Title: The First Five Days: A Government Remade at Speed
Content:
```markdown The second Trump administration did not begin with a transition period. It began with a flood. In the space of five days, the federal government was reordered across immigration, civil rights, energy policy, and the machinery of oversight itself, mostly through unilateral executive action signed before opposition could organize a response. By week's end, courts had already intervened on at least one front, but on most others, policy changes had taken hold in the real world well before any legal challenge could catch up.

**The Weekend**

The pace was set on inauguration day itself. Trump signed dozens of executive orders in a single sitting, touching immigration, energy, diversity programs, federal hiring, and the structure of government — more first-day orders than any modern president had issued. The volume was itself a strategy: by acting simultaneously across nearly every domain of federal policy, the administration made it difficult for Congress, courts, or the public to focus resistance on any single front. Paired with this was the declaration of simultaneous national emergencies at the southern border and over domestic energy production, unlocking military deployment authority, environmental review waivers, and a request for legal advice on invoking the Insurrection Act. Emergency powers meant for genuine crises were being activated as tools for standing policy goals.

Nowhere was the day's ambition clearer than in the treatment of the January 6 Capitol attack. Roughly 1,500 people charged or convicted in connection with the assault — including leaders convicted of seditious conspiracy — received pardons or commutations, and the Justice Department was directed to drop any remaining cases. This was not an isolated act of clemency but the start of a coordinated effort to unwind legal accountability for an attack on Congress, one that would continue later in the week when House Republicans formed a new panel to challenge the findings of the earlier bipartisan investigation into Trump's own culpability.

Also signed that day was an executive order attempting to end birthright citizenship for children born in the United States to undocumented or temporary-visa parents — a direct challenge to the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause. States and civil rights groups sued almost immediately, opening a legal battle that would develop over the following days. Alongside it came Executive Order 14168, declaring that the federal government would recognize only two biological sexes. Its effects cascaded quickly: passport denials, military discharges, exclusion from shelters, and the reassignment of transgender detainees and prisoners according to sex assigned at birth, stripping transgender Americans of federal recognition across multiple systems at once.

Immigration policy shifted just as fast. The CBP One appointment app, used to schedule lawful asylum appointments, was shut down within hours of the inauguration, cancelling roughly 30,000 scheduled appointments without notice or alternative. The border emergency declaration paired this closure with the deployment of active-duty troops and Marines, even though border crossings were then at multi-year lows. Meanwhile, the administration moved against the federal workforce itself, reinstating Schedule F to strip job protections from tens of thousands of policy-influencing employees, freezing federal hiring, and ending remote work — the opening move in a broader effort to make the civil service answerable to political loyalty rather than institutional continuity.

Not every first-day action carried equal weight. Trump directed the Justice Department not to enforce a law — upheld by the Supreme Court — banning TikTok, citing the app's popularity with young voters, a notable instance of an administration declining to enforce a validly enacted statute. The United States also began withdrawing from the Paris climate accord and the World Health Organization, while a national energy emergency expedited fossil fuel permitting and rolled back electric-vehicle and offshore-wind policy. DEI programs across the federal government were eliminated, staff placed on leave, and a 1965 nondiscrimination requirement for federal contractors was revoked. Smaller but telling moves rounded out the weekend: security clearances were stripped from roughly 50 former intelligence officials and John Bolton over a 2020 letter regarding Hunter Biden's laptop, and Trump and Melania Trump launched personal cryptocurrency tokens just before and after the inauguration, reportedly generating billions in paper value with promotion from exchanges under federal investigation.

**Tuesday**

By Tuesday, the government had moved from declaration to implementation. The Department of Homeland Security rescinded guidance that had limited immigration enforcement near sensitive locations, opening schools, churches, and hospitals to arrest, and raids intensified in communities near Mar-a-Lago and elsewhere. At the State Department, deputy assistant secretaries in the Bureau of Consular Affairs were removed the morning after inauguration and replaced with members of an ideologically aligned, immigration-restrictionist fellowship — an early sign that career expertise across the foreign service would be subordinated to political loyalty. DEI policy moved from proclamation to agency-level execution, with Executive Order 14173 directing formal termination of diversity practices and the revocation of the 1965 Equal Employment Opportunity order that had underpinned federal contractor nondiscrimination requirements for sixty years. The National Treasury Employees Union filed suit against Schedule F that same day, and Democratic state attorneys general began a wave of litigation against the administration's executive orders, while a public-interest law firm sued over the newly created Department of Government Efficiency for alleged transparency violations. Litigation, rather than legislative pushback, was emerging as the primary check on the pace of executive action.

**Wednesday**

Attention turned to the press and to internal purges. The new FCC chairman reinstated Trump campaign complaints against ABC, NBC, and CBS over alleged election coverage bias and reopened an investigation into CBS's editing of a Kamala Harris interview — a probe later leveraged during review of a corporate merger. Enrique Tarrio, the Proud Boys leader convicted of seditious conspiracy, was pardoned and released, emboldening far-right groups even as the Justice Department's national security and criminal divisions saw senior career officials removed and reassigned. A presidential memorandum restructured National Security Council decision-making, and dozens of acting officials were installed across agencies, sidestepping normal Senate confirmation timelines. Smaller actions that day included a Foreign Terrorist Organization designation for the Houthis and a $2 billion investment in Jared Kushner's private equity firm from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, made over the objection of the fund's own investment committee.

**Thursday**

Thursday brought the week's clearest judicial rebuke. U.S. District Judge John Coughenour issued a temporary restraining order blocking the birthright citizenship executive order, calling it "blatantly unconstitutional" — a rare instance of a court moving as quickly as the administration itself, and evidence that some constitutional limits remained enforceable even amid the surrounding velocity of change. The same day, House Republicans formally launched their new select subcommittee to revisit January 6, aiming to challenge the conclusions of the earlier bipartisan investigation. An executive order deregulating cryptocurrency followed days after the president's own crypto ventures launched, revoking consumer protections and establishing a Presidential Working Group on Digital Asset Markets. Smaller developments rounded out the day: the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology was reestablished under new leadership, assassination records related to JFK, RFK, and Martin Luther King Jr. were ordered declassified, a House resolution proposed amending the two-term presidential limit in terms that would exclude a prior president while opening a path for a third Trump term, and Purdue Pharma reached a $7.4 billion opioid settlement with the Sackler family — one of the week's few developments unconnected to the administration's own agenda.

**Friday**

The week closed with two of its most consequential moves. The administration fired at least 12 inspectors general across major federal agencies in a single action, reportedly without the 30-day congressional notice required by law — removing internal watchdogs en masse before their oversight of the week's other actions could even begin. Separately, Trump threatened to withhold wildfire disaster relief from California unless the state adopted mandatory voter ID requirements and altered its water policy, tying humanitarian aid to unrelated political demands against a state governed by the opposing party. An executive order reasserted Hyde Amendment restrictions on federal abortion funding, extending the week's broader pattern of reproductive-rights reversal. The Senate confirmed Pete Hegseth as defense secretary by a 50-50 vote broken by Vice President JD Vance, despite allegations of sexual assault and financial mismanagement and opposition from two Republican senators — a confirmation that tested how far the Senate's advice-and-consent function could bend under party pressure. A FEMA Review Council was established the same day, following Trump's public suggestion that disaster response might shift entirely to the states.

**The Week in Sum**

Across the five days, several threads ran continuously beneath the surface of individual headlines. Executive action consistently outpaced the capacity of Congress, courts, and the public to respond in real time. Accountability for the January 6 attack was both legally erased through pardons and historically contested through a new congressional panel. Immigration enforcement moved from a system of prioritized targeting toward something closer to a dragnet, with legal pathways closed and enforcement zones widened into schools and hospitals. Transgender Americans lost federal recognition across passports, the military, shelters, and prisons within days. And the internal watchdogs meant to check all of this — inspectors general, career civil servants, career diplomats — were removed or restructured before they could act. Against all of it, the first institutional counterweights appeared just as quickly: a federal judge blocking an unconstitutional order, a union suing over civil-service protections, state attorneys general filing challenge after challenge. The week did not resolve any of these contests. It set their terms — a pattern of speed, volume, and unilateral action, met by a pattern of litigation as the first line of response — that would recur throughout the term to come. ```

Title: This Week in Democracy: The Opening Barrage
Content:
```markdown The second week of the new administration did not so much begin as detonate. In the span of seven days, the federal government moved on immigration, the military, civil rights, federal oversight, foreign trade, and the machinery of its own bureaucracy — often several fronts at once, often before the previous day's actions had been fully absorbed. The defining feature of the week was not any single order but the sheer simultaneity of them: watchdogs were fired, prosecutors were purged, courts intervened, and the administration pressed forward anyway.

**The Weekend**

The weekend set the tone. Trump pardoned or commuted the sentences of roughly 1,500 people convicted in connection with the January 6 attack on the Capitol, including Oath Keepers leader Stewart Rhodes, who had been found guilty of seditious conspiracy. Some of the pardoned defendants publicly declined the clemency, and the Justice Department later took down the public database that had documented the underlying charges. Alongside the pardons came a cluster of first-day executive orders: a national emergency declared at the southern border, the cancellation of resettlement flights for 1,600 Afghan refugees already in the pipeline, the dismantling of diversity and affirmative-action programs, the disbanding of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and new authority for immigration agents to enter schools and churches, spaces long treated as off-limits. By Sunday, ICE and partner agencies had launched coordinated raids in Chicago and other cities, arresting more than 950 people in a single weekend at some of those same sensitive locations. In North Carolina, a judge's attempt to discard 60,000 certified votes in an effort to overturn a state supreme court race drew immediate, organized pushback from civil society groups — an early sign that election results themselves would be contested terrain.

The weekend's most structurally significant move came quietly: the dismissal of at least seventeen inspectors general across federal agencies, carried out without the thirty-day congressional notice the law requires. The Council of Inspectors General warned the firings might be unlawful; objections came from both parties. Days later, Acting Attorney General James McHenry fired more than a dozen career Justice Department prosecutors who had worked on cases against Trump, citing distrust in their willingness to carry out the administration's agenda. These were not isolated personnel decisions — they were the opening moves in what would become a running story of independent oversight being cleared out from inside the executive branch.

**Monday**

By Monday, the focus shifted to the military. Trump signed a cluster of orders banning transgender service members, eliminating diversity offices at the Pentagon and the Department of Homeland Security, and reinstating — with back pay — the roughly 8,000 troops discharged for refusing the COVID-19 vaccine. These were three distinct policies aimed at three distinct groups, unified mainly by their departure from institutional continuity in favor of ideological and loyalty-based sorting.

The same day, a federal judge issued an administrative stay blocking the funding freeze the administration had announced days earlier, a freeze that threatened to disrupt healthcare, education, and disaster-relief programs nationwide. It was the first of several judicial interventions that would define the week. Also on Monday, according to reporting rather than any formal order, White House aide Stephen Miller was said to be pressuring Justice Department officials to compile lists of FBI agents who had worked on the January 6 and classified-documents investigations, with the bureau's acting director reportedly resisting full compliance.

Elsewhere, the administration moved to strip civil service protections from career federal employees under a new "Schedule Policy/Career" designation and offered a buyout to federal workers with pay through September. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth revoked the security detail and clearance of retired Gen. Mark Milley, a past critic of Trump. And a diplomatic dispute with Colombia over deportation flights escalated within roughly a day into cancelled visas and 25 percent tariffs, before flights resumed.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought some of the week's most consequential — and most immediately felt — actions. An executive order cut off federal funding, insurance coverage, and institutional support for gender-affirming medical care for anyone under nineteen. Hospitals including NYU Langone and Denver Health paused treatment for young patients within hours. The administration also pursued an order attempting to end birthright citizenship, a guarantee written into the 14th Amendment; twenty-two state attorneys general sued, and a federal judge quickly blocked the order, calling it "blatantly unconstitutional." Trump also invoked the Alien Enemies Act to announce plans for a 30,000-person migrant detention facility at Guantánamo Bay, a military prison long associated with human rights abuses now being repurposed for civilian immigration detention. Meanwhile, the funding freeze that had been blocked a day earlier continued to cause disruption — including reports of Medicaid portal outages — prompting a second judicial restraining order.

**Wednesday**

By Wednesday, the Guantánamo plan moved from announcement to formal policy: a presidential memorandum directed the Secretaries of Defense and Homeland Security to expand the detention center to full capacity, and Trump signed the Laken Riley Act mandating detention for undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related offenses. The same day saw a wave of education orders — targeting what the administration called "radical indoctrination" in K-12 schools, reviving the 1776 Commission on patriotic education, expanding federal support for school choice, and directing federal agencies to investigate, and potentially move to deport, pro-Palestinian student activists under an anti-antisemitism framework.

In Washington, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. faced pointed questioning in Senate confirmation hearings over his history of vaccine misinformation and shifting positions on abortion, drawing opposition from thousands of physicians. And the funding freeze took another turn: the Office of Management and Budget formally rescinded its freeze memo, only for the White House press secretary to immediately clarify that the underlying executive orders "remain in full force and effect" — leaving the actual status of federal funding, and the government's own position on it, genuinely unclear.

**Thursday**

Thursday was the busiest single day of the week. Trump signed an order requiring independent regulatory agencies — including the SEC and FTC — to submit their policy priorities and budgets for White House approval, undoing decades of structural independence that Congress had built into those agencies. He also signed a further set of orders restricting transgender rights: banning transgender athletes from women's sports categories, transferring transgender women held in federal prisons to men's facilities while cutting their access to gender-affirming treatment, and declaring English the official language of the United States.

On trade, the administration imposed 25 percent tariffs on Canada and Mexico and 10 percent on China, triggering a stock market drop and threats of retaliation from Ottawa, before carving out exemptions for USMCA-covered goods and autos within days. Elon Musk's role in federal operations expanded sharply: Trump signed an order broadening Musk's oversight of a centralized federal payment system, and a senior career Treasury official resigned after associates of Musk demanded access to sensitive payment infrastructure — a demand connected to an earlier whistleblower lawsuit alleging that federal employee data was being collected for a Musk associate under the guise of official communications.

The day also brought a batch of deregulatory and industrial orders — reviving the coal industry, expanding tree-cutting on public lands, boosting deep-sea mining, creating a sovereign wealth fund and a strategic bitcoin reserve, and pausing enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Amid all of this, a federal judge issued a formal injunction — stronger than the earlier temporary blocks — preventing the administration from impounding federal funds owed to states. And in his own confirmation hearing, FBI director nominee Kash Patel declined to rule out politically motivated investigations of Trump's opponents.

**Friday**

The week closed on Friday with three threads converging. Trump signed a sweeping deregulation order requiring agencies to repeal at least ten existing regulations for every new one issued, with a mandate that net new regulatory costs for the fiscal year be significantly less than zero. The FBI purge, previously reported anonymously, became visible: at least five senior officials in major field offices were ordered to resign or were terminated, part of a broader campaign against career agents tied to the January 6 and Trump-related investigations, drawing a warning from the FBI Agents Association about the resulting loss of institutional capacity. The National Labor Relations Board was left without the quorum needed to issue significant rulings after Trump fired its general counsel and chair.

Reporting also revealed that donors with tax matters pending before the IRS had paid off more than $130,000 in campaign debt for Billy Long, Trump's nominee to lead the agency, shortly after his nomination was announced — and that a young engineer connected to Musk's companies had gained direct access to Treasury payment systems, following the Treasury official's resignation earlier in the week. In a smaller but telling move, DHS dissolved an internal advisory board that had reviewed local police immigration partnerships for civil rights concerns, removing oversight just as those partnerships were expanding.

**The Pattern**

Taken as a whole, the week established a pattern that would recur throughout the young administration: rapid, wide-ranging assertions of executive authority, followed almost immediately by legal challenge, and in several cases by outright judicial rejection — on the funding freeze, on birthright citizenship, on the impoundment of state funds. Courts emerged as the most consistent institutional check on the week's actions, intervening not once but repeatedly, sometimes within days of an order's signing. At the same time, the administration's response to those checks was not always to comply cleanly; the funding freeze was rescinded on paper while its substance was reasserted in the same breath, a maneuver that blurred the line between compliance and defiance.

Inside the executive branch, the machinery of independent oversight — inspectors general, career prosecutors, FBI leadership, an independent labor board — was cleared out in overlapping waves, while regulatory agencies built for independence were placed under direct White House control. For immigrant communities, transgender Americans, and federal civil servants alike, the week's policies were not abstract: hospitals halted treatment, arrests spiked into the thousands, and career officials lost their positions within days of an inauguration. Whether measured by volume, speed, or the breadth of institutions touched, it was a week that tested, in real time, how far executive power could be extended before the other branches of government were able to respond. ```
Excerpt: This was the administration's opening week of governing, and it moved on nearly every front at once.

Title: The Week the Government Was Taken Apart From the Inside
Content:
```markdown The first week of February 2025 began with an extraordinary concentration of executive action and ended with courts, unions, and career officials straining to hold the line against it. In the span of seven days, the federal government experienced a spending freeze and its reversal, the gutting of independent oversight bodies, the effective dismantling of a federal agency, a private takeover of Treasury payment systems, three separate judicial rulings against the same executive order, and a new set of sanctions aimed at an international court. The throughline was consistent: rapid assertions of executive power, followed by institutional and legal pushback that only partially caught up by week's end.

The weekend opened with an attempt to freeze trillions of dollars in federal grants and loans, a move that disrupted Medicaid, childcare, and other programs before a federal judge blocked it and the administration rescinded its own memo amid public confusion. It was the first sign of a pattern that would recur throughout the week — bold executive action, swift real-world disruption, and an eventual, often grudging, retreat under legal pressure. That same weekend, eighteen inspectors general were fired without the notice required by law, board members at the NLRB and EEOC were dismissed before their terms ended, and a new order stripped civil service job protections while pressuring roughly two million federal employees toward resignation. The effect was to remove, in a single motion, many of the internal watchdogs designed to check executive misconduct.

USAID became an early casualty of the broader consolidation. The administration moved to fold the independent, congressionally established agency into the State Department, placing security officials who resisted DOGE's access on leave, locking staff out of headquarters, and having Secretary of State Marco Rubio declare himself acting administrator. The action foreshadowed a theme that would define the week: agencies and systems built with statutory independence being absorbed into direct executive control, often over the objections of the career staff meant to administer them.

The weekend also saw Trump issue pardons to roughly 1,600 people connected to the January 6 attack on the Capitol, nearly the entire universe of those convicted or charged, while a separate executive order attempted to reinterpret the 14th Amendment's guarantee of birthright citizenship. Both actions drew immediate legal and political opposition, and the citizenship order in particular would become one of the week's central storylines, as three separate federal judges — appointed by presidents of both parties — moved to block it over the following days. Simultaneously, new tariffs of 25 percent on Canada and Mexico and 10 percent on China were declared under emergency powers, prompting swift retaliatory measures from all three countries before a partial one-month delay was negotiated in exchange for border security concessions.

Rounding out the weekend, the Pentagon began rotating established outlets like the New York Times and NPR out of its press pool in favor of more favorable coverage, the White House denied Reuters access to a cabinet meeting, and a HuffPost reporter was removed from the press pool altogether. Executive orders also targeted transgender athletes and federal use of gender pronouns, while decentralized protest movements such as 50501 and Tesla Takedown began organizing nationally, and Democratic state attorneys general launched what would become a coordinated litigation campaign eventually producing more than 170 court rulings against administration actions.

By Monday, the tariffs on Mexico and Canada were formally paused until March 4, with the administration reserving the right to reimpose them at will — a resolution that left the underlying leverage over trade policy intact even as the immediate crisis eased. Far more consequential was the deepening of Elon Musk's DOGE team's access to Treasury payment systems, which manage roughly $6 trillion annually. Career officials had resisted, but DOGE-affiliated staff obtained access anyway, prompting federal employee unions to sue over what they characterized as violations of federal privacy law. The same day brought a new executive order directing the Treasury and Commerce Departments to draft a plan for a U.S. sovereign wealth fund within 90 days, with suggestions it could facilitate a TikTok purchase — a novel financial vehicle assembled without congressional authorization. Higher education associations sued over DEI-related funding threats, and two groups of FBI agents sued the Justice Department to block the collection of information on agents who had worked January 6 investigations, an early sign of the retaliatory pattern that would harden as the week went on. North Carolina, meanwhile, enacted criminal penalties for mask-wearing and road-blocking at protests, and Secretary of State Rubio announced that El Salvador had offered to imprison deportees of any nationality, including U.S. citizens, for a fee.

Tuesday brought the judiciary's first major counterpunch. A federal judge reaffirmed the block on the spending freeze as unconstitutional, while judges in Maryland and Washington state separately halted enforcement of the birthright citizenship order — the first two of what would become three consecutive rulings against it. A federal judge also issued a temporary restraining order stopping the transfer of transgender women from federal women's prisons to men's facilities, preserving hormone therapy access for sixteen incarcerated individuals and finding the underlying policy discriminatory. Even as courts pushed back, DOGE's control over Treasury systems deepened further, enabling the cancellation of the free IRS Direct File tax-filing program — a concrete illustration of how much authority the team had assumed without formal accountability. The CDC and other health agencies were separately ordered to purge public resources on contraception, gender-affirming care, and HIV. The Senate advanced Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s nomination to lead Health and Human Services along party lines and confirmed Chris Wright, a climate skeptic, as energy secretary. In foreign policy, the administration withdrew the United States from the UN Human Rights Council, halted funding to the Palestinian refugee agency UNRWA, and issued a memorandum relaunching a maximum-pressure campaign against Iran, directing federal agencies to drive Iranian oil exports to zero and pursue Iranian-linked networks domestically.

Wednesday combined a formal executive order banning transgender athletes from women's sports — directing federal agencies to enforce this reading of Title IX and threatening funding cuts to noncompliant schools — with a second nationwide injunction against the birthright citizenship order, this one from Judge Deborah Boardman. Senate Democrats staged an all-night filibuster against Russell Vought's nomination to lead the Office of Management and Budget, citing fears that a key architect of Project 2025 would use the position to target Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security; his confirmation proceeded along party lines two days later regardless. The day's most unexpected development came during a joint press conference with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu, when Trump announced that the United States would "take over" Gaza, administering and redeveloping the territory — a proposal that drew bipartisan criticism and visible unease even among his own advisors. Elsewhere, West Point disbanded twelve student cultural and identity organizations, including the Society of Women Engineers and an LGBTQ+ support group, following DEI-related orders. The Justice Department ended civil rights investigations and police reform agreements tied to the killings of Breonna Taylor and George Floyd in Louisville and Minneapolis. And the Senate confirmed Pam Bondi as attorney general largely along party lines, positioning her to lead a Justice Department already reshaped by personnel purges — a role she would move on immediately.

Thursday opened with an executive order sanctioning officials of the International Criminal Court, blocking their assets and barring their entry into the United States over the court's investigation into alleged war crimes by U.S. and Israeli personnel. Bondi wasted little time asserting her new authority, eliminating the Justice Department's foreign bribery unit and its Kleptocracy Initiative and scaling back enforcement of the Foreign Agents Registration Act, redirecting resources toward drug and smuggling cases instead. The Justice Department separately sued Chicago and Illinois over their sanctuary immigration laws, escalating a federal-state conflict over enforcement authority. In North Carolina, Judge Griffin sought to discard roughly 60,000 ballots in an effort to overturn a certified state Supreme Court race, prompting public campaigns to defend the result. Protests over Musk's Treasury access and broader concerns about a private takeover of government functions intensified nationwide, accompanied by reports that ICE had altered timestamps on years-old press releases to make them appear as fresh enforcement actions, and by Trump's public call for CBS to lose its broadcast license over an edited "60 Minutes" interview with Kamala Harris. Amid this, a federal judge issued an order restricting Treasury access to two DOGE-affiliated staff on a read-only basis pending further litigation — a narrower but still significant judicial check.

That check hardened by Friday, when a federal judge issued an emergency order halting DOGE's access to Treasury systems altogether and ordering the destruction of any downloaded records, prompting Musk and Vice President Vance to publicly suggest the administration might simply ignore the ruling. It was the most forceful judicial intervention of the week, and it tested directly whether the executive branch would comply with a court order it disagreed with. The same day, Judge John Coughenour, a Reagan appointee, issued the third ruling against the birthright citizenship order, calling it "clearly unconstitutional" and criticizing the administration's disregard for the rule of law — a rebuke made more striking by the ideological range of the three judges who had now reached the same conclusion. The administration also suspended aid to South Africa over its land expropriation law while directing the State Department to prioritize resettlement of Afrikaner refugees, escalating diplomatic tension through a reshaping of refugee policy along ethnic lines. After a weeklong standoff, the FBI complied with a Justice Department demand to submit details on 5,000 to 6,000 agents connected to January 6 investigations, a disclosure that, despite excluding names, raised concerns about retaliation against career law enforcement personnel. The week closed with further censorship measures: a Department of Defense memo ordering military schools to purge books and lessons tied to gender and race, affecting 67,000 military-family students; the Education Department's decision to stop investigating school book bans; OSHA's order to destroy workplace safety publications flagged for unrelated keyword matches during a DEI purge; and the firing of the Archivist of the United States, whose office had played a role in retrieving classified documents from Mar-a-Lago.

Taken as a whole, the week illustrated a government being reshaped from the inside at a pace that outstripped the ordinary machinery of oversight. Independent watchdogs were removed before they could object, a private team gained hands-on access to the nation's payment infrastructure before the courts could catch up, and a constitutional guarantee was challenged by executive order before the ink on the order had dried. But the week also showed where resistance held: judges blocked the funding freeze and struck down the citizenship order three times over; unions and attorneys general filed suit after suit; and by Friday, a court order had forced at least a temporary halt to DOGE's Treasury access, even as the administration's response suggested compliance was not guaranteed. Whether that judicial and civic pushback could keep pace with the speed of executive action remained, at week's end, an open question — one the weeks to come would begin to answer. ```

Title: The Week the Guardrails Were Tested
Content:
```markdown This was the week the machinery of the federal government came under direct, sustained pressure from an executive branch testing how far it could move before something pushed back — and the week made clear that plenty did push back, even as compliance with those pushes remained uneven. Between February 8 and 14, courts blocked funding freezes, mass firings, and citizenship changes; career prosecutors resigned rather than execute a political order; and the vice president stood in Munich and told European allies, in effect, that the old alliance no longer held. By Friday, the week's disparate threads — an efficiency initiative run by a private citizen, a prosecutorial crisis in New York, a foreign-policy realignment toward Moscow — had converged into a single, unmistakable pattern.

It began over the weekend with a burst of executive action. Trump announced he would personally chair the Kennedy Center's board, dismissing its sitting leadership in an unprecedented assertion of presidential control over a congressionally chartered cultural institution. At the same time, Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency team made its opening moves against the federal bureaucracy: targeting NOAA for elimination, disrupting operations at more than fifteen agencies, and seeking access to sensitive data systems. The CIA offered buyouts to its entire workforce; thousands of USAID staff were placed on leave. Courts moved almost immediately. A federal judge halted the USAID leave order. Another issued an emergency block on DOGE's access to Treasury payment systems. Separate rulings in two courts blocked the administration's attempt to end birthright citizenship, and a deadline tied to federal-worker buyouts was paused. The judiciary, in other words, was active from day one — not a passive backdrop but an immediate counterweight.

Immigration policy hardened in parallel. The Justice Department cut funding to sanctuary jurisdictions and sued Chicago and Illinois directly, while the ACLU sued over an order suspending asylum law. Trump moved to end legal status for more than 530,000 immigrants from four countries even as he prioritized resettlement for Afrikaner refugees, and the first deportation flight to Guantanamo Bay departed. Meanwhile, the earliest signs of a broader pressure campaign against institutions capable of checking the administration appeared: Musk and Senator Tom Cotton publicly attacked the judge who had blocked DOGE's Treasury access, calling for his impeachment, and the White House canceled its Politico subscriptions while the FCC opened an inquiry into a radio station's immigration coverage. Trump also signed a proclamation formalizing the renaming of the Gulf of Mexico and, standing beside Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu, said the United States would "take over" Gaza and relocate its Palestinian population — language widely condemned as describing ethnic cleansing. Amid all this, congressional phone lines were overwhelmed by tens of millions of calls opposing the administration's moves, an early sign of the public reaction building beneath the institutional story.

By Monday, the pace had not slowed. Trump signed an order pausing enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act for 180 days, halting prosecutions under a decades-old anti-bribery law on the argument that enforcement harmed American competitiveness — a significant retreat from a central pillar of international anti-corruption law, paired with smaller, more symbolic moves like eliminating the Federal Executive Institute and reversing restrictions on single-use plastics. Courts kept intervening: one judge found the administration in violation of a prior order and demanded frozen funds be restored; another blocked the mass federal-worker buyout plan; a third ordered the CDC and FDA to restore health webpages scrubbed under an anti-DEI directive. But the attacks on judicial independence sharpened as well. Senators Cotton and Lee called an adverse ruling a "judicial coup." Representative Eli Crane announced plans to draft impeachment articles against the judge who had ruled against DOGE. Musk shared a post revealing personal details about that judge's daughter. Separately, the NSA began purging "banned words" like "privilege," "bias," and "inclusion" from its systems in chaotic, overbroad fashion, and the White House laid rhetorical groundwork — branding the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau "weaponized" — for its eventual defunding. The day closed with the firing of the director of the Office of Government Ethics and new 25 percent tariffs on steel and aluminum imports from allies including Canada, the European Union, Japan, and the United Kingdom.

Tuesday brought a direct confrontation with the press. The White House indefinitely barred Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office and Air Force One after the wire service declined to adopt the "Gulf of America" name, drawing swift condemnation from press-freedom groups. The pattern of watchdog removals continued as USAID's independent inspector general was fired shortly after his office issued a critical report on the agency's dismantling — following the earlier removal of eighteen inspectors general government-wide. Reporting also revealed that the NIH was still blocking grant funding in direct violation of two federal injunctions, a defiance that would only end once internal staff confirmed the freeze was unlawful and the agency reversed course by midweek. Elsewhere, Steve Bannon pleaded guilty to a state fraud charge tied to a border-wall fundraising scheme and avoided jail time, even as data showed roughly 60 percent of charges against pro-Palestinian protesters nationwide had been dropped — a contrast in prosecutorial treatment that did not go unnoticed. The American Bar Association publicly condemned the administration's actions as undermining the rule of law, and five former Treasury secretaries warned jointly about the constitutional risks of DOGE's access to sensitive financial systems. Courts, meanwhile, blocked a proposed cap on NIH research funding after twenty-two states sued, even as Trump signed a new order banning openly transgender individuals from military service.

Wednesday marked the week's decisive foreign-policy turn. Trump and Vladimir Putin agreed to begin ceasefire negotiations over Ukraine, with Trump suggesting Kyiv might need to cede territory and abandon NATO membership. Defense Secretary Hegseth announced a strategic pivot away from European security commitments toward China, while Treasury Secretary Bessent proposed exchanging continued U.S. support for half of Ukraine's mineral resources — a deal President Zelensky rejected outright. The administration disbanded the task force responsible for seizing sanctioned Russian assets just as these talks opened, removing a key point of economic leverage at a pivotal moment. Trump also signed an order asserting exclusive presidential authority over foreign policy, empowering the Secretary of State to discipline or dismiss Foreign Service officers who deviated from the administration's line — a structural move toward politicizing the diplomatic corps. And in New York, federal prosecutors Danielle Sassoon and colleagues resigned in protest after DOJ leadership pressured them to drop corruption charges against Mayor Eric Adams, reportedly in exchange for his cooperation on immigration enforcement — the opening act of a crisis that would consume the rest of the week. Courts issued mixed rulings that day: one allowed the federal buyout program to proceed after finding unions lacked standing, another blocked enforcement of restrictions on gender-affirming care for transgender minors. The eight fired inspectors general filed suit challenging their dismissals as unlawful, and Senator Durbin accused FBI director nominee Kash Patel of directing an agent purge while a private citizen — a claim that, if true, would contradict his confirmation testimony.

Thursday, the Adams case reached its breaking point. DOJ leadership reportedly gave Public Integrity Section lawyers one hour to decide who would sign the motion to dismiss the indictment, threatening mass firings if none complied. An internal memo openly acknowledged the dismissal was for political reasons unconnected to the evidence. Prosecutor Hagan Scotten resigned in protest, joining Sassoon from the day before. Elsewhere, Trump signed an order establishing a Make America Healthy Again Commission chaired by newly confirmed HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., granting it broad authority to reshape federal health research priorities. Immigration enforcement disputes multiplied: the Justice Department sued New York over its driver's-license law for undocumented residents, Mayor Adams separately announced plans to reestablish an ICE presence at Rikers Island despite the city's sanctuary laws, and Denver's public school system sued the administration over a policy permitting ICE access to schools. The White House also announced a coordinated, multi-agency campaign of investigations and lawsuits against jurisdictions it deemed "noncompliant," spanning education, immigration, and environmental regulation. Trump signed a memorandum directing development of a "Fair and Reciprocal" tariff plan, while the Department of Veterans Affairs cut 1,000 employees and the Department of Energy cut 300 staff from the office overseeing nuclear weapons security. The Senate confirmed Tulsi Gabbard as director of national intelligence over Democratic objections and one Republican dissent.

The week closed on Friday with three converging climaxes. DOGE's mass terminations arrived at scale: roughly 24,000 probationary federal employees were fired across agencies including the Forest Service, the VA, the USDA, and HHS, with minimal notice and inconsistent implementation of the court-ordered reinstatements that followed. In the Adams case, prosecutors formally filed to dismiss the corruption charges after six more attorneys resigned in protest, bringing the week's total resignations in that single case to seven — a cascade many likened to the 1973 Saturday Night Massacre. And at the Munich Security Conference, Vice President Vance delivered a speech attacking European allies' democratic values, declined to name Russian aggression as a threat, and met with Alice Weidel, leader of Germany's far-right AfD party — breaking a longstanding taboo in German politics and drawing sharp condemnation from European leaders. A readout of a call between Secretary of State Rubio and Russian Foreign Minister Lavrov suggested discussions of easing sanctions on Moscow, extending the week's pattern of warming toward Russia even as its war in Ukraine continued. Closer to home, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro sued to compel release of more than $3 billion in federal funds withheld from the state, arguing the administration had violated Congress's constitutional appropriations authority — one more instance, alongside a separate ruling elsewhere ordering the release of impounded foreign aid, of a federal judge confronting the administration's refusal to justify withholding funds. The White House, for its part, published a self-congratulatory release cataloging the week's achievements — a contrast that captured the tension running through the entire seven days: between judicial rebuke and executive self-narration, between resignation and resistance, between what the law required and what the government did anyway until someone made it stop.

Taken as a whole, the week showed an executive branch probing the outer edges of its authority on nearly every front — agency staffing, prosecutorial independence, judicial compliance, alliance commitments, watchdog oversight — while courts, career officials, and, in the case of Adams, prosecutors willing to resign rather than comply, offered the most visible resistance. That resistance was real but partial: injunctions were issued, but not always obeyed promptly; officials resigned, but the underlying orders they objected to still went through. The pattern that emerged by Friday was not one of unchecked power nor of an unbroken rule of law, but of a system under sustained strain, its guardrails tested in public view, holding in some places and giving way in others. ```

Title: The Week the Guardrails Were Tested
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which nearly every check on executive power was tested at once, and in most cases the executive did not yield. A corruption case against a sitting mayor collapsed under apparent political pressure, a new cost-cutting body pushed into the government's most sensitive data systems, courts issued rulings the administration sometimes ignored, and a state governor's public refusal to comply with a presidential directive brought immediate federal retaliation. By week's end, the country's institutional guardrails had been pushed in nearly every direction, with mixed and often unresolved results.

The week began over the weekend with an eruption inside the Justice Department. Acting US attorneys and senior officials in the Southern District of New York and the Public Integrity Section resigned rather than carry out an order to drop corruption charges against New York Mayor Eric Adams, a case critics said was being traded away in exchange for Adams' cooperation on immigration enforcement. The resignations were the opening move in what would become a running story through the middle of the week. Alongside the Adams fallout, Trump signed executive orders empowering the newly formed DOGE committee, led by Elon Musk, to shrink the federal workforce, and ended COVID-19 vaccine mandates in schools by threatening to withhold federal education funding. The administration also faced accusations of ignoring court orders altogether, including a pause on USAID staff leave that employees said was disregarded when they were turned away from their offices anyway. Elsewhere, DOJ fired more than two dozen immigration judges even as 3.5 million cases sat backlogged, the Associated Press was barred from White House coverage over its refusal to rename the Gulf of Mexico, and workforce cuts hit the Forest Service, Park Service, USDA's animal disease lab network, and the CFPB.

By Monday, the Adams case moved a step closer to resolution as the Justice Department formally requested dismissal of the charges, and another senior DOJ official, Denise Cheung, resigned rather than follow a directive she considered unethical. The same day, the IRS began reviewing a request to give DOGE personnel access to classified taxpayer records, prompting a lawsuit from 19 state attorneys general over similar access sought at Treasury. Courts, meanwhile, issued a mixed batch of rulings on emergency motions tied to DOGE and personnel actions, including continuing uncertainty over the fate of Special Counsel Hampton Dellinger, whose removal was headed toward the Supreme Court.

Tuesday brought one of the week's most consequential single actions: an executive order asserting direct presidential control over independent regulatory agencies including the SEC and FTC, requiring them to submit proposed rules for White House review and declaring the president's and attorney general's legal interpretations controlling across the executive branch. That same day, the Justice Department formally dismissed the corruption case against Adams, closing the loop that had begun with weekend resignations and confirming, for many observers, that prosecutorial power had been used as political leverage. On a separate but related front, twenty-two red states and oil industry groups sued to block climate superfund laws in New York and Vermont, while the federal solicitor general opposed reviving the youth-led Juliana climate case — a coordinated legal push against state-level climate accountability efforts. Courts also issued a dense batch of rulings on pending motions touching DOGE, agency firings, and diversity-related orders, granting some relief and denying other requests, underscoring how much of the week's activity remained legally contested.

Wednesday was the busiest day of the week by a wide margin. Trump signed an executive order attempting to reinterpret the 14th Amendment to deny automatic citizenship to children born to parents without permanent legal status — a move estimated to affect roughly 255,000 births annually — only to have a federal appeals court deny the administration's request to reinstate the policy. The same day, DOGE was formally established by executive order with Musk named to lead it, even as later court filings would claim he held no formal decision-making authority within it. A cluster of additional orders restricted undocumented immigrants' access to federal benefits, directed agencies to review and potentially rescind regulations deemed unconstitutional, and eliminated several federal entities and advisory committees. In the Adams matter, acting deputy attorney general Emil Bove appeared before a Manhattan judge to defend the dismissal, arguing that continued prosecution would impede Adams' cooperation with immigration enforcement; the judge questioned the rationale sharply without ruling. On foreign policy, following a call with Vladimir Putin, Trump publicly blamed Ukraine for the ongoing war and suggested President Zelensky should hold elections — language that echoed demands long made by Moscow. Federal websites also saw references to Black Americans removed during Black History Month, and the National Park Service stripped references to transgender people from its pages. Separately, a federal judge allowed the administration's mass firings of federal workers to continue, rejecting a union bid to halt them, even as another judge questioned whether the DOJ itself understood the scope of its own personnel actions.

Thursday's developments centered on two parallel institutional tests. Courts intervened repeatedly against DOGE's expanding data access: lawsuits sought to block the group from Department of Labor, Education, and Treasury systems, and federal judges restricted DOGE's access to Treasury data to two vetted staffers, one of whom resigned after past racist posts surfaced. At the same time, the Senate confirmed Kash Patel as FBI director in a narrow 51-49 vote, installing an election denier and Trump loyalist who has spoken of targeting "deep state" officials and media organizations atop federal law enforcement. The Justice Department also declared job protections for administrative law judges unconstitutional, moving to bring them under more direct presidential control, extending the week's broader pattern of subordinating independent adjudicative bodies. In a separate move, the US Marshals Service was ordered to deputize Musk's private security detail, granting armed authority on federal property without standard vetting. The administration also directed New York City to end congestion pricing and froze congressionally approved EV subsidies. Away from the executive branch, Mitch McConnell announced he would not seek re-election in 2026, and Senator Angus King warned that the administration's impoundment actions represented the most serious constitutional assault in the country's history.

The week closed on Friday with its sharpest confrontation between federal and state power. At a White House meeting, Trump told Maine Governor Janet Mills to comply with his ban on transgender athletes in girls' sports or lose federal funding, declaring "we are the federal law." Mills responded, "see you in court." Within hours, multiple federal agencies opened investigations into Maine's policies — a rapid sequence that made explicit how quickly institutional defiance could draw federal retaliation. The same day, Trump fired Gen. CQ Brown Jr., chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, along with the Navy chief, the Air Force vice chief, and senior military lawyers, reportedly over their resistance to diversity policies — a sweeping removal of military leadership that raised concerns about the politicization of the armed forces. A federal judge in Maryland separately blocked enforcement of the administration's anti-DEI directives as likely unconstitutional, finding they probably violated the First Amendment. Labor unions filed suit alleging DOGE had unlawfully accessed Social Security data, extending the week's pattern of legal challenges to the group's reach. Elsewhere, a judge cleared the way for more than 2,000 USAID workers to be placed on leave while the Forest Service and Interior Department continued firing probationary employees, and the SEC agreed to drop its enforcement lawsuit against Coinbase without penalty as Attorney General Pam Bondi told Fox News that Jeffrey Epstein case files were "sitting on my desk." The week's final loose thread involved January 6 defendants: several pardoned participants, including Enrique Tarrio, announced a lawsuit against the Justice Department over their original prosecutions, even as Tarrio was arrested near the Capitol days later for allegedly assaulting a protester.

Taken as a whole, the week showed executive power probing nearly every seam in the system built to constrain it — prosecutorial independence, regulatory autonomy, judicial protections, military leadership, press access, and constitutional citizenship guarantees among them. Courts intervened repeatedly, sometimes decisively, as with the birthright citizenship rebuff and the DEI injunction, and sometimes only partially, as with the piecemeal restrictions on DOGE's data access. Career officials resigned rather than comply with directives they viewed as improper, while a state governor chose public defiance over compliance and drew immediate federal scrutiny in return. None of these confrontations reached final resolution by Friday; instead, the week left behind a docket of unresolved lawsuits, pending appeals, and open investigations that will shape how much of this contested authority ultimately survives legal and institutional review. ```
Excerpt: This was a week in which executive power tested nearly every institutional check available to it, often successfully.

Title: The Week the Bureaucracy Fought Back
Content:
```markdown This was the week the machinery of a second Trump administration met the machinery of American government, and neither yielded cleanly. It began with a triumphant speech at a conservative conference and ended with a Social Security agency bracing to lose half its staff, a Voting Rights Act challenge freshly filed, and House Republicans quietly told to avoid their own constituents. In between, courts issued injunction after injunction, federal workers resigned rather than comply with an unelected billionaire's demands, and the press lost its traditional claim on access to the president.

**The Weekend**

The week's tone was set at CPAC, where Trump used a single speech to preview nearly everything that would follow: sweeping federal workforce cuts, the termination of Haitian temporary protected status, a renewed push to end birthright citizenship, a ban on transgender athletes backed by funding threats, and a repeated, false claim about the scale of his 2024 vote total. The speech worked less as a policy announcement than as a table of contents for the days ahead. That weekend also brought pardons for roughly 1,500 January 6 defendants, including Proud Boys leader Enrique Tarrio, whose seditious conspiracy conviction was wiped away along with those of hundreds of others. The bipartisan criticism that followed was still settling when a bomb threat targeted an anti-Trump conservative conference, naming a Capitol Police officer as its object — a reminder that clemency for insurrection and the threat of further political violence were not separate stories.

The same weekend introduced what would become the week's central drama: Elon Musk's push to reshape the federal workforce by fiat. An email sent through the Office of Personnel Management, at Musk's direction, ordered federal employees to document their weekly accomplishments or be treated as having resigned. The response was immediate and came from inside government itself. The FBI director told bureau staff to disregard the directive. The State Department did the same. It was the clearest early sign that an advisor with no Senate confirmation and no statutory authority over the civil service was going to have his authority tested by the civil service itself. Courts moved in parallel: a federal judge granted an injunction blocking Musk's Department of Government Efficiency team from accessing Americans' personal data in the Treasury payment system, the first of several early rulings that would define the week's legal architecture. The weekend closed with another fight taking shape, as the Associated Press sued the White House after being barred from presidential events for declining to adopt the term "Gulf of America" in its copy — a dispute over three words that would grow into something much larger.

**Monday**

The pattern of judicial pushback deepened. A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order stopping the Education Department and the Office of Personnel Management from sharing personal data with DOGE, ruling that the arrangement likely violated the Privacy Act, after labor unions sued to stop it. The same day, interim US Attorney for the District of Columbia Ed Martin described himself on social media as "President Trump's lawyer," a remark that would soon draw a congressional inquiry into whether he had used his office to pursue Musk's critics. It was a small sentence with large implications: a federal prosecutor publicly renouncing the independence his office is supposed to embody.

Inside DOGE itself, the strain was becoming visible. More than twenty civil servants resigned from the initiative, saying they would not use their expertise to dismantle the public services they had spent careers building — the first significant defection from within Musk's own operation. Meanwhile, the National Institutes of Health found itself blocked from submitting new grant notices to the Federal Register, apparently in violation of a standing court order, stalling roughly $1.5 billion in medical research funding even as a judge's restraining order sat unenforced. And in the press fight, a Trump-appointed judge declined to immediately restore the AP's access, leaving the constitutional question for a later hearing but allowing the ban to continue in the meantime.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought the week's most pointed act of legal retaliation. A presidential memorandum suspended security clearances for employees of the law firm Covington & Burling who had assisted former special counsel Jack Smith, and directed federal agencies to terminate their contracts with the firm — framed by the White House as correcting the "weaponization of government." It was a different kind of escalation than the workforce fights playing out elsewhere: not an attempt to reshape an agency, but a direct punishment of lawyers for performing lawful legal representation of a political adversary. The same day, Trump floated a "Trump Gold Card" proposal that would sell green-card privileges and a pathway to citizenship for a $5 million payment, drawing criticism for attaching a price tag to a status the Constitution treats as equal and foundational.

There was, however, a retreat to register alongside the escalations: after days of confusion, resignations, and legal challenges, the Office of Personnel Management formally reversed Musk's resignation ultimatum, clarifying that ignoring the "accomplishments" email would not cost anyone their job. It was a rare instance of sustained pushback producing a clear, if belated, walk-back.

On Capitol Hill, the House narrowly passed a budget resolution combining $4.5 trillion in tax cuts with roughly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts, while the Senate advanced a competing resolution adding $175 billion for border enforcement — establishing, in a single day, the fiscal trade-off that would recur through the week. A cluster of court rulings capped the day: judges blocked a freeze on federal loans and grants, blocked the suspension of the refugee admissions system, and extended protections against transferring transgender women in federal prison to men's facilities. And the press story took its sharpest turn yet, as the White House announced it would now decide, on its own, which reporters join the pool covering the president — displacing the White House Correspondents' Association's decades-old role.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday turned the week's separate threads into policy. An executive order dramatically expanded DOGE's authority over federal spending, creating a centralized payment-tracking system, mandating review of existing contracts for termination, freezing government credit cards for thirty days, and formalizing "DOGE Team Leads" embedded across agencies and reporting to Musk's administrator. The order did more than continue the week's disputes — it tried to make DOGE's reach permanent and structural rather than improvised. Its first casualties arrived almost immediately: the new credit-card freeze halted NIH purchases needed for ongoing cancer and Alzheimer's research, leaving scientists with only a cumbersome exception process to keep experiments running.

The press-access fight was formalized the same day, as the administration confirmed AP and Reuters would lose their traditional standing in the pool. NOAA absorbed a roughly one-third budget cut alongside demands for DOGE access to its internal systems, threatening its climate and weather research capacity. And at the Washington Post, the opinion editor resigned after owner Jeff Bezos redirected the section toward "personal liberties" and "free markets," a move that raised its own questions about editorial independence under ownership pressure — a quieter echo of the press fight unfolding at the White House. The Justice Department, meanwhile, dismissed four Biden-era civil rights lawsuits against police and fire departments over hiring discrimination, framing the dismissals as ending "DEI-driven enforcement."

**Thursday**

Thursday delivered both the consequence of Wednesday's order and a check on it. NOAA fired hundreds of employees, with layoffs falling hardest on probationary staff, including workers hired through disability and veteran-focused programs — drawing warnings from lawmakers about damage to weather forecasting and national security. Hours later, Judge William Alsup ruled that the Office of Personnel Management lacked the authority to order such firings and directed agencies to rescind termination notices, protecting thousands of jobs pending further review. It was, by Thursday, a familiar rhythm: executive action, then judicial restraint, then an uncertain interval in which agencies had to decide how far to comply.

Elsewhere, Attorney General Pam Bondi released roughly 200 pages of declassified Epstein files while publicly accusing the FBI of withholding additional material and setting an aggressive compliance deadline, raising as many questions about the disclosure's politics as it answered about its substance. Jared Kushner advanced a plan to redevelop Gaza following the removal of its Palestinian population, even as his private equity firm's $2 billion in Saudi funding drew renewed conflict-of-interest concerns given his informal but substantial policy role. And during a high-profile Oval Office meeting between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, a reporter from Russian state media outlet TASS retained access while the Associated Press and Reuters were reportedly excluded — a small moment that crystallized the administration's selective approach to who gets to watch power up close.

**Friday**

The week closed with four developments that, taken together, showed the breadth of what had shifted in six days. The Securities and Exchange Commission paused its securities fraud case against Chinese crypto entrepreneur Justin Sun shortly after his $75 million investment in a Trump family-linked crypto venture, prompting immediate questions about whether regulatory enforcement now bent around political proximity. Republican lawyers filed a new legal challenge to Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, aiming at protections against racial discrimination in voting with implications reaching far beyond any single state. The Social Security Administration announced a restructuring that could eliminate up to half of its 57,000 employees, extending the week's workforce-reduction arc into a program relied upon by tens of millions of Americans. And on the ground, two smaller but telling developments emerged: the People's Union USA organized a twenty-four-hour consumer boycott protesting corporate retreats from diversity commitments, and House Republican leadership reportedly advised members to stop holding in-person town halls after facing sustained constituent anger over the week's policies.

Read end to end, the week traced a single, repeating shape: an administration testing the limits of executive power over the workforce, the press, the courts, and the law itself, met at nearly every turn by an institutional response — a judge's injunction, a union's lawsuit, an FBI director's countermanding order, a mass resignation, a boycott, a lawmaker's retreat from public accountability. Courts emerged as the most consistent check, issuing a steady stream of restraining orders even as the administration in several instances appeared to slow-walk or defy compliance. None of the resistance fully stopped the underlying momentum — DOGE's authority was formalized rather than curtailed, the press lost ground it may not recover, and a budget combining tax cuts with deep Medicaid reductions kept moving through Congress. But the week also made clear that the machinery of American government, however strained, still had moving parts capable of pushing back — and that the outcome of this contest was not yet settled by either side alone. ```
Excerpt: This week opened with a CPAC victory lap and closed with the machinery of an administration straining against its own courts, its own employees, and its own contradictions.
