Title: This Week in Democracy: The Machinery Turns
Content:
```markdown The first week of March opened with a burst of executive activity so dense it was hard, at the time, to see its shape. By the time the week closed seven days later, the pattern was clearer: federal money, immigration law, and executive orders were being used as instruments of pressure against universities, law firms, immigrants, and independent officials, while courts intervened repeatedly but only partially to check it.

The weekend set the tone. The administration issued an executive order threatening to withhold funding from universities it judged to have "hostile environments," a designation that froze $2.2 billion at Harvard and pushed Columbia into accepting sweeping administrative concessions in exchange for restored funding. Warning letters went out to 60 universities; San Jose State was targeted before an investigation into it had even concluded. That same weekend, the Department of Homeland Security eliminated three of its own oversight offices — the ones responsible for civil rights, detention conditions, and citizenship services — laying off most of their staff and later limiting complaints to an English-only online portal. Immigration enforcement turned personal and specific: Columbia graduate Mahmoud Khalil was arrested without a warrant over pro-Palestinian activism, Rümeysa Öztürk was detained over an op-ed she had written, and Yunseo Chung had her green card revoked. A father with no criminal record was deported and separated from his 12-year-old son. Four U.S. citizen children, including one being treated for brain cancer, were deported alongside their undocumented parents.

Elsewhere that weekend, Trump fired Democratic FTC Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter, asserting a unilateral removal power over an independent agency despite decades-old statutory protections; she sued immediately. An executive order stripped collective bargaining rights from roughly two-thirds of federal employees. Other orders reached into cultural and civic terrain: dismantling Voice of America and the U.S. Agency for Global Media, directing the Smithsonian to remove content deemed "anti-American," ordering the removal of slavery and Native American removal exhibits from national parks, and declaring English the official language in a move that revoked federal language-access protections. Trump also attacked federal judge James Boasberg over an adverse deportation ruling, calling him a "radical left lunatic" and urging impeachment — an escalation echoed separately by Rep. Eli Crane and Elon Musk regarding judges who ruled against Musk's cost-cutting initiative, and pointed enough to draw a rare public rebuke from Chief Justice Roberts. An executive order aimed at mail-in voting sought proof-of-citizenship requirements and the elimination of ballot-receipt grace periods, drawing immediate legal challenges. Amid all this, resistance was visible too: hundreds confronted Vice President Vance in Vermont, Boston's mayor defended sanctuary policy before Congress, and a new hotline network mobilized volunteers to track ICE activity.

By Monday, the focus shifted to trade. The administration imposed 25 percent tariffs on Canada and Mexico and raised tariffs on China to 20 percent. Retaliation was immediate and substantial: Canada announced C$30 billion in counter-tariffs, China imposed 15 percent tariffs on U.S. farm products along with export restrictions, and Mexico's president promised her own response. The same day, the American Bar Association condemned the intimidation of judges, even as the Justice Department opened a review of a politically sensitive election-fraud conviction and Rep. Mike Turner was removed from the House Intelligence Committee for contradicting the administration's account of Russian cybersecurity threats. Health and law enforcement independence also came under strain: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. claimed it was "very very difficult" for measles to kill a healthy person and promoted cod liver oil as treatment, this during an active outbreak in which children with no underlying conditions had already died in Texas. In New York, senior FBI official James Dennehy was forced to retire after resisting a purge of agents who had investigated the January 6 Capitol assault, following the earlier removal of eight other FBI officials. The Associated Press, meanwhile, amended its First Amendment lawsuit over its exclusion from the White House press pool after refusing to rename the Gulf of Mexico. And an order expanding logging across 280 million acres of national forest directed agencies to bypass standard Endangered Species Act review.

Tuesday belonged to Trump's first joint address to Congress. The guest list was built around hardline immigration and transgender policy themes, and the speech included a claim that Musk's Department of Government Efficiency initiative had uncovered "hundreds of billions" in fraud — a figure later shown to be false, with documented savings under $9 billion and some cited examples fabricated outright. Inside the chamber, Democratic Rep. Al Green was forcibly removed by the sergeant-at-arms after repeatedly interrupting the speech to shout that Trump had "no mandate" to cut Medicaid, a protest and ejection that would return to the story two days later. Away from the Capitol, Rep. Richard Hudson, who leads House Republicans' campaign arm, directed members to stop holding town halls in order to avoid drawing attention to public backlash over government cuts — a quieter but telling retreat from constituent accountability. And State Street, the investment firm behind the Fearless Girl statue, quietly dropped its requirement that companies in its index funds maintain gender-diverse boards, part of a broader corporate pullback from diversity commitments under political pressure.

Wednesday brought the week's clearest judicial pushback. The Supreme Court, in a 5–4 decision, rejected the administration's attempt to continue freezing nearly $2 billion in foreign aid. The same day, a federal court ruled that Trump's firing of National Labor Relations Board member Gwynne Wilcox had been illegal, ordering her reinstatement and stating plainly that the president is "not a king." A third check followed from the Merit Systems Protection Board, which ordered the USDA to temporarily reinstate nearly 6,000 fired probationary employees, finding reasonable grounds that the terminations had violated federal law. Even as courts pushed back, pressure on universities widened rather than narrowed: the Justice Department opened a Title VII civil rights investigation into the University of California system over alleged failures to address antisemitic harassment, extending federal scrutiny from private universities to a major public system, and Barnard College announced the expulsion of several student protesters following the pattern set at Columbia. In Alabama, a federal court held a hearing on the state attorney general's threats to prosecute groups that help women travel out of state for abortions — a novel test of interstate reproductive rights. And reports surfaced that DOGE was planning to cut up to half the IRS workforce and as many as 83,000 jobs at Veterans Affairs, reducing staffing to 2019 levels despite rising demand for services.

Thursday's developments carried a distinctly personal dimension. Trump signed an executive order creating a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and Digital Asset Stockpile just ahead of a "crypto summit," a move that legitimized and boosted the value of bitcoin holdings, including his own, while exposing public funds to risk for unclear public benefit. The same day, he signed an order suspending security clearances and terminating federal contracts tied to Perkins Coie, a law firm that had represented Hillary Clinton and other Democratic clients, citing its past Steele dossier work and its diversity hiring practices — a continuation of a pattern that had begun the prior weekend with a similar order against Jenner & Block. A separate memo directed agencies to enforce bond requirements on plaintiffs seeking injunctions against the government, a change legal experts warned would raise the financial cost of challenging executive action in court.

Yet judicial and legislative checks continued in parallel: a federal judge ruled that Trump lacked authority to freeze congressionally appropriated funds, issuing a preliminary injunction, while the House voted to formally censure Al Green for his outburst two days earlier, with ten Democrats joining Republicans. Elsewhere, the Justice Department dismissed a Biden-era environmental lawsuit against a Louisiana chemical plant accused of emitting carcinogens near a majority-Black community, framing the dismissal as an end to "environmental justice" enforcement, and a congressional investigation into oil industry disinformation was allowed to lapse under Republican control.

The week closed on Friday with the formal culmination of its central throughline. The Justice Department, joined by HHS, the Education Department, and the General Services Administration, announced the immediate cancellation of $400 million in federal grants and contracts to Columbia University — described as the first phase of a broader campaign. An executive order narrowed eligibility for Public Service Loan Forgiveness, directing the Education Department to exclude organizations judged to have a "substantial illegal purpose," a category that could include those aiding immigration violations or civil disobedience. The State Department announced plans to use artificial intelligence to screen the social media activity of foreign students, aiming to revoke visas from those perceived as sympathetic to Hamas, a program that could affect tens of thousands of visa holders. Despite multiple court orders blocking the practice, transgender women not named in existing lawsuits continued to be transferred to men's federal facilities. A German permanent resident of nearly two decades was detained and allegedly mistreated by border officials at Boston's airport, prompting a formal inquiry from the German government. And, in a rare non-adversarial note, Trump signed an order establishing a White House task force, which he would chair himself, to coordinate federal preparations for the 2026 World Cup.

Taken as a whole, the week showed an administration comfortable using the tools available to it — appropriated funds, enforcement discretion, executive orders, and personnel authority — against institutions and individuals it viewed as adversarial, while courts, an independent labor board, and a merit board offered resistance that was real but incomplete. Universities lost hundreds of millions of dollars over their handling of protest and speech. A green-card holder and several students faced detention or deportation for political expression. A father was separated from his child; American children were deported with their parents. Judges faced calls for impeachment over their rulings, and a sitting member of Congress was removed from the floor and later censured for a floor protest. Courts blocked a foreign-aid freeze and ordered federal employees reinstated, but tariffs, a bitcoin reserve tied to the president's own holdings, and mounting pressure on universities moved forward largely on schedule. The week's clearest counterweight came not from any single institution but from the layered response of courts, an independent board, a legal association, and ordinary people organizing hotlines and showing up at town halls — a reminder that accountability, in this period, was being tested and defended at once, often within the same day. ```

Title: The Week Immigration Enforcement Became a Speech Test
Content:
```markdown The week of March 8 to 14 opened with an arrest that would echo through nearly every day that followed. Immigration agents detained Mahmoud Khalil, a legal permanent resident and recent Columbia graduate, and moved him to a detention facility in Louisiana without filing criminal charges. The administration invoked a rarely used provision allowing deportation over alleged foreign-policy risk, and President Trump said the arrest was only the first in a campaign against pro-Palestinian activists. That declaration proved accurate: over the following days, the case against Khalil widened into a broader pattern of using immigration law as a tool against political speech—one of the week's defining threads.

The weekend also brought other signs of institutional friction. The Supreme Court rejected an attempt by the administration to freeze nearly $2 billion in foreign aid that Congress had already approved, reaffirming that spending power does not belong to the executive alone. At the same time, the Justice Department dropped a long-running environmental-justice case tied to Louisiana's "Cancer Alley," and Trump dismissed the chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff along with other senior military leaders—a move sudden enough that five former defense secretaries called for immediate congressional hearings over fears the armed forces were being reshaped along political lines. Meanwhile, the DOJ removed senior national-security officials in favor of ideological allies, and DHS began polygraphing its own employees to hunt for leaks about ICE operations. Outside government, the pushback was already visible in the streets: protests against Elon Musk's role in the administration spread to Tesla dealerships nationwide, more than 150 "Stand Up for Science" events took place, and Bernie Sanders' "Fighting Oligarchy" tour drew large crowds.

By Monday, courts had begun to answer back. U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman ordered that Khalil not be deported while his case proceeded, offering the first judicial check on the new campaign against activist students—though it did nothing to slow the broader effort. That same day, Attorney General Pam Bondi dismantled Task Force KleptoCapture, paused enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act for six months, and disbanded the FBI's foreign-influence taskforce, stripping away institutional capacity built to track oligarch wealth and foreign interference. Elsewhere, a federal judge ordered Musk's DOGE office to comply with transparency law and release internal records, and a separate ruling found that a presidential pardon for a January 6 defendant did not extend to an unrelated plot to kill federal agents. Trump also endorsed a stopgap funding bill that would boost defense spending while cutting non-defense programs, setting up a fight that would carry into the following days.

Tuesday sharpened two threads that would define the rest of the week. The Department of Education fired more than 1,300 employees in a single day, cutting its workforce roughly in half and eliminating more than half of its Civil Rights Division offices—a preview of a formal dismantling order still to come. Separately, a presidential memorandum instructed federal agencies to ask courts to impose financial bonds on parties seeking injunctions against government action, calling recent court rulings against the administration "meritless." A federal judge in Boston blocked planned cuts to teacher-training funding, and new FBI director Kash Patel relocated as many as 1,500 agents amid concern the bureau's focus would shift toward left-leaning protest groups rather than far-right extremism. The day's most serious lapse, however, involved national security directly: National Security Adviser Mike Waltz accidentally added a journalist to a Signal group chat where officials were discussing classified strike planning in Yemen. Trump later dismissed the breach as a minor "glitch," even as the Senate Armed Services Committee demanded a Pentagon inspector general investigation.

Wednesday brought the week's clearest run of judicial resistance. Federal Judge Beryl Howell ruled that Trump's executive order stripping security clearances and contracts from the law firm Perkins Coie violated the First Amendment, comparing it to an unconstitutional bill of attainder—an early sign of a pattern that would recur before the week was out. Judge William Alsup found the government's stated justifications for mass federal layoffs to be false and ordered reinstatement of workers across multiple agencies, while another court compelled DOGE to produce records on its cost-cutting operations. Those operations came under further strain when an independent tracker found that Musk's claimed $105 billion in government savings was verifiable only to about $8.6 billion—a gap Musk criticized without addressing. Trade policy also escalated that day: 25 percent tariffs on imported steel and aluminum took effect, prompting the European Union to announce roughly $28 billion in retaliatory tariffs and Canada about $21 billion. And in a case with implications beyond any single individual, Judge Paula Xinis found that the government had acted with no legal basis in detaining and deporting Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant with legal work authorization, despite a prior court order—calling the government's conduct "wholly lawless."

Thursday deepened both the education and immigration threads. More than twenty Democratic attorneys general, led by New York's Letitia James, sued to block the Education Department layoffs, arguing the cuts were unconstitutional and would harm students with disabilities and low-income households—setting up a direct legal test of whether the executive branch could unilaterally gut a cabinet agency. On the immigration front, attorneys alleged that ICE had obtained a search warrant on false pretenses, framed as an investigation into Columbia "harboring aliens" but aimed instead at pro-Palestinian activist students Yunseo Chung and Ranjani Srinivasan; agents searched dorm rooms, and Srinivasan left the country after her visa was revoked. Their cases were distinct from Khalil's, but part of the same expanding campaign. Far more severe in scale, federal agents secretly flew at least 252 Venezuelan migrants to a "terrorism confinement" prison in El Salvador based on gang-affiliation allegations, without a public registry of names or charges; many families learned of the transfers only through news reports weeks later. Separately, nearly 100 protesters were arrested at Trump Tower after occupying its lobby to demand Khalil's release, and in the Senate, ten Democrats joined Republicans to advance the House funding bill via cloture, prompting sharp criticism within their own party over how much spending discretion the deal ceded to the administration.

Friday consolidated nearly every strand of the week into a single, dense set of executive actions. Trump signed an order directing Education Secretary Linda McMahon to begin dismantling the department outright, formalizing what the layoffs had already begun—though full elimination would still require Congress. Days after a court struck down the punitive order against Perkins Coie, Trump signed a nearly identical order against Paul Weiss, suspending security clearances, terminating government contracts, and restricting building access over the firm's past representation of January 6 defendants—confirming that the targeting of law firms was a pattern rather than an isolated case. Trump also invoked the Alien Enemies Act, an 1798 wartime statute, to declare members of the Tren de Aragua gang subject to summary apprehension and removal without standard immigration due process—an extraordinary use of law rarely invoked outside declared wars, extending the logic of Thursday's covert deportations into formal policy. That expansion of unilateral authority was matched by an explicit challenge to the courts themselves: a senior DOJ official told immigration lawyers that deportation flights "need to take off, no matter what," and that if a court tried to stop them, the department might tell the court "f— you." At a Justice Department event the same day, Trump denounced former special counsel Jack Smith and other investigators as "bad people" who had tried to turn America into a "third-world country," while separately celebrating the dismissal of a corruption case against New York's mayor. A further executive order moved to eliminate or shrink seven federal entities, including the U.S. Agency for Global Media, defunding Voice of America and Radio Free Asia and putting contracted journalists in authoritarian countries at heightened personal risk. Even amid this surge, the judiciary did not go silent: Judge James Bredar issued a temporary restraining order blocking further firings at eighteen federal agencies, finding the government likely engaged in an illegal scheme, adding to Wednesday's reinstatement ruling.

Taken as a whole, the week showed two forces moving in direct tension. Federal courts intervened repeatedly and specifically—blocking a deportation, reinstating fired workers, striking down a law firm sanction, halting further firings—demonstrating that institutional checks were still functioning and willing to rule against the executive branch on the merits. But the week's final days revealed something new: an official readiness, voiced plainly by a senior Justice Department lawyer, to disregard a court order altogether if it stood in the way of deportation flights. Paired with the invocation of a wartime statute to bypass ordinary due process, the dismantling of a cabinet department by executive order, and a second law firm punished despite a court's rebuke of the first, the week marked less a single crisis than an accumulation—each action testing how far unilateral power could reach before the courts, Congress, or the public pushed back, and whether that pushback would still be enough. ```

Title: The Week the Courts and the White House Went to War
Content:
```markdown This was the week the tension between the executive branch and the judiciary stopped being theoretical. Over seven days, the administration deported hundreds of people under a rarely invoked wartime statute even after a federal judge ordered the flights turned back, the President called for that judge's impeachment, and the Chief Justice of the United States felt compelled to respond in public. By Friday, a Cabinet department had been ordered closed, a law firm had been coerced into concessions, and an agency head was threatening to shut down Social Security rather than comply with a court's data-access order. Few weeks of the year offer as clear a picture of how power moves when it meets resistance.

**The Weekend**

It began over the weekend of March 15 and 16, when the administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 to deport roughly 250 Venezuelan and Salvadoran men to a mega-prison in El Salvador, bypassing individual hearings entirely. The government's evidence of gang membership included tattoos that turned out to carry no gang significance at all — in one case, a religious symbol inked on a gay makeup artist with no criminal record. Judge James Boasberg ordered the flights halted and directed that any planes already in the air be turned around. The administration argued the aircraft had already left U.S. airspace and were therefore beyond the court's reach, and the flights continued anyway. Whether that argument was a genuine legal position or a pretext for ignoring a judicial order became the defining question of the week.

Among those swept into the operation was Kilmar Ábrego García, a Maryland man who held a 2019 legal order specifically protecting him from deportation to El Salvador. He was sent to the same notorious prison, known as CECOT, as the others. The government first called this an "administrative error," then reversed course, labeling him a gang member without offering evidence and refusing to facilitate his return — a refusal that held even after courts, and eventually the Supreme Court, ordered the government to bring him back. The case would recur throughout the week as a stark example of an error the government declined to undo, even when instructed to by the nation's highest court.

The weekend carried other weight as well. Reporting revealed that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had shared detailed strike plans for a Yemen operation — targets, weapons systems, timing — over the commercial messaging app Signal, in a chat that inadvertently included a journalist. A second Signal chat, involving his wife and brother, contained similarly sensitive material. Separately, an executive order eliminated the US Agency for Global Media, the parent organization of Voice of America, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, and Radio Free Asia, placing more than 1,300 VOA employees on leave and severing contracts with major wire services. Columbia University lost $400 million in federal funding over its handling of campus protests, the University of Maine had funding frozen over transgender athlete policy, and cybersecurity support for state and local election security was cut — three separate signals that federal money would now be wielded as leverage over institutional behavior.

**Monday**

The confrontation over the deportation flights sharpened into something more personal. Trump called Judge Boasberg a "Radical Left Lunatic" and demanded his impeachment over the restraining order. Chief Justice John Roberts, who rarely comments on political disputes, issued a public statement asserting that impeachment is not an appropriate response to disagreement with a judicial ruling. It was an extraordinary moment: the head of the judicial branch publicly defending a lower-court judge against the head of the executive branch.

The same day brought a cluster of other developments. Immigration agents detained Georgetown researcher Badar Khan Suri over alleged Hamas ties and pro-Palestinian social media activity, and separately detained longtime immigrant rights advocate Jeanette Vizguerra outside a Denver store. A Brown University professor was deported despite a judge's order requiring 48 hours' notice before removal. In Texas, a midwife became the first person criminally charged under the state's near-total abortion ban, facing felony counts that could carry decades in prison. And employees from Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency gained access to the US Institute of Peace after initially being denied entry, replacing leadership and canceling contracts at the independent, congressionally created institution — even as a separate federal judge ruled that DOGE was likely subject to Freedom of Information Act requests.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought a string of judicial setbacks for the administration. A federal judge blocked the transgender military service ban, calling it "unabashedly demeaning." Separate rulings protected USAID from further dismantlement by DOGE and temporarily blocked a $20 billion EPA climate grant clawback. Yet the same day, Rep. Brandon Gill formally introduced articles of impeachment against Judge Boasberg, asserting without support that he was "guilty of high crimes and misdemeanors" — translating Trump's rhetoric into actual legislative action. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty and the US Institute of Peace both filed lawsuits challenging the funding cuts and takeover attempts against them, testing whether courts would protect institutions built to operate independently of the White House. In a smaller but telling moment, Trump praised Judge Aileen Cannon, who had ruled in his favor in a classified documents case, calling her a model judge — a contrast that made his attacks on Boasberg look less like a matter of judicial philosophy than a matter of outcomes.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday shifted the week's center of gravity toward the machinery of federal government itself. Trump signed an executive order directing the Education Secretary to begin closing the Department of Education, an action critics immediately said required congressional approval that had never been sought. New York's attorney general announced a legal challenge, warning the move would disproportionately harm low-income and disabled students who rely on federal education protections. The same day, the Justice Department withdrew eleven pieces of guidance on Americans with Disabilities Act compliance, the EEOC and DOJ issued joint guidance recasting workplace diversity programs as potential civil rights violations, and the Department of Education found Maine in violation of Title IX over its policy allowing transgender athletes to compete.

In North Dakota, a jury ordered Greenpeace to pay Energy Transfer more than $660 million over its role in Dakota Access pipeline protests — a verdict civil liberties groups warned could chill protest activity nationwide, given its scale. A judge did bar the administration from deporting Badar Khan Suri while his case proceeded, but the Social Security Administration quietly froze a program that automatically issued Social Security numbers to work-authorized noncitizens — a change made without public announcement that risked overwhelming field offices and delaying benefits for millions.

**Thursday**

Thursday made the Department of Education order formal. Trump signed Executive Order 14242, declaring the agency had spent "$3 trillion with virtually nothing to show for it," and barred federal education funds from supporting diversity or "gender ideology" programs. The same day brought a cluster of additional executive orders: consolidating federal procurement under the General Services Administration, directing agencies to share unclassified data across government in the name of fighting "waste, fraud, and abuse," and accelerating mineral production on federal lands by bypassing standard environmental review. Each, in its own way, concentrated authority that had previously been distributed or reviewed.

The day's most consequential judicial check came from Judge Ellen Lipton Hollander, who issued a temporary restraining order blocking DOGE from accessing Social Security Administration data, calling the effort a "fishing expedition" undertaken without any articulated legal basis, and ordering the deletion of data DOGE had already obtained. Separately, ICE arrested Mahmoud Khalil, a green card holder and former Columbia graduate student, under a rarely used provision permitting deportation of noncitizens deemed to pose "adverse foreign policy consequences" — an arrest that quickly became a flashpoint in the broader campaign against campus protest. In a smaller moment that nonetheless underscored unresolved tensions around outside influence in government, Trump acknowledged that Elon Musk should not be briefed on war plans involving China, given Musk's business interests there.

**Friday**

By Friday, several threads converged. The Department of Homeland Security announced the revocation of temporary legal status for more than 530,000 immigrants from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Venezuela, ending a Biden-era parole program effective April 24 and exposing all of them to potential deportation.

Acting Social Security Commissioner Leland Dudek responded to Judge Hollander's data-access ruling by threatening to shut down the agency's operations entirely, claiming — inaccurately, according to the judge herself — that the order required halting all of the agency's IT systems. Judge Hollander issued unusual public clarification letters insisting that benefit payments were not at risk and that Dudek's reading of her order was mistaken, an exchange that left open the question of whether the threat reflected confusion or resistance.

Trump also issued a memo directing the Attorney General to identify "partisan" lawsuits against the federal government and recommend sanctions against the attorneys and firms bringing them, along with a retroactive review of litigation conduct reaching back to 2017 — a move that followed the administration's earlier pressure campaign against the law firm Paul Weiss, which had been coerced into concessions after facing an executive order targeting its business. And the $1.7 trillion federal student loan portfolio, covering 42 million borrowers, was transferred from the Department of Education to the Small Business Administration, an agency that simultaneously announced a 43 percent reduction in its own workforce. The week's final act came quietly: federal funding supporting legal representation for 26,000 unaccompanied immigrant children was cut, with a White House memo describing immigration legal advocacy itself as "fraud."

Taken as a whole, the week did not turn on any single event so much as on a pattern repeated across immigration enforcement, agency restructuring, and the treatment of dissenting institutions: courts issued orders, and the administration either tested their limits, argued around them, or in some cases appeared simply to disregard them. Some judicial checks held — the transgender military ban stayed blocked, USAID retained court protection, and DOGE's access to Social Security data was constrained, at least for the moment. Others produced open confrontation, as with the deportation flights and the Social Security shutdown threat, where compliance itself became contested territory. The Chief Justice's willingness to publicly rebuke a sitting president over an attack on judicial independence was itself a measure of how far the week's events had traveled from ordinary political disagreement. What remained unresolved by Friday evening was not whether the courts could rule, but whether their rulings would be obeyed — a question that history suggests matters as much as any single policy decided along the way. ```
Excerpt: This week centered on a direct confrontation between the executive branch and the judiciary.

Title: The Week the Guardrails Were Tested
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which nearly every institutional check on presidential power was tested at once, and in which the pressure ran in both directions — coercion from the White House met, unevenly but persistently, by lawsuits, injunctions, and public resistance. Law firms were punished for representing the president's opponents. A federal judge was defied over deportation flights and then threatened with impeachment. Students were detained for political speech. A voting-rules order threatened to complicate registration for millions. And in the middle of it all, a magazine editor found himself accidentally added to a group chat where the nation's most senior security officials were discussing live strike plans on a commercial messaging app.

**The Weekend**

The weekend set the tone. Trump issued executive orders against the law firms Perkins Coie and Covington & Burling, extending a campaign that had already hit Paul Weiss, and the White House revoked security clearances for sixteen former officials. The stated justification was that these firms had represented his opponents or employed lawyers tied to investigations against him; the practical effect was to make representing the administration's adversaries carry a cost. At the same time, Trump publicly denied signing his own deportation proclamation invoking the Alien Enemies Act, even though his signature appeared in the Federal Register — a small but telling episode in a week full of questions about who was actually directing consequential policy. Judge James Boasberg, meanwhile, opened an inquiry into whether the administration had defied his order halting deportation flights; 137 Venezuelan migrants had been deported anyway, and officials, including deportation czar Tom Homan, said openly that they did not care what the judge thought. Trump compared Tesla vandalism to the January 6 attack and called for twenty-year sentences, months after pardoning convicted January 6 rioters — a jarring contrast in how political violence was being treated depending on its target. He also pressured Maine Governor Janet Mills over her refusal to comply with a transgender sports ban, threatening the state's federal funding. Beneath these clashes, a "TeslaTakedown" protest movement was gathering strength, and a Harris Poll found one in five Americans planning permanent boycotts of companies aligned with the administration's agenda.

**Monday**

By Monday, the week's most consequential single revelation had surfaced: The Atlantic's Jeffrey Goldberg revealed that he had been mistakenly added to a Signal chat in which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Vice President JD Vance, and other senior officials discussed detailed operational plans for strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen — on an unsecured commercial app, with messages set to auto-delete. It was, on its face, a serious operational security failure, and it would occupy the week's remaining days. The same day, Trump signed an order directing the Education Secretary to begin dismantling the Department of Education, while Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced plans to eliminate FEMA, the government's primary disaster-response agency — both attempts to use executive action to accomplish what would normally require Congress. Attorney General Pam Bondi warned Democratic Representative Jasmine Crockett to "tread very carefully" after she supported a Tesla protest rally, and separately labeled pro-Palestinian student protesters "domestic terrorists." A 21-year-old Columbia green card holder, Yunseo Chung, sued the administration after ICE tried to arrest and deport her over her participation in campus protests, alleging retaliation for protected speech. Trump named his former personal attorney, Alina Habba, who had no prosecutorial experience, as interim U.S. Attorney for New Jersey; she said she intended to help "turn New Jersey red." And the Department of Government Efficiency fired 11,000 IRS employees, part of a broader cut expected to reach 20,000 workers and reduce federal tax revenue by roughly $500 billion this year.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday deepened several of these threads at once. Trump signed a sweeping executive order overhauling federal election rules, requiring documentary proof of citizenship for voter registration and threatening funding cuts to noncompliant states — despite noncitizen voting being exceedingly rare and roughly 21 million eligible voters lacking ready proof of citizenship on hand. The law firm campaign expanded again, with a new order suspending security clearances and terminating federal contracts for Jenner & Block, which employed former special counsel deputy Andrew Weissmann. The pattern of targeting political speech through immigration enforcement widened as well: Tufts doctoral student Rumeysa Ozturk was detained and transferred to Louisiana in apparent violation of a court notice requirement after co-authoring a pro-Palestinian op-ed, and University of Alabama student Alireza Doroudi was detained without stated justification. The State Department expanded visa screening based on applicants' social media activity. But the day also brought a check: a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order blocking ICE from detaining or transferring Yunseo Chung, finding the government had not shown sufficient basis for its claims. And the Signal chat fallout intensified as the watchdog group American Oversight sued Hegseth and other officials for violating federal record-keeping law, while Hegseth, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, CIA Director John Ratcliffe, and Trump himself all publicly denied that classified information had been shared — denials that would not survive contact with the primary source.

**Wednesday**

By Wednesday, that source arrived: The Atlantic published the actual screenshots, contradicting the officials' denials outright. Also that day, Columbia University, having lost $400 million in federal funding, agreed to overhaul its protest policies and hire an internal security force empowered to remove people from campus — a concession that alarmed faculty concerned about academic freedom. A federal appeals court, in a split decision, upheld Judge Boasberg's block on further deportations under the Alien Enemies Act, even though the administration had already deported hundreds of people without complying with his earlier order to turn planes around. House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters that Congress had the authority to "eliminate an entire district court," as House Republicans pursued impeachment resolutions against judges who had ruled against the administration — a direct escalation from criticizing rulings to floating the elimination of courts themselves. And in a smaller but telling moment, Fox News stopped putting national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin on air after she accurately reported that the Signal chat contained sensitive operational details, not vague generalities.

**Thursday**

Thursday brought the week's largest single blow to organized labor: an executive order excluded dozens of federal agencies from labor-management relations coverage, citing national security grounds, and stripped collective bargaining protections from more than a million federal workers. The administration simultaneously sued unions in Texas to affirm its authority to void existing bargaining agreements outright. The same day, a separate order titled "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History" directed Vice President Vance to remove content on race and gender from Smithsonian museums and restore pre-2020 Confederate monuments, conditioning future funding on ideological compliance. The law firm campaign reached a fifth target, WilmerHale, whose order cited its employment of former special counsel Robert Mueller and its pro bono immigration and voting rights work. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced roughly 10,000 additional layoffs at HHS, bringing total losses across the FDA, CDC, and NIH to around 20,000 workers. Judge Boasberg, acting on the watchdog lawsuit, ordered officials to preserve all Signal communications from the relevant days and file a status report on compliance. And new messages surfaced suggesting Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller had invoked presidential authority to greenlight the Yemen strike, while Vance indicated uncertainty about whether Trump himself was fully aware of the decision — raising a pointed question about who, precisely, held the authority being exercised.

**Friday**

Friday showed the law firm campaign splitting into two distinct paths. Jenner & Block and WilmerHale filed federal lawsuits challenging the orders against them as unconstitutional retaliation, joining a resistance track. Skadden Arps, by contrast, reached a preemptive $100 million settlement, following Paul Weiss's earlier capitulation. And Perkins Coie won an actual court block on its order — the first successful legal challenge to the entire campaign, proof that the strategy was not unstoppable. Elsewhere, the University of Michigan closed its diversity office, which had measurably increased enrollment among first-generation and low-income students, citing the same federal funding pressure that had reshaped Columbia's policies days earlier. Trump commuted the sentence of Ozy Media's Carlos Watson and pardoned Nikola founder Trevor Milton, who had donated roughly $2 million to his campaign, eliminating hundreds of millions of dollars in restitution obligations tied to fraud convictions. Dr. Peter Marks, the FDA's top vaccine regulator, resigned after being told to resign or be fired, warning publicly that Health Secretary Kennedy wanted "subservient confirmation" of misinformation rather than scientific accuracy — a resignation that landed in the middle of an active measles outbreak. In Wisconsin, a state Supreme Court race became a flashpoint after Elon Musk spent more than $20 million and offered direct cash payments to voters and petition signers, prompting the state's attorney general to sue to block the payments as illegal vote-buying. Markets fell sharply amid inflation data that exceeded the Federal Reserve's target and new uncertainty over auto tariffs. And two fired Federal Trade Commission commissioners, Rebecca Kelly Slaughter and Alvaro Bedoya, sued over their removal, arguing it violated statutory protections meant to insulate independent agencies from direct presidential control.

Taken as a whole, the week amounted to a test of how many institutional buffers could be pressed at once — the legal profession, the judiciary, the civil service, universities, independent agencies, and the electoral process itself — and how each would respond. Some yielded: Paul Weiss and Skadden settled; Columbia and Michigan reshaped their policies under funding threats. Others resisted and, in at least one case, won outright: Perkins Coie's injunction, and the protective orders shielding Yunseo Chung and Rumeysa Ozturk, showed that courts retained real capacity to intervene when presented with a case. The Signal chat scandal, running from Monday's revelation through Thursday's preservation order, demonstrated both how casually classified military planning could be handled at the highest levels and how difficult it was proving to hold anyone directly accountable for it. None of these threads resolved by Friday. What the week made clear was that the pressure was sustained, coordinated across many fronts simultaneously, and met by a response that was real but far from uniform — a system under strain, still functioning in places, bending in others. ```
Excerpt: This week showed a presidency testing the limits of nearly every institutional check at once.

Title: Tariffs, Term Limits, and the Price of Defiance
Content:
```markdown This week, spanning the last weekend of March through the first Friday of April, brought together two forces that would define its shape: a steady tightening of executive pressure on universities, courts, and immigrants, and a sudden economic shock the president brought on himself. By week's end, a research university had surrendered part of its academic governance, a senator had spoken for a full day on the Senate floor, a wrongfully deported man remained in a Salvadoran prison despite a judge's order, and the stock market had lost more value in forty-eight hours than at almost any point in American history.

The weekend set the tone. Facing a threatened $400 million cut in federal funding over allegations that it had failed to address antisemitism on campus, Columbia University placed its Middle Eastern studies department under outside receivership and imposed new restrictions on pro-Palestinian protest. The university's interim president resigned within days. Faculty unions sued, students and alumni protested, and some graduates publicly destroyed their diplomas. It was a stark demonstration of how directly federal money could reshape what a university teaches and permits its students to say — and it would not be the last such demonstration this week. At the same time, the administration moved against individual activists: Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended revoking visas from student protesters, and the government pursued deportation of Columbia graduate Mahmoud Khalil under rarely invoked provisions of immigration law, even as a federal judge blocked a similar action against another Columbia student. Institutional capitulation on one side, individual targeting on the other — the pairing became a pattern that would recur all week.

Also over the weekend, in an NBC interview, Trump said he was "not joking" about seeking a third term and claimed unspecified "methods" existed for bypassing the 22nd Amendment. Days later his own attorney general, Pam Bondi, publicly downplayed the idea, calling it "a heavy lift" — a rare instance of a senior official contradicting the president on the constitutional limits of his own power. Separately, Elon Musk turned a Wisconsin Supreme Court race into a spectacle of money in politics, spending more than $20 million backing a candidate and personally handing out $1 million checks to voters who signed a petition. A state lawsuit challenging the payments went nowhere on procedural grounds, while "Tesla Takedown" protests spread to 253 cities. Meanwhile the administration sued CBS News for $10 billion and the Des Moines Register over a pre-election poll, and the FCC opened investigations into NBC, NPR, and PBS — a widening effort to use litigation and regulatory power against unfavorable coverage.

By Monday, the week's central act of legislative resistance began. Senator Cory Booker took the Senate floor at 7 p.m. and did not stop talking for twenty-five hours, breaking the record Strom Thurmond had set in 1957. Booker used the time to catalog what he called threats to democracy — economic disruption, cuts to health and education programs, erosion of due process — turning a procedural tool into a sustained act of public protest that would be invoked again and again through the week as a symbol of resistance within institutions still capable of resisting. His speech landed alongside a wave of federal agency retrenchment: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin terminated $14 billion in climate grants and moved to cut more than 1,100 scientist positions, plans a federal judge would later block. The administration also froze Title X family-planning funds, canceled $1 billion in food-bank funding, and, at HHS, began laying the groundwork for what would become mass layoffs the next day.

Monday also produced the week's clearest instance of admitted government error met with refusal to correct it. In a court filing, the government acknowledged it had deported Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a legal resident with protected status, to a Salvadoran prison due to "administrative error" — but argued it lacked the authority to bring him back. Vice President JD Vance compounded the episode by falsely claiming on social media that Abrego Garcia was a "convicted" gang member. The case would anchor the week's due-process concerns, alongside a lawsuit alleging ICE had deported three U.S.-citizen children, including a four-year-old with stage-4 cancer, without due process or the chance to arrange alternative custody. Elsewhere, House Republican leadership tried and failed to block a bipartisan proxy-voting measure for new parents — a minor but telling sign of diminished control over their own caucus — and federal judges blocked the firing of CIA and ODNI employees tied to DEI programs and delayed termination of Temporary Protected Status for Venezuelan migrants, with one judge calling the government's justification "predicated on negative stereotypes." Democratic attorneys general filed the first of three lawsuits challenging Trump's executive order imposing proof-of-citizenship and mail-ballot restrictions on federal elections.

On Tuesday, the administration's campaign against federal health capacity reached its fullest expression. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. oversaw layoffs eliminating roughly a quarter of the HHS workforce — about 10,000 employees — hitting programs on lead poisoning, tobacco policy, bird flu surveillance, and maternal health monitoring, even as measles and whooping cough outbreaks remained active. The same day, the administration announced a review of $9 billion in federal grants to Harvard, extending the funding-pressure template first applied to Columbia, while USCIS said it would begin monitoring immigrants' social media for "antisemitic activity" — a policy with clear potential to target pro-Palestinian speech broadly. Pressure on the judiciary also intensified: Trump and Musk escalated attacks on judges who had ruled against the administration, including calls to impeach Judge James Boasberg, while House Republicans displayed "Wanted" posters of judges outside their offices and held a hearing on curbing judicial power. In a related development, a federal judge dismissed corruption charges against New York City Mayor Eric Adams with prejudice, finding the arrangement "smacks of a bargain" tied to his cooperation on immigration enforcement — a judicial finding that prosecutorial discretion had been traded for policy compliance. House Republicans also advanced the SAVE Act, requiring documentary proof of citizenship for voter registration, and a Trump appointee referred New York Attorney General Letitia James to the DOJ for criminal investigation, part of a broader pattern of federal law enforcement being turned against officials who had resisted administration directives.

Wednesday belonged almost entirely to one event. Trump signed an executive order imposing a 10 percent baseline tariff on all imports, with country-specific rates as high as 49 percent for major trading partners, justified by a declared national emergency over trade deficits. He called it "Liberation Day." The market response was immediate and historic: a two-day loss of $6.6 trillion in value, the largest in American history, as economists across the political spectrum called the underlying tariff formula incoherent. The scale of the shock briefly cracked party discipline — four Republican senators joined Democrats to pass a resolution rescinding tariffs specifically on Canadian goods, defying a direct public appeal from Trump to block the measure, though the House was expected to let it expire without a vote. The law firm settlement pattern continued as well, with Milbank LLP becoming the latest major firm to commit $100 million in pro bono work to avoid a threatened executive order, following a similar deal struck by Willkie Farr & Gallagher days earlier — coercion of the legal profession running in parallel with coercion of the university system.

By Thursday, the consequences of Wednesday's announcement were spreading internationally and domestically. China imposed 34 percent retaliatory tariffs, restricted exports of rare earth minerals critical to defense and technology manufacturing, and blacklisted several U.S. defense firms, while American markets extended their losses and economist Lawrence Summers publicly derided the tariff methodology. Health Secretary Kennedy acknowledged that roughly 20 percent of the prior week's HHS layoffs had been made in error and would be reversed, an admission that undercut the administration's stated justification for the cuts in the first place. The Pentagon's inspector general opened a formal investigation into Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's use of the Signal messaging app to discuss classified military operations, after a journalist was inadvertently included in the chat. Two more lawsuits were filed against Trump's election executive order, bringing the total to three, and the Social Security Administration briefly canceled Maine's vital-records contracts in apparent retaliation against the state's governor before reversing course under public pressure — a small but revealing episode in the use of federal agency power as political punishment. North Carolina's General Assembly introduced a bill making it illegal to use standard voter registration forms in registration drives, extending the week's pattern of new restrictions on voter access to the state level.

The week closed on Friday with direct confrontation between the executive branch and a federal court. Judge Paula Xinis ordered the government to return Kilmar Abrego Garcia by April 7, finding his deportation "wholly lawless" and a "clear constitutional violation." Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller responded by calling her a "Marxist judge," and the White House publicly disputed her authority over the case — turning what had begun as an admitted administrative error into an open dispute over whether a court order would be obeyed at all. In North Carolina, a divided Court of Appeals ruled that a Republican candidate who had lost a state supreme court race by 734 votes could proceed with a challenge seeking to invalidate more than 65,000 ballots, prompting an appeal from his opponent and raising the prospect of a court overturning an election outcome rather than a recount or a new vote. The U.S. Supreme Court, in a 5-4 emergency order, allowed the administration to freeze $65 million in teacher-training grants tied to diversity programs, overturning a lower court's restraining order and testing the boundaries of congressional spending authority. And as markets continued their historic decline, Trump held a $1 million-per-person fundraiser at Mar-a-Lago for his super PAC and skipped the dignified transfer ceremony for four service members killed in a training accident, attending a golf tournament at his resort instead. Former President Obama, in a public speech, urged universities, law firms, and citizens to resist executive coercion and defend academic freedom and due process even at financial cost — a coda that echoed Booker's speech from six days earlier.

Across the week, a recurring thread ran beneath the individual stories: officials speaking with confidence about things that were not true. A DOGE staffer made false claims about noncitizen Social Security numbers and voting; Kennedy falsely claimed vitamin A shipments had reached Texas measles communities; Vance misdescribed a wrongfully deported man as a convicted gang member; a member of Congress promoted a decades-old assassination conspiracy theory on national television. No single instance dominated the news, but together they formed a steady erosion of the assumption that government statements could be taken at face value.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government testing the outer edges of several restraints at once — the two-term limit, the separation of trade authority between Congress and the presidency, the independence of universities and law firms from federal financial coercion, and the finality of judicial orders concerning wrongful deportation. Some of these tests met resistance: a bipartisan Senate vote, a federal judge's order, a former president's public appeal, a marathon speech meant to hold public attention. Others met little resistance at all: a university surrendered without a fight from its trustees, a market absorbed trillions in losses without altering the policy that caused them, and a deportation error remained uncorrected past the deadline a court had set. The week did not resolve any of these tensions. It simply made clear how many of them were now open at the same time. ```
Excerpt: This week combined a slow-building campaign against institutions with a sudden, self-inflicted economic shock.

Title: Tariffs, Takedowns, and Two Weeks in El Salvador
Content:
```markdown The week of April 5 through April 11 opened with the largest coordinated street protests of the young administration and closed with the government openly defying a unanimous Supreme Court order. In between, financial markets convulsed under a self-inflicted tariff shock, universities faced an escalating campaign to bend them to federal demands, law firms were pressured into pledging nearly a billion dollars in "voluntary" legal tribute, and a single wrongfully deported man in a Salvadoran prison became the clearest test yet of whether the executive branch would answer to the courts at all.

The weekend began with numbers. Organizers with the 50501 Movement and Indivisible drew well over a million people into the streets of more than 1,300 cities under the banner "Hands Off," with tens of thousands filling the Washington Mall. Organizers billed it not as a single event but as the opening move of a sustained resistance effort ahead of the midterms. That same weekend, Trump declared a new tariff regime — a 10% universal tariff followed swiftly by escalating "reciprocal" rates, including 34% on Chinese goods — and markets responded immediately: the Dow lost more than 2,000 points in two days, trillions in value evaporated, and economists began warning openly of recession. Away from the cameras, the Justice Department placed career attorney Erez Reuveni on indefinite leave after he told a federal judge, truthfully, that the deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia to El Salvador had no legal basis. Attorney General Pam Bondi made clear that DOJ lawyers were expected to advocate zealously rather than candidly. At the same time, immigration authorities revoked roughly 300 student visas linked to pro-Palestinian activism, canceled all South Sudanese visas en masse, and detained Venezuelan Temporary Protected Status holders despite their statutory protections. Amid it all, more than 80 former employees of the law firm Skadden Arps publicly condemned its decision to settle with the administration rather than fight an executive order — an early sign of the pressure building on the legal profession.

By Monday, the week's central threads had begun to interlock. The Supreme Court, in a 5-4 ruling, allowed the administration to continue deportations under the 1798 Alien Enemies Act, requiring notice and habeas review but declining to block the practice through a nationwide injunction. Hours later, in a separate case, U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis found that Abrego Garcia's deportation had been "wholly lawless" and ordered the government to bring him back from the Salvadoran prison where he had been sent by what officials called an administrative error. The administration responded not with compliance but with an emergency motion to block the order. The law firm story split further that day: Willkie Farr, Milbank, and Skadden struck deals to perform pro bono work for causes aligned with the administration, while Perkins Coie, Jenner & Block, and WilmerHale won court injunctions blocking similar executive orders against them. Trump, meanwhile, turned his attention to the judiciary itself, calling for the impeachment and disbarment of Judge James Boasberg over an adverse deportation ruling — prompting a rare public rebuke from Chief Justice John Roberts — while the Justice Department separately sought to remove Judge Beryl Howell from a law firm case after she ruled against the government. Trump also proposed a $1 trillion defense budget, a sharp reversal from his February calls for reduced military spending, and bipartisan lawmakers introduced bills to reclaim tariff authority from the White House, though party leadership signaled it would keep the measures off the floor.

Tuesday brought a cluster of executive orders reshaping energy and environmental policy: directives to remove barriers to coal production, a two-year exemption for coal plants from mercury emissions standards, and instructions to the Attorney General to halt enforcement of state climate laws in New York, Vermont, and California. The same day, the D.C. Circuit ordered the reinstatement of two independent agency heads — Cathy Harris of the Merit Systems Protection Board and Gwynne Wilcox of the NLRB — citing a 90-year-old precedent shielding such officials from at-will removal, a ruling that set up a likely Supreme Court fight over presidential removal power. The university funding campaign began in earnest, with the administration freezing nearly $1 billion to Cornell and $790 million to Northwestern over allegations tied to campus activism and antisemitism. In smaller but telling developments, a federal judge — a Trump appointee — ordered the Associated Press's White House access restored, finding that barring the wire service over its refusal to adopt the phrase "Gulf of America" violated the First Amendment. And the case of 19-year-old Jose Hermosillo surfaced: a U.S. citizen held for nearly ten days by Border Patrol after an agent falsified a transcript claiming he had admitted to being undocumented.

Wednesday was dominated by the tariff standoff reaching its most volatile point. Trump raised tariffs on China to 104%, then to 125%, as Beijing vowed to "fight to the end." Hours after new reciprocal tariffs took effect against dozens of countries, Trump abruptly announced a 90-day pause for most of them while continuing to escalate specifically against China — a whiplash sequence that left allies and markets uncertain what U.S. trade policy actually was, and prompted questions in Congress about possible insider trading around the reversal. The same day, an executive order targeted Susman Godfrey, the firm that had represented Dominion Voting Systems in its $787.5 million defamation settlement against Fox News, stripping its lawyers of security clearances and restricting its federal contracts. Trump also directed the Justice Department to investigate former CISA director Chris Krebs, who had defended the integrity of the 2020 election, and former DHS official Miles Taylor, who had written critically about Trump; both lost their security clearances. A follow-on executive order required federal agencies to build automatic one-year sunset clauses into energy regulations unless affirmatively renewed, shifting the deregulatory default further in industry's favor.

Thursday delivered the week's most consequential single ruling. The Supreme Court, unanimously, ordered the government to facilitate Abrego Garcia's release from custody in El Salvador — a 9-0 rebuke from a court with a conservative supermajority, though ambiguous language about "effectuating" his return left room for the executive to maneuver. The university pressure campaign widened sharply the same day: the administration suspended dozens of research grants to Princeton, opened a review of $9 billion in contracts with Harvard, and paused $175 million to Penn over transgender athlete policies. Law firms kept adding to the running tally of concessions, with Milbank, Paul Weiss, and Willkie Farr each committing tens of millions more in pro bono work, prompting the American Bar Association to formally condemn what it called a "clear and disconcerting pattern" of attacks on judges and lawyers. Away from Washington, the North Carolina Supreme Court ruled that thousands of overseas and military voters must prove their eligibility within 30 days or have their already-cast ballots discarded — a decision that could overturn Democratic Justice Allison Riggs's narrow November victory and inject retroactive uncertainty into a certified election.

By Friday, the Abrego Garcia case reached its starkest point yet. A government attorney told the court he had no information about Abrego Garcia's whereabouts and that no steps had been taken to comply with the Supreme Court's order; Judge Xinis responded by ordering daily compliance updates as the administration continued to stall. The same day, Harvard became the week's most prominent institution to say no: its lawyers publicly rejected federal demands to install "viewpoint-diverse" faculty, eliminate diversity programs, and cede control over admissions and academic content in exchange for restoring $2.2 billion in frozen funding. Elsewhere, a presidential memorandum created a military buffer zone along the southern border, authorizing active-duty troops to detain migrants as trespassers, with a report due on whether to invoke the 1807 Insurrection Act. Five more major firms — including Kirkland & Ellis and Latham & Watkins — agreed to $600 million in pro bono commitments, pushing the week's total past $1 billion in coerced legal tribute. In a smaller but revealing episode, DOGE staffers attempted to embed personnel within the independent nonprofit Vera Institute of Justice before withdrawing once it became clear the group had already lost its DOJ funding.

Taken as a whole, the week showed an executive branch testing the outer edges of its authority on nearly every front at once — economic, judicial, academic, and legal — while the institutions built to check that authority responded unevenly. Courts pushed back with real force in several instances: reinstating fired agency officials, restoring press access, and, most significantly, ruling unanimously against the government in the Abrego Garcia case. Yet that unanimous order was met not with compliance but with silence and delay, raising a question more fundamental than any single policy dispute: whether judicial rulings still bind the executive when the executive simply declines to answer them. Congress, for its part, showed flickers of bipartisan resistance on tariffs but declined to force a vote. Universities and law firms split between capitulation and resistance, with Harvard's public refusal standing as the week's clearest institutional line drawn against federal coercion. And in North Carolina, a certified election faced the prospect of being unwound after the fact — a reminder that threats to democratic settlement do not always arrive from Washington, and do not always announce themselves as crises until the rules have already changed beneath the voters who trusted them. ```
