Title: The Week the Government Said No to the Courts
Content:
```markdown This was the week the machinery of American government tested, in public, whether a president could simply say no to the courts — and whether anyone could stop him. Over seven days, a wrongly deported Maryland man became the fulcrum for a constitutional confrontation that widened by the day, a state governor's family survived a firebombing of their home, one of the nation's oldest universities refused to bend to federal pressure and paid for it within hours, and by Friday the FBI was leading a sitting judge out of her own courthouse in handcuffs.

The week began badly and got worse before Monday even arrived. Overnight between Saturday and Sunday, a man named Cody Balmer scaled a fence around the Pennsylvania governor's residence, broke in with a hammer, and firebombed the building hours after Governor Josh Shapiro's family had finished their Passover Seder. State troopers evacuated Shapiro, his wife, and their four children before the fire spread further. Balmer was arrested and later told investigators he hated Shapiro over his position on Israel; he was charged with attempted murder, terrorism, and arson, and held without bail. It was, by any plain reading, a political attack on an elected official's family in their home — the kind of event that in past eras would have drawn immediate, unified condemnation from the nation's leadership. That weekend also brought fresh economic turbulence: Trump paused most tariffs for 90 days while keeping a 145 percent tariff on China, a reversal that came only after a near-collapse in the government debt market and a sharp slide in the dollar — the kind of capital flight more often associated with unstable economies than with the United States. Tens of thousands turned out for rallies in Los Angeles and Boise against the administration, and in Washington, a Social Security Administration IT executive was physically dragged from his office after objecting to a policy targeting immigrants' bank access.

By Monday, the week's central storyline sharpened into focus. In a staged Oval Office meeting with El Salvador's president, Nayib Bukele, Trump signaled that his administration would not facilitate the return of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland man the government had already admitted was wrongly deported — this despite a unanimous Supreme Court order directing the administration to facilitate his return. A hot microphone caught Trump telling Bukele he wanted to go after "home-growns" next, and the two discussed building more prison capacity to hold American citizens abroad. Asked directly, Attorney General Pam Bondi and Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt both declined to rule out that the administration could lawfully deport U.S. citizens. The administration then filed a court declaration containing a claim from senior aide Stephen Miller that the Supreme Court had ruled 9-0 in the government's favor — a description of the ruling that did not match its actual text. Asked about the Shapiro firebombing nearly a day after it happened, Trump said he had not heard about it, then dismissed the attacker as "probably just a whack job."

Monday also delivered the week's second defining confrontation. Harvard University's legal team formally rejected federal demands to dictate its governance, admissions, and hiring practices in exchange for continued funding, arguing plainly that no government should tell a private university what it may teach. The retaliation was immediate: within hours, the administration froze $2.2 billion in grants and a $60 million contract. This was not passive resistance — Harvard also mounted a public defense of its position, making clear it intended an active fight rather than a quiet standoff. Elsewhere that day, ICE detained Mohsen Mahdawi, a Columbia University student and lawful permanent resident, during his own naturalization interview in Vermont, in what his lawyers said was retaliation for pro-Palestinian campus activism; a federal judge blocked his deportation that same day. The White House, meanwhile, again denied Associated Press journalists access to the Oval Office despite a standing court order requiring it, and issued an official statement branding NPR and PBS purveyors of "radical, woke propaganda."

Tuesday brought the judiciary's first sharp answer. U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis declared that "nothing has been done" to comply with the Supreme Court's order in the Abrego Garcia case, rejected the administration's argument that the Bukele meeting satisfied that order, and directed depositions and sworn testimony from up to six officials. Trump, who had briefly signaled he might respect the Court's order, reversed himself again, insisting his administration lacked the power to bring Abrego Garcia back — even as he separately said he would "love" to send American citizens to El Salvador's mega-prison, with Leavitt calling the idea "a legal question the president is looking into." The same day, the IRS began preparing to revoke Harvard's tax-exempt status, an action legal experts noted appeared to violate a 1998 law barring the president from directing IRS enforcement; the Education Department confirmed a separate $2.3 billion funding freeze. Civil society pushed back on multiple fronts: the American Association of University Professors sued over the Harvard freeze, the NAACP sued over anti-DEI school policies, labor groups sued over canceled child-labor programs, and Protect Democracy sued over the removal of a federal spending database. A whistleblower also revealed that DOGE staff had accessed National Labor Relations Board data in a manner resembling unauthorized intrusion, including a login attempt traced to a Russian IP address, while the group scrubbed identifying information from its own website. Amid all this, Trump's media company launched investment products explicitly built to profit from his own tariff decisions, and a federal judge in Boston blocked the administration from abruptly ending legal status for roughly 500,000 migrants from four countries. Barbara Lee won Oakland's mayoral race by ranked-choice vote, and North Carolina's contested judicial election dispute deepened as a losing candidate pressed a challenge to roughly 260 ballots built on flawed residency data.

Wednesday opened a second, legally distinct front in the standoff between courts and the executive. Chief U.S. District Judge James Boasberg, in a separate case concerning deportation flights conducted under the Alien Enemies Act, issued a 46-page opinion finding probable cause that administration officials had committed criminal contempt by failing to recall those flights despite his earlier order — and warned he would appoint an independent prosecutor if the administration would not prosecute itself. This was not the Abrego Garcia case; it involved different facts, a different judge, and a different legal theory, but it landed in the same week and compounded the same underlying message — that the executive branch was treating judicial orders as optional. California's governor and attorney general sued separately that day, arguing Trump's unilateral tariffs exceeded authority reserved to Congress. The Justice Department sued Maine over its transgender-athlete policy, following earlier threats to withhold the state's entire $250 million K-12 budget — threats a federal judge had already partially blocked. North Carolina's election board, after investigative reporting found dozens of challenged voters had documented histories of living in the state, committed to restoring wrongly invalidated ballots. An immigration judge denied bond to Rümeysa Öztürk, a Turkish doctoral student detained over a campus op-ed about Gaza, ruling her a "danger to the community" even though the government itself had argued only flight risk — a case distinct in its facts from both Abrego Garcia and Mahdawi, but part of the same widening pattern of immigration enforcement reaching political speech. The State Department closed its office monitoring foreign disinformation, and police used stun guns on protesters at a Marjorie Taylor Greene town hall in Georgia. Senator Chris Van Hollen traveled to El Salvador to see his constituent Abrego Garcia and was told a meeting might not be possible, even as officials confirmed the U.S. was paying El Salvador to hold him.

Thursday's ruling tied the week's judicial threads together. A three-judge panel of the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals — including J. Harvie Wilkinson, a Reagan appointee — unanimously rejected the administration's appeal in the Abrego Garcia case, writing bluntly that the government was "asserting a right to stash away residents of this country in foreign prisons without the semblance of due process." Coming a day after Boasberg's contempt finding, the ruling made clear that judicial resistance to the administration's posture was not confined to one court or one party's appointees. The same day, Trump escalated a different institutional fight, publicly attacking Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell as "always too late and wrong" and declaring that "Powell's termination cannot come fast enough" after Powell warned that tariffs would hit the economy harder than expected; Powell publicly rejected the pressure and reaffirmed the Fed's independence. DOGE staff terminated roughly 1,500 of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's 1,700 employees despite concerns the move violated a standing court order. The administration extended the federal hiring freeze through mid-July and signed orders deregulating commercial fishing and opening marine monuments to review. Markets fell sharply on new chip export limits and Powell's warning, manufacturing orders hit their lowest level since April 2020, and China diverted purchases of oil, soybeans, aircraft, and beef away from American suppliers — hard evidence that the tariff turmoil begun over the weekend was inflicting real damage on the sectors it was meant to protect. The FCC chair threatened Comcast over its coverage of the Abrego Garcia case, a U.S.-born citizen remained jailed on an ICE detainer even after a judge authenticated his birth certificate, and a gunman killed at least two people at Florida State University, prompting Trump to say only that "the gun doesn't do the shooting, the people do."

The week closed with its most direct assault yet on judicial independence. FBI agents arrested Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Hannah Dugan, alleging she had helped a defendant evade a federal immigration arrest team inside her own courtroom; FBI Director Kash Patel posted a photograph of her in handcuffs captioned "No one is above the law." This was a separate matter from the Abrego Garcia and Boasberg proceedings — a different court, a different defendant, a different theory of liability — but arriving on the same Friday as those other threads, it read as the culmination of a week in which the executive branch had moved from resisting judicial orders to directly confronting the judges who issue them. That same day, Trump signed an executive order requiring documentary proof of citizenship to vote, and the House passed the SAVE Act imposing similar federal requirements, while legislatures in seven states advanced parallel restrictions. A federal judge blocked a policy that would have allowed rapid deportation of migrants to third countries without a chance to show they faced persecution. Judge Amy Berman Jackson blocked the CFPB layoffs a day after they had proceeded. The Office of Personnel Management moved to strip civil service protections from roughly 50,000 federal workers, and the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division was redirected away from its traditional protective mission toward pursuing claims of discrimination against white applicants and unauthorized voting. Trump instructed advisors to study whether he had legal authority to remove Powell. The IRS's acting commissioner was ousted days after his appointment, Pentagon aides were fired amid a leak investigation tied to disputed surveillance claims, and the official dismantling USAID was in turn fired by the secretary of state. By week's end, Van Hollen finally secured his meeting with Abrego Garcia in El Salvador and relayed a message to his wife back home.

Taken as a whole, the week did not produce a single dramatic rupture so much as an accumulation of tests, each probing whether existing checks on executive power still held. Courts at every level — a district judge, a chief judge finding probable cause for contempt, a conservative-majority appellate panel, another district judge blocking a deportation policy hours after it was announced — answered with unusual unanimity that they did not intend to yield. Universities, states, unions, and advocacy groups filed suit rather than comply. The Federal Reserve chair, in his own domain, said the same. Whether those institutional answers translate into enforceable consequences, or whether verbal defiance from the executive branch hardens into settled practice, is the question the week leaves behind — one no single ruling will resolve, but that will be answered by whether the pattern set this week continues, or breaks. ```
Excerpt: This week centered on one unresolved standoff: the Trump administration's refusal to bring home a wrongly deported Maryland man despite a unanimous Supreme Court order.

Title: The Week the Courts Pushed Back — and the Executive Pushed Harder
Content:
```markdown The week of April 19 to 25 opened with courts intervening to stop deportations already in motion and closed with the FBI arresting a sitting judge. In between, a university refused to bend to federal pressure, a Cabinet secretary's handling of classified information collapsed into a full leadership crisis, and the administration signed nine executive orders in a single day rewriting how the federal government enforces civil rights. By any measure, it was a week in which the branches of government tested each other's limits — at one point prompting a federal appellate judge to warn publicly of constitutional breakdown.

The weekend began with an overnight emergency order from the Supreme Court halting the deportation of Venezuelan men already loaded onto planes bound for removal under the Alien Enemies Act. Justices Thomas and Alito dissented, but the majority acted again hours later for a second group headed to El Salvador. At the same time, the administration was telling a separate court that it had no obligation to correct the wrongful deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, even after admitting in filings that the removal had been a mistake. The juxtaposition — courts intervening in real time to stop removals, while the government resisted fixing an acknowledged error — set the tone for the week ahead.

That same weekend, the White House opened a new front, announcing funding freezes against Brown, Northwestern, Princeton, and Cornell as part of a campaign pressuring universities over curriculum, admissions, hiring, and diversity programs — the opening move in what would become one of the week's defining confrontations. Meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of people turned out in more than 400 cities in protests organized by groups including 50501 and Indivisible, timed to the 250th anniversary of Lexington and Concord and citing due-process violations and fears of executive overreach. After Senator Chris Van Hollen visited Abrego Garcia in El Salvador, the White House posted a digitally altered image purporting to show gang tattoos on his hand and doctored a New York Times headline to falsely label him an MS-13 member — a fabrication of evidence aimed at a person still subject to contested legal proceedings. Away from these clashes, the administration promoted coal expansion while cutting nearly 900 positions at the agency that screens miners for black lung disease and pausing enforcement of a new silica dust rule, a quieter but consequential retreat from worker protection.

By Monday, a new crisis was emerging at the Pentagon. Reporting revealed that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had shared detailed information about a Yemen strike — including flight schedules — in a private Signal chat with his wife, brother, and personal associates, a second such disclosure separate from an earlier chat involving National Security Adviser Mike Waltz. Trump publicly defended Hegseth, but the secretary's own former spokesman published an editorial describing "total chaos" inside the department. The story would not go away; it would deepen across the week. Monday also brought fresh evidence of enforcement reaching citizens and legal residents: a 19-year-old American, Jose Hermosillo, had been held for ten days by Border Patrol despite his family providing his birth certificate; an Irish green card holder was detained at San Francisco's airport over decades-old, expunged convictions; a Palestinian green card holder was detained during his own naturalization interview. In Congress, the House passed the SAVE Act, which would require in-person proof of citizenship to register to vote and ban counting of late-arriving mail ballots — a measure with uncertain prospects in the Senate but clear implications for ballot access. Detained activist Mahmoud Khalil was denied release to attend the birth of his son, participating only by phone, while the EEOC sent unsolicited surveys to Barnard College employees asking about Jewish or Israeli identity as part of an antisemitism inquiry. At the Interior Department, Secretary Doug Burgum delegated control over 70,000 employees and the full budget to an unconfirmed political appointee, sidestepping the Senate's constitutional role in appointments.

Tuesday sharpened the university confrontation. Harvard became the first institution to sue the administration, challenging the freeze of $2.2 billion in funding and threats to its tax-exempt status after refusing to submit to government audits of viewpoint diversity or dismantle its diversity programs. University President Alan Garber said Harvard would not surrender its independence. The same day, Judge Royce Lamberth ordered the restoration of Voice of America, ruling that the administration's attempt to dismantle the congressionally funded broadcaster was a direct affront to legislative authority. In comments that crystallized the week's central conflict, Trump stated that judges could not require trials before deportation, even as allied commentators publicly floated ignoring the Supreme Court altogether or deporting judges themselves. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a sweeping State Department reorganization eliminating bureaus for democracy promotion, human rights, and refugee assistance and cutting over 700 positions. A congressional delegation visited detained students Khalil and Rümeysa Öztürk, calling their detention political imprisonment, while reporting revealed DOGE was consolidating immigration, tax, Social Security, and voting records into a single government database.

Wednesday was the week's most concentrated exercise of unilateral power. President Trump signed nine executive orders in a single day, eliminating disparate-impact liability across federal civil rights statutes, overhauling college accreditation standards to target diversity programs, rescinding Obama-era guidance on racial disparities in school discipline, mandating foreign-funding disclosure by universities, and launching new initiatives on historically Black colleges and AI education. The disparate-impact change alone removed a legal tool used for decades to address systemic discrimination in employment, housing, and education — a shift whose practical consequences would surface within a day. That same Wednesday, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals denied the administration's request to halt orders requiring compliance in the Abrego Garcia case, and Judge Harvie Wilkinson — a Reagan appointee — warned that continued defiance risked the branches "grinding irrevocably against one another." Elsewhere, a federal jury found the New York Times not liable in Sarah Palin's defamation retrial, reaffirming the actual-malice standard that protects reporting on public figures. Hegseth, for his part, blamed ousted officials for leaking word of his Signal use and defended his reliance on encrypted messaging, even as reports surfaced of an unsecured internet line installed in his office to bypass Pentagon security protocols. On Ukraine, Rubio withdrew from scheduled peace talks in London, the U.S. recast its proposal as a "final offer," and Trump publicly pressured Ukrainian President Zelensky to accept Russian control of Crimea, blaming him for prolonging the war.

Thursday showed the disparate-impact order's consequences almost immediately: the Justice Department dropped a 2023 settlement that had protected a majority-Black Alabama community from raw sewage exposure, calling the agreement an unlawful diversity initiative. A separate executive order stripped job security from probationary federal employees, shifting the burden onto workers to justify their continued employment and enabling faster, less accountable dismissals — a structural change to the civil service beyond any single firing. Trump also directed the Justice Department to investigate ActBlue, the Democratic Party's primary fundraising platform, based on unsubstantiated claims of fraud, a move widely read as targeting the opposition's financial infrastructure ahead of the midterms. Yet the week's pattern of judicial pushback continued at scale: federal judges blocked eleven separate administration actions within days of each other, including the dismantling of Voice of America, Alien Enemies Act removals in Colorado and New York, anti-diversity education rules, funding impoundment against noncompliant cities, and the elimination of federal collective bargaining rights. The volume of rulings illustrated courts functioning less as isolated obstacles than as a sustained, cumulative check. Separately, the Interior Department invoked a disputed energy emergency to cut environmental review timelines for fossil fuel permits from years to 28 days, drawing immediate legal challenges, while a leaked HHS draft proposed eliminating disability services and research even as the NIH announced it would begin collecting private medical records to study autism.

Friday delivered the week's most dramatic single event: the FBI arrested Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Hannah Dugan at her own courthouse, accusing her of helping a defendant evade ICE agents during a courtroom proceeding. Attorney General Pam Bondi called judges "deranged" on television and warned of prosecuting officials who "harbor fugitives." It was the first known criminal arrest of a sitting local judge over a discretionary courtroom decision, landing as the culmination of a week that had already seen a sitting president reject due process as a precondition for deportation and a federal appellate judge warn of the branches grinding against one another. Two more rulings that day reinforced the pattern of judicial resistance: Judge William Orrick found the administration's threats to withhold funding from sanctuary cities unconstitutional, and Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly blocked the executive order requiring proof of citizenship for voter registration, ruling that the president lacked authority to bypass Congress on the matter. But Friday also brought the week's gravest human toll: ICE deported three U.S. citizen children, including one with Stage 4 cancer sent without medical consultation, and separately deported a two-year-old citizen to Honduras — a removal a federal judge called "illegal and unconstitutional" while scheduling an emergency hearing. These were not documented immigrants caught in enforcement error; they were American children, removed alongside detained mothers. Elsewhere, former congressman George Santos was sentenced to 87 months in prison for fraud and identity theft, a reminder that ordinary accountability mechanisms continued to function even amid broader strain. The administration also reversed its earlier revocation of thousands of foreign student visas after 104 lawsuits and more than 50 injunctions across 23 states forced its hand, and China canceled over 12,000 metric tons of American pork purchases in retaliation for tariffs, with effective duties reaching 172 percent and rural exporters absorbing the cost.

Taken as a whole, the week showed two things happening at once. Courts, at every level from district judges to the Supreme Court to a Reagan-appointed appellate judge, repeatedly intervened against executive actions on deportation, funding, worker protections, and broadcasting — and largely prevailed in the sense that their orders were issued and, for now, stood. Universities, led by Harvard, demonstrated that institutional resistance to federal pressure remained possible. Yet the administration met that resistance not with retreat but with acceleration: a single day of nine executive orders narrowing civil rights enforcement, a president publicly rejecting the premise of due process, and, by week's end, the arrest of a judge for a discretionary act on the bench. The deportation of citizen children — one gravely ill, one a toddler — stood apart even within a week already marked by wrongful detentions, a signal that the machinery of enforcement was reaching people the law was never meant to touch. Whether the courts' persistence or the executive's escalation would define the weeks ahead was, by Friday, still an open question, but the shape of the confrontation was no longer in doubt. ```

Title: The First 100 Days End With a Judge in Handcuffs and a Country in Contested Terrain
Content:
```markdown The week that closed out the first hundred days of Donald Trump's second term did not offer the traditional rituals of a presidential milestone. Instead it delivered a sitting judge in handcuffs, a permanent court order against a wartime deportation law, a Supreme Court justice's public rebuke of her own government, and a Cabinet meeting held against the backdrop of a shrinking economy. Across seven days, courts, universities, and news organizations each became sites of new pressure from the executive branch, while the judiciary pushed back with a force that was neither uniform nor guaranteed to last.

The weekend set the tone. FBI agents arrested Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Hannah Dugan on obstruction charges, accusing her of helping a man evade immigration agents inside her own courthouse. The FBI director publicized the arrest with a handcuffed photograph, an unusual move for a sitting judicial officer, and the image circulated widely within hours. That same weekend, Trump took to Truth Social to argue that due process was impractical for the "millions and millions" of people he said the government intended to deport, insisting that officials already knew who among them was a criminal. An arrest inside a courtroom and a public argument against courtroom process itself arrived together — and would recur throughout the week.

Universities absorbed a parallel wave of pressure. The administration continued threatening federal funding for schools, including Swarthmore, over claims they had failed to address antisemitic harassment, while Columbia, Harvard, and other institutions moved to discipline students involved in pro-Palestinian protests. Critics said the discipline fell disproportionately on Palestinian, Arab, Muslim, and other minority students. This became one of two distinct storylines involving federal leverage over civil society: one running through campuses and protest discipline, the other, emerging days later, through the Justice Department's own civil rights enforcement staff.

Press freedom eroded on several fronts at once. The Associated Press was barred from the Oval Office and the presidential pool. The Department of Justice, under Attorney General Pam Bondi, rescinded a policy that had shielded journalists from being compelled to reveal confidential sources. Trump separately singled out a New York Times reporter by name, calling her "biased and untalented," while legal pressure built against ABC, CBS, and the Des Moines Register. Funding threats against NPR and PBS were already in motion — a thread that would culminate later in the week with an executive order.

Congress, meanwhile, advanced a budget framework enabling large tax cuts alongside proposed reductions to Medicaid and SNAP, plus $68.8 billion in new border security spending. Republican divisions over savings targets surfaced almost immediately. And in one of the week's most disturbing enforcement stories, ICE deportations swept up U.S. citizen children along with their immigrant mothers — including a four-year-old with cancer sent abroad without her medication — with little chance for legal intervention beforehand.

By Monday, the administration had moved from rhetoric to formal executive action. Trump signed a cluster of orders requiring English proficiency for commercial drivers, directing agencies to identify and defund "sanctuary jurisdictions," and expanding legal protections for police officers, including a review of consent decrees that had constrained local law enforcement. The same day, reporting revealed a new private club in Georgetown, backed by Donald Trump Jr. and megadonor Omeed Malik, charging more than half a million dollars for membership and direct access to administration officials — already reportedly carrying a waiting list. Separately, the administration quietly ended federal investigations and lawsuits against 89 corporations, a number of which had donated heavily to Trump's inaugural fund.

Not every institutional signal Monday favored the executive branch. A federal appeals court restored an injunction blocking the administration's attempt to fire 90 percent of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's staff, and another judge ordered the restoration of congressionally appropriated funds to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty — a reminder that the executive cannot unilaterally withhold money Congress has already approved. But the day's other major development cut the opposite way: Trump's DOJ appointees removed senior civil servants overseeing the department's voting rights section and directed attorneys to drop active cases, the start of a hollowing-out that would leave the Civil Rights Division a fraction of its former size within days. That evening, Hakeem Jeffries and Cory Booker led a twelve-hour sit-in on the Capitol steps opposing the proposed cuts to Medicaid and SNAP, while Bishop William J. Barber II was arrested during a related demonstration.

Tuesday's developments were quieter in volume but no less consequential. Human Rights Watch described the detention of Venezuelan migrant Neiyerver Rengel and at least 252 others as "enforced disappearances," after families lost track of relatives deported to El Salvador on gang-affiliation accusations. House Republicans added a procedural rule blocking a vote on investigating Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's use of Signal for sensitive communications, narrowing Congress's ability to examine a potential security lapse. The Peace Corps began a second round of deferred resignations tied to a DOGE review, and Hegseth formally ended the Pentagon's Women, Peace and Security program, which had originated in Trump's first term. Nearly 400 scientific contributors to the National Climate Assessment were dismissed the same day a federal appeals court upheld an injunction blocking DOGE from accessing sensitive Social Security data — one action reducing scientific capacity, the other preserving a check on executive reach into personal records. By day's end, the Federal Election Commission lost its quorum after a second commissioner resigned, leaving the country's campaign finance watchdog unable to act.

Wednesday arrived as the symbolic marker of the administration's first hundred days, and the day split cleanly between image and consequence. Trump held a Cabinet meeting celebrating the milestone, during which Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. repeated debunked claims about child trafficking under the previous administration, while Trump responded to a newly reported GDP contraction by blaming his predecessor. Away from the cameras, the legal ground was shifting. U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. — a Trump appointee — ruled that the administration's invocation of the 1798 Alien Enemies Act "exceeds the scope" of the statute and permanently enjoined its use against a certified class of Venezuelan migrants in the Southern District of Texas. The same day, the Supreme Court issued an emergency order blocking the deportation of Javier Salazar, a 19-year-old Venezuelan migrant with no criminal record, preserving his chance to contest removal. A separate federal judge ordered the release of Palestinian Columbia student Mohsen Mahdawi from ICE detention, ruling that his continued confinement would likely chill protected speech and comparing the administration's approach to McCarthyism. At a Michigan rally that evening, Trump attacked "communist radical-left judges" and called on the Supreme Court to intervene on his behalf — rhetoric that extended directly from the weekend's arrest of Judge Dugan. Beneath all of it, the economic numbers were real: the Bureau of Economic Analysis reported the first GDP contraction in three years, and weekly unemployment claims rose to their highest level since February, both linked in part to tariff disruption.

Thursday deepened both the press-freedom and economic threads. Trump signed an executive order directing the Corporation for Public Broadcasting to end funding for NPR and PBS, accusing the outlets of biased coverage; PBS President Paula Kerger called the move "blatantly unlawful," and both organizations signaled they would challenge it in court. The order followed directly from the weekend's press restrictions and the DOJ's rollback of source protections, forming a single continuous story about the administration's effort to reshape the country's information environment rather than a series of disconnected incidents. The same day, Trump signed an order creating a Religious Liberty Commission, naming Dr. Phil McGraw among its members. On the economic front, UPS confirmed plans to lay off 20,000 employees and close 73 facilities, while port executives in Los Angeles and Oakland projected shipping volumes could fall more than 35 percent because of tariffs — concrete, verifiable consequences following directly from the contraction reported a day earlier. Congress declined to check the president's tariff authority: House Republicans used a procedural rule to block a Democratic effort to challenge the national emergency tariff declaration, and Senate Republicans voted down a related measure. Reporting also confirmed that the Civil Rights Division had lost 70 percent of its attorneys since January — more than 250 departures or reassignments — a stark measure of the institutional hollowing that had begun on Monday. And in a moment that captured the week's central tension, Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson publicly condemned the administration's rhetoric toward judges as deliberate intimidation undermining the rule of law, a direct rebuke that traced back to the president's Michigan rally remarks and, further still, to the arrest of Judge Dugan five days earlier. Oklahoma's new social studies standards, meanwhile, drew criticism for requiring students to analyze supposed 2020 election discrepancies and for sharply increasing religious content in public school curriculum.

The week closed with two of its major throughlines reaching a form of resolution, both contested. Judge Rodriguez certified a class of Venezuelan detainees and issued his permanent injunction against use of the Alien Enemies Act, cementing the judicial limit first announced Wednesday. And Trump announced on Truth Social that his administration would revoke Harvard University's tax-exempt status, escalating a monthslong standoff over funding and diversity policy — a threat that remained unresolved and contested rather than a settled outcome. Swarthmore issued interim suspensions without full due process to nine students involved in a protest encampment, extending the week's pattern of campus discipline. The Justice Department paused Foreign Corrupt Practices Act prosecutions for six months and abruptly closed its cryptocurrency crime unit following criticism from industry donors, echoing Monday's decision to drop investigations into 89 corporate donors. In Oklahoma City, ICE agents posing as U.S. Marshals raided the wrong home, taking a citizen family's belongings despite the family not being the intended target. Former pardon attorney Liz Oyer said Trump's recent pardons of white-collar offenders had erased more than $1 billion in restitution and penalties owed by wealthy Americans. And in a smaller but telling coda, Maine's federal child-nutrition funds were restored after the state sued over a funding freeze tied to its refusal to bar transgender athletes from girls' sports — a reminder that even contested federal leverage over states still had to answer, eventually, to legal process.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government testing the outer edges of executive power on several fronts simultaneously — over courts, campuses, the press, immigration enforcement, and the machinery of civil rights enforcement itself — while the judiciary, unevenly but repeatedly, pushed back. A judge was arrested and handcuffed; another judge, appointed by the same president, ruled his invocation of an 18th-century wartime statute unlawful. A justice of the Supreme Court warned publicly that attacks on the judiciary amounted to intimidation, even as the president continued making them. Public broadcasters faced defunding while a private club sold access to Cabinet officials for half a million dollars a seat, and pardons erased more than a billion dollars in penalties owed by the well-connected even as ordinary families lost their possessions to a mistaken immigration raid. None of these threads resolved neatly by Friday. Litigation over Harvard's tax status, the fate of NPR and PBS funding, and the broader reach of the Alien Enemies Act ruling all remained open. What the week made clear was less a verdict than a pattern: the steady, simultaneous testing of institutional limits across courts, universities, the press, and federal agencies, met by a judiciary that in several instances held the line — and in several others did not yet have the chance to. ```
Excerpt: This week bridged the end of Trump's first 100 days with an accelerating pattern of executive pressure across courts, universities, immigration enforcement, and the press.

Title: This Week in Democracy: Media Silenced, a Mayor Arrested, and Due Process in Doubt
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which words about the law started turning into acts against it. By its end, a sitting mayor had been arrested by federal agents, a senior White House adviser had floated suspending one of the oldest protections in Anglo-American law, and courts across the country were straining to keep pace with an executive branch testing how far it could go. The week's throughline was simple to state and unsettling to watch: a president publicly wondered aloud whether due process applied to everyone, and by Thursday that wondering had produced an arrest.

**The Weekend**

The weekend set the tone. On Saturday, Judge Beryl Howell permanently struck down Trump's executive order targeting the law firm Perkins Coie, ruling that it violated the First, Fifth, and Sixth Amendments and calling it unprecedented retaliation against attorneys for the clients they had represented. Roughly 1,500 lawyers rallied outside a Manhattan courthouse the same weekend in support of the ruling — on its face, a clear win for judicial constraint on executive power.

But the weekend also brought a wave of personnel moves inside the security apparatus: the firing of NSA and Cyber Command chief Tim Haugh, plans to cut 1,200 CIA jobs, and the elimination of diversity programs across intelligence agencies, all consistent with a pattern of stocking sensitive institutions with loyalty rather than continuity. And in a *Meet the Press* interview, Trump said he wasn't sure that everyone in the United States was entitled to due process, framing the constitutional guarantee as an obstacle to the deportations he said he was elected to carry out. The administration also announced a June 14 military parade timed to the president's 79th birthday and the Army's 250th anniversary, at a cost of tens of millions of dollars, and Trump said he would not rule out using military force to gain control of Greenland.

**Monday**

By Monday, the Supreme Court had entered the picture in a way that cut against the weekend's judicial momentum. The Court granted a stay allowing Trump's ban on transgender military service to take effect while litigation continued, overriding lower court blocks and drawing dissent from three liberal justices. It was a reminder that the judiciary was not a uniform check — the same week that produced Perkins Coie also produced a green light for a contested policy to take hold before its legality was settled.

Monday brought lighter theater too: an order to reopen Alcatraz as a federal prison for "ruthless offenders," widely read as symbolic messaging rather than serious policy. More consequential were mounting reports of foreign business deals tied to the Trump family — a Trump-linked crypto firm's role in a $2 billion Abu Dhabi-backed Binance transaction, a new Trump hotel project in Dubai with Saudi-linked partners, and a $5.5 billion golf club deal with Qatar's government-owned Qatari Diar — each renewing questions about an ethics agreement meant to bar exactly this kind of foreign entanglement.

National security leadership shifted again as Mike Waltz was removed as national security adviser following the Signal chat controversy over Yemen war plans, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio installed as his acting replacement, doubling up critical roles under one trusted official. Civic dissent broadened as well: California State University students began a hunger strike over Gaza aid, Bernie Sanders launched his "Fighting Oligarchy" tour, Tesla protests continued abroad, and Bishop William Barber's Moral Mondays campaign targeted proposed cuts to Medicaid and SNAP alongside rising military spending. A federal court also ordered North Carolina to certify Democrat Allison Riggs as the winner of a contested state supreme court race, rejecting a Republican effort to discard more than 60,000 ballots after months of dispute.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday shifted focus to institutions being hollowed from within. The EPA eliminated its office of science and technology, cut $300 million from its budget, and forced 1,500 research staff to reapply for roughly 400 remaining positions — a restructuring critics said would strip the agency of independent scientific capacity just as it was needed most. Harvard, meanwhile, lost access to new federal research grants after rejecting a list of demands from an administration antisemitism task force, compounding an earlier freeze of $2.2 billion; the university responded with a lawsuit.

At the FCC, a "news distortion" investigation opened into CBS over a *60 Minutes* interview with Kamala Harris — echoing Trump's own lawsuit against the network — while Paramount's chair reportedly intervened in CBS coverage and softened diversity policies to help clear the way for merger approval. It was a clear instance of regulatory leverage appearing to bend editorial judgment at a major news organization. Campus protest also continued: more than two dozen demonstrators were arrested at the University of Washington after occupying an engineering building to demand the school cut ties with Boeing over military contracts with Israel.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday's defining story had been building for weeks. Voice of America remained off the air, with 1,300 employees still on leave months after an executive order dismantled its parent agency. The D.C. Circuit, sitting en banc, restored some district court protections for other USAGM grantees, including Radio Free Asia, but staffing relief for VOA itself stayed limited — a case study in how executive action can outlast even partial judicial intervention.

The same day, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem appeared before Congress and refused to answer whether the Constitution guarantees due process to everyone, echoing the president's earlier equivocation, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent dodged questions about who actually bears the cost of tariffs. Elsewhere, the legal system pushed back: a federal appeals court upheld an order requiring Tufts student Rümeysa Öztürk, detained for weeks after co-authoring an op-ed critical of Israel, to be transferred to Vermont for hearings on her detention's legality. And at a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing, Senator Susan Collins pressed the administration on funding cuts, grant cancellations, and layoffs in health agencies that appeared to conflict with enacted appropriations law.

**Thursday**

Thursday delivered the week's most visible confrontation. Newark Mayor Ras Baraka was arrested by federal agents outside Delaney Hall during a protest and oversight visit joined by members of Congress, who accused ICE of staging the encounter. He was released after several hours, but allies described the arrest as an act of intimidation against a sitting local official — a marked escalation from earlier threats made against Wisconsin's governor.

The same day brought a cluster of safety-oversight rollbacks: the administration halted an outside review of air traffic control practices after a deadly crash, kept a hiring freeze in place despite controller shortages, removed the NTSB's vice chair, began dismantling the Consumer Product Safety Commission, and had the FAA approve a fivefold increase in SpaceX launches over environmental objections.

Then came the sharpest rhetorical turn of the week: senior adviser Stephen Miller said the administration was considering suspending the writ of habeas corpus — a measure the Constitution reserves for invasion or insurrection — suggesting it would hinge on how courts ruled against the administration going forward. Against that backdrop, courts kept intervening on behalf of detainees: a judge ordered Öztürk's release from ICE custody citing First Amendment and due process violations, and Irish green card holder Cliona Ward was freed after 17 days in detention following a court's reversal of decades-old convictions used against her. Meanwhile, NYPD arrested about 75 pro-Palestinian protesters after they occupied Columbia University's main library, at the request of the university's own president. And in North Carolina, Republican candidate Jefferson Griffin conceded his state supreme court race to Allison Riggs, closing out a six-month legal battle in favor of the judicially certified result.

**Friday**

Friday closed the week with a scattering of smaller but telling moves. The American Bar Association filed suit over the termination of federal grants, part of an escalating conflict that has also touched the ABA's law school accreditation authority. A resurfaced letter from Pope Francis, rejecting Vice President Vance's theological defense of prioritizing national interests over migrants, drew renewed attention after Cardinal Robert Prevost publicly backed the Pope's position and former border czar Tom Homan told the pontiff to keep to church matters.

Trump signed a cluster of executive orders — establishing a veterans homelessness center, limiting criminal enforcement of regulatory offenses, and speeding up Federal Register publication — while the GSA rescinded workplace nondiscrimination guidance tied to gender identity, and the White House blocked a chief-of-staff pick favored by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Finally, Judge Susan Illston granted a temporary restraining order pausing reductions in force tied to an executive order restructuring the federal workforce; the administration appealed immediately to the Ninth Circuit.

**Looking Back**

Taken as a whole, the week showed two institutions moving in opposite directions at once. Courts struck down retaliatory orders, restored some protections to detained students, forced the certification of a contested election, and briefly paused workforce cuts — the ordinary machinery of judicial review still functioning under pressure. But the same week saw the Supreme Court clear the way for a disputed military policy, a mayor detained by federal agents at a protest, a public broadcaster left dark months after being dismantled, and a senior official openly discussing the suspension of habeas corpus. Individually, each of these might be read as a policy dispute or a legal skirmish. Together, they described a government increasingly willing to test whether constitutional guarantees are conditions to be negotiated rather than limits to be obeyed — and a judiciary, a press corps, and a public still finding, unevenly, the means to answer that test. ```
Excerpt: This week combined sustained institutional pressure with a few sharp, visible confrontations.

Title: The Qatar Jet, a Mayor's Arrest, and a Week of Executive Testing
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which the machinery of American government strained visibly against its own limits, and in which the courts, more than any other institution, kept pulling that machinery back toward its constitutional moorings. Over seven days, a president moved to accept a $400 million jet from a foreign monarchy, a sitting mayor was arrested at a protest, a deputy chief of staff floated suspending one of the oldest legal protections against arbitrary detention, and the Supreme Court twice intervened to stop the executive branch from moving faster than the law allowed. By week's end, the president himself was publicly uncertain whether due process was a right at all.

The weekend set the tone. Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, suggested the administration was weighing whether to suspend habeas corpus — the centuries-old legal mechanism that prevents the government from holding people without charge or judicial review. Republican senators, asked about the remark, declined to say it was off the table. The same weekend brought confirmation that the administration intended to accept a Boeing 747-8 valued at roughly $400 million from Qatar's royal family, intended for use as Air Force One, with White House counsel and the Department of Justice concluding it broke no bribery or emoluments law. In Newark, ICE agents arrested Mayor Ras Baraka while he stood outside a private detention facility alongside members of Congress; the Department of Homeland Security suggested the lawmakers present might face arrest as well. Elsewhere, the Pentagon ordered military academies to disregard race and sex in admissions and directed the removal of DEI and gender-related books from base libraries, extending political directives into military education. Federal courts, meanwhile, were already pushing back on immigration enforcement — blocking a deportation to Libya, ordering the release of Turkish student Rümeysa Öztürk, and halting removals of Venezuelan detainees to conditions resembling El Salvador's mega-prison. A coalition of Democratic state attorneys general sued over the dismantling of the Department of Health and Human Services, after roughly 10,000 employees were fired and entire agencies shuttered.

By Monday, the Qatar jet had become the week's most persistent thread. Reports detailed the administration's legal rationale even as scrutiny of the emoluments clause intensified. Trump signed an executive order aiming to tie U.S. drug prices to the lowest prices paid abroad, a move critics — including Senator Bernie Sanders — predicted would collapse in court for lack of legislative authority. SpaceX secured a $6 billion Pentagon contract and remained a frontrunner for the proposed "Golden Dome" missile shield, prompting more than 40 members of Congress to demand review of Elon Musk's influence after a nominated Inspector General was fired. The United States and China reached a Geneva agreement sharply reducing tariffs — from 145 percent to 30 percent — continuing a pattern of abrupt reversals in trade policy. The head of the U.S. Copyright Office was dismissed shortly after publishing a report skeptical of rushing government intervention on AI and copyright, a firing that read, to many observers, as retaliation for an inconvenient finding. Beneath these headline events, courts processed a steady stream of filings across immigration, agency-cuts, and tariff litigation — evidence that judicial review was operating continuously, even when it wasn't making headlines.

Tuesday sharpened the Qatar story into a direct confrontation between the legislative and executive branches. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer announced he would block all Justice Department nominations until the White House answered questions about the jet's constitutionality, demanding that Attorney General Pam Bondi testify. Republicans, for their part, still would not disavow Miller's habeas corpus comments, even as Trump's own remarks about upholding the Constitution remained notably vague. In Pennsylvania, a federal judge allowed conditional use of the Alien Enemies Act to speed deportation of accused Venezuelan gang members — but only with three weeks' notice and an opportunity to contest removal, a ruling that set up further Supreme Court review. The Qatar entanglements multiplied further: the Trump Organization struck a $5.5 billion golf resort deal in the country, and the U.S. approved a $2 billion arms sale to the same government whose jet gift was under scrutiny. Trump also signed an executive order aimed at dismantling the Department of Education, an action critics said bypassed Congress's authority over federal agencies entirely.

Wednesday was the week's densest day, its developments pulling in several directions at once. Attorney General Bondi — who had previously worked as a registered representative for the Qatari government — concluded that transferring the jet to the Defense Department and eventually to Trump's presidential library was legally permissible, a ruling whose independence was immediately questioned given her prior client. Hours later, the U.S. and Qatar signed a $243 billion defense and aviation agreement, including Qatar's purchase of up to 210 Boeing aircraft and more than $38 billion in future defense investment — a deal signed the same week as the disputed jet, deepening the sense that personal and state interests were becoming difficult to separate. On the immigration front, federal judges ordered the release of three detained activists — Badar Khan Suri, Rümeysa Öztürk, and Mohsen Mahdawi — rejecting the government's argument that their pro-Palestinian speech justified detention on foreign policy grounds. The Justice Department, meanwhile, announced plans to investigate former prosecutors who had brought cases against Trump, including Jack Smith, Alvin Bragg, and Fani Willis — a move distinct from the mayor's arrest days earlier, but part of the same broader pattern of law enforcement being turned toward political opponents. The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on Trump's executive order seeking to deny birthright citizenship to children born in the U.S. to noncitizen parents; even justices generally sympathetic to the administration asked skeptical questions — a separate legal matter from the Alien Enemies Act cases running in parallel. In the House, Republicans advanced budget proposals cutting Medicaid, SNAP, and child tax credit eligibility for mixed-status families, and Capitol Police arrested 25 disability rights protesters during the debate. A provision advanced alongside it would let the Treasury Secretary strip nonprofits of tax-exempt status on loosely defined "terrorist supporting" grounds. Away from Washington, the owner of the Los Angeles Times intervened to block a Kamala Harris endorsement and spike a mildly critical op-ed on Trump's cabinet picks, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was found to have quietly rerouted his own wife's flight away from Newark Airport even as he publicly insisted the airport, beset by radar outages and controller shortages, was safe.

Thursday brought the week's clearest resolution to an escalating legal question. The Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that the administration must halt deportations of alleged gang members under the Alien Enemies Act without adequate due process, rejecting a 12-hour notice period the government had proposed as insufficient under the Fifth Amendment — the culmination of a thread that had run from Tuesday's conditional lower-court ruling to this definitive check. The House Budget Committee, meanwhile, voted down the broader reconciliation bill 16–21, as Freedom Caucus members demanded deeper cuts, exposing Republican divisions that stalled Trump's tax and spending agenda. Moody's downgraded the United States' credit rating for the first time since 1917, citing federal deficits projected to reach nearly 9 percent of GDP by 2035 — a distinct economic signal, separate from the week's tariff and trade news, about confidence in federal fiscal management. The administration terminated nearly 600 Voice of America contractors, most of them journalists, in defiance of a standing court order to maintain operations; many now face deportation because their visas were tied to their jobs. Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard fired the acting chair and deputy chair of the National Intelligence Council after their analysis contradicted Trump's claims about Venezuela's ties to a Salvadoran gang. Amid this, Newark's airport crisis worsened, operating with just three of fourteen required air traffic controllers, a shortfall linked to earlier federal cuts. Ben & Jerry's co-founder Ben Cohen was arrested protesting during a Senate hearing, and in Omaha, voters elected Democrat John Ewing as the city's first Black mayor, unseating a Republican incumbent in what was widely read as a rebuke of Trump-aligned politics — a reminder that ordinary electoral processes continued even amid the turbulence.

The week closed on a note of stark contrast. On Friday, Trump publicly questioned whether people in the United States have a right to due process at all, despite its explicit guarantee under the Fifth Amendment — remarks that landed just a day after the Supreme Court had enforced exactly that right. The Court formalized its injunction in A.A.R.P. v. Trump, blocking Alien Enemies Act deportations pending further proceedings, with Justices Alito and Thomas dissenting, and remanded the case to the Fifth Circuit — bringing the week's central legal arc to a firm, if temporary, resolution. A federal judge in South Dakota separately blocked the deportation of Priya Saxena, an Indian doctoral graduate whose student visa had been revoked over a minor traffic violation, extending the week's pattern of judicial pushback against aggressive visa actions. Inside the Democratic Party, a subcommittee recommended invalidating the vice-chair election of David Hogg and Malcolm Kenyatta over procedural irregularities — a minor but telling sign of internal strain. And in two unrelated but resonant notes, Harvard Law School confirmed that a document long believed to be a copy was in fact an original 1300 Magna Carta, one of only seven surviving originals, while Bruce Springsteen, performing in Manchester, criticized the abandonment of allies and deportations carried out without due process.

Taken together, the week offered a case study in how constitutional systems are tested — not through a single dramatic rupture, but through accumulation: a foreign gift accepted and then legally blessed by an official with ties to the giver; a mayor arrested for standing outside a detention facility; a due process guarantee affirmed by the Supreme Court and then publicly questioned by the president himself days later; prosecutors threatened with investigation for prior cases; journalists and intelligence analysts dismissed for producing unwelcome findings. Against all of this, courts functioned as the most consistent counterweight, intervening repeatedly and, in the case of the Alien Enemies Act, decisively. Whether that check holds, or whether rhetoric about suspending habeas corpus and doubting due process hardens into policy, will depend on what comes next — but this week made clear how many fronts were open at once, and how much weight the judiciary was being asked to bear. ```

Title: This Week in Democracy: A Megabill, a Missing Plaque, and a Jet From Qatar
Content:
```markdown This week in American governance was defined by a single number — 215 to 214 — and by the accumulating weight of decisions made above, below, and around that vote. The House narrowly passed a sweeping tax-and-spending package touching nearly every corner of federal policy, even as the courts and the executive branch pulled in opposite directions on due process, institutional independence, and retaliation. By week's end, the country had a clearer picture of how much power can move in five business days: through legislation, through judicial rulings, through emergency Supreme Court orders, and through the quieter mechanics of agency directives and prosecutorial discretion.

**The Weekend**

The week began with a jolt: ABC News reported, and Trump confirmed, that the administration intended to accept a Boeing 747-8 valued at roughly $400 million from the Qatari royal family, to be refitted for use as Air Force One. Officials described it as a routine Defense Department transaction, but the arrangement immediately drew scrutiny under the Constitution's emoluments clause. It would not be the last time all week that the line between presidential duty and personal or foreign benefit came into question.

Alongside the jet story came a quieter but consequential shift inside the FBI. Director Kash Patel confirmed that agents had been told to deprioritize white-collar crime investigations in favor of immigration enforcement, and the bureau disbanded a squad dedicated to investigating corruption among members of Congress. Combined with reported cuts to IRS enforcement, the moves suggested a systematic retreat from financial accountability for the politically connected, even as the administration intensified enforcement elsewhere.

That "elsewhere" was the immigration system, where courts spent the weekend pushing back against Alien Enemies Act deportations. An appeals court dismissed a bid to overturn a restraining order, and the Supreme Court itself ruled that 24 hours' notice was insufficient to satisfy due process before removal. In Wisconsin, federal prosecutors indicted Judge Hannah Dugan on charges of helping an immigrant evade arrest; she pleaded not guilty and called the case unconstitutional, setting up a fight over whether judges can be criminally targeted for actions taken from the bench. Meanwhile, North Carolina's legislature advanced a cluster of bills touching immigration, protest rights, library book bans, and voter registration — a reminder that state legislatures were pursuing their own restrictive agendas in parallel with events in Washington.

**Monday**

The Supreme Court issued its first major emergency order of the week, granting a stay that allowed the administration to proceed with ending Temporary Protected Status for roughly 350,000 Venezuelans, over Justice Jackson's dissent. The ruling stripped legal protection from a large population while their underlying appeal continued in a lower court — a pattern of emergency-docket decisions that would recur throughout the week. That same day, Trump traveled to Capitol Hill to personally lobby House Republicans on the reconciliation bill, working through concerns over the SALT deduction and waving off deficit hawks. His direct involvement signaled how central the bill had become to the administration's agenda, and how much presidential pressure was being applied to secure votes.

Monday also brought warning signs about the bill's cost. Moody's downgraded the United States' credit rating for the first time since 1917, citing the deficit impact of the pending legislation, while the Congressional Budget Office and independent analysts projected that millions could lose health coverage and that income losses would fall hardest on lower earners. These were not abstract concerns; they described the practical consequences of a bill still working its way through the House. Separately, the administration continued its effort to gut the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, attempting to fire most of its staff despite a court order blocking the move, and moving to rescind dozens of consumer protections, including medical-debt safeguards. In the media world, CBS News president Wendy McMahon resigned amid disagreements tied to a lawsuit Trump had filed over a Kamala Harris interview — one more sign of pressure reaching into newsroom leadership. And in a Senate hearing whose theme would recur later in the week, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem incorrectly described habeas corpus as a presidential power to remove people from the country, prompting a correction from Senator Maggie Hassan that habeas corpus is, in fact, a protection against unlawful detention.

Monday's most pointed confrontation, however, involved a dispute over congressional oversight. After a group of House Democrats visited an ICE detention facility and DHS threatened them with arrest, the Justice Department dropped trespassing charges against Newark Mayor Ras Baraka while continuing to prosecute Representative LaMonica McIver on charges of assaulting law enforcement during the same incident. McIver called the charges politically motivated, and the disparity between the two outcomes — one dropped, one pursued — became a storyline that would run through the rest of the week. The Senate also confirmed Charles Kushner, previously pardoned by Trump for tax evasion and father of Jared Kushner, as ambassador to France, in a 51-45 vote that drew criticism over nepotism.

**Tuesday**

The Qatari jet story continued, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent comparing the gift to historical precedents like the Statue of Liberty, even as CNN reported that the administration had actively negotiated for the aircraft rather than simply receiving an unsolicited gift — a detail that complicated the "transparent transaction" framing officials had used days earlier. Trump also announced a costly new "Golden Dome" missile defense initiative, projected to cost up to $540 billion over two decades, with a Space Force general appointed to lead it and initial funding already allocated by congressional Republicans. Verizon announced it would end its diversity, equity, and inclusion programs the same day the FCC approved its $20 billion acquisition of Frontier, a pairing that suggested regulatory approval was being used as leverage over corporate policy. Trump also said he would investigate whether Joe Biden was aware of executive orders signed via autopen, extending a broader effort to question the legitimacy of his predecessor's official acts. Noem again misdefined habeas corpus before senators, while lawmakers separately raised concerns about delayed FEMA assistance for storm victims in Mississippi and Missouri.

By day's end, the Justice Department had formally confirmed it was dropping all charges against Mayor Baraka, sharpening the contrast with the ongoing case against Representative McIver — and a federal judge ordered the administration to maintain custody and control of migrants being removed toward South Sudan, citing possible violations of an earlier injunction. That order would prove prophetic within twenty-four hours.

**Wednesday**

This was the week's most consequential day for institutional confrontation. DHS Secretary Noem sent Harvard University a letter immediately revoking its ability to enroll international students, requiring current students to transfer or leave the country over what the department described as noncompliance with reporting requirements. The move, following earlier cuts of $450 million in federal grants to the university, marked a sharp escalation in the administration's campaign against Harvard — one that legal challenges were expected to meet quickly.

That same day, Judge Brian Murphy found that the administration had in fact violated his earlier order by deporting at least six men to South Sudan without a meaningful opportunity to raise fear-based claims, and he ordered remedial interviews with counsel and interpreters. It was among the clearest judicial findings of the week that the executive branch had defied a direct court order. The Justice Department also opened new civil rights investigations into Harvard and the Harvard Law Review over alleged discrimination against white applicants — a separate track from the funding and visa disputes — while also opening a civil rights probe into the city of Chicago. Elsewhere, the department moved to cancel police reform consent decrees in Minneapolis and Louisville, established after the deaths of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor.

ICE agents conducted arrests at immigration courts in multiple cities, and Mahmoud Khalil remained detained in Louisiana, denied a contact visit with his newborn son. In Congress, Representative Nancy Mace filed a resolution to expel Representative McIver following her indictment, intensifying the standoff over the ICE facility incident, and Democratic Representative Gerry Connolly died at 75, the third House Democrat to die in office in three months, further narrowing an already tight chamber.

**Thursday**

Thursday delivered the week's defining legislative moment. The House passed the "One Big Beautiful Bill" by a vote of 215 to 214, extending the 2017 tax cuts, cutting Medicaid and food assistance, funding a historic expansion of immigration detention and deportation capacity, and including provisions limiting federal courts' contempt powers. The bill now moves to the Senate, but its passage alone marked one of the most consequential single legislative actions of the year, reshaping tax policy, the social safety net, and immigration enforcement in one package.

The same day, the Supreme Court handed down another major emergency ruling, allowing Trump to remove board members from the National Labor Relations Board and the Merit Systems Protection Board in a 6-3 decision that advanced "unitary executive" theory over the objections of three dissenting justices — weakening statutory protections designed to insulate independent agencies from direct presidential control. Yet the same day also saw courts push back hard against the administration elsewhere: Judge William Illston issued a preliminary injunction halting planned mass layoffs and reorganizations across 22 federal agencies, finding that neither the president nor the agencies had shown authority to act without Congress, and Judge Allison Burroughs issued a temporary restraining order blocking DHS's revocation of Harvard's ability to host foreign students — protecting more than 7,000 visa holders from Noem's order two days earlier. A separate nationwide injunction blocked the arrest, detention, or deportation of over 4,700 international students whose visas had been abruptly revoked without notice. A 4-4 Supreme Court deadlock, with Justice Barrett recused, left in place a lower court ruling blocking taxpayer funding for a Catholic charter school in Oklahoma.

Trump, meanwhile, reportedly considered re-privatizing Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac amid rising mortgage rates and hosted a dinner for top investors in his personal cryptocurrency, including a billionaire under SEC investigation — one more instance of blurred lines between the presidency and private financial interests. Several major corporations, including AT&T, Comcast, T-Mobile, Uber, and United Airlines, publicly endorsed the reconciliation bill despite their own hunger-relief partnerships, a juxtaposition that drew notice given the bill's food-assistance cuts.

**Friday**

Friday brought a final wave of executive and judicial action. Trump signed a series of orders aimed at accelerating nuclear energy development, expediting reactor approvals, restructuring the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, and cutting its workforce, with a goal of three operational experimental reactors by mid-2026 — concentrating regulatory authority over a safety-critical industry in the executive branch with limited public deliberation.

In a significant check on executive retaliation, Judge John Bates ruled that Trump's executive order targeting the law firm Jenner & Block was unconstitutional, calling it "null and void" for violating the First Amendment and permanently enjoining its enforcement. A federal court also blocked the deportation of eight men to South Sudan, ruling they must be given at least fifteen days to legally challenge removal and allowing torture-related claims — reinforcing, once again, the due process standards the administration had already been found to have violated earlier in the week.

Internal documents obtained by The Guardian revealed disarray at the Department of Veterans Affairs, including unit closures and exam backlogs following layoffs of 2,500 workers and the cancellation of hundreds of contracts. The Pentagon issued new press restrictions confining reporters to limited areas under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Senator Katie Britt reportedly called Capitol Police on a group of fired federal workers protesting budget cuts. The week closed with confirmation that the reconciliation bill's Medicaid and SNAP cuts would leave millions without healthcare and food assistance as it moved to the Senate, and with the Justice Department seeking to dismiss criminal charges against an MS-13 leader in order to facilitate his deportation — a move that raised its own questions about subordinating prosecution to political ends.

**Looking Back**

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government pulling in several directions at once. The legislative branch delivered, by the narrowest possible margin, a bill that will reshape taxation, healthcare access, and immigration enforcement for years. The judiciary spent the week functioning as the most consistent check on executive action — blocking deportations without due process, halting mass layoffs, striking down retaliation against a law firm, and pausing an attempt to expel Harvard's international students — even as the Supreme Court's emergency docket simultaneously expanded presidential removal power over independent agencies and let stand the termination of protected status for hundreds of thousands of migrants. Meanwhile, questions of foreign gifts, prosecutorial selectivity, and institutional pressure on universities and the press accumulated across the week rather than resolving in it. None of these threads concluded by Friday; several — the Senate's handling of the reconciliation bill, the Harvard litigation, the McIver prosecution, the South Sudan deportations — will continue to test how far executive power can reach before the courts, Congress, or public accountability draw a firm line. ```
