Title: Pardons, Purges, and Pushback: A Week of Executive Overreach and Judicial Resistance
Content:
```markdown This was a week defined by two competing forces: an executive branch testing how far institutional pressure could be pushed, and a judiciary that pushed back at nearly every turn, even when its rulings didn't always hold. By week's end, Harvard remained locked in open legal war with the administration, a cluster of pardons had raised fresh questions about who gets mercy and why, and a Supreme Court decision had stripped legal protection from hundreds of thousands of migrants, even as lower courts kept finding that other enforcement actions had gone too far.

The weekend set the tone. An executive order dismantling diversity, equity, and inclusion programs reached into West Point, where student clubs were disbanded and materials removed, part of a broader pattern that also saw a critically ill child's humanitarian parole revoked and a Mexican singer's visa canceled. In Alabama, a U.S.-born citizen named Leonardo Garcia Venegas was detained for hours while filming an ICE operation, despite presenting valid identification—an early sign that aggressive enforcement tactics were not reliably distinguishing citizens from targets. And in Massachusetts, the administration made its opening move against Harvard, revoking the university's certification to enroll international students. Harvard sued immediately, and within a day Judge Allison Burroughs had issued a temporary restraining order blocking the action. Elsewhere, Trump announced a 50% tariff on European Union goods effective June 1, then extended the deadline to July 9 after the European Commission asked for more time—part of a now-familiar pattern of trade brinkmanship conducted through personal announcement rather than institutional process. The weekend also saw the Indivisible movement organize what it called the largest day of protest of Trump's second term, spanning more than 1,300 cities, while federal judges began quietly discussing whether they needed their own independent security force, wary that the Justice-Department-controlled U.S. Marshals Service might be pressured to withdraw protection from judges who ruled against the administration.

By Monday, the week's second major thread emerged: a cluster of pardons that critics said rewarded loyalty and access rather than legal merit. Trump pardoned former Virginia sheriff Scott Jenkins, convicted of bribery, and Paul Walczak, a nursing-home executive convicted of tax crimes whose mother had attended a high-priced Mar-a-Lago fundraiser. The same day, the administration's proposed federal budget revealed its priorities in stark terms, sharply increasing funding for ICE and the Pentagon while proposing steep cuts to SNAP and Medicaid that would shift costs onto states and threaten benefits for millions. NPR filed a First Amendment lawsuit challenging an executive order that barred federal funds for NPR and PBS, arguing the order retaliated against the network for unfavorable coverage. Federal judges, meanwhile, continued rejecting the administration's attempts to sidestep due process in deportation cases, finding that DHS had mischaracterized prior court orders in its efforts to remove protections for deportees bound for South Sudan and Djibouti. Separately, Republican-led efforts in several states moved to raise the threshold for ballot initiatives and referendums, narrowing one of the few tools voters have to bypass unresponsive legislatures.

Tuesday brought an escalation on nearly every front. Federal agencies were ordered to sever all ties with Harvard, canceling roughly $100 million in contracts and grants and pushing the funding fight well beyond the original enrollment dispute even as courts kept intervening. The same day, Trump signed his 152nd executive order since returning to office, a pace unmatched by any recent predecessor at this point in a term and a marker of a governing style built on unilateral action rather than legislative negotiation. The pardon pattern continued as well, with clemency for Todd and Julie Chrisley, the reality television couple convicted of defrauding banks of more than $30 million, following advocacy from their daughter. Elsewhere, Boeing admitted in legal filings that its employees had deliberately misled the FAA about risks in the 737 MAX's flight-control system, contributing to two fatal crashes, while reporting also tied the company to close financial and lobbying relationships with the administration. A federal judge delivered one clear check on executive overreach, striking down Trump's order targeting the law firm WilmerHale over its association with Robert Mueller and ruling that the order violated the First Amendment. But that same day, Trump used a Memorial Day social media post to call judges ideologically opposed to the country and accuse them of protecting criminals, extending a running campaign against judicial legitimacy. A flurry of other rulings touched tariffs and DOGE authority, including one requiring Elon Musk to face a lawsuit over the initiative's constitutional footing, reflecting how broadly litigation against the administration had spread.

Wednesday deepened the Harvard confrontation and delivered the week's most consequential legal ruling on tariffs. Backed by a letter from more than 200 college presidents opposing federal overreach, Harvard formally sued the administration and refused to comply with a list of demands tied to its funding and enrollment status. In Congress, the House passed the sprawling "One Big Beautiful" tax-and-spending bill, which extends Trump-era tax cuts, funds mass deportations, and cuts safety-net programs, drawing public backlash even as it moved to the Senate. On tariffs, two federal courts ruled that Trump had exceeded his authority by using emergency powers to impose sweeping duties without congressional approval—a significant assertion that trade policy belongs to Congress. But the win was immediately complicated: the administration's appeal produced a temporary stay, keeping the tariffs in effect despite the ruling against them. Immigration enforcement escalated further as Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller ordered ICE to triple its daily arrest target to 3,000 people, raising concerns about due process and detention capacity given the earlier wrongful detention of a U.S. citizen. In response to the mounting pressure across these fronts, grassroots organizing continued to widen, with new or expanding campaigns including Tesla Takedown, the 50501 movement, a general strike effort, and a boycott campaign aimed at Fox News. Trump also pardoned former Chicago gang leader Larry Hoover, commuting his life sentence, and issued two dozen additional pardons—a contrast critics drew against the administration's harsher stance toward undocumented immigrants without criminal records. Separately, Elon Musk officially ended his formal role atop the Department of Government Efficiency, though Trump indicated he would remain informally involved.

Thursday's developments ranged across the courts and the states. The Supreme Court issued a unanimous 8-0 ruling narrowing environmental review requirements under the National Environmental Policy Act, a decision favoring a Utah oil railway project and, more broadly, fossil fuel infrastructure expansion for years to come. In a very different arena, Idaho and Montana followed Utah's lead in banning LGBTQ+ Pride flags at government buildings, part of a wave of 31 similar bills introduced across 17 states. Twenty-two young plaintiffs, ages 7 to 25, filed suit against the administration's fossil-fuel-promoting executive orders, arguing they violated constitutional rights to life and liberty. The tariff fight took another turn as a federal appeals court granted a temporary stay on the earlier ruling against Trump's tariffs, keeping them in force while the administration pursued further appeals, potentially all the way to the Supreme Court. And in the Harvard case, Judge Burroughs issued an injunction expanding protection for the university's ability to enroll international students, preserving the status quo while litigation continued. In Oklahoma, parents organized under the name "WOKE" used a state opt-out law to resist a new social studies curriculum embedding 2020 election conspiracy theories and Christian nationalist themes, while a separate lawsuit challenged how the curriculum had been approved.

Friday closed the week with some of its most consequential rulings. In a 7-2 decision, the Supreme Court allowed the administration to end humanitarian parole and temporary protected status for hundreds of thousands of Cuban, Haitian, Nicaraguan, and Venezuelan migrants, reversing a lower court's block and exposing many to expedited removal even as related litigation continued. The State Department, meanwhile, notified Congress of plans to build an "Office of Remigration," restructuring the Bureau of Population, Refugees, and Migration around deportation tracking and cutting more than 300 offices and thousands of positions in the process. The Harvard fight escalated again as the administration directed U.S. consulates worldwide to conduct social media screening for all visa applicants tied to the university, citing concerns about antisemitism and extending scrutiny to students, faculty, and other visitors alike. Amid these federal actions, Virginia's legislature advanced a constitutional amendment to codify abortion rights, a measure that must pass again next year before reaching voters. A federal judge in Boston halted a deportation flight to South Sudan after finding the administration had violated a prior order guaranteeing detainees the right to challenge removal to third countries, leaving affected men stranded in Djibouti. And in an unusual coda, an AI-generated voice impersonating White House chief of staff Susie Wiles was used by an unknown actor to contact her associates requesting pardons and cash transfers, prompting an FBI investigation into the security breach.

Taken as a whole, the week illustrated a widening gap between what courts were willing to block and what ultimately stayed in force. Judges ruled against the administration on tariffs, on due process in deportations, on retaliation against a law firm, and repeatedly in Harvard's favor, yet appeals and a receptive Supreme Court preserved much of the underlying policy anyway. Pardons flowed toward the well-connected even as enforcement intensified against migrants with no such access, and a growing infrastructure of grassroots protest and litigation tried to keep pace with the scope of executive action. The week did not resolve any of these tensions; it sharpened them, leaving courts, universities, protesters, and Congress each holding a piece of an unfinished argument over where presidential power ends. ```

Title: This Week in Democracy: Tariffs, Travel Bans, and a Public Feud Over Power
Content:
```markdown This was a week that moved on several tracks at once, each reinforcing the others. The Supreme Court repeatedly sided with executive power even as lower courts pushed back on it. The president doubled tariffs and signed a sweeping new travel ban. The House narrowly passed a budget bill that will touch millions of Americans' health coverage and food assistance. Federal disaster agencies entered hurricane season stripped of staff. And a public feud between the president and the world's richest man exposed just how thoroughly private wealth and government power had become entangled.

The weekend set the tone. Trump announced a doubling of steel and aluminum tariffs to 50 percent, timed to a Pennsylvania rally celebrating a Nippon Steel investment deal, and formalized the increase by executive order days later. The move added fresh uncertainty to trade relationships, including a recently negotiated tariff reduction with the United Kingdom. At nearly the same time, the U.S. Court of International Trade ruled that Trump's broader "Liberation Day" tariffs were illegal, finding that only Congress has the constitutional authority to levy tariffs — but the Federal Circuit paused that ruling on appeal, letting the tariffs stand while the case proceeded. The dispute went straight to the question of who actually controls American trade policy, and it remained unresolved by week's end.

The Supreme Court also acted early, allowing the administration to end parole protections for roughly 500,000 people from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Venezuela, and separately ending Temporary Protected Status for Venezuelans. Both rulings stripped legal status from enormous populations while their court challenges were still pending — part of a pattern in which the Court allowed policy to take effect before the underlying legal questions were settled. That same weekend, federal officers entered Representative Jerry Nadler's Manhattan office and handcuffed a staff member, falsely accusing him of harboring a migrant. Nadler and other Democrats called it intimidation, and it would not be an isolated incident. Meanwhile, the House passed a budget package cutting Medicaid and SNAP while adding work requirements and increasing border and detention funding by $160 billion — the opening move in what would become the week's central legislative story.

By Monday, courts were pushing back forcefully in several directions. Judges blocked the Department of Homeland Security from ending TSA officers' collective bargaining rights, halted the deportation of a detained student pending review, ordered continued treatment access for a plaintiff class, and reaffirmed limits on retaliation against the law firm Jenner & Block. Even as the Supreme Court moved to expand executive latitude, lower courts were drawing lines around it. That same day, a man threw an incendiary device into a rally supporting Israeli hostages in Boulder, Colorado, injuring eight people; the FBI treated it as terrorism and a hate crime, and the administration moved almost immediately to fold the attack into its argument for tougher deportation policy. Monday also brought unsettling news on disaster preparedness: staffing cuts and a hiring freeze had left more than a dozen Gulf Coast National Weather Service offices understaffed, and the new acting head of FEMA reportedly did not know the United States has a hurricane season — the first of several alarming disclosures that week about the state of federal disaster infrastructure. Enforcement actions continued as well, with ICE agents raiding a San Diego restaurant using flash-bang grenades to disperse protesters, and the arrest of international student Rümeysa Öztürk over a campus op-ed about Gaza.

Tuesday's dominant story was the House's passage of Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill," which combined major cuts to healthcare and social programs with a provision preempting state and local regulation of artificial intelligence for a full decade — a sweeping removal of state authority over a fast-moving technology, with almost no offsetting federal oversight built in. The same day, the administration explicitly connected the Boulder attack, committed by a man who had overstayed his visa, to calls from Trump and Stephen Miller for stricter deportation policy and a revival of travel-ban style restrictions. Elsewhere, nineteen corporations — including Anheuser-Busch, Toyota, Booz Allen Hamilton, and Deloitte — withdrew Pride sponsorships, leaving funding gaps in cities including New York and Washington. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered the Navy to strip Harvey Milk's name from a ship during Pride month, part of a broader campaign to rename vessels honoring historical figures in favor of what he called warrior-culture branding. And two developments raised concerns about the integrity of federal science: an executive order reportedly granting political appointees new authority to override research findings, and a proposed 43 percent cut to National Institutes of Health funding that would threaten cancer and biomedical research nationwide.

Wednesday brought the first open break between Trump and Elon Musk. After Musk publicly denounced the spending bill, Trump suggested Musk's government contracts and subsidies could be cancelled; SpaceX responded by announcing it would begin decommissioning the Dragon spacecraft used to resupply the International Space Station. The exchange revealed, in stark terms, how deeply a private billionaire's business empire had become woven into core federal operations — including the country's access to space. The same day, courts continued reinforcing due-process protections: a federal judge ruled that more than 100 migrants sent to a Salvadoran prison must be allowed to challenge their deportations, another ordered the return of a wrongly deported Guatemalan asylum seeker, and a third temporarily blocked deportation of the Boulder suspect's family. The administration also threatened to withdraw billions in federal funding from California's high-speed rail project, giving the state 30 days to demonstrate compliance, while further FEMA cuts emerged — nearly $4 billion in cancelled infrastructure resilience grants and a proposal to eliminate the agency outright, compounding the staffing concerns raised days earlier. A House Democrat called for subpoenaing Musk over alleged drug use during his time inside the administration, an early sign that the rift was becoming a matter of formal oversight rather than private grievance.

The week's final stretch, spanning Thursday into Friday, carried the heaviest concentration of consequential developments. Trump signed a proclamation restricting entry from 19 countries effective June 9, reviving and expanding first-term travel-ban policy and drawing warnings about family separation and discriminatory impact — a direct continuation of the rhetoric that had followed the Boulder attack earlier in the week. Separately, Trump signed an order suspending entry of foreign nationals seeking to study at Harvard, escalating his conflict with the university; a federal judge blocked the policy almost immediately, finding it would cause irreparable harm. The administration also opened an investigation, led by Attorney General Pam Bondi, into whether aides had effectively run the government during Biden's presidency due to alleged cognitive decline, while the House Oversight Committee sought testimony from former Biden aides and the Justice Department opened a separate inquiry into Biden's pardons — an unusually direct use of executive and prosecutorial power against a predecessor's legitimacy.

The reconciliation bill's passage in the House, by a single vote, 215-214, was among the week's most consequential developments. It extended the 2017 tax cuts, funded a major expansion of immigration enforcement, and cut Medicaid and food assistance, even as the Congressional Budget Office projected it would add trillions to the deficit and cause millions to lose health coverage — directly contradicting the administration's public claims. Passed on the thinnest possible margin, the bill now heads to the Senate as the week's largest structural reshaping of the federal safety net.

The Trump-Musk rupture reached its most explosive point on Friday. Trump publicly criticized Musk and again raised the possibility of cancelling his government contracts; Musk responded by claiming Trump appeared in files related to Jeffrey Epstein, a claim that drew immediate national attention before the dispute began to cool. Whatever its ultimate resolution, the episode left a lasting record of how entangled personal loyalty, private fortune, and federal contracting authority had become at the center of government.

The Supreme Court closed the week with a cluster of major rulings issued in a single sitting: it struck down Mexico's lawsuit against American gunmakers, expanded a religious tax exemption for Catholic Charities, eased the path for reverse-discrimination claims in Ames v. Ohio, and allowed the Department of Government Efficiency to continue accessing Social Security records while litigation proceeds. Each ruling shifts legal terrain that will outlast this particular week — on corporate liability, religious exemption, discrimination law, and executive access to Americans' private data.

Enforcement actions also escalated on the ground. David Huerta, president of the Service Employees International Union, was arrested and hospitalized during an immigration raid on a Los Angeles garment factory; the Department of Homeland Security maintained he had assaulted an officer, despite video evidence showing officers using force against him. It was the most prominent instance yet of enforcement activity touching a national labor leader rather than an individual immigrant, following the same week's incidents at Nadler's office and the San Diego restaurant raid. Separately, a federal appeals court allowed the administration to continue barring the Associated Press from the Oval Office, Air Force One, and Mar-a-Lago while litigation proceeds, narrowing press access to the presidency even as it preserved some access to East Room events. And the administration announced it would no longer enforce federal guidance requiring emergency rooms to perform necessary abortions under emergency care law, narrowing federal protection for reproductive care nationwide.

Taken as a whole, the week showed two branches of government pulling in different directions on the same underlying question: how much latitude the executive should have to act unilaterally, and how quickly. The Supreme Court extended that latitude on immigration status, government data access, and workplace removals; district and appellate courts kept insisting that due process, contractual rights, and institutional independence still bound executive action, even under pressure. Congress, for its part, used its narrowest possible majority to pass a bill that will reallocate resources across the entire country for years. And the public dispute between a president and a businessman whose companies now perform core government functions offered an unusually plain illustration of how personal, financial, and political power had come to occupy the same space — a condition future historians will likely find easier to name than to reverse. ```

Title: This Week in Democracy: Los Angeles Becomes the Test Case
Content:
```markdown This week, Los Angeles became the place where the country's arguments about immigration enforcement, federal power, and dissent stopped being abstract. What began as a series of workplace raids grew, over six days, into a National Guard deployment fought out in federal court, a sitting senator forced to the ground in handcuffs, and finally the largest coordinated day of protest of the term. The throughline connecting these moments was not accident but escalation: each step built on the one before it, and each drew a response that raised the stakes further.

The pattern started over the weekend. Department of Homeland Security agents conducted coordinated raids across Los Angeles workplaces, including a Home Depot and a clothing manufacturer, arresting at least 45 people without warrants. Agents used flash-bang grenades and military-style tactics; among those detained was the president of SEIU California. Governor Gavin Newsom and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass condemned the operation immediately, setting up a conflict between federal enforcement priorities and local government that would define the rest of the week. The administration moved on several other fronts at once: a ban on entry from twelve countries, suspension of Harvard's student visa program, rescission of emergency abortion guidance, a filing to resume mass federal firings, and new investigations into Joe Biden's pardons and mental competency. Federal judges pushed back almost immediately, blocking deportations under the Alien Enemies Act, blocking cuts to gender-affirming care in federal prisons, and stopping the elimination of Job Corps. But even as courts intervened, a more basic form of oversight failed: Representatives Jimmy Gomez, Luz Rivas, Norma Torres, and Lou Correa were turned away from federal detention facilities in Los Angeles despite holding statutory authority to inspect them, with reports that detainees lacked access to food, water, and medicine.

By Monday, the numbers themselves became the story. ICE detained more than 2,200 people in a single day, the largest daily total in the agency's history, after deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller reportedly demanded a minimum of 3,000 arrests per day and warned of firings if the pace didn't increase — enforcement driven by a political target rather than individualized case review. The same day, President Trump directed cabinet members to "liberate" Los Angeles from what he called a migrant invasion, casting protests against the raids as violent riots against federal law enforcement, a characterization the Los Angeles Police Department's own public statements did not support. That framing would become the rationale for federalizing the state's National Guard. Congressional access problems recurred, with Democratic members again denied entry to detention facilities in both Los Angeles and New York. Separately, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard was accused by senior Democrats of "illegal interference" after firing the acting counsel to the intelligence community's inspector general, raising concerns about the independence of internal watchdogs. And journalists covering the Los Angeles protests, including CNN's Jason Carroll and Australian reporter Lauren Tomasi, were struck by rubber bullets or briefly detained, prompting a coalition letter warning of First Amendment violations.

Tuesday was the week's densest day for institutional pressure. California Attorney General Rob Bonta and Governor Newsom filed suit against the federalization of the state's National Guard, arguing it violated the Tenth Amendment and state sovereignty — a case that would move with unusual speed over the following days. On the public health front, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. dismissed all seventeen members of the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices in what he called a "clean sweep," replacing an independent scientific panel with appointees answerable directly to him. At Fort Bragg, Trump announced plans to restore Confederate-derived names to Army installations, reversing a bipartisan congressional decision. Pressure on institutions perceived as adversarial broadened considerably: the administration threatened school funding over lessons on systemic racism, escalated its dispute with Harvard over admissions and hiring, banned federal grants that used "gender ideology" terminology, threatened university funding over allowing protests, pulled American Bar Association grants after the group's criticism of the administration, and moved to defund NPR and PBS while continuing to retaliate against the Associated Press. The State Department revoked roughly 800 student visas tied largely to pro-Palestine protest activity, and USCIS announced plans to monitor immigrants' social media for "antisemitic activity." Even symbolic space came under scrutiny, as the Department of Defense ordered nearly 400 books removed from the Naval Academy library and banned pride flags from State Department and VA offices.

Wednesday offered a partial check and a grim illustration of enforcement's reach. A federal judge ruled that the administration could not detain Columbia activist Mahmoud Khalil on the theory that his presence posed foreign policy consequences, though a separate immigration charge kept him in custody — a narrow but real limit on a novel executive theory for detaining noncitizens over political speech. Meanwhile, ICE raids disrupted essential labor: about 75 workers were detained at a Nebraska meatpacking plant, and raids hit produce farms in Ventura County, California, unsettling immigrant workforces central to the food supply. Governor Newsom delivered a prime-time address condemning both the raids and the National Guard federalization, urging peaceful protest while warning against the erosion of civil liberties. And in Downey, California, unidentified federal agents detained a man outside a church, with one agent pointing a rifle at a pastor who tried to intervene — a small, sharp episode that crystallized concerns about accountability among unidentified enforcement personnel operating in civilian spaces.

Thursday produced the week's starkest images. California Senator Alex Padilla, a ranking member of the Senate's immigration subcommittee, was forced to the ground and handcuffed by federal agents after attempting to ask Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem a question during a press conference on the Los Angeles operations. He was released without charge, but the incident — a sitting senator physically restrained while attempting oversight — drew immediate bipartisan condemnation and became one of the week's defining moments. Hours earlier, in a legal sense, the week's central constitutional question had reached a verdict: Judge Charles Breyer ruled that Trump's federalization of the California National Guard exceeded his statutory authority and violated the Tenth Amendment, ordering control returned to Governor Newsom. The victory was short-lived. Within hours, the Ninth Circuit issued an administrative stay, keeping the troops under federal control pending a hearing set for June 17 — a sequence that showed how quickly a district court check on executive power could be blunted by appellate procedure rather than resolved on the merits. The same day, Trump signed congressional resolutions overturning California's ban on new gas-powered car sales by 2035 and its truck emissions rules, prompting a new multistate lawsuit, while his earlier takeover of the Kennedy Center continued to generate falling ticket sales and performer cancellations. Ahead of planned nationwide demonstrations, governors and law enforcement officials in Texas, Missouri, South Carolina, Virginia, and Florida announced National Guard call-ups or zero-tolerance postures, and a Florida sheriff issued a widely criticized threat of lethal force against protesters. House Republicans, meanwhile, narrowly passed a $9.4 billion rescissions package defunding NPR and PBS, sending it to the Senate.

Friday brought the week to its intended culmination, on more than one front. A federal judge in Massachusetts issued an injunction against parts of Trump's executive order requiring proof of citizenship to vote and penalizing states over ballot deadlines, finding a "substantial risk" of voter disenfranchisement — the second such ruling after an earlier one from a judge in Washington, D.C. In New Jersey, the Justice Department indicted Representative LaMonica McIver on three counts of impeding federal officers during a protest and oversight visit to an ICE detention center in Newark; McIver called the charges political intimidation. Taken together with Padilla's removal two days earlier, the indictment meant that within the same week, one member of Congress had been handcuffed by federal agents and another criminally charged, both in connection with attempts to conduct oversight of immigration enforcement. Quieter but consequential actions moved alongside these headlines: the administration transferred personal data, including immigration status, for millions of Medicaid enrollees to DHS to support deportation efforts, and the EEOC's acting chair ordered a halt to processing gender-identity discrimination claims. Trump himself acknowledged that immigration enforcement was removing long-term agricultural workers and hurting farmers, an unusual admission of friction within his own administration's agenda.

And then, on Friday, the week's accumulated pressure found its expression in the streets. Organizers mobilized "No Kings" demonstrations across roughly 2,000 sites nationwide, explicitly framed as a response to the preceding days' raids, deportations, and confrontations, and to a military parade Trump had scheduled the same weekend. Millions were expected to participate across all fifty states, making it one of the largest single-day displays of coordinated public dissent of the term.

By the end of the week, no single institution had settled the underlying conflict. Courts had repeatedly found parts of the administration's immigration and election actions unlawful, only to see some of those rulings paused on appeal within hours. Congress had twice been physically or legally denied the oversight access its members are entitled to by law, and two of its elected members had been handcuffed or indicted in the course of trying to exercise that access. Local and state officials in California asserted authority over their own National Guard and environmental policy, only to have both contested or overridden by federal action within days. What the week made visible, more than any one ruling or statement, was how enforcement power, oversight power, and protest power were all being tested against one another in real time — with Los Angeles as the proving ground and the Friday demonstrations as the clearest public answer the country had yet given. ```
Excerpt: This week the conflict between federal enforcement power and local and constitutional limits moved from courtrooms into the streets.

Title: A Parade, a Purge, and a Political Assassination
Content:
```markdown The week of June 14th began with a jarring contrast and ended in an unsettled one. On Saturday, President Trump presided over a $40 million military parade in Washington, staged to mark both his 79th birthday and the Army's 250th anniversary. Attendance was thin, and the event drew criticism for its disorganization. That same weekend, more than five million people turned out for over 2,100 "No Kings" protests across the country — one of the largest coordinated demonstrations in American history, organized around objections to what participants described as an unchecked consolidation of presidential power. The split-screen — a state spectacle drawing modest crowds against a nationwide wave of dissent — set the tone for a week in which public sentiment and official display seemed to run in opposite directions.

The same weekend brought a far graver development. In Minnesota, a gunman posing as a police officer shot and killed State Representative Melissa Hortman and her husband, while wounding State Senator John Hoffman and his wife in a related attack. Governor Tim Walz called it a politically motivated assassination. The FBI opened a manhunt for the suspect, Vance Boelter, who was apprehended and later charged federally. The killing of a sitting legislator, and the wounding of another, marked one of the most serious acts of political violence against elected officials in recent American history, and it cast a shadow over the rest of the week, including a bout of misinformation that falsely tied the shooter to left-wing politics before facts emerged showing his views leaned in the opposite direction.

The weekend's unrest did not stay peaceful everywhere. In Los Angeles, police used tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse a protest that turned confrontational near a federal building. In Salt Lake City, a peacekeeper at a similar demonstration fatally shot a bystander while confronting an armed man. Against this backdrop, President Trump ordered thousands of National Guard troops and hundreds of Marines into Los Angeles without the consent of Governor Gavin Newsom — the first such unilateral domestic deployment since 1965. California challenged the move in court immediately, opening a legal fight that would run through much of the week.

Immigration enforcement lurched unpredictably over the same days. ICE briefly paused workplace raids in agriculture and hospitality after Trump acknowledged the economic damage they were causing, even as the administration simultaneously announced intensified deportation efforts aimed at Democratic-led cities and withdrew a list of "noncompliant" sanctuary jurisdictions. Elsewhere, an executive order shaped by adviser Stephen Miller sought to end birthright citizenship for children of undocumented immigrants, a direct challenge to the Fourteenth Amendment that remained pending before the Supreme Court. In a smaller but telling episode, the EPA dropped an enforcement case against the private prison operator Geo Group over toxic disinfectant use at a detention facility — a decision that followed substantial company donations to Trump and Republican leaders. The weekend closed with symbolic rollbacks as well: Trump removed a bust of Martin Luther King Jr. from the Oval Office without explanation, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered the renaming of a Navy ship that had honored LGBTQ rights pioneer Harvey Milk — early signs of a pattern that would recur later in the week around Juneteenth.

By Monday, the courts were pushing back. Judge William Young ruled that the administration's termination of hundreds of NIH research grants — many tied to DEI and LGBTQ health research — was unlawful and discriminatory, ordering the funds restored. Meanwhile, ICE raids continued in Los Angeles, sweeping through a Santa Fe Springs swap meet, a Home Depot parking lot in Montebello, and other sites, detaining day laborers and, in some cases, U.S. citizens, and prompting accusations of racial profiling. In Georgia, Spanish-language journalist Mario Guevara was arrested while covering a "No Kings" protest and, despite holding valid work authorization, was transferred into ICE custody — a move that blurred the line between immigration enforcement and press suppression. The American Bar Association filed suit the same day, alleging that executive orders targeting law firms were designed to intimidate lawyers away from challenging the administration in court. In a quieter but still notable set of developments, Trump fired an NRC commissioner without cause, the GAO found the administration had illegally frozen funding for libraries, archives, and museums, and the Trump family launched a new commercial venture, Trump Mobile, renewing questions about the mixing of the presidency with personal profit.

Tuesday's most striking moment came in New York, where NYC Comptroller and mayoral candidate Brad Lander was arrested by ICE and FBI agents while trying to accompany an immigrant out of a courthouse. Agents accused him of assaulting law enforcement, a claim disputed by video evidence; he was released hours later without charges. The arrest of a sitting elected official by federal agents raised alarm about the use of immigration enforcement as a tool of political intimidation. That same day, ICE raids on farms and hotels resumed after only four days of pause, under pressure from immigration hardliners pushing for 3,000 daily arrests — another turn in a week defined by enforcement whiplash. Congressional Democrats, including Senator Richard Blumenthal and Representative Jamie Raskin, opened inquiries into Trump's cryptocurrency dealings, including a dinner event for top purchasers of his memecoin, while Senator Jeff Merkley introduced legislation aimed at curbing crypto-related corruption. Elsewhere, a federal judge expanded protections allowing transgender and intersex citizens to update gender markers on passports, and congressional leaders began reviewing security arrangements for lawmakers in the wake of the Minnesota killing.

Wednesday brought two major Supreme Court developments in entirely separate domains. In *United States v. Skrmetti*, the Court's conservative majority upheld Tennessee's ban on gender-affirming care for minors, ruling that it did not constitute sex-based discrimination — a decision with implications for similar laws nationwide. Separately, a federal judge held Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier in contempt for continuing to enforce a state immigration law despite a court order blocking it, a direct rebuke of official defiance of judicial authority. The National Guard dispute in Los Angeles took another turn as well: a federal judge ordered control of the troops returned to Governor Newsom, only for an appellate panel to stay that ruling and leave federal control in place, with Hegseth suggesting he might not comply with an adverse decision regardless. The same day, corporate America's retreat from Juneteenth recognition became visible, as Amazon and Verizon withdrew financial support for celebrations and West Virginia's governor ended state backing for the holiday — developments that traced directly back to the MLK bust removal days earlier. Federal courts also blocked the administration from barring Harvard from admitting international students, part of a broader wave of rulings that day pausing or narrowing executive actions on education and environmental policy, even as the State Department announced it would begin reviewing the social media accounts of student visa applicants for signs of hostility toward the United States.

Thursday deepened several of the week's central conflicts. New DHS guidance required lawmakers to give 72 hours' notice before visiting immigration detention facilities, a rule that directly contradicted federal law; Representatives Dan Goldman and Jerry Nadler were subsequently denied entry to an ICE facility in Manhattan. The National Guard dispute reached a further stage when the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals overturned the lower court's order and allowed Trump to retain control of the deployed troops, finding sufficient evidence of violent protester conduct to justify the federalization — a ruling that, unlike Wednesday's stay, represented a more definitive step in the administration's favor. The administration also formally rescinded long-standing guidance that had shielded schools and churches from immigration arrests, forcing community organizations to strip these locations of their status as safe spaces. Trump renewed calls for a special prosecutor to investigate the 2020 election as fraudulent while separately dismissing his own intelligence community's assessment of Iran's nuclear timeline. Smaller acts of resistance surfaced too: the Los Angeles Dodgers denied ICE agents access to stadium parking lots, and an Australian writer was denied entry to the United States and deported after being questioned about his views on the Israel-Palestine conflict and his coverage of student protests.

The week closed on Friday with developments spanning media, energy, and environmental policy. The administration terminated 639 employees at Voice of America and its parent agency, part of a broader effort that had eliminated 1,400 positions since March and left nearly dismantled an organization that once reached 360 million people weekly. The Supreme Court, in a 7-2 ruling, allowed fossil fuel companies and Republican-led states to proceed with a challenge to California's federal waiver for stricter vehicle emissions standards, reopening a long-settled area of environmental law. Using emergency executive authority, the administration ordered a Michigan coal plant to remain open past its scheduled closure and delayed another plant's planned shutdown, overriding the state's clean energy law. Congress, meanwhile, used joint resolutions to reverse an Office of the Comptroller of the Currency rule on bank mergers and an EPA rule on pollution source classification, rolling back regulatory protections through ordinary legislative means.

Taken as a whole, the week traced several threads that would not resolve neatly by Friday. Political violence entered the machinery of elected governance directly, from the killing of a state legislator to the forceful, if brief, detention of a sitting city comptroller. Immigration enforcement swung between retreat and escalation, driven less by settled policy than by shifting economic and political pressure, while reaching further into spaces — courthouses, schools, churches, congressional oversight visits — previously treated as off-limits. The courts remained an active check on executive power, blocking grant terminations and expanding rights protections, even as appellate rulings and a major Supreme Court decision showed that judicial outcomes were far from uniformly resistant to the administration's aims. And alongside these confrontations, a quieter erosion continued: the paring back of Juneteenth recognition, the removal of civil-rights symbols, and the near-dismantling of an independent international broadcaster suggested that institutional memory and public voice were being narrowed even as the more visible battles over courts, troops, and protest dominated the week's attention. ```
Excerpt: The week opened with a jarring split-screen: a military parade in Washington marking Trump's birthday drew thin crowds while more than five million Americans joined 'No Kings'

Title: War Without Congress, Courts Without Teeth
Content:
```markdown This was a week that began with bombs falling on Iran and ended with the Supreme Court narrowing the tools courts use to check the president. In between, National Guard troops occupied the streets of Los Angeles, a Justice Department official accused of contemplating defiance of federal judges sat for Senate questioning, and immigration enforcement expanded into new detention facilities in California and the Florida Everglades. It was a week in which institutions pushed back against executive power almost daily—and one in which, by Friday, some of their sharpest tools had been dulled.

The weekend opened with the most consequential single act of the period: President Trump ordered B-2 bombers to strike three Iranian nuclear facilities—Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan—the first American bombing of Iranian soil in decades. No vote was held in Congress, and no War Powers Resolution process was observed. Trump declared the operation a "spectacular success" even as his own officials cautioned that damage assessments were premature. Within days, that claim collided with reality: intelligence assessments began circulating that contradicted the president's account of the strikes' effectiveness, setting up a dispute that would occupy the rest of the week. It was not the first time in recent months that Trump had brushed aside his intelligence agencies. Months earlier, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard had testified that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon; Trump publicly rejected that finding, saying flatly that "my intelligence community is wrong." By week's end, Gabbard had realigned her public position with the administration's.

The same weekend, roughly 4,000 National Guard troops and 700 Marines arrived in Los Angeles to reinforce immigration raids that had begun weeks earlier, deployed over the objections of state and local officials. The military presence deepened an already volatile standoff between protesters and federal agents. In Newark, that same enforcement climate produced a striking legal confrontation: Mayor Ras Baraka was charged with trespassing at an ICE facility, and Rep. LaMonica McIver was charged with assaulting and impeding law enforcement during the same standoff. A federal magistrate later rebuked prosecutors for the haste of the Baraka charge, which was quietly dropped, but the message sent by charging a sitting mayor and a member of Congress in connection with oversight of a detention facility was not lost on observers. Amid this, a rare judicial check landed in favor of due process: a federal judge ordered the release of Palestinian rights activist Mahmoud Khalil after more than 100 days in ICE detention without charge, finding no evidence he posed a flight risk. The administration appealed immediately.

By Monday, the legal system was engaged on multiple fronts. California sued over the federalization of its National Guard, and fifteen Democratic attorneys general sued over Trump's declared "energy emergency," arguing it improperly bypassed environmental review. A federal judge in New York blocked the administration's use of the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to treat Venezuelan migrants as an "invasion," rejecting a legal theory underpinning parts of the deportation campaign. Judge Burroughs issued an injunction against the administration's attempt to bar international students from Harvard, warning of efforts to "squelch diverse viewpoints," while Judge Young ordered hundreds of terminated NIH grants restored, calling the cancellations "bereft of reasoning." Yet the same day brought a very different signal from the Supreme Court, which paused a lower court ruling requiring a "meaningful opportunity" for migrants to contest deportation to third countries where they might face torture or persecution—over the dissent of the three liberal justices. And a DOJ whistleblower, attorney Erez Reuveni, came forward alleging that Emil Bove, a senior Justice Department official and Trump's nominee for a federal appellate judgeship, had suggested the department might proceed with deportations regardless of court injunctions. Beneath these headline fights, the human cost of expanding detention was becoming visible: a 68-year-old detainee died in transit—the first such death in at least a decade—and a pregnant woman in ICE custody miscarried after days of pleading for medical care.

Tuesday brought the week's clearest signal of congressional restraint. The House voted to table articles of impeachment over the unauthorized Iran strikes, with only 79 Democrats in support—a clear demonstration of limited appetite in Congress to use its strongest check on unilateral military action. Courts, meanwhile, kept working. An appeals court ordered the government to facilitate the return of a man deported to El Salvador in violation of a prior court order, and a separate judge blocked Trump's executive order stripping collective bargaining rights from more than a million federal employees. But the conflict between the executive and the judiciary sharpened further: California formally sued over the Guard deployment, and the Justice Department, in an unusual escalation, sued the entire federal bench in Maryland over a standing order that delayed deportations pending legal challenge. Additional reporting detailed the Reuveni whistleblower letter, alleging Bove had suggested defying court orders and that Reuveni himself was fired after refusing to mislead a court. Meanwhile ICE enforcement kept expanding—arrests surging past facility capacity, reports emerging of DHS messaging encouraging citizens to report immigrants, and revelations about Stephen Miller's undisclosed financial stake in ICE contractor Palantir. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spent the day defending budget cuts that eliminated entire public health offices.

Wednesday centered on Emil Bove's Senate Judiciary Committee testimony. He denied the whistleblower's account and faced pointed questions about his role in dropping corruption charges against New York City Mayor Eric Adams and in firing prosecutors who had worked January 6 cases; Democrats accused him of weaponizing the department he was being promoted out of. The same day, following the leak of a Defense Intelligence Agency report that undercut the administration's claims about the Iran strikes' success, officials moved to restrict Congress's access to classified information—an action that drew immediate criticism from Democratic lawmakers concerned about the erosion of oversight. Health policy also shifted meaningfully: Kennedy unilaterally appointed eight new members, several known for vaccine skepticism, to the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, alarming even some Republican senators. Attorney General Pam Bondi, meanwhile, claimed ignorance of ICE agents wearing masks during raids despite video evidence to the contrary, and reports surfaced that the administration was preparing to dismiss the asylum claims of potentially hundreds of thousands of immigrants, rendering them immediately deportable. Elsewhere, the administration moved to terminate 639 more Voice of America employees as part of dismantling the U.S. Agency for Global Media, and Trump revoked security clearances from former officials Mike Pompeo, Mark Milley, and John Bolton. Still, courts issued more checks: a nationwide injunction blocked the shutdown of Job Corps centers, and Kilmar Abrego Garcia was ordered released on bail, even as officials acknowledged he could face renewed ICE custody.

Thursday's docket included a major Supreme Court ruling limiting Medicaid patients' ability to sue over their choice of healthcare provider, a 6-3 decision that will allow states to exclude Planned Parenthood from Medicaid funding. The Justice Department's lawsuit against Maryland's federal bench, filed the day before, drew wider notice as an extraordinary escalation—an executive branch agency suing an entire court as a body over its handling of deportation cases. ICE and private prison contractor CoreCivic moved to convert a shuttered prison into California's largest immigration detention facility, backed by an initial $10 million contract, over strong local opposition. In New York, the political costs of enforcement rhetoric became personal: the NYPD's hate crimes taskforce opened an investigation into death threats against Zohran Mamdani, the Democratic mayoral primary winner, amid a surge of Islamophobic rhetoric following his win, while a U.S. citizen, Andrea Velez, was mistakenly seized by federal agents during an unrelated Los Angeles raid. Away from immigration matters, the Senate parliamentarian ruled that several Republican-added provisions in the reconciliation bill, including Medicaid tax changes, could not proceed under budget rules—prompting some Republicans to call publicly for her removal—and Governor Gavin Newsom filed a $787 million defamation suit against Fox News over allegedly deceptive editing of a Trump phone call.

Friday delivered the week's structural turning point. In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that federal courts likely lack authority to issue nationwide injunctions absent specific congressional authorization, limiting relief in the birthright citizenship case to named plaintiffs and leaving open whether class actions might achieve broader effect. The Court did not rule on the constitutionality of ending birthright citizenship itself—only on the scope of judicial remedy. The practical effect was immediate and far-reaching: many of the very tools lower courts had used throughout the week to block deportations, restore grants, and protect students depend on nationwide injunctions for broad effect, and that tool was now sharply constrained. The same day, in Mahmoud v. Taylor, the Court ruled that public schools must allow parents to withdraw children from lessons involving LGBTQ characters on religious grounds, with Justice Sotomayor warning in dissent that schools might respond by removing such content altogether rather than manage individual opt-outs. In Florida, the attorney general advanced a 5,000-bed migrant detention facility in the Everglades, and Governor DeSantis used emergency powers to seize the land from Miami-Dade County, prompting an environmental lawsuit. The University of Virginia's president, James Ryan, resigned as part of a settlement with the Justice Department over the university's diversity policies—federal investigative leverage translating directly into a change in university leadership. Republican Rep. Andy Ogles called publicly for the denaturalization and deportation of Zohran Mamdani, a naturalized citizen, sending a formal letter to the Attorney General. The Court also upheld a Texas law requiring age verification for pornography websites and, in Kennedy v. Braidwood, affirmed the structure of the ACA's preventive services framework while confirming the health secretary's broad authority over expert advisory panels. Outside the Russell Senate Office Building, activists were arrested protesting proposed Medicaid cuts as the Senate pushed toward a July 4 vote on the broader reconciliation bill.

Taken as a whole, the week traced a familiar but intensifying pattern in the relationship between the branches of American government: a president acting unilaterally on matters of war, intelligence, and domestic deployment; a Congress largely unwilling to invoke its formal checks even after being bypassed on a matter as consequential as military action; and a judiciary that remained active and often assertive throughout the week, blocking deportations, restoring funding, and ordering releases—only to see its principal nationwide remedy curtailed by the Supreme Court on the week's final day. Due process for migrants narrowed further, oversight of classified intelligence tightened around the executive rather than around the public, and institutions built for independent expertise—from vaccine advisory panels to university leadership to public broadcasting—came under direct political pressure. None of these developments occurred in isolation; each fed into the others, compounding across seven days into a portrait of executive power testing, and in several instances exceeding, the practical limits historically imposed by the other branches of government. ```

Title: The Bill, the Bombs, and the Border: A Week That Rewrote the Ledger
Content:
```markdown The week beginning June 28 and closing on Independence Day was defined by two intertwined stories: a sweeping fiscal and immigration bill that moved from contested procedure to presidential signature in seven days, and a steady narrowing of the judiciary's capacity to check executive action. Around those twin currents ran a dense set of enforcement actions, press pressure, and public dissent that gave the week its full shape.

The weekend opened with the Supreme Court's ruling that lower courts generally cannot issue nationwide injunctions, a decision arising from a challenge to Trump's executive order narrowing birthright citizenship. The 6-3 ruling did not settle whether the underlying order was constitutional, but it allowed enforcement to proceed unevenly, state by state, while litigation continued elsewhere—stripping courts of a tool they had used to halt contested policies nationwide in a single stroke.

That same weekend, the administration ended Temporary Protected Status for roughly half a million Haitians, and a Justice Department directive prioritizing denaturalization of naturalized citizens accused of crimes began drawing scrutiny. Both moves expanded executive discretion over who could claim secure legal standing in the country. Separately, following the earlier U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, the Senate voted 53-47 along party lines to reject a resolution that would have required congressional authorization for further military action, leaving decisions about escalation concentrated in the presidency. In the Senate, meanwhile, the reconciliation bill cleared its first procedural votes 51-49, even as the parliamentarian ruled several provisions—including Medicaid-related additions—out of order, previewing a fight over substance that would run through the entire week. ICE actions over the weekend detained the father, wife, and daughter of military veterans, and a deceased veteran's son, while Trump endorsed legislation to strip tax-exempt status from nonprofits linked to protests. Nationwide "No Kings" demonstrations drew millions of participants, and in Louisiana a Catholic school fired a longtime teacher after learning of his marriage to a man.

By Monday, the fight over the budget bill escalated sharply. Trump urged Senate Republicans to disregard the parliamentarian's rulings outright, and the chamber passed the bill 51-50, with Vice President Vance breaking the tie. Senators also voted to treat $3.8 trillion in tax cuts as costing nothing for scoring purposes—a maneuver that altered the accounting rules meant to constrain how sweeping fiscal legislation can pass. The same day brought a wave of arrests involving sitting officials: Senator Alex Padilla, Newark Mayor Ras Baraka, New York City Comptroller Brad Lander, and Representative LaMonica McIver were all detained in episodes connected to ICE facility visits and protests, following the earlier arrest of Wisconsin Judge Hannah Dugan. Taken together, these arrests raised serious concerns about law enforcement being used against officials engaged in oversight of executive conduct.

Courts pushed back on multiple fronts that same Monday. Sixteen Democratic attorneys general sued over cancelled school mental health funds, a federal judge blocked mass firings at HHS, and another judge blocked the termination of Haitian TPS. Reports also surfaced of overcrowded, inhumane conditions inside ICE facilities, and a 75-year-old Cuban detainee died in custody—the thirteenth such death of the fiscal year. Elsewhere, Trump lifted select Syria sanctions by executive order, while Delaware enacted the Freedom to Read Act limiting book bans. A different kind of pressure also began to surface: more than 600 EPA employees signed a formal dissent against agency policy, DHS's border czar urged investigating CNN over its coverage of an ICE-tracking app, and the administration warned Harvard over antisemitism compliance—an early signal of the funding and investigative leverage that would recur throughout the week.

Tuesday carried the bill to Senate passage. Republicans approved the reconciliation package with Vice President Vance again breaking a tie, sending it to the House. The bill extended the 2017 tax cuts, funded mass deportations, and cut Medicaid and SNAP, with the Congressional Budget Office projecting a $3.3 trillion increase in the deficit through 2034. The same day, Florida opened the Alligator Alcatraz detention facility in the Everglades, built with capacity for up to 1,000 detainees and expandable to 5,000, prompting an immediate environmental lawsuit over the absence of required review. Press pressure intensified in parallel: Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said the Justice Department was considering prosecuting CNN over its ICEBlock app coverage, while Trump separately threatened action over Iran-related reporting. In an unrelated but consequential development, Paramount agreed to pay Trump $16 million to settle a lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview—two distinct pressure points on the press arising the same day through different channels. The administration also froze $6.8 billion in congressionally appropriated K-12 funding covering after-school, English-learner, and adult education programs, testing the limits of executive discretion over money Congress had already approved. A federal appeals court rejected the detention of Georgetown scholar Badar Khan Suri during deportation proceedings, and Trump threatened to cut government subsidies to Elon Musk's companies amid their public feud. The University of Pennsylvania, meanwhile, announced new restrictions on transgender athletes in women's sports and erased Lia Thomas's swimming records, following an agreement with the administration.

Wednesday centered on a chaotic House effort to adopt the Senate's bill without amendment. Trump pressured wavering Republicans directly, including with threats of primary challengers, while House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries delivered a record eight-hour floor speech opposing the legislation. The bill was ultimately adopted after a marathon procedural vote kept open for hours. The same day, a federal judge ruled that Trump's proclamation of an "invasion" at the border, and the resulting asylum ban, exceeded presidential authority, giving the administration fourteen days to seek emergency relief—a reaffirmation of statutory limits on unilateral executive control over asylum access. A coalition of twenty states led by California's attorney general sued over the sharing of Medicaid enrollee data with DHS for immigration enforcement purposes, alleging privacy violations. Trump called for investigating former DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas and threatened to arrest New York mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani over unfounded citizenship claims, while separately suggesting that U.S. citizens who commit crimes should be deported—rhetoric that blurred constitutional boundaries around citizenship itself. In a smaller but telling episode, officers attempted to deport Ward Sakeik, a stateless Palestinian woman, despite a standing court order barring her removal; her belongings were placed outside her cell before the attempt was halted. Gail Lee, known for challenging voter registrations, was appointed to DeKalb County's elections board, and Trump visited the newly opened Florida detention facility.

Thursday brought the bill's final congressional passage. Following Jeffries' speech, the House gave final approval, sending the legislation to Trump's desk with its $3.3 trillion projected deficit increase, cuts to Medicaid, SNAP, and green energy incentives, and expanded immigration enforcement funding intact. The Supreme Court's conservative majority separately allowed the deportation of eight men to South Sudan to proceed, despite concerns about torture risk, overruling a lower court that had required a chance to contest such removals—a ruling that extended the same term's earlier curtailment of nationwide injunctions into a direct narrowing of protection for individuals facing removal to third countries. The Court also agreed to hear cases on state bans on transgender athletes and reaffirmed a ruling allowing parents to opt children out of LGBTQ+-themed school lessons, adding new fronts to an already active docket. On the ground, a 64-year-old Iranian woman with no criminal record was detained in New Orleans after decades of residency, and a citizen photographer filed a $1 million claim after being arrested while filming an ICE raid—two enforcement episodes distinct in character but united in showing how far the crackdown's reach extended.

Independence Day brought the week's culmination. At a White House ceremony, Trump signed the reconciliation bill into law as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, permanently extending the 2017 tax cuts, funding a $170 billion expansion of immigration enforcement, cutting Medicaid and SNAP, phasing out clean energy incentives, and raising the debt ceiling by $5 trillion. It was the completion of an arc that had run continuously from Saturday's procedural votes through a parliamentarian override, a tie-breaking vice-presidential vote, and a pressured House majority. The same day, five Democratic lawmakers were blocked from inspecting the Alligator Alcatraz facility, closing the loop on a site that had opened under environmental objection and now resisted legislative oversight. A Los Angeles school district demanded a federal investigation after ICE agents were filmed urinating on high school grounds before a raid. Ward Sakeik, the stateless Palestinian woman twice targeted for removal despite a court order, was released from custody after four months, following sustained legal effort by her and her American husband. And across the country, the 50501 Movement organized mutual-aid and community events for the holiday, a grassroots counterpoint to a week otherwise dominated by concentrated federal action.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government moving with unusual speed and coordination across its legislative, executive, and judicial branches toward a single outcome: a larger, more heavily funded enforcement apparatus paired with a smaller social safety net, achieved partly by setting aside the procedural friction normally built into each institution. The Senate's disregard for its own parliamentarian, the House's adoption of the bill under direct presidential pressure, and the Supreme Court's narrowing of the injunctions and protections traditionally available to litigants each removed a distinct brake on the exercise of power. Yet the week did not pass unopposed. Federal judges blocked firings and TPS terminations even as Congress advanced its bill; state attorneys general filed suit over data-sharing practices; agency employees signed public dissents; sitting officials were arrested for acts of oversight, and their arrests themselves became public controversies; and ordinary citizens organized protests and community events on the very day the legislation was signed. The result was a week in which the concentration of federal power and the persistence of institutional and civic resistance advanced side by side, leaving the country's checks strained but not silent. ```

Title: This Week in Democracy: Floods, Firings, and a Weaponized Federal Government
Content:
```markdown Central Texas was still counting its dead when the rest of the week's machinery began turning. Catastrophic flooding killed dozens of people and left hundreds missing, and in the days that followed, a familiar pattern emerged: the National Weather Service's warnings had been degraded by earlier staffing cuts, and a new Department of Homeland Security approval requirement delayed FEMA's search-and-rescue teams by more than three days. Rather than address the shortfall, DHS accused the media of "deliberate lying" about the disaster's causes. It was a preview of the week's dominant theme — a government stripped of capacity, then defensive about the consequences.

The weekend carried other, equally consequential news. The Supreme Court narrowed the ability of federal judges to block executive actions on a nationwide basis, a procedural shift that would ripple through nearly every legal fight against the administration for the rest of the year. Its first casualties were visible almost immediately: eight immigrants with no ties to South Sudan were deported there after a judge's authority to stop the move was curtailed by the very ruling handed down days earlier. Meanwhile, President Trump signed a sprawling reconciliation bill that made the 2017 tax cuts permanent, cut roughly $1.1 trillion combined from Medicaid and food assistance, and funneled $170 billion into immigration enforcement, including $51.6 billion for a border wall — adding an estimated $3.4 trillion to the deficit in the process. The same weekend brought a purge of national security leadership, with NSA Director Gen. Timothy Haugh and six National Security Council staffers fired after being named on lists supplied by an outside influencer, and an FBI agent resigning over what he described as political pressure and ideological screening. Trump also pardoned January 6 defendants while directing the Justice Department to investigate his critics, and Elon Musk, breaking publicly with the president over the budget bill, filed paperwork to launch a new political party.

By Monday, the Court's influence was compounding. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. dismissed all 17 members of the CDC's vaccine advisory panel, replacing them with vaccine skeptics, while promoting unproven measles treatments and reviving a long-discredited vaccine-autism claim — actions that would draw lawsuits from medical associations and a pregnant physician within days. In Los Angeles, federal agents and National Guard troops staged a militarized raid in the MacArthur Park neighborhood, complete with armored vehicles and horseback units; no arrests were made, and local officials called it intimidation, a "reality TV spectacle" with no evident law-enforcement purpose. It was the first of several such operations that would grow more violent as the week went on. Separately, the Supreme Court allowed the administration's plan for mass federal layoffs to proceed over a sharp dissent from Justice Jackson, and in Boston, a trial opened to determine whether immigration law had been used to deport pro-Palestinian foreign students over their political speech — a First Amendment test with implications well beyond the individual defendants. The day closed with a jolt to the administration's own coalition: the Justice Department announced it had found no evidence of an Epstein client list, reversing earlier promises and triggering backlash from MAGA-aligned figures and House Democrats alike, an unusual moment of shared frustration across the political divide.

Tuesday deepened the structural story. The Supreme Court ruled that a former president holds broad immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts, a decision that narrows the law's reach over the nation's most powerful office. That same day, even as flood recovery continued in Texas, the administration announced plans to dismantle FEMA entirely by the end of hurricane season, arguing states and private enterprise could manage disaster response instead. A presidential memo stripped security clearances from Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton, Kamala Harris, and a whistleblower attorney, prompting a lawsuit alleging unconstitutional retaliation. In San Francisco, an unmarked ICE vehicle drove through a crowd of protesters outside the immigration court, injuring at least one person, while agents used batons, pepper spray, and rifles against demonstrators with no visible police intervention. Trump floated the idea of a federal takeover of New York City should Zohran Mamdani win the mayoral race, and suggested Washington, D.C. might similarly come under direct federal control. The IRS, meanwhile, announced that churches could endorse political candidates without losing tax-exempt status, ending a seventy-year interpretation of the Johnson Amendment, and a new report showed the Pentagon budget approaching $1 trillion annually, with more than half of recent discretionary spending flowing to private contractors. Marines and National Guard troops were dispatched to Florida to support ICE operations, including a pilot program stationing agents at a Marine Corps base.

Wednesday brought the Supreme Court's third major intervention of the week, clearing the way for mass firings across nineteen federal agencies. The Justice Department sued California over its transgender athlete policies and subpoenaed more than twenty clinics providing gender-affirming care to minors. In Florida, the Miami City Commission voted to postpone its 2025 municipal election to 2026 without voter input, extending the terms of officials who would otherwise have faced reelection — a move critics called a direct assault on voters' right to choose their representatives. Trump escalated his tariff campaign, announcing a 50 percent tariff on Brazil explicitly tied to the domestic prosecution of former president Jair Bolsonaro, opening a trade investigation into Brazil's social media regulations, and issuing new tariffs against the Philippines, Algeria, Iraq, and other nations. ICE detained an Ohio imam whose asylum status had been abruptly terminated and separately arrested a mother of four U.S.-born children who had lived in the country since age three. Trump repeated his federal-takeover threats against New York and Washington, and Florida opened a new detention facility in the Everglades that was quickly reported to have inhumane conditions. He also signed Medicaid work-requirement legislation, with administration officials suggesting recipients could replace migrant farm labor lost to deportation — tying the week's healthcare cuts directly to its immigration crackdown.

Thursday offered the week's clearest picture of institutions adapting under pressure. A federal judge in New Hampshire blocked Trump's executive order ending birthright citizenship, certifying a nationwide class action — a narrower legal tool deployed precisely because the Supreme Court had foreclosed broader injunctions days earlier. It was a rare demonstration that courts could still constrain executive action, even after losing some of their sharpest instruments. But the same day, DHS eliminated its Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties along with two immigration ombudsman offices, removing internal oversight just as detention and enforcement were intensifying. A former DOJ attorney, Erez Reuveni, produced text messages supporting his claim that a senior Justice Department official had instructed lawyers to disregard court orders blocking deportations to El Salvador — evidence striking directly at the rule of law. In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott announced plans to redraw the state's congressional map mid-decade at the Trump administration's urging, aiming to secure additional Republican seats before the midterms. Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil filed a $20 million claim alleging false imprisonment after months of detention without charges tied to his campus activism, and Rep. Jared Moskowitz renewed calls for a congressional investigation into the DHS approval rule that had delayed flood rescue teams.

The week closed on Friday with the State Department issuing termination notices to more than 1,300 employees — roughly 15 percent of its domestic staff — as part of a reorganization built around an "America First" foreign policy. In California, federal agents and National Guard troops raided cannabis farms in Carpinteria and Camarillo, arresting 200 workers and using chemical munitions on protesters; a farmworker later died from injuries sustained during the operation, the grimmest point yet in a week of escalating enforcement violence. North Carolina lawmakers advanced legislation that would replace nonpartisan election board members with partisan appointees, alongside a separate bill critics said could restrict political expression on government property. And it was confirmed that DHS had canceled a $3 million grant meant to improve communication between the National Weather Service and local officials — the same kind of infrastructure whose absence had contributed to the Texas flood death toll, cut even as search and rescue operations were still underway.

Taken together, the week traced a government reorganizing itself around loyalty, force, and diminished oversight, often while insisting nothing had gone wrong. A disaster exposed what years of quiet budget cuts had hollowed out, and the response was not reinforcement but further retrenchment — a plan to eliminate the very agency meant to answer such disasters. Courts lost some of their broadest tools to check the presidency, then improvised narrower ones to preserve constitutional guarantees, an adaptation that succeeded this week but whose durability remains untested. Security clearances, silence orders, and personnel purges were turned against critics and career officials alike, while oversight offices built to catch abuses in immigration enforcement were dismantled just as that enforcement grew more forceful and, in California, fatal. Even the administration's own coalition found reason for public anger, when a long-promised disclosure evaporated into denial. None of these developments occurred in isolation; each fed the next, and by week's end the throughline was unmistakable — a widening gap between the institutions meant to check power and the pace at which that power was being exercised. ```
