Title: This Week in Democracy: Minneapolis, a Shutdown, and a Supreme Court Rebuke
Content:
```markdown This week began with the aftermath of federal force still raw. Immigration operations in Minneapolis had already resulted in the deaths of two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, and over the weekend federal agents pepper-sprayed observers even as enforcement continued, with thousands detained and protesters and journalists facing arrest. The administration then moved to withhold federal funding from Minnesota, a step widely read as retaliation against a state resisting the crackdown, while the Justice Department issued subpoenas to state officials. In a separate but overlapping story, a partial government shutdown began Saturday after the Senate failed to pass Department of Homeland Security appropriations. Democrats withheld their votes pending reforms — visible agent identification, body cameras, judicial warrants — but the leverage proved limited in practice: roughly ninety percent of DHS staff kept working without pay, and ICE and CBP operations continued largely unaffected under prior funding. The weekend also saw Trump announce, via social media, his intention to impose voter ID requirements and eliminate mail-in ballots without congressional authorization, a move paired with DHS's use of a flawed voter-verification tool that had misclassified naturalized citizens as noncitizens. Alongside these developments, disputes over the Epstein files continued, with the Justice Department claiming full compliance with the Epstein Transparency Act even as survivors and advocates alleged that roughly half the files remained withheld.

By Monday, the fallout from Minneapolis had migrated into unexpected venues. Broadway dancers staging a memorial performance for Good and Pretti at the Lincoln Memorial were stopped mid-performance by twenty-three officers after moving to the Kennedy Center; the White House Communications Director later dismissed the tribute as "weak, corny, and lame." The same day brought a development with broader implications for political media: new FCC guidance eliminating the blanket exemption for talk-show political interviews prompted CBS to block Stephen Colbert from airing his interview with Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. Colbert released it independently online, but the episode marked the start of a pattern that would recur through the week. Local governments, meanwhile, began pushing back on ICE expansion directly — establishing "ICE-free zones," blocking a warehouse sale intended for detention-center conversion, and canceling contracts tied to enforcement operations — even as DHS refused to share evidence in the ongoing investigation into the Pretti shooting. In a narrower but symbolically resonant case, a federal judge ordered the National Park Service to restore a dismantled slavery exhibit at Independence National Historical Park, rejecting the administration's removal of the display. The day closed with Democratic lawmakers announcing a boycott of the upcoming State of the Union and reports that DHS had subpoenaed tech companies for identifying data on social media accounts critical of ICE.

Tuesday was among the most consequential days of the week. House Democrats filed articles of impeachment against DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, citing violations of public trust and obstruction of oversight tied directly to the Minneapolis shootings — a formal congressional accountability mechanism activated in direct response to lethal enforcement action. The same day, the House Oversight Committee compelled filmed depositions from Bill and Hillary Clinton after threatening contempt, while Jeffrey Epstein associate Les Wexner also testified about his past ties to Epstein — a rare instance of subpoena power reaching the highest tier of former officials. Outside Washington, a coordinated National Day of Lobbying brought constituents to nearly one hundred congressional district offices, organized by groups including Citizens' Impeachment and the 50501 Movement, demanding impeachment proceedings and, in some cases, the abolition of ICE. Personal-enrichment threads also surfaced this day for the first time as a distinct pattern: Trump filed trademark applications tied to his name for use on an airport, Florida's legislature advanced a bill to rename Palm Beach International Airport after him, and reporting raised self-dealing allegations connected to a DHS spokesperson's $220 million ad campaign, alongside scrutiny of Trump family business dealings with the UAE and an Israeli defense contractor. Amid this, the human cost of enforcement practices came into sharp focus: a two-month-old, Juan Nicolás, was deported to Mexico the same day he was discharged from hospital treatment for bronchitis. Separately, an immigration judge blocked the deportation of Palestinian activist Mohsen Mahdawi, ruling government evidence inadmissible.

Wednesday brought further expansion of detention infrastructure alongside new institutional friction. The federal government finalized a $128 million purchase of a warehouse in Social Circle, Georgia, to convert into a 10,000-person detention facility, proceeding despite objections from local officials who cited infrastructure strain and a lack of consultation. DHS separately sought approval to purchase a $70 million luxury jet — featuring a bedroom, showers, and a bar — for deportation flights and Cabinet travel, a proposal that drew criticism for its contrast with the conditions faced by those being deported. The media-freedom story from Monday escalated rather than resolved: CBS again blocked Colbert's interview citing FCC concerns, while the FCC opened a formal investigation into a similar interview aired by ABC's "The View" — applying its equal-time rule to television but notably not to talk radio, a selectivity that drew scrutiny in its own right. On the environmental front, the EPA repealed the 2009 greenhouse gas endangerment finding along with related vehicle emissions standards, prompting an immediate lawsuit from health and environmental groups. Perhaps most significant institutionally, the administration acknowledged in a New Jersey court filing that it had violated federal court orders more than fifty times over ten weeks, including deportations carried out despite standing injunctions and missed bond-hearing deadlines — a rare admission of sustained noncompliance with judicial authority. The day closed with a mistrial declared in the first-ever terrorism prosecution of alleged antifa protesters at an ICE facility, after a defense attorney's clothing was deemed potentially prejudicial to the jury.

Thursday deepened several of these threads while opening new ones. A DHS memo authorized ICE to detain legally admitted refugees indefinitely for "rescreening" under a program called Operation Parris, reversing a 2010 policy and appearing to conflict directly with a standing Minnesota federal court order blocking further refugee arrests. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed broad recommendations for six routine childhood immunizations the same day the CDC's vaccine advisory panel meeting was postponed amid a legal challenge from the American Academy of Pediatrics questioning the panel's legitimacy. In Illinois, Governor J.B. Pritzker used his State of the State address to announce the elimination of $1 billion in medical debt while directly accusing the administration of illegally withholding $8.4 billion in appropriated federal funds from the state — a pointed instance of a state executive publicly confronting federal funding pressure. New lawsuits also emerged Thursday challenging Trump's proposed twenty-five-story "Independence Arch" near the Lincoln Memorial for bypassing statutory review, and separately seeking to block the destruction of federal records at NASA's Goddard archive. HUD, meanwhile, proposed a rule that could evict tens of thousands of families with undocumented members from public housing, including nearly 37,000 US citizen children — extending immigration enforcement into a new domain of federal policy.

The week's sharpest institutional confrontation arrived on Friday. The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that Trump had exceeded his authority in imposing tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, reaffirming that the power to tax rests with Congress — a significant and relatively rare judicial check on unilateral executive trade authority. Within hours, Trump announced a new 10 percent global tariff, soon raised to 15 percent, invoking Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 and its 150-day emergency authority to route around the ruling almost immediately. The speed of the workaround raised an open question about how durable the Court's constraint would actually prove in practice. The same day, Senator Susan Collins cast the fiftieth vote for a measure critics describe as undermining free and fair elections, while Trump promoted the legislation in Georgia, framing it as a guarantee of Republican victories for decades — a claim that drew immediate criticism given the bill's implications for ballot access. California lawmakers moved in the opposite direction, introducing legislation to bar ICE agents from polling places. Florida's legislature finalized its bill renaming Palm Beach International Airport after Trump the same day he announced a $10 billion U.S. commitment to his "Board of Peace," an unauthorized spending pledge that critics said belonged to Congress, alongside a proposal for a costly American alternative to the World Health Organization. The week closed with Judge Sunshine Sykes accusing the administration of terrorizing immigrants through its mass detention practices and ordering DHS to notify detainees of bond eligibility, while, inside the Justice Department itself, employees hung a protest banner depicting Trump — a small but telling sign of friction within the federal workforce carrying out these policies.

Taken as a whole, the week traced several overlapping struggles over where authority actually resides in American government. Federal enforcement power collided with local resistance and judicial oversight in Minneapolis and Georgia; congressional appropriations power collided with an executive determined to keep enforcement running regardless of funding status; and the Supreme Court's tariff ruling collided almost instantly with an executive workaround that tested whether a constitutional check could be absorbed and bypassed within a single afternoon. Courts remained the most consistent site of resistance to executive overreach, issuing rulings on detention, deportation, historical preservation, and admitted violations of their own orders — even as new detention and surveillance authorities expanded elsewhere. Meanwhile, a persistent undercurrent of personal branding and financial entanglement, from airport trademarks to a luxury jet to an unauthorized nine-figure fund, ran alongside these institutional confrontations, a reminder that the exercise of power and the pursuit of personal gain were, this week as in prior weeks, difficult to fully separate. ```

Title: Tariffs Defied, a Court Report Sealed, and a Congressman Removed Twice
Content:
```markdown This week began with a defeat for the presidency and ended, in practice, as something closer to a demonstration of how little a defeat can mean. On Saturday, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that President Trump's global tariffs, imposed under emergency economic powers, were unconstitutional — a reminder that the power to tax and regulate commerce belongs to Congress, not the executive alone. Within a day, the White House announced a new 10 percent global tariff under a different statute, then raised it to 15 percent. Confusion followed almost immediately: businesses were unsure whether refunds were owed, European trade officials paused a pending ratification, and legal analysts debated whether the new tariffs were simply the old ones wearing a different label. It was the first and clearest expression of a pattern that would recur throughout the week — adverse rulings treated not as boundaries but as prompts to find another route to the same destination.

The weekend also brought a string of courtroom setbacks for federal immigration enforcement. Judges in Minneapolis and Los Angeles dismissed assault charges against men accused of confronting ICE officers, in both cases because sworn statements from federal agents conflicted with video evidence or were internally inconsistent. These were not isolated technical dismissals; they raised pointed questions about the reliability of the government's own account of enforcement encounters. Meanwhile, a government funding standoff forced TSA to suspend PreCheck and Global Entry over staffing shortages — PreCheck was restored within twelve hours after industry pressure, but Global Entry remained down, a small but telling sign of how quickly a funding fight can degrade everyday public services. Elsewhere over the weekend, the Justice Department intervened to back a lawsuit challenging Los Angeles school district equity policies as discriminatory against white students, a federal appeals court allowed Louisiana's mandatory Ten Commandments classroom law to take effect, and ICE detained a longtime Michigan resident with a pending deportation appeal along with a British tourist holding a valid visa for six weeks — cases that, together with continuing protests in North Carolina against a planned detention center expansion, showed enforcement pressing against even settled legal residents and visitors.

By Monday, three threads had emerged that would run through the rest of the week. The Department of Justice's release of files related to Jeffrey Epstein continued to ripple through academic and media institutions, prompting resignations, faculty reviews, and cancellations at Columbia, Harvard, Yale, and CBS as previously hidden connections came to light. Separately, Judge Aileen Cannon — a Trump appointee — permanently blocked the release of the second volume of Special Counsel Jack Smith's report on the handling of classified documents, with the Justice Department declining to contest the motion. That decision effectively sealed a significant investigative record on a former president's conduct from both Congress and the public, permanently. And a former ICE training instructor, Ryan Schwank, testified to Congress that officer training hours had been cut and that instruction had included guidance on entering homes without warrants — testimony serious enough that he resigned in protest after giving it. A Texas judge, meanwhile, ordered the release of a five-year-old asylum seeker who had been detained with his father, criticizing the government's justification for holding a child. On the tariff front, FedEx sued for refunds and Illinois Governor JB Pritzker sent the White House a symbolic $8.7 billion invoice for tariff-related costs to state families — early signs that industry and state governments intended to keep pressing the legal question the Court had just settled. House Republicans also passed a resolution using the Congressional Review Act to overturn a mining moratorium near Minnesota's Boundary Waters, part of a broader effort to apply the expedited tool retroactively to environmental protections.

Tuesday's State of the Union address turned into the week's most visible flashpoint. Aliya Rahman, a disabled guest of Rep. Ilhan Omar, was forcibly arrested by Capitol Police for standing silently in the gallery. Rep. Al Green was separately removed for holding up a sign protesting a racially charged video the president had shared about the Obamas. Both incidents put security power on public display, aimed not at any disruption but at symbolic and silent dissent inside the chamber itself. At least 40 Democratic members of Congress skipped the speech entirely, opting instead for a "People's State of the Union" event on the National Mall organized by outside groups — a boycott large enough to represent real institutional estrangement from a presidential ritual rather than a scattered protest. In his remarks, Trump claimed the Supreme Court's tariff ruling had actually given him "far more powers" and threatened higher tariffs on countries that "play games," even as House Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledged, separately, that Congress had no appetite to formally codify the tariffs Trump was already imposing — a gap between claimed authority and actual legislative backing that went largely unresolved. The same day, Senate Democrats opened an investigation into whether FCC Chair Brendan Carr and Paramount had blocked a Stephen Colbert interview to benefit the administration amid a pending merger review.

Wednesday deepened the Epstein-files story considerably. NPR and the New York Times reported that the Justice Department had withheld more than 50 pages of FBI interviews with a woman accusing Trump of sexual abuse as a minor — a disclosure gap that appeared to conflict directly with the Epstein Files Transparency Act Congress had passed. House Democrats opened a formal probe. It was the clearest evidence yet that transparency commitments around the Epstein files might bend when they touched the president himself, and it connected directly back to the sealed Jack Smith report from two days earlier — two separate legal mechanisms, in the same week, both working to keep records concerning the president's conduct out of public view. There was a countervailing note: a magistrate judge blocked the Justice Department from searching the electronic devices of Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson, criticizing the government's legal filing and citing First Amendment concerns — a rare, clean press-freedom win. The Justice Department also sued UCLA over alleged campus antisemitism tied to pro-Palestinian protests, part of a widening legal campaign against universities in Democratic-led states. And Vice President Vance announced that the administration would withhold $259.5 million in Medicaid reimbursements from Minnesota over fraud concerns; state officials called the move politically motivated, and later reporting connected it to sentiment surrounding the state's Somali population — the clearest instance yet of federal spending power being wielded against a specific, disfavored state population rather than applied neutrally.

Thursday brought a case that fused several of the week's concerns into one episode. DHS agents, posing falsely as police searching for a missing child, arrested Columbia student Elmina Aghayeva; she was released only after direct intervention from both President Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, drawing criticism for the use of deception as an enforcement tactic. In Kansas, lawmakers overrode the governor's veto to enact a law invalidating transgender residents' driver's licenses and permitting private lawsuits against transgender people in restrooms, stripping legal recognition from an entire class of state residents in one legislative stroke. DHS separately awarded a $250,000 public-relations contract to a Republican consulting firm with ties to former Trump campaign officials, following a 31-hour bidding window that reportedly required demonstrated loyalty to administration policy — a striking departure from standard procurement neutrality. An Oregon federal judge, meanwhile, ruled against the administration's abandonment of a Biden-era agreement protecting endangered Columbia and Snake River salmon, finding the government had presented evidence contradicting the established scientific record. And the EPA repealed the endangerment finding that underlies federal greenhouse gas regulation, while rolling back offshore wind approvals and clean energy incentives — a move tied to an estimated 170,000 clean energy jobs lost or delayed, and one that dismantled a foundational legal basis for climate policy built up over more than a decade.

Friday extended several of these threads to their sharpest points. The EPA followed its repeal of the endangerment finding with blanket exemptions for 71 coal plants from mercury and air toxics rules dating to 2024, in some cases granting longer exemptions than requested even where compliance technology already existed. Federal authorities arrested 25 more people connected to a January anti-ICE protest at a St. Paul church, bringing the total charged to 39 — a scale of prosecution over a single demonstration that signaled a widening use of criminal charges against organized dissent. A nearly blind Rohingya refugee, released from federal custody and driven miles from his home without notice to his family or attorney, was later found dead; the agency described the drop-off as a courtesy, a characterization that sat uneasily against his evident vulnerability. Elsewhere, a federal judge blocked DHS from detaining lawfully admitted refugees solely for not yet adjusting to permanent resident status, reaffirming statutory limits on detention authority, and raids at California fast food locations triggered fear and walkouts among workers, prompting a local union to draft a pledge urging employers to require judicial warrants before granting ICE access to workplaces. Community pressure in Concord, North Carolina led property owners to publicly reject leasing space for a planned ICE facility, even as a state elections board advanced new voting restrictions based on unsubstantiated noncitizen-voting claims. Perhaps most consequentially, right-wing activists circulated a draft executive order that would declare a national emergency over debunked 2020 election-interference claims in order to assert federal control over voting processes, including bans on mail-in ballots and voting machines — a proposal legal experts described as unconstitutional on its face. A separate Republican legal filing sought to revive the independent state legislature theory, aiming to insulate gerrymandered maps from state court review.

Taken as a whole, the week displayed a government whose formal checks were functioning — courts dismissed weak prosecutions, blocked improper detentions, protected a journalist's sources, and struck down an unlawful tariff regime — while the executive branch and allied state legislatures worked, often successfully, to route around each of those checks rather than absorb them. A Supreme Court ruling became a same-day workaround. A congressional transparency law met a records gap. A disabled bystander's silence in a public gallery met physical removal. A state's Medicaid funding met a freeze tied to who its residents were. None of this required the machinery of government to break; it required only that adverse rulings be treated as starting points for negotiation rather than as settled boundaries — a distinction that, multiplied across a single week, says a great deal about where authority in American governance was actually being tested. ```

Title: War Without a Vote
Content:
```markdown This was a week defined by a president who acted first and asked no one—not Congress, not the courts, not the public—and by the halting, often failed efforts of other institutions to catch up. It opened with strikes on Iran announced by video and closed with those strikes still underway, Congress having twice declined to reassert its own constitutional authority. In between, a cabinet secretary lost her job under bipartisan pressure, a court-ordered tariff refund gave way to a new tariff within days, and a private AI company found itself squeezed by the machinery of national-security law over a policy disagreement. Threaded through all of it were older, unresolved stories—Epstein-related testimony, election-integrity claims, protest restrictions—that moved without resolving.

**The Weekend.** It began with President Trump announcing military operations against Iran in a Truth Social video, calling for regime change and warning of a long conflict. The strikes proceeded even though Pentagon officials would later tell Congress there was no intelligence pointing to an imminent Iranian threat. Regional airspace closed and Iran's internet went dark within hours—consequences arriving before any public deliberation had occurred. The same weekend, the administration moved on a different front: after Anthropic refused Pentagon demands to loosen its AI safety guidelines, the Defense Department labeled the company a national-security supply-chain risk, a designation ordinarily reserved for foreign adversaries, and terminated its government contracts with the firm. Domestic frictions ran in parallel. A DHS memo instructed agents to flag naturalized citizens who had registered or voted before naturalization, reviving fears about noncitizen voting despite its rarity. The FBI searched Fulton County's election office over recycled 2020 fraud claims, and Los Angeles superintendent Alberto Carvalho was placed on leave after an FBI raid connected to a defunct ed-tech contractor—raising questions about whether the investigation was tied to his resistance to immigration enforcement near schools. Bill Clinton, meanwhile, testified for more than six hours before the House Oversight Committee on Epstein, the first former president compelled to testify under threat of contempt.

**Monday.** Trump confirmed the start of full combat operations, again bypassing ordinary channels, while Senator Tim Kaine and Representative Thomas Massie began pushing bipartisan war powers resolutions. The Pentagon's private assessment—that Iran had not been planning an unprovoked attack—stood in stark contrast to the administration's public rationale. New reporting added a further complication: Jared Kushner's firm had received Saudi and Emirati investment, and a Trump-branded development deal in Saudi Arabia was underway, even as both nations lobbied for military action against Iran. The financial entanglements did not prove motive, but they hung uncomfortably over a war launched without public debate. Florida lawmakers used the same day to advance a slate of bills criminalizing "foreign influence" political activity, restricting university funding tied to activism, empowering officials to designate groups as terrorist organizations, and creating a new state counterintelligence unit—a coordinated expansion of state power over dissent. In Washington, Senator Thom Tillis and colleagues grilled DHS Secretary Kristi Noem over the detention of American citizens, FEMA failures, and a $220 million advertising contract tied to a politically connected firm; Tillis called outright for her resignation. Courts, meanwhile, continued their quieter work, limiting DHS grant conditions on localities and protecting the *New York Times*' FOIA rights in a national-security case.

**Tuesday.** Two threads sharpened that would recur through the week. The House passed the SAVE America Act, 218-213, requiring proof of citizenship with documents matching a voter's current legal name—a technical requirement that could affect an estimated 69 million women who changed their names after marriage, with harsh penalties attached for election workers who err. And DHS's own inspector general told Congress that the department had refused to cooperate with a federal criminal investigation carrying national-security implications, part of a broader pattern of obstructed oversight. Noem faced renewed scrutiny before the Senate Judiciary Committee, refusing to retract her description of two Minnesotans killed by federal agents as "domestic terrorists" and denying enforcement quotas existed despite her own earlier public statements to the contrary. The Justice Department, days after signaling it would drop its defense of Trump's executive orders penalizing law firms tied to disfavored clients, abruptly reversed course and resumed the defense—a whiplash that suggested political pressure shaping litigation strategy. Separately, reporting surfaced that new Polymarket accounts had profited nearly a million dollars betting on a U.S. strike on Iran before it happened, while a fabricated war map had been used elsewhere to fake a Russian advance for betting gain, exposing how thinly regulated prediction markets can be exploited around matters of war.

**Wednesday.** The week brought its first formal reckoning on war powers. The Senate voted 47-53 against Kaine's resolution requiring congressional approval to continue military action, largely along party lines, leaving Trump free to proceed. The same day, a House Judiciary hearing turned up new discomfort for Noem: Trump had publicly contradicted her testimony that he personally approved the DHS ad campaign, and reports surfaced of internal turmoil tied to her relationship with a senior adviser. In Texas, a Republican-dominated state supreme court blocked a lower court's order extending primary voting hours in Dallas and Williamson counties amid widespread confusion over polling locations, ordering late ballots set aside rather than counted. The House Oversight Committee voted 24-19 to subpoena Attorney General Pam Bondi over the DOJ's handling of Epstein files, following the accidental release of survivors' names and unexplained redactions. And in a smaller but telling move, the DOJ opened an inquiry into former President Biden's use of an autopen, reportedly at Trump's own urging, without yet building any criminal case.

**Thursday.** The week's institutional consequences reached their conclusions. The House voted 212-219 against its own companion war powers resolution, following the Senate's rejection a day earlier—leaving both chambers, within 48 hours of each other, unwilling to reclaim authority the Constitution assigns to Congress. Kristi Noem was fired as DHS Secretary. After weeks of bipartisan criticism over the ad campaign, the Minnesota enforcement deaths, and contested testimony, Trump removed her and named Senator Markwayne Mullin as her replacement, effective at month's end; Noem was reassigned to a new envoy role. The change registered as a genuine break in personnel, but not in policy—the hardline enforcement approach that had drawn criticism showed no sign of softening under new leadership. The same day, a coalition of 24 states led by New York Attorney General Letitia James sued to block a new 15 percent tariff imposed under different statutory authority, arguing that Trump still lacked the power even after the Supreme Court had struck down his earlier "liberation day" tariffs. The administration escalated its pressure on Anthropic further, threatening to cut the company off from partners like Nvidia and Microsoft before abruptly shifting its own AI partnership to OpenAI. Elsewhere, a Haitian asylum seeker named Emmanuel Damas died in ICE custody of septic shock after staff failed to act on weeks of reported severe pain, and a gunman attacked a Dallas detention facility linked to ICE—two incidents, one of neglect and one of violence, both reflecting how volatile immigration enforcement had become. The DOJ also proposed a rule that would shield its own attorneys from state bar discipline pending internal review, even as Bondi separately directed staff to "zealously advance" the president's interests.

**Friday.** The week's loops closed, though rarely toward resolution. Trump reimposed 15 percent global tariffs under new legal authority just days after the Supreme Court's ruling against his earlier tariffs had forced refunds—refunds that Customs and Border Protection began processing at nearly the same moment the new tariffs took effect. Senator Richard Blumenthal opened a perjury investigation into Noem over whether she had misled Congress about adviser Corey Lewandowski's role in DHS contracting decisions. The White House ballroom project advanced despite overwhelming public opposition: the Commission of Fine Arts approved the $400 million plan to replace the East Wing, even as the National Capital Planning Commission postponed its own vote after receiving more than 35,000 comments, 97 percent opposed, and a federal judge declined to halt construction. Trump announced Mullin's appointment to succeed Noem via social media, ahead of any Senate confirmation process. Representative Tony Gonzales ended his re-election bid amid an ethics investigation tied to a past affair. CMS began migrating Medicare systems affecting 70 million Americans to Oracle's cloud platform, including generative AI tools, with little congressional scrutiny of the privacy implications. Kansas overrode its governor's veto to pass new anti-trans restrictions, and similar legislation advanced in Missouri, even as North Carolina primary voters rejected three anti-trans incumbents—a split verdict on the same underlying fight. The California State University system sued the Department of Education over Title IX conditions tied to a transgender athlete case, testing whether federal funding could be used to dictate university policy. And the DOJ quietly retreated from the autopen investigation into Biden, concluding there was no credible basis to proceed—a small instance of institutional resistance holding, even under direct presidential pressure.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government whose formal checks kept convening, arguing, and voting—and kept losing. Congress held hearings, drafted resolutions, and issued subpoenas, but failed twice on the one vote that would have reasserted its constitutional claim over war. Courts continued to rule against the executive on trade power, only to watch the same authority reassembled under a different statute within days. A cabinet secretary was removed under real bipartisan pressure, yet the policies she oversaw continued unaltered under her successor. Private companies, universities, and law firms found themselves treated as instruments to be pressured rather than institutions to be persuaded. None of this occurred through any single dramatic rupture; it accumulated through ordinary mechanisms—hearings, memos, contract terminations, court filings—each individually explicable, collectively describing a system straining to hold executive power accountable and, this week at least, not quite managing to. ```

Title: War Without a Vote
Content:
```markdown This was a week defined by a war the president started on his own authority and then struggled to explain, alongside an escalating campaign to rewrite the rules of American voting, and a judiciary that kept intervening to check both. By week's end, gas prices had spiked to levels unseen in years, a synagogue and a university ROTC program had both been attacked, and courts in three separate cases had told the executive branch it had exceeded its lawful authority.

The weekend began with the launch itself. Trump initiated air and naval operations against Iran alongside Israel without seeking congressional war authorization, a break from precedent that Republican leaders defended as falling within the president's inherent powers. The rhetoric escalated almost immediately: a Miami summit floated using military force against Latin American drug cartels and even raised the possibility of regime change in Cuba, suggesting the administration saw the Iran operation as a template rather than an isolated action. That same weekend, a federal court intervened on a separate front: Judge Royce Lamberth ruled that Kari Lake's appointment as acting head of the U.S. Agency for Global Media had violated the Vacancies Act, voiding her mass layoffs of more than 1,000 Voice of America journalists and her reduction of the agency's broadcast languages from 49 to four. Lake said she would appeal, but the ruling stood as an early marker of judicial pushback against unconfirmed executive appointments — a pattern that would recur before the week was out.

Violence touched the weekend directly as well. Two teenagers who described themselves as ISIS supporters threw improvised explosive devices during dueling protests outside New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's residence. Neither device detonated, and both suspects were charged with federal terrorism offenses, but the incident underscored how the atmosphere of the moment was drawing extremist actors near the seats of elected officials. Separately, a three-year prosecution of a Cop City protester concluded with an Alford plea: John Mazurek avoided conviction but accepted a decade of probation barring him from anti-government protest activity, closing out a case that had involved extended pretrial detention and surveillance later found to raise Fourth Amendment concerns. And the EPA repealed the scientific finding underpinning federal greenhouse gas regulation, even as the Justice Department simultaneously argued in court that federal law preempted state climate superfund laws — a contradiction state attorneys general said undercut the government's own legal position.

By Monday, the administration's demand for a new voting law had become explicit. Trump began pressing Congress to pass the Save America Act — legislation requiring proof of citizenship, banning most mail voting, and folding in unrelated culture-war provisions — and said he would not sign other legislation until it passed. The same day, the Supreme Court struck down Trump's tariff regime as exceeding presidential authority, opening the door to potentially $175 billion in corporate refunds and triggering an immediate wave of lawsuits. Monday also brought a significant oversight story: reporting revealed that DHS's civil rights and detention ombudsman offices had been cut by more than 90 percent, even as at least 15 people died in ICE custody during fiscal year 2025 — the highest total in years — and congressional investigators documented 510 credible abuse allegations, some involving children. Separately, the White House ordered a hold placed on an FBI, DHS, and National Counterterrorism Center bulletin warning of elevated domestic threats tied to the Iran war, blocking it from reaching state and local law enforcement. A federal grand jury also subpoenaed Arizona's state legislature for records from its 2020 election review, which Trump celebrated publicly and Arizona's attorney general called an effort to weaponize federal law enforcement against a settled election. The administration additionally ended Temporary Protected Status for roughly 2,500 Somali nationals despite a documented hunger crisis and active terrorism risk in Somalia. And on the war itself, Trump's messaging began to fracture: he told one outlet the war was "very complete" while telling House Republicans "we have won in many ways, but not enough" — a contradiction that would deepen as the week went on.

Tuesday sharpened both storylines. Senators emerged from a classified Iran briefing frustrated by unanswered questions about war costs, the possibility of ground troops, and the absence of any coherent postwar plan; Senator Warren invoked Congress's power of the purse as a potential check. That same day, officials were caught in a string of false statements — Trump wrongly claimed Iran possessed Tomahawk missiles and denied U.S. responsibility for a strike on a girls' school, while Energy Secretary Chris Wright falsely claimed the Navy had escorted a tanker through the Strait of Hormuz before deleting the post. The Pentagon also revised its public estimate of wounded troops sharply upward, from fewer than a dozen to as many as 150, only after independent reporting forced the correction. Judicial pushback continued as well: Judge Matthew Brann ruled that three New Jersey federal prosecutors installed by Attorney General Bondi to bypass Senate confirmation had been illegally appointed, echoing an earlier ruling in the Alina Habba case and reinforcing the pattern of courts rejecting unconfirmed executive appointments. In Utah, Republicans moved to block withdrawal of signatures from an anti-gerrymandering repeal petition and expanded the state supreme court from five to seven justices, a maneuver critics described as court-packing meant to blunt adverse redistricting rulings. Meanwhile, the human and financial costs of the war became visible to ordinary Americans: gasoline in California topped $5 a gallon and oil prices hit their highest levels since 2022 as the Hormuz shipping crisis deepened, contradicting earlier administration claims that the situation was nearly resolved.

Wednesday brought the most direct challenge yet to the war's stated justification. U.S. intelligence agencies told congressional staff privately that available intelligence did not support Trump's claim that Iran had been preparing an imminent strike — the rationale originally given for launching the operation. The top Democrat on the intelligence committee said he had seen no evidence of such a threat. The same day, Trump said he did not know about a military investigation finding the United States responsible for a strike that killed at least 175 people, mostly children, at an Iranian girls' school, and separately claimed the U.S. had struck 28 mine-laying ships despite earlier reporting of only sixteen. Civil society responded in kind: a broad coalition including the ACLU, AFL-CIO, and Planned Parenthood Action Fund announced a national day of action for March 28, with more than 3,000 planned events aimed at surpassing an earlier mobilization of roughly seven million participants. Separately, organizers reported a surge in federal tax resistance, with training-session attendance jumping from a dozen to nearly 500 people in a single month. House Speaker Mike Johnson, meanwhile, declined to condemn explicitly Islamophobic remarks made by two Republican members of Congress, and the administration's Medicare and Medicaid overseer announced plans to remove millions more people from ACA coverage rolls.

Thursday was the week's most consequential day for the voting-rights storyline. The House passed the Save America Act, with its citizenship documentation requirements, voter ID mandates, mail-ballot restrictions, and criminal liability provisions for election officials, while Trump publicly pressured Senate Majority Leader Thune to gut the filibuster to force the bill through — a request Thune refused. The same day, Senator Tim Sheehy physically joined Capitol Police in ejecting an Iran-war protester, a Marine veteran, from a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing, an altercation that left the protester with a broken arm; Sheehy blamed the protester for "causing violence." Thursday's gravest event came in Michigan, where a naturalized U.S. citizen drove a vehicle into Temple Israel synagogue in West Bloomfield Township and was killed during the incident. The FBI later described the attack as retaliation for Israeli strikes that had killed the attacker's relatives in Lebanon; 140 children in the synagogue's preschool were unharmed. The Pentagon also disclosed that war costs had already surpassed $11.3 billion in six days, a figure covering munitions alone, while the White House dismissed as "fake news" reporting that it had badly underestimated Iran's willingness to close the Strait of Hormuz.

The week closed with a cluster of judicial rulings that, taken together, formed one of its clearest patterns. Judge James Boasberg quashed a grand jury subpoena targeting Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, finding "abundant evidence" that it was intended to pressure Powell over interest-rate policy rather than to investigate any actual wrongdoing. A federal judge in Oregon separately found that ICE had conducted warrantless arrests without probable cause, driven by a national quota of 3,000 daily arrests, and halted the practice while criticizing the agency's targeting methods. And FCC Chairman Brendan Carr threatened broadcasters with the loss of their licenses over coverage of the Iran war that the administration deemed "fake news," drawing bipartisan criticism, including from a Republican senator. Violence recurred as well: a gunman with a prior ISIS material-support conviction opened fire during ROTC training at Old Dominion University, killing one person and injuring two before being subdued and killed by students. On the international front, the administration eased sanctions on Russian oil shipments to calm markets rattled by the war, a move Germany's chancellor said allies had explicitly urged against. And new economic data showed the underlying strain: fourth-quarter GDP growth of just 0.7 percent alongside rising core inflation, as munitions depletion and mounting war costs pressed against the wider economy.

Taken as a whole, the week traced a single throughline across seemingly separate stories: a president exercising war powers without a vote, pressing for voting restrictions without full legislative consent, and encountering, again and again, a judiciary willing to say that specific exercises of executive power had crossed a legal line. Courts voided an unlawful media takeover, invalidated unconfirmed prosecutors, blocked a retaliatory subpoena against the central bank, and struck down warrantless immigration arrests — four distinct rulings against four distinct abuses of appointment and enforcement power, arriving within the same seven days. Meanwhile, the human costs mounted outside the courtroom: rising fuel prices, contradictory casualty figures, a synagogue attacked, a university classroom attacked, and immigration detention oversight hollowed out even as deaths in custody reached a multi-year high. None of these threads resolved by Friday. But together they showed a system under real pressure — from the executive branch pushing at the edges of its authority, and from courts, protesters, and ordinary institutional friction pushing back. ```

Title: War by Feeling, Government by Template
Content:
```markdown This was a week defined by two collisions: an undeclared war run on instinct rather than strategy, and a federal government repeatedly overreaching into courtrooms, statehouses, and newsrooms, only to be checked—sometimes forcefully—by judges, senators, and its own internal dissenters. By week's end, gas lines were lengthening, a career national security official had resigned in protest, and courts had blocked or questioned no fewer than five separate executive actions. Little of it resolved cleanly. Most of it simply hardened into precedent.

**The Weekend**

The tone was set early. Energy Secretary Chris Wright invoked Defense Production Act authority—a Cold War-era statute meant for wartime industrial mobilization—to force the reopening of an offshore oil pipeline in Santa Ynez, California, shuttered since a 2015 spill under a court-approved settlement. The pipeline began shipping oil within days, brushing aside state environmental law and prompting Governor Newsom to threaten suit. It was an early marker of a week in which federal power would repeatedly override negotiated legal arrangements rather than work within them.

Abroad, the war with Iran continued to defy conventional description. Trump told reporters the conflict would end "when I feel it in my bones," resisting any articulation of strategy or objectives. Reporting surfaced that he had waved off warnings from the Joint Chiefs chairman that striking Iran would trigger closure of the Strait of Hormuz—warnings that proved accurate almost immediately, catching the administration flat-footed as global oil markets convulsed. At home, that credibility gap collided with rising pressure on the press: Defense Secretary Hegseth publicly griped about unflattering war coverage and floated a Trump-friendly buyer for CNN, while FCC Chair Brendan Carr threatened broadcasters with license revocation over what he called "hoaxes and news distortions." Separately, Jared Kushner, still functioning as an Iran policy envoy, was soliciting at least $5 billion in fresh investment from Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE—the same governments lobbying him on the war—despite having pledged not to raise capital during his father-in-law's presidency. And in Texas, nine defendants were convicted on material-support-for-terrorism charges over a 2025 protest at an ICE facility, the first federal prosecution to allege that demonstrators belonged to an antifa terrorist cell, with sentences reaching life imprisonment.

Immigration enforcement, meanwhile, produced its own quiet emergencies: a Canadian citizen and her autistic seven-year-old daughter, both legally documented, were detained at a Texas checkpoint and pressured to self-deport; a federal judge ordered the release of an asylum seeker held 50 days in defiance of a court order barring his removal; and a 3,000-agent DHS operation in Minneapolis, the largest of its kind, ended with two U.S. citizens fatally shot.

**Monday**

The week's institutional battles came into sharper focus. The Justice Department's demand for unredacted voter rolls from all fifty states—and its lawsuits against five that refused—collapsed under an avalanche of its own errors: nonexistent statutes cited in court filings, misspelled attorney names, states misidentified as commonwealths, internal drafting notes left in public documents, and complaints struck by judges for procedural violations. Maine, Minnesota, New Hampshire, and West Virginia refused to comply; roughly a dozen states, including Ohio, did. It was a campaign that raised as many questions about competence as about intent.

The same day, Trump signed an executive order creating a Task Force to Eliminate Fraud with sweeping authority over Medicaid, SNAP, and other state-run programs, then directed it to investigate Rep. Ilhan Omar based on false citizenship claims, accompanied by disparaging remarks about Somalia. Courts pushed back hard: Judge Brian Murphy blocked RFK Jr.'s wholesale replacement of the vaccine advisory committee, ruling it likely violated federal law and halting changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Trump, for his part, responded to the Supreme Court's earlier rejection of his tariffs not by retreating but by reimposing them under a different statute, while publicly attacking the Court and demanding it validate his false 2020 election claims.

In a smaller but telling moment, Trump disclosed a sitting congressman's terminal medical diagnosis at a press conference without consent, prompting an immediate objection from Speaker Johnson; the congressman later announced his retirement. The press-freedom pressure from the weekend escalated further as Trump said he was "thrilled" the FCC was reviewing broadcast licenses and called for treason charges against unfavorable outlets. Immigration enforcement continued to generate grim data points—a 19-year-old's death in ICE custody in Florida, one of at least ten detention deaths in 2026, and a report showing ICE arrests of Asian Americans had nearly quadrupled compared to the prior administration.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought the week's most consequential act of internal dissent. Joe Kent, director of the National Counterterrorism Center, resigned, stating plainly that Iran posed no imminent threat and that the war had been driven by Israeli pressure rather than U.S. intelligence findings. Trump's response was immediate and public: he dismissed Kent as "weak on security," called him "just the coffee boy," and made clear that dissenters had no place on his team. The episode would escalate further as the week went on.

Separately, Trump claimed he could withdraw from NATO without congressional approval, a claim a fellow Republican publicly corrected as contrary to statute. The House Oversight Committee subpoenaed Attorney General Bondi to testify under oath about the DOJ's handling of Epstein-related files, and Chief Justice Roberts, without naming Trump directly, warned in a public address that attacks on judges were "dangerous" and needed to stop—a rare institutional alarm sounded amid rising threats against the judiciary. Speaker Johnson, meanwhile, declined to hold public hearings on the war's costs, calling the operations too sensitive and describing Trump's "feel it in my bones" approach as a legitimate gut decision informed by intelligence.

Trump simultaneously pressured Republican senators over the Save America Act, an expansive voter-eligibility bill critics warned could disenfranchise up to 21 million voters, threatening to withhold endorsements and demanding the filibuster's elimination to pass it. Immigration cases added further texture: a legally documented Texas court interpreter was detained for over a month without explanation, and pro-Palestinian activist Leqaa Kordia was released after a year in custody despite three judicial findings that she posed no threat.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday was the week's heaviest day for testimony and judicial rebuke. FBI Director Kash Patel admitted under oath that the bureau purchases Americans' location data from commercial brokers without a warrant, drawing bipartisan criticism, including from Republican Rep. Warren Davidson, who called it a Fourth Amendment violation. Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard's written statement asserted Iran's nuclear program had been "obliterated," but she omitted the claim in person and told senators only the president determines what counts as an imminent threat—directly at odds with the intelligence community's own March 2025 assessment that Iran was not building a weapon.

Judge Royce Lamberth ordered the reinstatement of more than a thousand Voice of America employees, ruling the administration's dismantling of the outlet unlawful and setting a March 23 deadline for a restoration plan. Attorney General Bondi, rather than complying with her subpoena, appeared at a closed-door, unsworn briefing; when she declined to commit to sworn testimony, Democratic committee members walked out. Separately, Judge Richard Leon called Trump's $400 million White House ballroom project "brazen" and signaled he might halt it outright.

Amid escalating war costs, Federal Reserve data showed producer prices rising at their fastest pace in a year, and White House economic advisor Kevin Hassett drew bipartisan condemnation for saying consumers were "the last of our concerns." In a smaller but revealing detail, White House communications staff produced "banger meme" videos splicing military strikes with football highlights and movie clips, aimed at young online audiences.

**Thursday**

Thursday brought the formal congressional reckoning with the war, and it did not go well for oversight advocates. The Senate voted 53–47, almost entirely along party lines, to block a Democratic resolution requiring congressional authorization for the ongoing conflict, even as strikes had by then killed more than 1,300 Iranians and hundreds of Lebanese civilians; only Rand Paul crossed party lines. In testimony that day, Senator Ossoff pressed Gabbard further, establishing on the record that the intelligence community itself had not assessed Iran as an imminent threat, and accused her of evading questions to protect White House messaging.

Elsewhere, a New York Times investigation into decades of alleged sexual abuse by labor leader Cesar Chavez triggered a rapid cascade of institutional responses: within a day, Arizona discontinued its Chavez Day holiday, the AFL-CIO withdrew its endorsement, and the United Farm Workers and LUPE canceled planned celebrations.

Reporting also documented systematic failures in deportation practice, with interviews of over a thousand deportees to Honduras revealing that ICE officers routinely failed to ask about children or arrange care before removal, violating the administration's own weakened family-separation directive; separately, a federal judge denied asylum to a five-year-old facing expedited removal. Courts continued to push back elsewhere: a First Circuit panel dismissed lawsuits alleging that pro-Palestinian protest slogans violated civil-rights law, and a federal judge ruled that RFK Jr. had exceeded his authority in restricting gender-affirming care for minors.

Senator Wyden accused Deputy Attorney General Blanche of blocking release of an unclassified Epstein-related memo to Congress, calling it part of a "continued coverup." And Treasury Secretary Bessent floated easing sanctions on stranded Iranian oil to relieve price pressure, even as the International Energy Agency declared the Strait of Hormuz closure the worst supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.

**Friday**

The week closed with more of the same institutional patterns settling into place rather than resolving. Republican leaders permitted only closed-door briefings on the war, with Senator Ron Johnson arguing that public division would undermine the war effort, and a second Democratic attempt to force congressional authorization was again rejected. The Senate Homeland Security Committee advanced Markwayne Mullin's nomination for DHS Secretary on a near party-line vote, with Democrat John Fetterman providing the deciding vote despite unresolved concerns about Mullin's truthfulness and past comments on political violence; Rand Paul, who had raised those same concerns days earlier, dissented.

The Justice Department formally invoked privilege to block release of the Epstein-related DEA memo, dismissing the House Oversight subpoena as "completely unnecessary" while acknowledging that roughly 200,000 pages remained withheld on similar grounds. And the earlier terrorism conviction of anti-ICE protesters widened into a broader pattern, as federal prosecutors filed conspiracy charges against demonstrators in Chicago, investigated Minnesota's governor and Minneapolis's mayor on the same theory, and charged two journalists who had been covering a protest. The week's final small note was almost fitting: Trump misrepresented a CNN poll, claiming 100 percent support for the war when the figure in fact reflected only MAGA Republicans, a group in which other polling showed meaningful dissent.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a presidency willing to act first and litigate the consequences later—overriding state law, reshuffling expert panels, demanding voter data, and reimposing tariffs after judicial rejection—while Congress, controlled by the president's own party, declined at nearly every turn to exercise the oversight authority the Constitution assigns it, whether over war-making, spending, or executive testimony. The judiciary emerged as the most consistent counterweight, reinstating fired broadcasters, blocking a reconstituted health panel, and questioning a quarter-billion-dollar construction project on federal historic ground. But courts move case by case, and much of what happened this week—a war conducted by feeling, a senior official pushed out for stating an inconvenient fact, and prosecutions reaching further into protest and journalism than before—will not be undone by any single ruling. It was a week that tested, in concrete and mostly measurable ways, how much institutional friction still stands between executive will and its exercise. ```

Title: War Without a Vote: Airports, Ballots, and a President Who Won't Say the Word
Content:
```markdown This was the week an undeclared war came home. It arrived in airport security lines, in a California sheriff's search warrant, and finally in the president's own words at a Republican fundraiser, where he admitted he was avoiding the word "war" for a specific reason: to skip the constitutional requirement that Congress approve one. Between March 21 and March 27, that admission sat at the center of a week that touched markets, elections, immigration enforcement, and the machinery of government funding all at once — each strand pulling on the others until, by Friday, the strain was visible almost everywhere at once.

The weekend set the tone. In Riverside County, California, Sheriff Chad Bianco — a Republican candidate for governor — used a search warrant to seize 650,000 ballots from the 2025 election, citing fraud that state officials said did not exist beyond a 103-vote discrepancy. A court moved quickly to appoint a special master to oversee a recount, but the seizure itself stood as a stark example of a law enforcement officer wielding his office's power over an election in which he was a candidate. At nearly the same moment, Trump escalated the confrontation with Iran, threatening on social media to destroy the country's civilian power infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz was not reopened within 48 hours — a threat that UN officials and legal experts said would itself constitute a war crime. Iran responded with its own threats against regional infrastructure. The weekend also brought an uglier note: Trump celebrated the death of former FBI Director Robert Mueller and separately declared the Democratic Party the nation's "greatest enemy," drawing condemnation that crossed party lines. Underneath these headline stories ran two quieter ones that would matter later: a ProPublica report on a $220 million DHS advertising contract steered to associates of Kristi Noem and Corey Lewandowski, and a Treasury decision to lift sanctions on Iranian oil at sea, delivering Iran an estimated $14 billion in relief during active conflict. Separately, oddly timed prediction-market bets on a US-Iran ceasefire, placed just before Trump's public statements, hinted that someone had advance knowledge of what was coming.

By Monday, that advance knowledge looked to have paid off. Trump announced a five-day pause on strikes, claiming Iran had agreed to nuclear disarmament and joint control of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's government denied any such negotiations had occurred, repeatedly and immediately. Market data showed unusual trading spikes in the minutes before Trump's announcement, and the president could not, or would not, name the Iranian official he claimed to be negotiating with. The same day, the domestic consequences of the DHS funding standoff became visible in a new and jarring way: ICE agents in tactical gear appeared at major airports nationwide, replacing TSA screeners who had gone six weeks without pay during a partial DHS shutdown, hundreds of whom had quit. Border Czar Tom Homan admitted there was no detailed operational plan beyond "guarding exits." New data-sharing between TSA and ICE led to the arrest of a mother and her nine-year-old daughter at a checkpoint. A former Trump strategist described the deployment openly as a "test run" for the 2026 midterms. Courts offered some resistance that day — a federal judge blocked a policy that would have exposed more than 100,000 refugees to arrest for lacking green cards, and Anthropic filed suit over Pentagon retaliation tied to its refusal to loosen AI safety guardrails for autonomous weapons.

Tuesday shifted the focus toward the ballot box in a different way. House Republicans floated using budget reconciliation — a procedure meant for fiscal matters — to pass voter ID and proof-of-citizenship requirements that could not survive a Senate filibuster on their own. Even the House Freedom Caucus called the strategy "gaslighting," and the Senate parliamentarian's approval remained doubtful. The Senate confirmed Markwayne Mullin as DHS Secretary by a party-line vote of 54-45, putting a Trump loyalist in charge of the agency at the center of both the airport deployment and the broader deportation push — timed, notably, to the same news cycle in which Trump claimed Iran was nearing "complete surrender." Separately, a deputy to U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro admitted in a closed hearing that the Justice Department had no evidence of wrongdoing by Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, despite public claims of "criminality." The Supreme Court, meanwhile, reversed a lower court's denial of qualified immunity for an officer who used force against a nonviolent protester, narrowing the path to police accountability even as the DOJ's own accountability gaps became public.

Wednesday brought the week's starkest human cost. José Guadalupe Ramos, a Mexican national with chronic health conditions, died after being found unconscious at the Adelanto ICE detention facility — the 14th such death in ICE custody in 2026, and the fourth at that facility alone since Trump took office. On the same day, White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller urged state legislatures to pass immigration laws that Congress itself could not, including ending public education for undocumented children, in direct tension with a 1982 Supreme Court ruling protecting that right — a strategy explicitly framed around the possibility that Democrats might control Congress after 2026. New reporting revealed that Trump had been receiving curated "highlight reel" war briefings rather than full intelligence assessments, while separate DOJ documents disclosed to Congress showed Trump had retained highly classified materials mingled with business records, prompting Rep. Jamie Raskin to renew demands for answers. Iran, for its part, formally rejected Trump's ceasefire terms, demanding reparations and security guarantees — confirming that the "breakthrough" claimed days earlier had not materialized. A California appellate court, meanwhile, declined to immediately halt the ballot recount tied to Sheriff Bianco's seizure, sending the matter to a lower court instead.

Thursday delivered the week's most explicit admission. At a Republican fundraiser, Trump acknowledged he was deliberately avoiding the word "war" specifically to bypass the constitutional requirement for congressional approval, calling the Iran campaign a "military operation" instead — an unusually direct statement of intent to sidestep a core constitutional check. The same day, Trump fired Kristi Noem amid the contracting scandal that had surfaced over the weekend, and the DHS Inspector General opened a formal investigation into contract handling involving Noem and Lewandowski, after complaining of prior obstruction. A federal judge granted Anthropic a preliminary injunction blocking the Pentagon's retaliatory ban, finding the government's action likely unconstitutional punishment for protected speech. And in a pair of moves that echoed each other, Trump publicly endorsed Viktor Orbán's reelection bid in Hungary while the administration quietly dropped sanctions on Russian oil in transit — injecting up to $10 billion a month into Russia's war effort even as U.S. markets fell sharply on Iran-driven inflation fears.

Friday closed the week with the clearest collision yet between executive action and legislative authority. Trump signed an order invoking emergency powers to have DHS pay 50,000 to 60,000 unpaid TSA agents directly, bypassing Congress's constitutional control over appropriations — while simultaneously demanding the Senate eliminate the filibuster entirely to pass the full SAVE America Act. The House did pass that bill's voter ID and citizenship-verification provisions the same day, in what was described as the most restrictive voting legislation in U.S. history, even as House Republicans separately rejected a bipartisan Senate-passed DHS funding deal, extending the shutdown into its seventh failed vote. Markets, meanwhile, fell to their lowest levels of the year, and consumer sentiment hit historic lows amid war-driven inflation — even as the Treasury announced that Trump's own signature would appear on U.S. currency, the first time in 165 years that a sitting president's signature has been used on legal tender. In smaller but telling moves, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed an executive order barring state officials from trading on insider information in prediction markets, criticizing federal inaction on the same suspicious trading patterns seen earlier in the week, while National Intelligence Director Tulsi Gabbard's ongoing election security review was reported to be amplifying unsubstantiated claims of foreign interference.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government straining against its own structure from several directions at once. A war proceeded without a congressional vote, its architect openly explaining why he avoided the word that would have required one. A funding standoff over homeland security metastasized into an improvised deployment of immigration agents into the nation's airports, justified after the fact as useful practice for an election year. A sheriff running for higher office seized ballots central to a disputed race, while lawmakers in Washington moved to rewrite voting rules through a budget procedure designed for something else entirely. Courts intervened where they could — blocking a detention policy, restraining retaliation against a company that refused to build autonomous weapons, opening an investigation into contracting misconduct — but did so unevenly, even as the Supreme Court narrowed protections for citizens facing police force. None of these threads resolved by Friday. What the week left behind was not a single crisis but a pattern: institutions bending under pressure from multiple directions, sometimes holding, sometimes not, while the public record of what was said, denied, admitted, and ruled grew longer and harder to look away from. ```
