Title: This Week in Democracy: Millions March, a Cabinet Purge, and a President in the Courtroom
Content:
```markdown This week began with the largest single-day protest in American history and ended with the president's attorney general fired days before a subpoenaed deposition. Between those two poles ran a familiar but intensifying pattern: a government shutdown grinding into its seventh week, courts repeatedly blocking executive actions, an escalating threat of war against Iran, and a president who attacked the Supreme Court publicly before appearing in its courtroom in person. It was a week in which the machinery of dissent and the machinery of institutional control both operated at full capacity, often in direct view of each other.

The weekend opened with numbers rarely seen in American civic life. On March 28, more than 8 million people took part in over 3,300 coordinated demonstrations across all fifty states and more than fifteen countries, under the banner "No Kings 3." Organizers and outside observers described it as surpassing the 2017 Women's March as the largest single-day protest in the nation's history. Nearly half the gatherings occurred in Republican-leaning areas, suggesting the discontent was not confined to traditional opposition strongholds. The White House response was dismissive, attributing the turnout to "leftist funding networks" rather than engaging with its substance. Yet even as most of the day passed peacefully, it did not end that way everywhere: near a federal detention facility in Los Angeles, police used pepper rounds and bean bags to disperse a crowd, and a Department of Homeland Security agent shot an 18-year-old student journalist with a less-lethal projectile, permanently blinding him in one eye — an incident his attorney said violated a standing federal injunction protecting journalists at protests.

Underneath the protests, the Department of Homeland Security shutdown was already in its sixth week, the longest partial government shutdown in American history. House Republicans, driven by a Freedom Caucus faction resistant to funding without accompanying immigration-enforcement reforms, had rejected a bipartisan Senate deal that would have funded most of the department. TSA workers went unpaid, absences and resignations climbed, and Trump responded not through negotiation but through unilateral executive orders and memoranda directing DHS to redirect funds to cover salaries — moves of uncertain legal footing that nonetheless kept the appearance of function without resolving the underlying impasse. Elsewhere over the weekend, a federal judge restored detained immigrants' access to confidential legal calls at a Florida facility, nine activists were convicted on terrorism charges in a Texas ICE-protest case despite the trial judge noting no organizational basis for that label, and the FBI director moved to release a decade-old file involving a Democratic congressman and gubernatorial candidate despite his prior cooperation and exoneration. Overseas, the war with Iran entered its fourth week without congressional authorization, straining the Strait of Hormuz and rattling oil markets.

By Monday, the administration's ambitions turned toward election administration itself. Trump signed an executive order directing DHS and the Social Security Administration to build a national voter eligibility list, instructing the Postal Service to send mail ballots only to voters on that list, and threatening to withhold federal funds from states that did not comply. Civil rights groups sued within hours, arguing the order intruded on constitutional authority reserved to the states. The same day, Trump publicly called the Supreme Court "stupid" and "dumb," two days ahead of oral arguments in the birthright citizenship case his administration was defending — an attempt to shape public perception of an outcome not yet decided. Iran policy hardened further, with Trump threatening to destroy the country's power plants, oil wells, and desalination facilities if the Strait of Hormuz remained closed; legal experts noted that strikes on civilian infrastructure, particularly desalination plants, could constitute war crimes, a question the White House press secretary declined to answer directly. Domestically, a federal judge blocked construction of Trump's $400 million White House ballroom project, ruling he lacked authority to proceed without congressional approval — a ruling Trump attacked on social media even as the Justice Department appealed. A separate judge found the administration's funding cutoff to NPR and PBS unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination. The Endangered Species Committee, convened for the first time in three decades, unanimously exempted Gulf of Mexico drilling from environmental review on national-security grounds tied to the Iran conflict, and the Pentagon quietly sat on dozens of wind-farm project reviews as Treasury yields climbed toward levels last seen during the 2008 crisis.

Tuesday brought the formal signing of the mail-in voting order, with additional detail: the Attorney General was directed to investigate election officials over mail-ballot distribution, and lawsuits followed almost immediately from state officials and voting-rights groups. The Endangered Species Committee finalized its Gulf drilling exemption. Three former FBI agents, two of whom had worked on the Jack Smith investigation, filed a class-action suit alleging they had been summarily fired without due process in retaliation for perceived disloyalty. The Justice Department separately sued Minnesota over transgender athletes' participation in school sports, while the Supreme Court ruled 8–1 that Colorado's conversion-therapy ban for minors was unconstitutional, casting doubt on similar bans in over twenty other states. In upstate New York, a medical examiner ruled the February death of a blind Rohingya refugee — left in a Buffalo parking lot on a freezing night by border patrol agents — a homicide, prompting a state investigation. Quietly, the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion arguing that the Presidential Records Act was unconstitutional and that Trump need not comply with it, a claim with implications for the preservation of his own administration's history.

Wednesday's defining moment came at the Supreme Court itself, where Trump became the first sitting president to attend oral arguments in person, sitting in the front row with his attorney general and commerce secretary for the birthright citizenship case he had derided two days earlier. He left after about ninety minutes, before the ACLU's argument, but not before several justices — including Kagan, Kavanaugh, and Gorsuch — voiced skepticism toward the government's position. The same day, the Justice Department removed a career prosecutor who had resisted pressure to bring insufficiently supported charges against former CIA Director John Brennan, a move that would prove to be a preview of larger changes at the department's top. Florida and Mississippi signed proof-of-citizenship voter-registration laws, joining South Dakota and Utah in a growing state-level trend. And Trump posted, falsely, that Iran's president had requested a ceasefire — a claim Iran's Foreign Ministry denied within hours.

Thursday was the week's sharpest institutional rupture. Trump fired Attorney General Pam Bondi by social media post, reportedly over her handling of the Epstein files and insufficient prosecution of political adversaries, timed just before her subpoenaed deposition on those files was to occur. He replaced her with Todd Blanche, his former personal defense attorney, who promptly stated that the president has the "right" to direct Justice Department investigations. Epstein survivors, family members, and lawmakers from both parties demanded that accountability efforts continue regardless of who held the office. On the same day, in a separate institution governed by different rules and different chains of command, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired the Army's Chief of Staff, General Randy George, after George refused an order to strike two women and two Black officers from a promotion list; two additional senior Army officers, including the head of the Chaplain Corps, were removed as well. The Joint Chiefs' leadership publicly honored George's service — a rare and pointed institutional rebuke delivered without direct confrontation. These were not the same event wearing two faces: one was the removal of the nation's chief law enforcement officer ahead of testimony on a politically sensitive matter, replaced by a personal loyalist; the other was the ouster of a senior military officer for refusing to execute a discriminatory personnel order. That they landed on the same day gave the week its most visible marker of institutional pressure converging from two directions at once. The day also brought new tariffs — 100% on patented pharmaceuticals, 50% on metals — with reduced rates offered to companies willing to onshore production or negotiate pricing, effectively creating a tiered system that favored firms with leverage to negotiate directly with the executive branch. A Trump-aligned planning commission approved the ballroom project just two days after a federal judge had blocked it, and at an Easter reception, Trump directed his budget director to end federal daycare funding, telling states to absorb the cost given wartime military spending.

The week closed on Friday with a budget request that made explicit what many of the week's threads had implied. The administration's proposed fiscal year 2027 budget nearly doubled 2024 defense spending, requesting $1.5 trillion, funded in part through 10% cuts to non-defense programs including healthcare, housing, and education, alongside $152 million to reopen Alcatraz as an active prison. A separate sequestration order mandated automatic cuts across non-exempt federal accounts. The DHS shutdown, now past forty-nine days, persisted as the House again declined to vote on the Senate's bipartisan compromise; Republicans instead pursued funding ICE through budget reconciliation to bypass a Democratic filibuster, while Trump signed yet another order directing full DHS pay through redirected funds. Reporting also revealed that DHS had been deploying BORTAC and BORSTAR — tactical units trained for high-risk warrants and cartel operations — in routine civilian immigration enforcement, involving extensive force and at least one fatal shooting of an unarmed civilian. Not every development ran in the administration's favor: a federal court struck down the seven-day advance-notice requirement that had constrained congressional oversight visits to ICE facilities, restoring lawmakers' ability to conduct surprise inspections. Overseas, the United States bombed a bridge in Iran's Karaj region, and Trump posted about seizing Iranian oil while threatening to bombard the country "back to the Stone Ages" — language delivered even as a U.S. search-and-rescue operation for a missing service member was still underway. Civil society's response continued to build: Washington state enacted its first income tax on millionaires, New York added wealth-tax provisions to its budget, California organizers advanced a billionaire wealth-tax ballot initiative, and labor and education groups announced a May Day "Workers Over Billionaires" day of action. Lawmakers from both parties pressed for Bondi's subpoenaed testimony to proceed despite her firing, while a DOJ whistleblower's attorneys alleged that the department's inspector general had failed to investigate serious misconduct amid what they described as unprecedented violations of court orders.

Taken as a whole, the week traced a familiar arc pulled taut in both directions at once. Millions of Americans mobilized in numbers without precedent, expressing broad and geographically diffuse unease with the concentration of power in the executive branch. At the same moment, that same branch moved to seize control of election administration, remove officials who would not bend to political direction, threaten force against a foreign civilian population, and reallocate the federal budget toward military priorities at the expense of domestic programs. Courts intervened repeatedly — on the ballroom, on public broadcasting, on detention-facility access, on congressional oversight — providing a check that held in specific instances even as the president publicly challenged the judiciary's legitimacy days before appearing in its own courtroom. Whether these countervailing forces would settle into a durable equilibrium or continue to strain against each other remained, at week's end, an open question resting on institutions still functioning, if unevenly, under considerable pressure. ```

Title: The Week the President Threatened to Erase a Civilization
Content:
```markdown This was a week that began with an American service member missing in hostile territory and ended, six days later, with a shattered ceasefire, a collapsing currency of trust in the presidency, and a growing bloc of lawmakers questioning whether the man in the Oval Office was fit to hold it. In between came a threat of civilizational destruction posted before dawn, a war-powers debate that Congress refused to even hold, and an economy visibly buckling under the strain of it all. Few weeks test the distance between rhetoric and restraint as starkly as this one did.

The weekend opened with a crisis and a silence. An F-15E had been shot down over Iran, and its weapons officer was missing. Rather than address the airman's fate, the president's public statements turned to Iranian oil and a threatened deadline: Iran would face "all Hell" within 48 hours if it did not comply with his demands. The White House imposed information lids on the incident, and Trump skipped his usual weekend routine of public appearances entirely, offering no reassurance to a public anxious about a missing service member. Behind the scenes, aides were reportedly advising him that Iranian civilian infrastructure counted as a legitimate wartime target — an argument outside experts say runs contrary to international law. Defense Secretary Hegseth embraced the idea, and one White House official floated that destroying power plants might stoke civil unrest inside Iran. At a press conference, Trump threatened to jail the journalist who had revealed the missing airman's identity unless the reporter's source was disclosed. In Texas, meanwhile, more than 2,000 people — conservatives, environmentalists, and ranchers alike — gathered at the state Capitol to oppose a planned border wall cutting through Big Bend National and State Parks, a rare show of bipartisan resistance to a federal land decision. And more than twenty state attorneys general sued over Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting, arguing it unconstitutionally seized state election authority ahead of the midterms.

By Monday, the war rhetoric had hardened further. Trump issued a 24-hour ultimatum threatening to destroy Iranian bridges and power plants, refused to rule out strikes on schools and hospitals when a reporter raised the question, and dismissed the war-crimes implications outright. He then turned the White House Easter Egg Roll — an event built around children — into an impromptu press conference, disparaging Iranian civilians and threatening continued war while exhibiting moments observers described as disorientation. At the same event, he made a string of claims that were quickly shown to be false: that all four living former presidents had privately endorsed his Iran strikes, that Joe Biden could not sign his own name, and that he personally deserved credit for killing Osama bin Laden. Courts, meanwhile, delivered a run of setbacks to the administration. A federal judge ruled that Attorney General Bondi had illegally appointed a "triumvirate" of federal prosecutors in New Jersey; another found that deportation policies targeting college activists violated the First Amendment; and a broader tally put the number of court rulings against the administration since early 2025 above 210. Reporting also revealed that the Department of Justice was pressing a sweeping effort to build a federal citizen list using the SAVE database — a system so unreliable that one Texas county found an 81 percent error rate among voters flagged as non-citizens — while a DOJ attorney admitted in court that the data would be shared with immigration authorities, contradicting the department's earlier denials. Separately, Elon Musk and Laura Loomer shared photos of federal judge James Boasberg's daughter online after his rulings against the administration, with some allies calling for violence against the judge's family. And Vice President Vance announced he would travel to Hungary to campaign for Prime Minister Viktor Orbán ahead of that country's election.

Tuesday brought the week's defining rupture. At 5:06 in the morning, Trump posted that "a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again," language that explicitly invoked "Complete and Total Regime Change" and that legal observers described as an unambiguous threat of genocide. Thirteen hours later, at 6:32 that evening, he announced a two-week ceasefire, claiming victory on the basis of a disputed account of Iran's proposal — then attacked CNN for reporting Iran's own version of the deal. Congress's response fractured along lines that did not track neatly with party. Some Republicans praised the escalation as overdue strength; Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene invoked the 25th Amendment; Representative Jim McGovern called on the Joint Chiefs to disobey illegal orders; and Democratic members demanded the House and Senate be recalled to end the war and pursue removal. Amid the chaos, a $1.7 trillion defense budget request — nearly double the pre-Trump baseline — moved forward, with $350 billion routed through reconciliation specifically to bypass the standard bipartisan appropriations process. Billions in Golden Dome missile-defense contracts were awarded to SpaceX, Palantir, and Blue Origin, companies tied to Elon Musk, Peter Thiel, and Jeff Bezos, all significant allies of the administration, despite independent analyses questioning whether the system was even feasible. Elsewhere, Wisconsin's Supreme Court flipped to a 5-2 liberal majority with implications for redistricting and election disputes in a critical swing state; ICE agents shot a man more than six times during a traffic stop in California before federal prosecutors charged him with assaulting an officer, omitting unsubstantiated gang allegations from the complaint; the DOJ opened an unusual civil-rights-division investigation into January 6 witness Cassidy Hutchinson's testimony; the Supreme Court vacated Steve Bannon's contempt-of-Congress conviction pending review of a Trump administration motion to dismiss; and Vance appeared in Budapest to formally endorse Orbán's re-election, framing the relationship as a defense of "Western civilization."

The ceasefire did not survive contact with Wednesday. Trump falsely claimed Iran had undergone a "productive regime change," then stated publicly there would be no uranium enrichment under the deal — directly contradicting the actual ceasefire framework, which permitted it — and shifted his own description of the agreement from a "10-point" plan to a "15-point" one, rewriting its terms in real time. He also floated a joint U.S.-Iran venture to charge shipping tolls through the Strait of Hormuz, calling it "a beautiful thing," despite Iran never agreeing to any such arrangement and having previously mocked the idea. On the accountability front, the Justice Department informed the House Oversight Committee that former Attorney General Bondi would not sit for her scheduled deposition on the Epstein files, arguing her subpoena lapsed the moment she left office — a legal theory Democrats disputed and threatened to challenge with contempt proceedings. A Florida judge dismissed Trump's defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over Epstein-related reporting, finding it failed to meet the actual-malice standard, though he was granted until April 27 to refile. A wave of reporting detailed surveillance mission creep — license-plate readers causing wrongful arrests, Flock camera data being used to track protesters and abortion-related searches — and a federal judge ruled the Pentagon's revised press-credential policy was simply a disguised continuation of restrictions already blocked in court. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, meanwhile, delivered the keynote at a Heartland Institute climate-denial conference, rejecting scientific consensus and celebrating the rollback of the endangerment finding that underlies most federal climate regulation.

By Thursday, the fallout in Congress had crystallized into open calls for removal. More than 85 House Democrats and two senators publicly called for impeachment, invocation of the 25th Amendment, or both. Representative John Larson filed articles of impeachment, and House leadership announced a formal briefing on the 25th Amendment process. Yet House Republicans refused to allow even a debate, let alone a vote, on an Iran War Powers Resolution, prompting Senate Democrats to schedule their own vote for the following week — though Senator Fetterman announced he would oppose it regardless. In an unannounced appearance at a White House podium, Melania Trump denied any friendship or connection with Jeffrey Epstein or Ghislaine Maxwell and called for congressional hearings featuring Epstein survivors; Trump later claimed, contrary to available evidence, that he had no advance knowledge of her statement. Survivors of a drone attack that killed six U.S. service members in Kuwait publicly disputed Defense Secretary Hegseth's account of the incident, saying their position had been unfortified and unprepared. And the economic costs of the week's turmoil became visible in hard numbers: the University of Michigan's Consumer Sentiment Index fell to a record 47.6, lower than both the COVID and 2008 financial-crisis troughs, even as economic advisor Kevin Hassett dismissed a historically bad market quarter and soaring oil prices as a "temporary distraction." A body reshaped by Trump appointees also issued a final removal order against Palestinian-rights activist Mahmoud Khalil, who says he is being punished for speech opposing the war in Gaza.

The week closed on Friday with the ceasefire's central premise collapsing in public view. Iran's Revolutionary Guard effectively shut down shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and began charging cryptocurrency tolls, directly contradicting the agreement's stated condition of open passage. Trump warned Iran to stop, even as his own economic advisor conceded the strait might not reopen for two months. He then posted that all U.S. military assets would remain positioned around Iran and that "the Shootin' Starts" bigger than ever if compliance did not follow — in the same stretch of posts promoting Palantir stock by ticker symbol. For the second consecutive day, House Speaker pro tempore Chris Smith refused to recognize Democrats attempting to force a war-powers vote, ending the session immediately. Representative Jamie Raskin formally requested that the president's physician conduct a comprehensive cognitive assessment, citing what he called Trump's "increasingly incoherent, volatile, profane, deranged, and threatening" public statements. Two days ahead of Hungary's election, Trump pledged to use "the full Economic Might of the United States" to support Orbán's economy, following Vance's campaign appearance earlier in the week. March inflation data confirmed the human cost of the crisis: prices rose at their fastest rate since May 2024, with gas prices up 21 percent in a single month — the largest one-month jump since national data collection began in 1967. The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had repeatedly offered to pardon "everyone who has come within 200 feet of the Oval Office," an offer the White House declined to deny while calling it a joke. Courts continued to push back on multiple fronts — a California judge found border agents had again violated a prior order on warrantless arrests, a Massachusetts judge blocked the termination of Temporary Protected Status for more than 5,000 Ethiopians, and a court in Eswatini ruled that four men deported by the United States and held without legal access for nine months had a right to counsel. And as the week ended, Kamala Harris and Pete Buttigieg both signaled interest in 2028 presidential runs, a small but telling sign that political life was already looking past the current crisis.

What this week revealed was not simply a foreign-policy emergency but a test of the mechanisms meant to constrain executive power in moments of crisis. A president's threat of civilizational destruction, issued before dawn and walked back by evening, exposed how little formal process now stands between impulse and consequence in matters of war. Congress's fractured response — some members praising the escalation, others invoking constitutional remedies rarely used, and the chamber's own leadership blocking any vote at all — showed an institution unable to agree on its role even as its war-powers authority was being visibly bypassed. Courts, for their part, continued to function as a check, ruling repeatedly against voter-data overreach, deportation practices, and press restrictions, even as judges themselves faced intimidation for doing so. And the week's economic toll, from record-low consumer confidence to the sharpest one-month gas-price spike in modern data collection, made concrete what the rhetoric had left abstract: that decisions made in the language of ultimatums and civilizational threats do not stay contained to foreign policy, but move directly into household budgets, market confidence, and public trust in the institutions meant to hold power accountable. ```

Title: Blockade, Blasphemy, and a Broken Congress
Content:
```markdown The week began, fittingly, with a joke that wasn't quite a joke. Trump told associates he would pardon any aide or official who came within 200 feet of the Oval Office once his term ended, a remark the White House waved off as humor while insisting his clemency power was "absolute." It landed against a backdrop of more than 1,800 pardons and commutations already issued, many for January 6 defendants, and set the tone for a week in which loyalty and legal exposure would repeatedly intersect. That same weekend, the administration fired immigration judges who had ruled against deportations, including some who had blocked the removal of pro-Palestinian university students, targeting jurists with immigrant-defense backgrounds and higher asylum grant rates. In Minneapolis, surveillance footage undercut an ICE account of a January shooting, revealing a 12-second encounter where officers had described a three-minute struggle; the agents involved were placed on leave. And in California, a widening crisis engulfed Rep. Eric Swalwell, the frontrunner in the state's governor's race, as multiple women accused him of sexual assault and misconduct, prompting a Manhattan DA investigation and public calls from Gavin Newsom, Hakeem Jeffries, and Adam Schiff for him to leave the race. Abroad, nuclear talks with Iran collapsed in Islamabad amid disputes over the Strait of Hormuz, frozen assets, and reparations, with Trump posting mocking content about Iran even as negotiations were still live and both governments offered irreconcilable accounts of a naval incident. Away from all of it, a civic march of more than a thousand people set out from Philadelphia toward Washington, a 160-mile echo of an earlier demonstration, framed by organizers as sustained resistance rather than a single protest.

By Monday the diplomatic collapse had become military policy. Trump ordered a full naval blockade of Iranian ports, following the breakdown of Vice President Vance's talks in Islamabad, threatening to destroy Iranian infrastructure and eliminate any approaching vessels; CENTCOM confirmed the blockade was operational. It was a unilateral use of force at one of the world's most sensitive chokepoints, ordered without congressional authorization. Domestically, the Swalwell story reached its first resolution: facing an imminent expulsion vote and the collapse of support from his own party's leadership, he resigned from Congress. Within hours, a fifth accuser came forward alleging drugging and rape, and both the Manhattan DA and the Department of Homeland Security opened investigations — the latter tied to a complaint from a known conspiracy theorist, raising its own questions about federal investigative machinery being turned toward political ends. Trump, meanwhile, opened a new front, publicly calling Pope Leo XIV "weak on crime" for criticizing the war, then posting an AI-generated image of himself with divine healing powers. He deleted it after backlash and falsely claimed it had depicted him as a doctor or Red Cross volunteer, declining to apologize. Separately, Netanyahu reportedly told his own cabinet that Vance had been briefing him daily on the confidential Islamabad talks, an arrangement that raised questions about how sensitive diplomatic information was being shared. And the week's first economic signal arrived: inflation hit 3.3 percent, more than triple February's rate, driven substantially by tariffs, with gasoline prices up over 21 percent.

Tuesday compounded the whiplash. Rep. Tony Gonzales, facing expulsion over an affair with a staffer who had later died by suicide, announced his own resignation — a second congressional departure within hours of Swalwell's. Two members of Congress leaving office in a single stretch reflected both the accumulation of institutional dysfunction and, in a narrower sense, the fact that expulsion mechanisms were actually working. The Swalwell scandal kept widening regardless: a fifth accuser, Lonna Drewes, came forward publicly in Beverly Hills with an account of being drugged and raped in 2018. Trump's feud with the Vatican escalated in parallel — he attacked the Pope in an Italian interview and separately called Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni "unacceptable," reversing earlier praise after she defended the Pope. Elsewhere in the executive branch, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard issued criminal referrals against the 2019 Ukraine-call whistleblower whose complaint had triggered Trump's first impeachment, and against the inspector general who had processed it — an apparent attempt to punish protected disclosures years after the fact. The Justice Department, meanwhile, moved to dismiss the seditious conspiracy convictions of Oath Keepers and Proud Boys leaders, extending a pattern that had already cleared more than 1,600 January 6 defendants through pardons and commutations. The administration also repealed the federal "endangerment finding" that underpins greenhouse gas regulation, celebrated at a climate-denial conference as a signature win, while a White House event featuring a gig worker delivering food to Trump was exposed as a staged promotional stunt for a "no tax on tips" policy. And former Attorney General Pam Bondi simply didn't show up for a scheduled House Oversight deposition on her handling of the Epstein files, with the Justice Department arguing that congressional subpoenas lapse once an official leaves office.

Wednesday brought the week's most direct institutional response to what had come before. Rep. Jamie Raskin and fifty co-sponsors introduced legislation to create a formal commission to assess Trump's fitness for office under the 25th Amendment, citing both his threats against Iran and his religious-imagery posts as evidence of erratic conduct — a rare formal invocation of a constitutional mechanism seldom used and almost never seriously proposed. The same day, OMB Director Russell Vought defended the administration's withholding of congressionally appropriated PEPFAR and global health funding, calling the choice ideologically motivated even after the Government Accountability Office had found the impoundment illegal; the funding freeze has been linked to an estimated 780,000 deaths in its first year. On the bench, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson delivered a pointed public critique of her own court, describing the Supreme Court's use of emergency "shadow docket" orders favoring the administration as "scratch-paper musings" lacking real explanation — an unusual public airing of internal judicial strain. Reporting also surfaced a broader pattern of state legislatures moving against judges who had ruled on redistricting or voting access: an attempted impeachment in Kentucky was blocked by that state's supreme court, while similar retaliatory efforts were documented in West Virginia, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, and Utah. North Carolina's elections board voted along party lines to share voter registration data with DHS for citizenship cross-checks against a database known to be error-prone. And nationwide, Tax Day protests connected opposition to war spending, mass deportation, and private detention, while activists staged a sit-in at the offices of Senators Schumer and Gillibrand demanding limits on arms sales to Israel.

Thursday was the week's fullest day of institutional friction. House Democrats, led by Rep. Yassamin Ansari, filed six articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over an unauthorized Iran strike, earlier boat strikes, and Signal-channel leaks. Raskin separately opened an investigation into Jared Kushner's financial ties to Saudi Arabia, and a new congressional task force was formed to examine Trump family self-dealing more broadly — three parallel accountability efforts converging in a single day. Congress also came close to reasserting its own war powers: a resolution to constrain military action against Iran failed in the House by a single vote, 213 to 214, while a Senate effort led by Bernie Sanders to block arms sales to Israel failed 40 to 59, though the margin reflected a growing bloc of Democratic dissent. Vought returned to testify before the Senate, this time denying that any funds had been illegally withheld — an assertion Senator Merkley accused him of fabricating — and separately refused to disclose the cost of the Iran war when asked directly. In the courts, Judge Richard Leon halted above-ground construction on Trump's planned White House ballroom project, ruling that national security concerns do not grant a blank check for otherwise unlawful activity; Trump responded with repeated public attacks calling him "Trump Hating." The feud with the Vatican deepened into open theological argument, as Vice President Vance and House Speaker Mike Johnson publicly challenged Pope Leo XIV's understanding of just war doctrine, while Defense Secretary Hegseth compared journalists to biblical Pharisees and restricted briefings to conservative outlets. Elsewhere, the administration withheld $73.5 million in federal funding from New York over a driver's license dispute, renewed threats to remove Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, and canceled an $11 million Catholic Charities contract serving migrant children in what appeared to be retaliation for the Pope's criticism — three coercive funding actions against a state, an independent central banker, and a religious charity within a single day. Amid all of it, the House passed a bipartisan bill extending Temporary Protected Status for roughly 350,000 Haitians, 224 to 204, pushing back against the administration's termination effort.

The week closed on Friday with Trump declaring the Iran conflict over in a burst of thirteen posts claiming sweeping victory — that Iran had agreed to keep the Strait of Hormuz open, to surrender enriched uranium, and that Israel had been "prohibited" from bombing Lebanon. Iranian officials disputed the uranium claim specifically, and independent reporting indicated substantial disagreements remained unresolved. By week's end, the gap between the president's public account and the underlying facts was difficult to close. Elsewhere, accountability moved forward on narrower fronts: Minnesota prosecutors filed a felony assault charge against the ICE officer who had pointed a gun at highway occupants, the first criminal charge of its kind against a federal immigration agent, and acting ICE Director Todd Lyons announced his resignation amid mounting criticism of enforcement conduct. At a Florida detention facility known as "Alligator Alcatraz," attorneys reported that guards had cut off detainee phone access and used force in direct defiance of a judge's protective order. The Senate voted to reopen Minnesota's Boundary Waters wilderness to mining, clearing the way for a Chilean-owned subsidiary to pursue copper-sulfide extraction upstream from the protected area, reversing a two-decade moratorium. The House passed its Haitian TPS bill again, with eleven Republicans joining Democrats, as the Supreme Court prepared to hear related arguments later in the month. California's Supreme Court upheld the disbarment of John Eastman, the lawyer behind the fake-elector scheme to overturn the 2020 election, finding gross negligence and false statements without meaningful investigation. And on campuses nationwide, a coordinated Day of Action for Higher Education brought teach-ins and protests responding to federal funding threats against university independence.

Taken as a whole, the week measured the distance between what a government claims and what it can verify, and between institutions that still function and those bending under pressure. A blockade was ordered and then, in substance, abandoned, with victory declared before the other side agreed to the terms. Two sitting members of Congress left office in a single stretch under threat of expulsion, evidence that accountability mechanisms, however belatedly, still worked when misconduct became undeniable. Courts pushed back against a ballroom project and against retaliation targeting judges, even as the Justice Department worked to erase convictions tied to an attack on the Capitol and referred a protected whistleblower for prosecution. A sitting justice publicly criticized her own court's process. And a formal congressional effort to examine the president's fitness for office, alongside impeachment articles against his defense secretary, suggested that unease about the exercise of executive power had moved from commentary into legislative text. Whether these mechanisms could keep pace with the events generating them remained, at week's end, an open question. ```

Title: War by Ultimatum, Government by Grievance
Content:
```markdown This week can be read as a study in how a single unresolved crisis abroad and a set of hardening habits at home fed off each other. A ceasefire with Iran, declared and re-declared throughout seven days, never actually held. Around that instability, federal power kept turning toward critics, courts kept pushing back against executive overreach, and the Pentagon's command structure was reshaped in the middle of an active conflict.

**The Weekend**

The weekend set the tone. President Trump announced that Iran had effectively surrendered and agreed to keep the Strait of Hormuz open. Iran said no such thing had been agreed. Ships attempting to pass through the strait came under fire, and Tehran would not confirm a planned meeting in Pakistan meant to formalize a deal. Trump responded by threatening to resume bombing and to destroy Iranian power plants and bridges — a claimed diplomatic breakthrough dissolving within hours into fresh threats of infrastructure destruction.

In the same stretch of days, Trump and his sons filed a $10 billion lawsuit against the IRS over a leaked tax record, an extraordinary spectacle of a sitting president suing the agency he oversees. An appeals panel let construction resume on a $400 million White House ballroom despite an unresolved question of presidential authority to demolish the East Wing without Congress's approval. And the Justice Department's civil rights division, under Harmeet Dhillon, opened investigations into Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson over hiring remarks and into Cassidy Hutchinson, the January 6 committee witness — a break from norms of investigative confidentiality that, by week's end, would connect to the appointment of Joe diGenova, a longtime Trump loyalist, to lead a Florida-based probe into the officials who had once investigated Trump himself.

FBI Director Kash Patel, meanwhile, denied an Atlantic report alleging excessive drinking and unavailability, and promised to sue — a promise he would keep within days. Treasury quietly reversed a stated policy against renewing Russian oil sanctions waivers, extending relief without explanation. Congress, unable to agree on a longer renewal of surveillance authority under FISA, settled for a bare ten-day extension. And roughly 1,000 animal-rights protesters attempting to breach a Wisconsin breeding facility were met with tear gas and rubber bullets.

**Monday**

By Monday, the administration's response to the Iran crisis had shifted from diplomacy to unilateral mobilization. In a single day, Trump issued six separate Defense Production Act determinations declaring coal, petroleum, natural gas, and grid infrastructure essential to national defense — each waiving standard permitting and review requirements. Energy Secretary Chris Wright admitted publicly that gas prices were unlikely to fall below $3 before 2027, tying the delay to the war; Trump called him "totally wrong" even as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve was drawn down at its fastest rate since 2022.

Reporting surfaced showing repeated instances of large trades executed minutes before Trump's own market-moving statements on Iran, including bets that anticipated the timing of airstrikes. And an analysis of 202 news articles found that only six mentioned Jared Kushner's firm's multibillion-dollar financial relationship with the Saudi government, even as Senator Ossoff raised the conflict publicly — the first documented instance of a financial-conflict thread that would recur throughout the week.

Patel formalized his lawsuit against The Atlantic, seeking $250 million. The House rejected both a five-year and an 18-month extension of Section 702 surveillance authority, leaving only the short-term patch in place. A federal judge in California denied an emergency DOJ motion for statewide voter records, adding to a string of judicial rejections of the administration's voter-roll campaign, while DOJ expanded a citizenship-verification program to allow bulk sharing of voter data with DHS. The Labor Department moved to repeal more than 60 workplace protections. And 71 veterans, carrying tulips for Iranian civilian casualties, were arrested in a Capitol Hill office building after demanding a war-powers meeting with the Speaker.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought the ceasefire's collapse into sharper focus. Iran refused to send negotiators to Islamabad, calling the ongoing US naval blockade an act of war; at least one Iranian tanker broke through it regardless. Trump backed off his own bombing deadline, extending the ceasefire unilaterally while telling CNBC he still expected bombing to resume — a pattern of contradiction that would define the week's foreign policy. CNN later reported that Trump's own officials privately acknowledged his social-media claims of Iranian concessions, which Tehran denied, had actively damaged the negotiations he was claiming credit for.

Separately, the Justice Department indicted the Southern Poverty Law Center on an 11-count fraud case that a whistleblower said had been rushed forward under political pressure despite internal doubts about its strength. Environmental groups sued to block BP's Kaskida deepwater drilling project, timed to the anniversary of the Deepwater Horizon disaster. And ICE detained the wife of a deploying US Army sergeant at a Louisiana base before releasing her following media attention.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday compressed several distinct institutional confrontations into a single day. In Virginia, a court invalidated a voter-approved congressional redistricting map — passed just a day earlier by a narrow but clear margin — after a Republican-backed lawsuit challenged it; the state's attorney general vowed an appeal to defend the referendum's legitimacy. Trump, after the Supreme Court struck down his tariffs and ordered $159 billion in refunds, published a lengthy public attack on the Court and on Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson personally, calling her a "Low IQ person," while pre-emptively denouncing an anticipated ruling against his birthright citizenship policy.

The SPLC indictment was formalized with an added conspiracy-theory framing, alleging the organization staged false-flag violence tied to January 6 — a claim critics called legally baseless. Reporting connected a proposed Treasury-funded bailout for the United Arab Emirates, floated as the UAE warned of dollar destabilization from war-related damage, to a Sheikh who had invested hundreds of millions in Trump family businesses and secured chip export approvals shortly afterward — the clearest instance yet of the Kushner-adjacent financial-conflict undercurrent running through the week.

At the Pentagon, Defense Secretary Hegseth fired Navy Secretary John Phelan amid a dispute over shipbuilding and direct communications with Trump, replacing him with Hung Cao — the first move in what would become a broader purge. Eric Trump appeared on Fox News promoting a $24 million Pentagon robotics contract awarded to his company, drawing a rebuke from Senator Warren. The House, defying both Speaker Johnson and the administration, passed bipartisan protections restoring Temporary Protected Status for 350,000 Haitian immigrants. And the American Library Association reported a record 5,668 book bans in 2025, with 92 percent originating from organized pressure campaigns.

**Thursday**

By Thursday, the week's threads of executive unilateralism and legal retaliation converged directly. The Justice Department launched what officials described as the largest denaturalization effort in history, assigning litigators across 39 regional offices to file a first wave of cases against 384 naturalized citizens under unusually broad criteria. Separately, a federal judge in Oregon struck down the administration's ban on gender-affirming care for minors, calling the government's arguments "a bald-faced lie" in a 49-page ruling.

The FBI's investigation of New York Times reporter Elizabeth Williamson came to light — agents had queried databases and interviewed Patel's girlfriend after Williamson reported that Patel used bureau personnel to escort her, prompting the Times to call the probe unconstitutional. House Judiciary Democrats formally demanded Patel undergo alcohol screening.

Trump, with the War Powers Act's 60-day window closing within days, declared the law unconstitutional and said he had "all the time in the world" to continue operations without congressional authorization. The Senate advanced $140 billion in multi-year ICE and CBP funding through reconciliation, sidestepping the filibuster and removing Congress's annual leverage over enforcement conduct.

The Pentagon fired the Stars and Stripes ombudsman after she warned publicly about efforts to control the military newspaper's content. Trump reposted a Newsmax segment using dehumanizing language about Chinese and Indian immigrants while calling for a referendum ending birthright citizenship — amplification that landed squarely alongside the day's denaturalization news. A Colorado CBP officer was criminally charged for placing a protester in a chokehold. And a proposed $500 million bailout for Spirit Airlines advanced over internal administration disagreement.

**Friday**

The week closed on Friday with three major developments landing in close succession. The Justice Department announced an expansion of federal execution methods — firing squads, electrocution, and nitrogen gas — ending roughly 17 years of federal restraint on capital punishment, and authorized death sentences against 44 defendants while directing the Bureau of Prisons to expand death-row capacity. The department also dropped its criminal investigation into Federal Reserve Chair Powell's building renovations after a senator threatened to block a Trump nominee's confirmation, referring the matter to the Fed's inspector general — only for the White House Press Secretary to publicly contradict that closure, saying the investigation "still continues."

And the Pentagon purge that had begun Wednesday with the Navy Secretary's removal culminated in a sweeping shake-up: Hegseth removed senior generals and admirals from nearly every service branch except the Marine Corps and Space Force, along with senior military lawyers and the Army's chaplain corps head, part of a wave of at least 15 defense-official departures. Reporting that same day revealed the Iran war had severely depleted US munitions stockpiles, burning through the bulk of long-range stealth cruise missiles and years of Tomahawk and Patriot interceptor production. An inspector general opened an audit into the department's compliance with the Epstein Files Transparency Act after missed deadlines and criticism over redactions. And the CDC was reported to have blocked publication of a peer-reviewed finding on COVID-19 vaccine efficacy among healthy adults.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government operating less through settled process than through improvisation and pressure. A war policy conducted by presidential social-media post, rather than negotiated agreement or congressional authorization, produced contradictory ceasefires and a documented case of diplomacy undermined by its own principal negotiator. Federal legal power moved with unusual directness against a civil rights organization, a congressional witness, journalists covering a law enforcement official, and hundreds of naturalized citizens, even as courts in Virginia, Oregon, and California pushed back against specific instances of executive reach. Personal and family financial interests — around Kushner's Saudi ties, a proposed UAE bailout, and a Pentagon contract awarded to a presidential relative — ran alongside the war and drew only scattered public scrutiny. And in the middle of an active conflict, the Defense Department's senior leadership was reorganized around loyalty rather than continuity, even as the military's own resource base was reported critically strained. None of these threads resolved by week's end; each was left open, unsettled, and carried forward. ```

Title: A Shooting, a Ballroom, and the Voting Rights Act: One Week of Escalation
Content:
```markdown This was a week that began with a gunshot near a black-tie dinner and ended with a federal court restricting access to a common medication, a president bypassing a war-powers deadline by letter, and thousands of Americans marching under a banner declaring workers over billionaires. In between, the Supreme Court issued a ruling likely to be remembered as one of the most consequential decisions of the decade, and a governor in Louisiana did something with almost no precedent: he suspended an election that voters had already started voting in.

**The Weekend**

The week opened on Saturday night, when an armed man was apprehended near the White House Correspondents' Association dinner, prompting the evacuation of the president and First Lady. The basic facts stayed murky for days—cable networks disputed for a time whether the gunman had even fired a weapon—but confusion did not slow the political response. Within hours, administration officials and allied lawmakers were citing the incident to demand that the National Trust for Historic Preservation drop its lawsuit blocking construction of a new White House ballroom, and to argue that taxpayer funding for the project was now a security necessity.

That same weekend, ICE agents re-detained an Egyptian mother and her five children within days of a federal judge ordering their release. A Colorado judge had to order their deportation flight turned around mid-transit before the family was freed again, their attorney calling the episode open defiance of judicial authority. Elsewhere, ICE ended decades-old protections that had shielded houses of worship from enforcement action, drawing a multi-faith lawsuit, while new guidance threatened green-card denial for pro-Palestinian protest activity, and reporting surfaced plans for a children's detention facility on a PFAS-contaminated site in Louisiana. Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer resigned amid a misconduct investigation, blaming "deep state actors," even as Senate Republicans quietly made closure of a criminal probe into Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell a condition for supporting Kevin Warsh's nomination to replace him.

**Monday**

By Monday, the ballroom fight had become a coordinated legislative campaign. Senators Lindsey Graham, Rand Paul, and Tim Sheehy each introduced overlapping bills to authorize $400 million in public funds for the project, while Representative Randy Fine introduced a "Build the Ballroom Act" explicitly designed to override the pending court injunction. The Justice Department simultaneously renewed pressure on the National Trust to abandon its suit.

That same day, in a 60 Minutes interview, Trump attributed the weekend's shooting to the "No Kings" protest movement—a movement with a well-documented record of nonviolence—and administration officials, including the press secretary, extended the blame to "the entire Democrat party." A separate confrontation was building over speech and media: after Jimmy Kimmel joked about Melania Trump, both the president and First Lady called publicly for his firing, and FCC Chair Brendan Carr warned ABC affiliates that the agency could act against their licenses "the easy way or the hard way." Florida's governor, meanwhile, unveiled a congressional redistricting map that could hand Republicans as many as four additional House seats, Arizona sued over a $700 million detention-facility procurement it said skipped environmental review, and the administration resumed housing migrant families with young children at the Dilley, Texas facility, a site with a documented history of inadequate medical care.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought two escalations that, while both involving the Justice Department, were fundamentally different in kind. First, a grand jury indicted James Comey for a second time—this time over a year-old Instagram photo of seashells arranged to spell "86 47," which prosecutors characterized as a threat against the president. Comey denied any such intent, and legal observers, including some Republican senators, questioned the strength of the charge; his earlier indictment had already been dismissed by a federal judge over an improperly appointed prosecutor. Separately, and distinctly, the FCC ordered an accelerated review of eight ABC-owned station licenses, citing an unrelated diversity-practices inquiry even as the timing made the connection to the Kimmel controversy hard to ignore.

The ballroom fight also advanced in court: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche filed a motion attacking the National Trust's legitimacy and arguing the injunction should be lifted on security grounds, formalizing what had until then been political pressure. And in a speech welcoming King Charles III, Trump described the American founding in terms of blood and cultural inheritance rather than the Declaration's language of universal equality, a framing amplified by a White House social-media post reading "TWO KINGS" that drew criticism for blurring constitutional and monarchical language around the presidency. Quieter developments continued alongside these: EPA rollbacks of PFAS, mercury, arsenic, and pesticide protections advanced, with Bayer a notable beneficiary of prior campaign contributions, and reporting revealed growing unease among Senate Republicans over Defense Secretary Hegseth's removal of senior military officers.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday was the week's structural turning point. In a 6–3 decision in *Louisiana v. Callais*, the Supreme Court ruled that Louisiana's creation of a second majority-Black congressional district amounted to an unconstitutional racial gerrymander, holding that plaintiffs must now prove intentional discrimination rather than discriminatory effect to prevail under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Justice Kagan's dissent warned that the ruling renders Section 2 "all but a dead letter." The decision took effect immediately, without the customary waiting period, and the consequences were not abstract.

Within hours, Florida's legislature passed the new map expected to yield four additional Republican seats. Mississippi and Tennessee officials announced special legislative sessions aimed explicitly at eliminating their states' remaining majority-Black districts, with Tennessee Senator Marsha Blackburn describing the move as advancing the president's agenda. Alabama moved as well. A federal tool that had governed voting-rights litigation for six decades was, in the space of a single day, converted into concrete, targeted losses of representation for Black voters across the South.

Separately that day, House Democrats filed a civil contempt resolution against former Attorney General Pam Bondi for refusing to appear for a deposition on the Epstein files, the House passed a budget resolution setting up fast-track reconciliation for up to $70 billion in immigration-enforcement funding, and Georgia's attorney general—running for governor—filed new felony charges against Cop City protesters just before the statute of limitations expired on four-year-old conduct.

**Thursday**

The redistricting scramble reached its most extraordinary point on Thursday. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry declared a state of emergency and suspended the state's May 16 primary just before early voting was to begin—despite more than 100,000 absentee ballots already having been distributed, and some already returned and counted. A congressional candidate immediately sued, arguing the suspension violated federal election-timing law and basic due process. Halting an election already in progress, with ballots already cast, is not an ordinary use of executive emergency power; it is a step with almost no modern precedent, undertaken specifically to secure a redistricting outcome made possible by the Court's ruling two days earlier.

The same day, Congress ended the longest agency shutdown in U.S. history, passing bipartisan legislation to fund most of the Department of Homeland Security while deliberately excluding ICE and CBP funding, which remains tied to the separate reconciliation track. Trump publicly called on the Senate to eliminate the filibuster, writing that doing so would let Republicans "not lose for 50 years"—an explicit linking of a procedural rule change to permanent partisan advantage. At a Senate hearing, Senator Jack Reed accused Defense Secretary Hegseth of giving the president "dangerously exaggerated" assessments of the ongoing Iran conflict, now in its eighth week, as the Strait of Hormuz standoff pushed gas prices to four-year highs and contributed to the collapse of Spirit Airlines.

**Friday**

The week closed on Friday with several threads converging at once. As the 60-day War Powers Act deadline for the Iran conflict arrived, Trump sent Congress a notice claiming that hostilities had "terminated" in early April—despite continued U.S. military presence and an ongoing blockade—and separately made the false claim that no prior president had ever sought War Powers authorization. Senate Majority Leader Thune declined to challenge the interpretation, leaving the assertion effectively uncontested by the chamber constitutionally charged with checking it.

The same day, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the FDA's 2021 decision permitting mail distribution of mifepristone, reinstating an in-person dispensing requirement over the agency's own scientific findings; the drug's manufacturer immediately asked the Supreme Court to intervene. Against this backdrop, the May Day Strong coalition—including 50501, No Kings, Indivisible, and major labor unions—organized more than 3,000 rallies, marches, and coordinated economic actions under the banner "Workers Over Billionaires," demanding higher taxes on the wealthy and curtailment of ICE operations. It was one of the largest coordinated civic mobilizations of the year.

Elsewhere, House Democrats opened an inquiry into whistleblower claims that DOJ leadership pressured prosecutors to rush charges against the Southern Poverty Law Center, Comey appeared in court to deny the seashell-post charges as reporting emerged of additional charges being pursued against him, and less than 72 hours after the weekend's shooting, DOJ filed a new emergency motion arguing the ballroom injunction "cannot defensibly continue." Investigative reporting that day also detailed a pattern of Trump family financial arrangements—promotion of family business interests documented 110 times since taking office, a $24 million Pentagon contract and Air Force drone purchases from companies backed by the president's sons, and a $1.6 billion federally supported mining venture in which his sons had acquired a stake.

**Looking Back**

Taken as a whole, the week showed how quickly a single legal ruling can reorder the machinery of representation, and how readily a security scare, once invoked, can be stretched to serve unrelated ends. The Voting Rights Act's practical dismantling did not wait for appeals or slow implementation; it produced special sessions, new maps, and a suspended election within forty-eight hours. Executive and legislative actors tested the limits of war powers, prosecutorial independence, and broadcast regulation largely without institutional resistance from the bodies traditionally expected to provide it—a Senate leader declining to contest a war-powers claim, a court overriding an agency's own scientific findings, an FCC chair explicitly threatening a network.

Yet the week did not pass unopposed: lawsuits were filed within hours of nearly every major action, a sitting judge turned around a deportation flight, and several thousand demonstrations unfolded across the country on its final day. Whether these countervailing efforts can keep pace with the speed of the changes they are answering remained, at week's end, an open question. ```

Title: The Week the Voting Rights Act Was Gutted, and States Raced to Cash In
Content:
```markdown This was the week the Supreme Court rewrote the practical meaning of the Voting Rights Act, and the country found out within hours what that meant. It was also a week in which a war the administration insisted had ended kept producing casualties, costs, and contradictions; in which federal law enforcement turned repeatedly toward journalists rather than away from them; and in which the human toll of immigration enforcement became harder to look past. Courts pushed back in places, unevenly, even as other institutions bent quickly to new pressure. Taken together, the seven days from May 2 through May 8 showed how fast the machinery of government can move once a single legal restraint is removed.

**The Weekend**

The weekend opened with the Supreme Court's ruling in *Callais v. Louisiana*, which required plaintiffs to prove discriminatory intent rather than discriminatory effect in redistricting cases—a standard that, in practice, eliminated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act as a workable tool against racial gerrymandering. The response was immediate. Alabama sought expedited review of a map already found unlawful. Indiana moved to dismiss a pending challenge. Courts in Mississippi and Florida reopened settled matters. Louisiana suspended an active congressional primary outright. The ACLU, the NAACP, and Louisiana voters filed suit within the same weekend, but the pace of state action was already outrunning the pace of legal response—a dynamic that would define the entire week.

The same weekend brought a second jolt: the Justice Department, under Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, indicted former FBI Director James Comey over a deleted Instagram post spelling "86 47" in seashells, a post Comey had already apologized for. The timing—days after a violent incident at the White House Correspondents' Dinner, and alongside a Republican senator's public acknowledgment that the phrase wasn't criminal—fed concerns that federal prosecutorial power was being aimed at a prominent critic rather than a genuine threat.

Trump closed out the weekend with a rapid-fire sequence of social media posts: fabricated images placing himself as a fifth face on Mount Rushmore, a golden self-portrait, a comparison of a reflecting pool's condition to the Obama years—interspersed with a racially charged attack on House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries calling for his impeachment. Separately, the administration argued that the conflict with Iran had "terminated," a claim meant to sidestep War Powers Resolution obligations, even as a naval blockade continued and Trump issued a 24-hour ultimatum threatening major air strikes. Senator Tammy Duckworth publicly disputed the "ended" framing, pointing to ongoing missile exchanges in the Strait of Hormuz. The war's costs were already visible in daily life: Spirit Airlines shut down entirely, eliminating roughly 17,000 jobs and citing fuel costs tied to the conflict; gas prices jumped more than thirty cents in a week; farmers reported being priced out of fertilizer.

**Monday**

The administration's attention turned to a different kind of project—converting a public golf course in Washington into a private course and expanding a "National Garden of American Heroes" monument park, without congressional approval. Democracy Forward sued, and a judge ordered the administration to begin producing internal communications about the plan. The same day, the Supreme Court, through Justice Alito, issued an administrative stay preserving mail and telehealth access to the abortion medication mifepristone after the Fifth Circuit had moved to restrict it—one of several moments this week where a court intervened against an executive or lower-court action, keeping the picture from being one of uniform institutional collapse.

Monday also brought a grimmer pattern into focus: multiple documented cases of medical neglect in ICE detention—an untreated ovarian cyst, appendicitis, a chest lump, chronic cardiovascular disease—alongside reporting that deaths in ICE custody had risen more than fivefold since medical reimbursements were cut. A federal judge, Melissa DuBose, said DHS had endangered her safety by publishing a false claim that she had knowingly released a murder suspect, and indicated she was weighing contempt proceedings. Smaller but telling incidents rounded out the day: a clash between ICE agents and protesters outside a Brooklyn hospital, renewed and baseless claims from Trump that a Texas municipal election had been "rigged," and antisemitic vandalism at synagogues and homes in Queens.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday belonged largely to Tennessee. Governor Bill Lee called a special legislative session aimed squarely at eliminating Memphis's only Democratic, majority-Black congressional district, and Republican leadership rejected Democratic requests for extended public comment or advance disclosure of the new map, compressing what would normally take weeks into days.

The same day, the Justice Department sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to compel release of sensitive voter data, including driver's license and Social Security numbers—part of a broader data campaign that multiple federal courts had already rejected. A U.S. attorney separately subpoenaed personal contact information for Fulton County's 2020 election workers, directing responses to his own office rather than a grand jury; Fulton County moved to quash the subpoena as politically motivated. In Indiana, voters ousted five of seven state senators who had resisted a Trump-aligned push to redraw maps, following a roughly $7 million ad campaign—a result suggesting that primary pressure alone could enforce redistricting compliance. Tom Homan, Trump's border advisor, promised an escalation of ICE deployment into resistant jurisdictions, declaring that "mass deportations are coming." Quietly, a DHS funding bill advanced through reconciliation carrying $1 billion for a White House ballroom project alongside billions for ICE and CBP.

**Wednesday**

The Supreme Court let its own *Callais* ruling take effect ahead of its standard 32-day waiting period, over a sharp dissent from Justice Jackson, clearing the way for Louisiana Republicans to redraw maps before the general election—a procedural acceleration that drew accusations the Court was actively managing the ruling's practical rollout rather than simply issuing it.

The same day, the FBI opened a criminal "insider threat" investigation into leaks made to journalist Sarah Fitzpatrick over her reporting on FBI Director Kash Patel's conduct—an unusual application of that tool to a reporter rather than a classified-information case. Hours later, the FBI raided the office of Virginia Senate President Pro Tempore L. Louise Lucas, an 82-year-old Black legislator who had led the state's redistricting reform efforts; Fox News' apparent advance presence at the scene suggested the raid had been tipped to friendly media beforehand.

Elsewhere, HHS confirmed the FDA had blocked publication of peer-reviewed, taxpayer-funded studies finding certain vaccines safe, and the *Washington Post* reported that the government had pressured satellite imagery firms to withhold damage assessments from the Middle East, forcing journalists to rely on Iranian and European sources to verify the war's toll. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick gave roughly 400 answers in a closed-door, unsworn session about his continued contact with Jeffrey Epstein after Epstein's 2008 conviction, including a 2012 visit to Epstein's island he called "inexplicable." The Justice Department also asked the Supreme Court to substitute itself as the defendant in E. Jean Carroll's $83.3 million defamation verdict against Trump—a maneuver that would result in dismissal, since the government cannot be sued for defamation—while DOJ closed San Francisco's major immigration court, relocating 120,000 pending cases to an already understaffed facility.

**Thursday**

Thursday brought the week's clearest and fastest-moving demonstration of what the *Callais* ruling had unleashed. Tennessee's Republican supermajority repealed a 1972 law banning mid-decade redistricting, passed a new map splitting Memphis across three Republican-leaning districts, and Governor Lee signed it into law the same day. State troopers cleared the House gallery of protesters, and Representative Justin Jones burned a Confederate flag in the Capitol rotunda in protest. The NAACP's Tennessee State Conference filed an emergency lawsuit within three hours of the bill's signing. Alabama's attorney general moved the same day to reinstate a map already found racially gerrymandered, while the governor urged defiance of a federal injunction—part of a wave that already included Ohio, Missouri, North Carolina, Texas, and Florida, with South Carolina and Louisiana still in progress.

Separately, the Southern Poverty Law Center was indicted on fraud charges that legal experts called weak, tied to standard informant-payment practices used in monitoring extremist groups. The human costs of immigration enforcement sharpened further: a federal judge ordered the release of the detained parents of an 18-year-old U.S. citizen with terminal cancer, who died a day after their reunion in Mexico; ProPublica documented at least 79 children injured by tear gas and pepper spray during enforcement operations; and reporting showed a 50 percent rise in children entering foster care due to parental detention.

On the press-freedom front, Kash Patel filed a $250 million lawsuit against *The Atlantic* and reporter Sarah Fitzpatrick, while the FBI separately investigated a *New York Times* reporter over coverage of his girlfriend's security detail, and Patel ordered polygraph tests of more than two dozen staff to find leakers. A confidential CIA assessment, meanwhile, found that Iran could sustain the ongoing blockade for three to four months and retained roughly 75 percent of its missile launchers—directly contradicting public claims by Trump and Defense Secretary Hegseth of an imminent Iranian collapse. Gas prices hit $4.56 a gallon, with 81 percent of Americans reporting financial strain, even as Shell posted a 24 percent jump in profits and Whirlpool described a "recession-level industry decline." Trump also publicly attacked Pope Leo XIV as "WEAK on Crime" over the pope's criticism of U.S. Iran and immigration policy.

**Friday**

Friday's rulings cut in different directions. Virginia's Supreme Court, in a 4–3 partisan decision, struck down a redistricting map nearly 3 million Virginians had approved by referendum just weeks earlier to counter Republican gerrymandering elsewhere, ruling on procedural grounds that the amendment process had begun before early voting concluded; the decision restored maps favoring Republicans, and Trump celebrated it as a "huge win." The same day, the Court of International Trade ruled Trump's global "Liberation Day" tariffs illegal, ordering a permanent injunction and refunds with interest—even as Trump simultaneously threatened "much higher" tariffs against the European Union if a trade deal wasn't reached by July 4.

Vice President Vance said the administration would threaten to withhold federal health funding from states resisting fraud-audit compliance, while CMS froze new hospice and home-health enrollments for six months, despite legal experts noting HHS lacks authority to withhold Medicaid funds broadly. Courts also pushed back elsewhere: a federal judge blocked sanctions against a UN rapporteur for criticizing Israel on First Amendment grounds, South Carolina's Supreme Court overturned Alex Murdaugh's convictions for jury interference, and a pardoned January 6 rioter was sentenced to prison for an unrelated burglary.

The week's press-freedom thread continued when Trump, during a Lincoln Memorial inspection of reflecting-pool repairs, called ABC reporter Rachel Scott's question about gas prices "stupid" and used a derogatory slur to describe her to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who laughed. A 22-foot golden Trump statue was unveiled at a Miami golf course amid a cryptocurrency financing dispute, a Gold Star mothers' luncheon was held at a Mar-a-Lago-style White House replica, and contaminated East Wing demolition debris was dumped at a public golf course without environmental review. Consumer sentiment, meanwhile, hit a record low of 48.2, and the administration projected a $2.1 trillion deficit for the fiscal year. California, separately, reached a $12.75 million settlement with General Motors over illegal sale of drivers' location data and pursued enforcement against State Farm over wildfire insurance claims—a reminder that some forms of institutional accountability continued regardless of federal dynamics.

By the end of the week, the throughlines were unmistakable. A single Supreme Court ruling had, within days, been converted by state legislatures into the elimination of decades-old minority representation, executed faster than courts, advocacy groups, or the public could respond in kind. A war described as over kept generating casualties, costs, and intelligence contradictions that officials struggled to reconcile with their own public statements. Federal law enforcement, meanwhile, turned its investigative and legal tools not only toward political opponents engaged in lawful voting-rights work but toward the journalists covering the officials who wielded that power. And running beneath all of it was a steady accumulation of harm to ordinary people—detainees denied medical care, children exposed to chemical agents, families separated, consumers absorbing rising costs while corporate profits climbed—that did not make headlines on their own but, taken together, described the week's real cost. Courts intervened in places, unevenly, preserving some rights and vacating others; legislatures moved with a speed that outpaced deliberation; and the public record of the week stands less as a single event than as a demonstration of how quickly the removal of one legal constraint can cascade through a system built to depend on it. ```
