Title: The Maps Come Down, the Bills Come Due
Content:
```markdown This was a week defined by speed: how quickly a single Supreme Court decision could travel through statehouses and courtrooms, how quickly war costs could outrun their own accounting, and how quickly the machinery of the presidency could be turned toward private benefit. By Friday, six states had moved to eliminate or dilute Black-majority congressional districts, an active election had been halted mid-vote, a defense secretary had threatened a sitting senator, and a taxpayer-funded compensation fund for January 6 defendants was taking shape. Courts and legislatures often reached opposite conclusions on the same questions, leaving the week's institutional picture mixed rather than uniform.

The pattern began before the week technically did. In the days following the Supreme Court's decision in Louisiana v. Callais, which weakened Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, courts across the country issued conflicting rulings on redistricting almost simultaneously. A federal court upheld California's voter-approved congressional map. Utah's Supreme Court protected a citizen-enacted anti-gerrymandering law. But Virginia's Supreme Court struck down a voter-approved map that could have benefited Democrats, and Florida's governor signed a new gerrymander that was challenged in court within days. Illinois Democrats, watching the pattern unfold, shelved their own voting-rights amendment rather than risk it meeting the same fate. The weekend also brought turmoil inside the Food and Drug Administration, where the president pressured the commissioner to approve flavored vapes over staff objections, the vaccine center overruled its own scientists on Covid vaccine access, and a director quit after one month on the job. Separately, a no-bid contract to repair the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool went to a company tied to the president's golf clubs, invoking an emergency exemption never used before and nearly tripling his original public estimate. And over the weekend, the president's social media account began posting fabricated images of destroyed Iranian military assets alongside AI-generated attacks on domestic critics — a preview of a pattern that would resurface later in the week. Amid all this, Hungary offered a rare counter-example: Péter Magyar was sworn in as prime minister after his party's landslide win over Viktor Orbán, pledging to restore rule of law and press freedom.

By Monday, the redistricting story had a sharper edge, and a second story — over war powers — opened in earnest. Louisiana suspended its congressional primary after more than 100,000 absentee ballots had already been distributed and roughly 42,000 votes cast, halting an election in progress in order to redraw districts and eliminate a Black-majority seat. At the same time, President Trump rejected Iran's ceasefire counterproposal as "a piece of garbage" and continued relying on a fragile truce to avoid seeking congressional authorization for war, even though the War Powers Act's 60-day deadline had expired ten days earlier. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth threatened a military tribunal against Senator Mark Kelly after Kelly discussed depleted weapons stockpiles on television — information Kelly said had come directly from Hegseth's own prior public testimony. Trump also floated "seriously considering" annexing Venezuela as a 51st state, citing its oil reserves. And reporting surfaced showing federal agencies and school curricula scrubbing civil rights history ahead of the nation's 250th anniversary, even as the reflecting-pool contract and an undisclosed UFC fundraiser on the White House lawn deepened questions about public resources being used for private benefit.

Tuesday sharpened both threads further. The Supreme Court, in an unsigned order, vacated a lower-court injunction and allowed Alabama to use a congressional map that a three-judge panel had already found intentionally discriminatory — offering no explanation, over a sharp dissent from the Court's three liberal justices. In Tennessee, the House Speaker stripped every Democratic legislator of committee assignments after they protested a special-session vote eliminating the state's only majority-Black district, a move Democratic lawmakers said stripped nearly two million Tennesseans of representation. Overnight, the president posted 55 times in roughly three hours, making false and conspiracy-laden claims against former President Obama and others, including a fabricated quote falsely attributed to a sitting Republican senator, while demanding the acting attorney general pursue indictments. Separately, after the Supreme Court ruled his tariffs unconstitutional, Trump publicly attacked two of his own appointees and called to "PACK THE COURT." A federal judge revealed that a Justice Department criminal investigation into Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell had been a "pretext" to pressure interest-rate policy, dropped only after a senator blocked a Fed nominee who was later advanced on a party-line vote. Hegseth's conflict with Kelly escalated further with a formal referral to Pentagon lawyers. And in Congress, Epstein survivors testified at a House Democratic field hearing about prosecutorial failures, even as Senate Democrats moved to block $1 billion in reconciliation funding earmarked for security around a White House ballroom project.

Wednesday brought Georgia into the redistricting story, as its governor called a special session to redraw maps, while Louisiana's legislature advanced its own bill to eliminate one of the state's two majority-Black congressional districts. Epstein testimony continued, with a survivor describing how the Justice Department had exposed her identity hundreds of times in released documents while redacting the names of her abusers. A federal appeals court granted Trump a delay in paying the $83.3 million E. Jean Carroll defamation judgment while he sought Supreme Court review. Separately, the Justice Department entered settlement talks over Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against the IRS — a case in which he was effectively both plaintiff and defendant — with one option under discussion eliminating mandatory presidential audits before a judge could even rule on the case's validity. The EPA, meanwhile, used a never-before-invoked national security provision to exempt facilities from regulations on ethylene oxide, a carcinogen found more dangerous than previously assessed. And NBC reported that military leaders were weighing whether to rename combat operations against Iran specifically to reset the expired 60-day War Powers Act clock.

Thursday delivered the seventh consecutive Senate rejection of a war-powers resolution to end U.S. involvement in the Iran conflict, failing 49-50 with only three Republicans crossing party lines. The redistricting wave widened further: Mississippi's governor announced plans to eliminate the state's only majority-Black district and specifically target its longest-serving Black congressman, South Carolina's governor was expected to call a special session for the same purpose, and Alabama petitioned the Supreme Court to cut its required majority-Black districts from two to one. Louisiana's state senate passed its bill 27-10, reshaping a 250-mile majority-Black district into a predominantly white suburban seat and potentially giving Republicans a 5-1 congressional majority in the state. Meanwhile, Pentagon officials testified that their $29 billion Iran war cost estimate excluded roughly $12 billion in documented damage to U.S. bases and left uncertain whether arms transfers to Israel were counted at all. Miami residents sued Trump, Florida's governor, and Miami Dade College over the transfer of nearly three acres of waterfront land, valued in the hundreds of millions, to Trump's presidential library foundation for a nominal sum. Against this, the Supreme Court, in a 7-2 decision, blocked a lower-court ruling that would have restricted nationwide mail-order access to mifepristone, preserving uniform federal drug authority. The VA reinstated a ban on abortion counseling for veterans, and Vice President Vance announced withholding $1.3 billion in Medicaid payments from California over disputed fraud claims.

The week closed on Friday with Tennessee's governor formally signing the new congressional map, eliminating the state's sole majority-Black district and positioning Republicans to hold all nine of its congressional seats — the culmination of the week's central story. Colorado's governor commuted the prison sentence of Tina Peters, convicted of unauthorized access to voting systems, following months of pressure, a symbolic federal pardon from Trump, and threats to withhold federal funds from the state. The IRS settlement talks produced a concrete figure: a taxpayer-funded $1.7 billion compensation fund for people claiming harm from alleged Biden-era DOJ targeting, including roughly 1,600 individuals convicted in the January 6 Capitol attack, with Trump retaining removal power over the fund's commissioners. New reporting detailed roughly $4 billion accumulated by the Trump family through cryptocurrency and business ventures, $5 billion raised by Jared Kushner from Middle Eastern investors while he served as a U.S. negotiator in the region, and more than $2 billion raised from wealthy donors for Trump's projects, some of whom later received pardons or jobs. Watchdog groups separately petitioned the Senate Judiciary Committee to investigate whether Justice Alito's oil-industry stockholdings had compromised his participation in energy-related cases. And at the state and local level, Providence's mayor vetoed a rent stabilization ordinance after months of tenant organizing, Minnesota Democrats staged an overnight legislative sit-in after a gun-violence bill was blocked from a vote, and Virginia's governor vetoed a bill that would have restored collective bargaining rights to 500,000 public workers. An independent analysis, largely unchallenged by major outlets, placed the true cost of the Iran war at $50 to $72 billion — roughly double the Pentagon's official figure.

Taken together, the week showed how quickly a single judicial ruling can cascade through the machinery of representation, and how unevenly the checks meant to contain executive power performed under pressure. Six states moved in near-lockstep to eliminate or dilute Black political representation within days of each other, while Congress failed repeatedly to reassert its constitutional authority over war-making and spending, and a sitting president pursued personal financial arrangements alongside official acts with little separation between the two. Not every institution yielded: courts preserved mifepristone access and blocked some gerrymanders, and Hungary's peaceful transfer of power stood as a reminder that democratic reversal is not inevitable. But the dominant story of the week was one of speed and coordination — how rapidly legal openings can be converted into lost representation, unaccounted costs, and blurred lines between public duty and private gain, and how much depends on which institutions still have the will and capacity to say no. ```

Title: The Slush Fund Week
Content:
```markdown This was the week a lawsuit the president filed against his own government quietly became a constitutional problem for his own party. It began on Monday with a routine-sounding announcement and ended on Friday with Senate Republicans burying their own immigration bill rather than let Democrats force a vote on it. In between, courts pushed back hard against prosecutorial abuse, Congress twice flinched from a war-powers vote it seemed poised to win, and the border and detention system kept producing casualties that no single week's news cycle could contain.

**The Weekend**

The weekend set a grim tone before the fund story even existed. Six migrants, including a 14-year-old, died of heat exposure in a sealed railcar near Laredo — a tragedy tied to a "prevention through deterrence" strategy that pushes border crossers into deadly terrain, compounded by a former Border Patrol agent's claim that agents are trained to sabotage water stations left by humanitarian groups. At the same time, ICE dropped its degree requirements and age caps while dangling $50,000 signing bonuses, raising alarms about who exactly would be given detention and deportation authority. In Colorado, the governor, under sustained pressure from Trump, commuted the sentence of Tina Peters, convicted of tampering with voting machines — a decision state election officials called a dangerous precedent. A Long Island Rail Road strike stranded 250,000 commuters, thousands rallied in Selma and Montgomery for voting rights following the Supreme Court's rollback of key protections, and reports surfaced of DHS agents intimidating journalists covering ICE operations.

**Monday**

By Monday, the week's defining story had begun, though it did not yet look like one. Trump and his sons dismissed, with prejudice, a $10 billion lawsuit they had filed against the IRS. In its place, the Justice Department announced a $1.776 billion fund — quickly dubbed the "Anti-Weaponization Fund" — drawn from the government's Judgment Fund and overseen by a five-member commission the president could remove at will. Reporters noted almost immediately that the fund's structure could allow it to compensate January 6 defendants. House Democrats filed an amicus brief calling it an unprecedented specter of corruption. On its first day, it was already more than a settlement.

Monday carried other weight too. A California state report on seven ICE detention facilities documented medical neglect linked to four deaths, contaminated food and water, overcrowding at 125 percent of capacity, and degrading strip-search practices — a systemic, state-verified record of abuse. A Brookings study estimated that more than 145,000 U.S. citizen children had lost all co-resident parents to immigration detention since January, with DHS's own figures judged a substantial undercount. A Third Circuit ruling narrowed judicial review for detained activist Mahmoud Khalil, blocking First Amendment retaliation claims from federal court until deportation proceedings concluded. In South Carolina, Republicans opened a special session to redraw the state's only Black-majority congressional district, acting on Trump's urging after the Supreme Court weakened Voting Rights Act protections. And on the National Mall, an eight-hour taxpayer-funded evangelical rally featuring top administration officials opened a broader "Freedom 250" anniversary program that had bypassed Congress's own bipartisan commission in favor of soliciting corporate donations for access to the president.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday deepened the fund story rather than letting it rest. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche signed an order permanently barring the IRS from investigating or prosecuting Trump, his family, and affiliated businesses — halting, among other things, a live audit potentially worth more than $100 million. Senate Democrats immediately demanded preservation of related documents. Then came a signal from inside the administration itself: Brian Morrissey, the Treasury general counsel responsible for approving Judgment Fund disbursements, resigned as the fund was announced, a move widely read as an internal legal objection. Elsewhere, a federal judge barred ICE from making arrests at three lower Manhattan immigration courthouses except in exceptional circumstances, and Trump signed executive orders easing fintech regulation while directing financial regulators to treat immigration status as a risk factor in banking decisions. The New York Times sued over a Pentagon policy requiring journalist escorts, and Trump gave the press an extensive tour of his fortified White House ballroom project, describing drone-proofing and titanium fencing in terms more befitting a bunker than a banquet hall.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday made the fund's ambitions explicit — and, simultaneously, exposed their fragility. Blanche signed an amended agreement declaring the government would "forever discharge" Trump, his sons, and affiliated entities from all IRS claims and audits, a legal shield with no clear precedent for a sitting president. Almost in the same breath, Judge Kathleen Williams dismissed Trump's original IRS lawsuit and found that its withdrawal referenced no actual settlement of record at all, undercutting the very origin story the fund had been built on. Capitol Police officers Daniel Hodges and Harry Dunn, both injured defending the building on January 6, filed suit arguing the fund was illegal and could end up compensating the people who attacked them. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson published an unusually candid public warning that the Supreme Court risked losing the public's confidence, citing the gutting of the Voting Rights Act and a pattern of emergency orders favoring Trump administration policies. And after the Senate parliamentarian blocked $1 billion in ballroom funding, Trump demanded Senate Republicans replace her with a loyalist and eliminate the filibuster outright, threatening political consequences for anyone who refused. The Senate, separately, advanced an Iran war-powers resolution by a 50–47 vote, with four Republicans joining Democrats to require congressional authorization for continued military operations. A federal judge also ordered the White House to comply with the Presidential Records Act, including preservation of Signal and WhatsApp communications, rejecting a separation-of-powers defense.

**Thursday**

Thursday brought the fund story to open crisis inside the Republican Party. Roughly two dozen GOP senators — including Mitch McConnell, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis, and Rand Paul — publicly and privately denounced the fund as "morally wrong," "stupid," and unprecedented, during a nearly two-hour, openly hostile meeting with Blanche. Representatives Fitzpatrick and Suozzi began drafting bipartisan legislation to kill the fund outright, and Speaker Johnson reportedly declined an Oval Office summons over the matter. The same day, the House quietly pulled its own Iran war-powers vote — one likely to pass with bipartisan support — adjourning early rather than let it reach the floor, a second retreat from a vote Congress seemed prepared to win.

Courts, meanwhile, delivered two forceful rebukes of prosecutorial conduct. Judge Waverly Crenshaw dismissed vindictive-prosecution charges against Kilmar Ábrego García, finding the Justice Department had reopened a closed case specifically to punish him after he successfully challenged his unlawful deportation — an act the judge called "an abuse of prosecuting power." Separately, federal prosecutors dropped all charges with prejudice against the "Broadview Six," Chicago ICE protesters, after a judge found prosecutors had improperly manipulated a grand jury, including removing jurors unwilling to indict. Elsewhere, a panel composed entirely of Trump appointees approved a 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery over 600 letters of public opposition. Eighteen young Americans filed a constitutional challenge against February's rollback of vehicle emissions standards, and Trump dismissed $43.6 billion in Iran-conflict-related fuel costs to American households as "peanuts."

**Friday**

By Friday, the fund's political cost had become tangible and immediate. Senate Republican leadership quietly shelved a $72 billion immigration and border enforcement bill — already stripped of $1 billion in ballroom funding — for fear that bringing it to the floor would let Democrats force a public reckoning over the fund. The same day, the fund's real-world purpose came into sharper focus: Proud Boys leader Enrique Tarrio, Mike Lindell, Michael Cohen, and others announced they would formally apply for payouts ranging into the hundreds of millions of dollars, even as Trump publicly described the fund as an act of generosity. Federal courts in Maine and Wisconsin rejected Justice Department demands for sensitive state voter data, continuing a pattern of judicial pushback seen in at least eight states. At Delaney Hall, a New Jersey detention facility, roughly 300 to 400 detainees escalated a hunger and labor strike over medical neglect, spoiled food, denial of bond, and stalled case processing, citing violations of their Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Amendment rights. Trump repeatedly promoted an online casino illegal in at least seventeen states shortly after its co-owner donated $1 million to his super PAC. And in Virginia, a judge dismissed charges against a school administrator who had ignored warnings that a six-year-old brought a gun to school, closing off criminal accountability despite an earlier $10 million civil verdict against her.

By week's end, a single thread ran through nearly everything: a fund conceived to close out one lawsuit had, within five days, become a permanent tax shield for a sitting president, a potential payday for people convicted of attacking the Capitol, and a source of open revolt within the president's own party — forceful enough to stall unrelated, urgent legislation on immigration enforcement. That its collapse into scandal took place alongside courts rejecting vindictive prosecutions, throwing out manipulated indictments, and blocking improper demands for voter data suggests an institutional system still capable of friction against concentrated executive power, even as Congress twice declined to test that power directly on questions of war. Meanwhile, the human costs of policy — migrant deaths in the desert, children separated from detained parents, detainees on hunger strike over medical neglect — persisted in the background, largely untouched by the week's institutional drama, a reminder that accountability fights in Washington do not automatically reach the people most affected by the policies in question. ```

Title: This Week in Democracy: A Slush Fund Blocked, a Senator Pepper-Sprayed, and a President's Face on the Money
Content:
```markdown This week began with a foreign policy announcement that didn't survive the weekend. The administration floated a memorandum that would have released $25 billion in frozen Iranian assets and lifted the naval blockade, but the framework collapsed almost as soon as it was announced. Iran's state media disputed the terms outright. Prime Minister Netanyahu called Trump directly to demand full nuclear dismantlement instead. Senate Republicans, including Marco Rubio's predecessor Mike Pompeo along with Ted Cruz, Lindsey Graham, and Roger Wicker, publicly denounced the framework as a giveaway. By the next day, Trump was telling reporters the blockade remained in force after all — a reversal suggesting the announcement had been made without securing buy-in from allies or his own party.

That same weekend, Trump's ongoing effort to punish Republican dissenters claimed new casualties. Senator Bill Cassidy lost his Louisiana primary, a defeat tied directly to his 2021 vote to impeach Trump. Five Indiana state senators who had resisted redistricting demands lost their seats as well, and Trump publicly attacked Representative Brian Fitzpatrick over independent votes. Yet the purge carried an unintended consequence: freed from electoral pressure by his own defeat, Cassidy indicated he would now support a war powers resolution challenging Trump's Iran policy — a reminder that removing the incentive to survive can also remove the incentive to comply.

Elsewhere over the weekend, a federal judge dismissed a criminal indictment against Kilmar Ábrego García, finding that the administration would not have prosecuted him had he not challenged his unlawful deportation to a Salvadoran prison — an unambiguous finding of vindictive prosecution, in which the government used the criminal justice system to punish a man for exercising his legal right to contest his own deportation. Separately, an overheating tank of methyl methacrylate at a Garden Grove aerospace facility forced evacuation orders for roughly 50,000 residents near Disneyland, prompting Governor Newsom to declare a state of emergency while firefighters worked through the weekend to cool the tank.

It was also over the weekend that the week's central story began to take shape, though almost no one recognized it yet. At the Delaney Hall immigration detention facility in Newark, New Jersey, roughly 300 detainees began a coordinated hunger and work strike, alleging worm-infested food, inadequate medical care, and pressure to self-deport. It would not stay a local story for long.

On Monday, Memorial Day, the Delaney Hall situation escalated sharply. Federal agents deployed pepper spray against roughly 150 protesters gathered outside the facility — and against Senator Andy Kim, who was present. The Department of Homeland Security later denied the incident had occurred at all, characterizing the protesters as dangerous rioters, a claim that stood in direct contradiction to video evidence showing the senator sprayed alongside demonstrators. The same day, Trump posted an AI-generated image depicting Representative Ro Khanna as a devil, along with violent AI-generated imagery of bombers attacking Iran and images suggesting territorial designs on Greenland, capping the holiday with a message attacking Democrats as disrespecting the military. Representative Thomas Massie, freshly defeated in his primary, used a television appearance to promise he would continue naming individuals from the Epstein files in the months ahead.

By Tuesday, the week's throughlines began to multiply. A three-judge federal panel — including two Trump appointees — found that Alabama's congressional map intentionally discriminated against Black voters and ordered a map with two majority-Black districts reinstated; Alabama announced it would appeal to the Supreme Court. In Texas, Governor Abbott designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations a foreign terrorist organization under state law and urged sheriffs to investigate alleged "sharia law" enforcement, while both Senate candidates in the state's runoff, John Cornyn and Ken Paxton, deployed anti-Muslim messaging in their campaigns — Cornyn going so far as to introduce a "Boot Sharia Law Act." At Delaney Hall, Governor Mikie Sherrill was refused entry to the facility she was attempting to inspect; DHS dismissed her visit as a "political stunt" as the hunger strike entered its fifth day. In a case with clear implications for the treatment of political speech, the Third Circuit paused re-detention of Palestinian-American activist Mahmoud Khalil pending Supreme Court review. And amid public concern over his visible health, Trump underwent a third physical examination at Walter Reed, after which he did not appear publicly for more than a week.

Wednesday brought the sharpest escalation yet at Delaney Hall. Senator Kim was pepper-sprayed a second time while attempting to enter the facility alongside Governor Sherrill. That evening, ICE agents deployed pepper spray and tasers against protesters, chasing some onto train tracks and spraying at least seven journalists in the process. DHS Secretary Mullin denied the hunger strike was even occurring and accused lawmakers of "spreading smears" — a claim increasingly difficult to square with the accumulating documentation. The same day, in South Carolina, the state senate rejected a mid-decade redistricting proposal targeting Representative Jim Clyburn's district by a 26–18 vote, with fourteen Republicans joining Democrats despite direct phone calls from Trump urging passage — a rare instance of the president's pressure campaign failing outright. Away from the political battles, a tank holding 600,000 gallons of caustic liquor ruptured at a paper mill in Longview, Washington, killing at least two workers with nine more missing and presumed dead, contaminating the Columbia River and prompting a federal safety investigation into what could become the deadliest industrial accident in the state's modern history.

Wednesday also surfaced a cluster of reporting on executive self-dealing. ProPublica revealed that a White House adviser had pressured the Pentagon into approving a $620 million loan to a startup linked to Donald Trump Jr. Separate reporting showed Trump had purchased Dell stock shortly before the Pentagon awarded Dell a $9.7 billion contract. The administration was also found to be diverting national park entrance fees to fund White House beautification projects, including an inflated no-bid contract for work on the Reflecting Pool. Elsewhere, the Office of Personnel Management circulated a draft nondisclosure agreement that would bar federal employees from speaking to journalists, backed by civil and criminal penalties. Reporting also disclosed that at least ten men had died by suicide in ICE custody since the start of Trump's second term, seven of them in the current fiscal year alone — the highest total in the agency's history. Trump, meanwhile, falsely claimed that Somali Americans in Minnesota are "all crooks," while the Justice Department refiled a $10 billion defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal over its Epstein-related reporting and separately argued in court that it holds unlimited power to fire federal employees for political reasons.

Thursday extended the self-enrichment thread into new territory. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a push for legislation to override an 1866 law banning the depiction of living persons on U.S. currency, with the Washington Post reporting that political appointees had pressured the Bureau of Engraving and Printing to design a $250 bill bearing Trump's likeness, reassigning the director who objected. DHS Secretary Mullin floated withdrawing customs agents from international airports in sanctuary cities to pressure local governments on immigration enforcement, a proposal the travel industry pushed back against forcefully. The Justice Department opened a criminal investigation into E. Jean Carroll, the writer who successfully sued Trump for sexual assault and defamation, examining whether she had committed perjury regarding funding for her lawsuits — though the Acting Attorney General recused himself given his prior work representing Trump. Economic data released the same day showed inflation had reached a three-year high, gross domestic product for the first quarter had been revised down, and the personal savings rate had plunged to its lowest level since 2022; Bessent characterized the collapsing savings rate as evidence of consumer confidence. Also on Thursday, a $106 million federal prison contract was awarded to a company led by a pardoned Trump fundraiser with a history of illegal lobbying, and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission gutted its cryptocurrency enforcement staff while retaliating against officials who had raised conflict-of-interest concerns involving firms tied to the president's family. At Delaney Hall, ICE deployed chemical spray and pepper balls against demonstrators again, striking some with batons and pushing others into traffic, and arrested six protesters after the hunger-strike leader was transferred to another facility.

The week closed with courts asserting themselves forcefully. A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order blocking the creation or disbursement of Trump's $1.8 billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund," after thirty-five former federal judges petitioned to reopen the underlying lawsuit, alleging the fund amounted to a collusive pretext and a fraud on the court; a hearing was set for June 12. Separately, another judge ruled that only Congress has the authority to rename the Kennedy Center, voiding its rebranding under Trump's name and blocking a board-approved closure. The same day, Trump signed an executive order directing the CDC to nearly halve the recommended childhood vaccine schedule, based on an assessment from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.; fifteen Democratic-led states sued within hours, arguing the change lacked scientific basis. Former Attorney General Pam Bondi appeared before the House Oversight Committee for a downgraded, unsworn interview on the Epstein files, acknowledging redaction errors while refusing to answer questions about Trump's involvement, as a Justice Department attorney repeatedly intervened to block such questions. At Delaney Hall, New Jersey announced that state police would assume public safety operations outside the facility and establish a protected protest zone, even as a fresh wave of federal agents arrived to investigate demonstrators and the Justice Department filed charges against a protester accused of assaulting an ICE officer. The Office of Management and Budget, under Director Russ Vought, proposed placing federal research grants under political appointee control rather than scientific peer review — a change estimated to potentially discontinue nearly half of NIH clinical trials, including more than a thousand cancer trials. The Justice Department also opened an inquiry into a nonprofit backed by Reid Hoffman that had helped fund Carroll's lawsuits, extending scrutiny of the president's critics into their financial networks. And in a scattering of related cases, a federal jury convicted three ICE protesters, including an Army veteran, on felony conspiracy charges; the Justice Department sued four additional states seeking unredacted voter data; a judge dismissed protest-related charges in Chicago over prosecutorial misconduct; and Minneapolis prosecutors charged a second ICE agent with assault.

Taken as a whole, the week recorded a government pulling in two directions at once. Federal power was used to disperse protesters and a sitting senator with chemical agents, to prosecute a plaintiff who had already won her case in court, to channel public money toward the president's family and allies, and to press for the president's image on the nation's currency. At the same time, courts intervened repeatedly and with unusual force — freezing a $1.8 billion fund, restoring a congressional map found to discriminate against Black voters, protecting a federally chartered cultural institution from unilateral rebranding, and pausing the re-detention of a political activist. Even within the president's own party, pressure did not always produce compliance: South Carolina Republicans rejected a redistricting map despite direct calls from the president, even as a Louisiana senator lost his seat for defying him months earlier. The week did not resolve which of these forces would prevail. It left, instead, a record of an executive testing the limits of its authority on multiple fronts simultaneously, and of institutions — judicial, legislative, and civic — testing whether those limits would hold. ```

Title: This Week in Democracy: A Slush Fund Dies, a Detention Center Erupts, and the Courts Split on Voting Rights
Content:
```markdown This was a week that seemed, for its first two days, like a run of genuine institutional pushback — and then spent the rest of its length demonstrating how quickly such gains can be undone, hedged, or quietly abandoned. Courts blocked a discriminatory map and a cultural-institution takeover. Congress forced a retreat on a $1.8 billion compensation fund. And yet by Friday, the map was back, the fund's fate was murkier than officials had claimed, and federal prosecutors were watching California count its votes while the president declared fraud before the count was finished.

The weekend set the pattern of courts asserting limits on executive power. A three-judge panel in Alabama, including two Trump appointees, unanimously found that the state's congressional map had been drawn with intentional discrimination against Black voters. That same weekend, a federal judge ruled that the Kennedy Center could not be renamed without congressional approval and blocked a planned two-year closure of the institution — prompting Trump to threaten to hand it back to Congress entirely and to launch a lengthy public attack on the judge who ruled against him. A third case added to the weekend's judicial scrutiny: a federal judge in Miami reopened Trump's $10 billion IRS lawsuit after 35 former federal judges alleged that the underlying settlement — which included a bar on auditing Trump's taxes and the creation of the $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund — was the product of collusion. The judge ordered a response by June 12 and signaled that DOJ officials, including the acting attorney general, could be compelled to testify.

The weekend's other defining story began at Delaney Hall, a New Jersey ICE facility, where roughly 300 detainees had launched a hunger and labor strike over conditions inside. DHS denied any problems existed. Then came pepper spray, deployed against detainees and, notably, against a visiting senator. Governor Sherrill deployed state police, and the response escalated further into teargas and mounted units against protesters outside the facility. A journalist covering the demonstrations reported being directly targeted with a flash-bang — something he said he had never experienced in years of covering similar protests. Alongside these major threads, Capitol Police officers who had defended the building on January 6 sued to block the weaponization fund on constitutional grounds, while more than a dozen Republican senators privately pushed to kill it, worried about political exposure ahead of the midterms. Smaller stories rounded out the weekend: an OMB proposal to let political appointees terminate university research grants outside peer review, and a cluster of reporting on federal contracts and loans flowing toward companies tied to Trump and his family, including a $9.7 billion Pentagon contract to Dell awarded after Trump personally bought and promoted the company's stock.

By Monday, the Supreme Court delivered a narrower kind of relief. In a 6-3 ruling, the Court struck down Trump's executive order attempting to deny citizenship to children born to undocumented or temporary-visa parents, preserving a constitutional principle affecting more than 250,000 children a year. But three conservative justices dissented, lending unusual credibility to fringe legal theories and signaling that birthright citizenship's constitutional footing, while intact, was not secure. The same day, a federal appeals court found the Pentagon's transgender military ban likely unconstitutional and driven by animus, protecting currently serving members even as new enlistment remained barred, and a separate federal judge blocked the administration's attempt to move a major atmospheric research supercomputing center out of Colorado, ruling it was likely retaliation tied to a dispute with the state's governor. Also on Monday, the administration announced — for the first time — that it was abandoning the $1.8 billion weaponization fund, following a meeting between Trump and Speaker Johnson. Senate Democrats introduced the "Drain the Slush Fund Act" to make the reversal permanent and retroactive, a sign that they did not trust the announcement to hold on its own. Elsewhere, the Pentagon reclassified its press office in a way that barred journalists without appointments, and Trump posted language announcing a Washington rally nearly identical to his December 2020 call that preceded January 6, alongside AI-generated images depicting himself in grandiose and racially charged terms.

Tuesday brought the fund saga into open congressional testimony. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche told Congress the Justice Department would not proceed with the fund, declaring it over "period" — but he declined to commit to that reversal in writing, an omission that would matter later in the week. House Republicans moved separately to block the fund and shelved $1 billion in White House ballroom security funding. The same day, Trump signed an executive order directing that bank accounts allegedly used to enable illegal immigration or store benefits be shut down, their funds seized and returned to taxpayers, framed as retaliation against "anti-ICE rioters." Separately, investigations revealed a network of purportedly progressive super PACs, funded through shell companies and vendors tied to House Republican leadership, coordinating to boost weak Democratic candidates and attack strong ones across multiple primary races. New Jersey's governor, attorney general, and Newark's mayor announced lawsuits against GEO Group over health conditions at Delaney Hall and the denial of state health department access — a distinct legal track from the protest-suppression story unfolding at the facility's gates. In a quieter admission, the administration cut tariffs on farm and construction equipment from 25 to 15 percent, tacitly conceding that tariffs had been driving up consumer prices after months of denying it.

Wednesday delivered the week's sharpest reversal. In an unsigned 6-3 decision, the Supreme Court overturned the prior weekend's lower-court finding on Alabama, permitting the state to use its redrawn map — the one found to intentionally discriminate against Black voters — for the midterms. The three liberal justices dissented sharply, accusing the majority of abandoning the rule of law. The whiplash was stark: a unanimous panel including two Trump appointees had found intentional discrimination just days earlier, and the nation's highest court erased that finding before the week was out. The same day, the House passed a war powers resolution 215-208, with four Republicans joining Democrats, directing Trump to end hostilities with Iran absent congressional authorization — the first such resolution to pass after months of blocked attempts, and only after Speaker Johnson had earlier tried to send members home early to prevent the vote. Trump signed a separate order stripping civil service protections from an estimated 8,000 to 10,000 senior federal employees, enabling their removal without due process — a restoration of a Project 2025 priority that had been rescinded under the previous administration. Trump also posted demanding that his New York criminal conviction and civil fraud judgment be dismissed, calling for the prosecution of Attorney General Letitia James and District Attorney Alvin Bragg. In smaller but pointed moments, the Senate parliamentarian ruled that ballroom security funding violated budget rules, forcing its removal from a reconciliation bill, and Representative Ted Lieu played footage during a House hearing showing Trump asleep in Cabinet meetings — footage Secretary Rubio denied witnessing despite sitting beside the president in it.

Thursday showed the Kennedy Center complying with the earlier court order, its general counsel directing staff to restore the institution's original name on signage by the following Friday — the clearest sign all week that judicial authority still carried practical weight somewhere. But the day's darker story came out of Louisiana, where Mamuka Artmeladze, 43, a detainee with no criminal record, was found unresponsive and pronounced dead at Winn Correctional Center. It was the 50th death in ICE custody under this administration and the 19th of the year, occurring after federal inspectors had already documented unsanitary conditions and excessive force at the facility. Separately, reporting found that fourteen of twenty-seven known corporate donors to Trump's White House ballroom project had secured new or expanded federal contracts worth more than $50 billion since donating, including Lockheed Martin, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Palantir. Trump also touted a "Trump Promenade" addition to the Lincoln Memorial without disclosing its funding, and described the ballroom project as incorporating a "DronePort" and other military elements. Oil reserves, meanwhile, fell to their lowest level since 2004, as the administration drained the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to manage price spikes tied to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the ongoing Iran conflict. Governor Sherrill announced a $12 million increase in immigration legal defense funding, a modest concession following weeks of protest pressure over the state's Delaney Hall response.

Friday closed the week with the weaponization fund's fate still genuinely unresolved. The Senate passed a $70 billion ICE and Border Patrol funding package, 52-47, through reconciliation, funding immigration enforcement through the end of Trump's term — but every amendment aimed at restricting the anti-weaponization fund had failed the day before, leaving it technically alive despite the acting attorney general's public claim that it was dead. As California's gubernatorial primary count continued, Trump declared a premature winner and accused the state of rigging the election without evidence; the Justice Department sent a federal prosecutor to observe ballot processing in Los Angeles County and announced unspecified fraud investigations, which state officials rejected outright. A federal judge struck down a Trump policy that had frozen immigration benefit processing for nationals of 39 countries, calling it impermissible animus — even as, in a separate and unrelated case over the White House ballroom, DOJ lawyers argued that courts lacked authority to halt the project's construction even if it violated the law, comparing judicial intervention to an inability to stop the demolition of the Statue of Liberty. At a Florida detention facility, detainees reported that guards withheld food and provided contaminated water to pressure them into signing documents in English they could not understand, and ICE's acting director quietly rescinded a requirement to report detainee deaths occurring within 30 days of release — following a year that had already recorded dozens of such deaths. New York's legislature approved a one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers pending the governor's signature, and senior U.S. officials, including Vice President Vance, used a British murder case to promote anti-immigration messaging abroad.

Taken as a whole, the week offers a study in how quickly institutional wins can be reversed, hedged, or left ambiguous even as they are announced. Courts blocked a discriminatory map, only to have the Supreme Court restore it days later. Congress forced a public retreat on a contested compensation fund, only for the Senate to leave it technically intact and for the president to keep advocating for it after his own attorney general declared it over. A cultural institution complied with a judicial order to restore its name, even as the Justice Department argued in a separate case that courts had no power to stop a president's construction project at all. Detainees at one facility faced escalating force from state and federal agents; detainees at another died after documented warnings went unheeded, while the agency responsible quietly narrowed its own reporting obligations. None of these threads resolved cleanly by Friday. What the week recorded, more than any single verdict, was the persistent gap between institutions asserting their authority and the administration's capacity — sometimes successful, sometimes not — to outlast, evade, or simply ignore that assertion. ```

Title: This Week in Democracy: War Powers on a Truth Social Feed
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which volatility at the top of the executive branch collided, again and again, with resistance built into the machinery beneath it. A president who could not sustain attention during an active attack on American forces spent the week lurching between threats of war and claims of peace, while federal judges, a divided Congress, and even a besieged nonprofit's own board became the last obstacles standing in his way. By Friday, the pattern was unmistakable: courts blocking, agencies defying, and money moving in directions Congress had explicitly forbidden.

The weekend set the tone. As Iran launched missile and drone strikes on U.S. facilities, Trump posted about golf course renovations at a military installation and shared AI-generated videos glorifying himself, then appeared to doze off during a signing ceremony. Days later, when NBC's Kristen Welker pressed him on his unsubstantiated claims that the 2020 election and a recent California election had been rigged, he called her "crooked or stupid," tore off his microphone, and walked out before flying to Bedminster. In between, Senator Andy Kim was denied access to detainees during an oversight visit to Delaney Hall in New Jersey, where he witnessed a detainee in apparent medical distress that staff refused to explain. A Justice Department attorney told the D.C. Circuit, in arguments over the administration's $400 million White House ballroom project, that courts have no authority to review executive demolition of federal property after the fact — unable to say whether the same reasoning would bar review of bulldozing the Statue of Liberty. A whistleblower separately revealed that Department of Government Efficiency officials had devised a scheme to falsely mark roughly 2.7 million people, including U.S. citizens, as dead in federal records to coerce self-deportation; about 6,100 people were actually entered into the Death Master File. At Normandy, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used a D-Day commemoration to describe European immigration as an "invasion," borrowing language associated with white nationalist ideology at a solemn Allied ceremony.

By Monday, courts began pushing back in earnest. Judge Leo Sorokin struck down Trump's $100,000 H-1B visa fee as an unlawful tax, ruling that only Congress holds the power to levy such charges. The same day, Judge Christopher Cooper ordered Trump's name stripped from the Kennedy Center, ruling that only Congress can rename a congressionally chartered institution, and temporarily blocked a related $257 million renovation. Elsewhere, border czar Tom Homan said he had reviewed plans to surge an unprecedented number of ICE agents into New York City, timed to coincide with major sporting events, in what read as retaliation for the state's new sanctuary law. Trump, in a separate NBC interview, declined to rule out using a nearly $1.8 billion fund to compensate people convicted of assaulting police during the January 6 attack — despite his own acting attorney general having previously called the fund dead. Reporting meanwhile deepened on the financial entanglements surrounding Trump's family: Jared Kushner's $2 billion in Saudi investment, a Kushner-Ivanka resort project in Albania drawing mass protest over environmental damage, and an $8 billion Penn Station plan raising fresh conflict-of-interest questions. In the Senate, Republicans blocked Democratic amendments that would have barred a presidential slush fund, prohibited William Pulte from holding two federal posts simultaneously, and restricted unapproved ballroom spending.

Tuesday introduced what would become the week's second major crisis. Trump announced that Pulte — the head of a housing finance agency with no intelligence background — would become acting Director of National Intelligence while retaining his existing post, and floated eliminating the DNI office altogether. The same day, after an Apache helicopter was reportedly shot down near the Strait of Hormuz, Trump ordered Central Command to strike Iranian radar and air-defense sites; Iran responded with strikes on U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, and Jordan. Vice President Vance said he would refer Minnesota's governor and attorney general for criminal investigation over unproven claims involving Somali immigrant fraud, drawing accusations of political retaliation against opposition officials. House Oversight Chair James Comer declined to subpoena Todd Blanche in connection with the Epstein matter even as the committee heard testimony from a longtime Epstein assistant. In Maine, Graham Platner won the Democratic Senate primary with 72 percent of the vote despite documented misconduct allegations against him, a result that raised its own questions about party accountability heading into a competitive general election.

Wednesday brought the two crises together. The House passed the $70 billion Secure America Act along strict party lines, 214–212, funding ICE and CBP through 2029 without any of the oversight reforms Democrats had sought following civilian deaths during enforcement operations. The Justice Department briefly established the $1.8 billion fund for Trump allies — including individuals convicted of assaulting police on January 6 — before abruptly cancelling it under bipartisan legislative pressure. At the same time, Trump doubled down on installing Pulte at DNI even as bipartisan opposition mounted, threatening the pending reauthorization of FISA Section 702 before it expired. ProPublica reported that Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani had invested at least $100 million in a Texas startup secretly tied to Donald Trump Jr. around the same period his family secured tariff exemptions and sanctions relief from the administration. Trump also pressed Congress to fast-track a $350 billion military spending bill alongside a restrictive voting measure requiring proof of citizenship and curbing mail-in ballots, and, asked about rising prices, said he "loves" inflation even as markets fell and oil prices spiked following the renewed strikes on Iran.

Thursday carried the Iran volatility to its sharpest point yet. Trump announced imminent "very hard" strikes on Iran and floated seizing Kharg Island and Iran's oil markets outright — then, hours later, claimed to have cancelled the strikes after reaching a deal, an account Israeli officials publicly disputed. The whiplash was matched by legislative collapse: the House failed even a short-term FISA extension in a 198–218 vote amid Democratic protest over the Pulte nomination, allowing the surveillance authority to lapse, though existing court certifications kept some collection running. The Department of Homeland Security published a waiver suspending the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, and tribal grave protections to build 17 miles of border wall and roads through Big Bend National Park — an area accounting for less than half a percent of unauthorized crossings. About 100 FBI agents raided the offices and homes of board members connected to the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a voter-registration nonprofit, citing a fraud justification despite the statistical rarity of such fraud. Separately, former and current FBI agents described a wave of departures — reportedly up to 2,800 since January 2025 — attributed to pressure to violate professional standards under Director Kash Patel. Federal prosecutors also unsealed charges against eight pro-Palestinian activists accused of an intimidation campaign tied to divestment demands at the University of Michigan.

Friday closed the week with the Kennedy Center saga reaching its resolution. After the D.C. Circuit denied Trump's emergency stay of the renaming order, the Kennedy Center's board amended its own bylaws to threaten bankruptcy if Trump's name were removed — a maneuver legal experts described as a violation of fiduciary duty. The name came down only after midnight. The same day, the administration diverted $352 million in Secret Service funds toward the ballroom project, despite earlier promises it would be privately financed and after Congress had explicitly refused to appropriate $1 billion for it. Judge Leonie Brinkema extended, then formalized, an injunction blocking the $1.8 billion allies' fund, ordering senior officials to certify compliance under penalty of perjury. Trump separately pressed Congress to pass a symbolic resolution nullifying his two impeachments, despite constitutional scholars noting no such mechanism exists in law; Speaker Johnson called it a priority for after the midterms. At Delaney Hall, nearly 40 women began a hunger and labor strike demanding the release of vulnerable detainees and improved conditions; ICE and its private contractor responded with new restrictions, police used tear gas and made arrests against supporting protesters outside the facility, and the Department of Homeland Security publicly denied the strike was happening at all. Reporting also revealed that Joint Chiefs Chairman Dan Caine had made a rushed secret trip to brief Trump on a plan for a ground invasion of Iran aimed at seizing enriched uranium — an operation Trump ultimately paused after warnings of severe retaliation. And in Minnesota, Vance Boelter pleaded guilty to murdering former House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband, and to wounding a state senator and his wife, in a politically motivated attack, receiving two consecutive life sentences.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a presidency operating at the edge of its own institutional restraints, and a system of checks straining, unevenly, to hold. War powers were exercised and reversed on a private social media timeline rather than through congressional debate. An unqualified political loyalist's path to the nation's top intelligence post proved so contentious that it took down a foundational surveillance law rather than reforming it. Courts intervened repeatedly and, in several instances, successfully — vacating an unlawful tax, enforcing a renaming order against an institution's own resistance, and blocking a fund that would have rewarded people convicted of assaulting police officers. But other checks bent rather than held: Congress passed enforcement funding without conditions even as detainees at a New Jersey facility went on hunger strike and were met with denial and force, and money continued to move — from Secret Service accounts to a ballroom, from foreign investors to family businesses — in patterns that outlasted any single day's headlines. The week's throughline was less about any one crisis than about how many simultaneous ones the country's institutions were being asked to absorb at once. ```

Title: A Birthday Party, an Arch, and a War Nobody Can Explain
Content:
```markdown This was the week the White House became a stage. Donald Trump turned his 80th birthday into a corporate-sponsored spectacle on the South Lawn, Congress let a surveillance law lapse without renewing it, and a hastily announced deal with Iran unraveled in full public view within days. Beneath the noise, courts kept intervening against the administration's excesses — sometimes successfully, sometimes only after visible delay and resistance. By week's end, an untested loyalist had taken charge of American intelligence, a mosque president had been freed from what a judge called retaliatory detention, and a small Georgia town had beaten back a federal detention center simply by refusing to accept it.

**The Weekend**

The weekend began with the UFC event, and it was no sideshow. Trump hosted a fight card on the White House lawn to mark his birthday, backed by at least $60 million in combined federal agency and UFC funding, cryptocurrency bonuses distributed through his family's World Liberty Financial venture, and his own stockholding in UFC's parent company. Legal efforts to stop the event failed in court, and when a fighter made a racist, sexist remark about Michelle Obama during the broadcast, Trump said nothing. Army ceremonial units more commonly reserved for visiting heads of state opened a related press conference at the Lincoln Memorial, blurring the line between military pageantry and personal promotion. The event's financing, political convenience, and symbolism would prove not to be a one-off; later reporting connected it to plans for a July 4 rally and to Trump's continued use of a foreign government's jet — part of a broader pattern of turning the presidency into an instrument of self-glorification.

Even as the party unfolded, courts pushed back elsewhere. A federal judge's order to strip Trump's name from the Kennedy Center's facade survived an emergency appeal, and workers quietly removed the signage overnight under tarps. The Trump-appointed board that runs the center voted to keep fighting the ruling anyway — a pattern of grudging, incomplete compliance that would recur throughout the week. Separately, Judge Leonie Brinkema blocked a $1.8 billion fund that had emerged from Trump's own legal settlement with the IRS, taxpayer money that could have been used to compensate his allies and January 6 defendants. A second court ordered the restoration of historical exhibits on slavery, civil rights, Indigenous history, and climate change that had been stripped from national parks the previous year, giving the administration three weeks to comply. Each ruling represented a check on an administration eager to rewrite institutions, records, and financial arrangements in its own image.

Immigration enforcement hardened over the same stretch. Trump signed a $70 billion Department of Homeland Security funding law locking in years of expanded ICE and CBP operations through 2029, stripped of the accountability measures — warrant requirements, body cameras — that Democrats had sought. In Ohio, FBI agents raided the Cleveland office of a voter registration group and visited affiliated individuals' homes, seizing devices as part of a broader push to investigate voter fraud ahead of the midterms. At midnight, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act lapsed for the first time in eighteen years, after Congress failed to renew it amid Democratic distrust of Trump's installation of a politically loyal acting director of national intelligence — a distrust that would prove well-founded by Friday. New Jersey's attorney general sued to force health inspections at Delaney Hall, an ICE-contracted facility in Newark, while the governor toured the site and protesters were arrested in solidarity outside. And the New York Times reported that the administration had seriously considered suspending habeas corpus to speed deportations after the Supreme Court affirmed migrants' right to challenge removal in court — a contemplated step, not an executed one, but a serious one nonetheless.

**Monday**

The week's second major storyline emerged Monday, when Trump announced via social media that a deal with Iran was complete and that the U.S. naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz would be lifted. The agreement's text was withheld even as Iran's foreign ministry began describing terms — on sanctions relief and Hormuz transit fees — that sharply contradicted the administration's account. The same day, Governor Gavin Newsom announced that Trump had directed Justice Department investigations into him and his wife, describing a year of federal scrutiny and grand jury activity aimed at a potential 2028 rival. The Justice Department also charged five men with plotting to attack the UFC event with explosive drones and snipers, a plot uncovered after a tip from one suspect's mother — a rare instance of the week's security apparatus functioning as intended, though its aftermath would raise separate concerns. Meanwhile, Shasta County, California, passed a ballot measure ending mail-in and early voting and mandating hand-counted ballots, prompting the state's attorney general to announce plans to sue. And Representative Jamie Raskin accused FBI Director Kash Patel of directing more than $1 million in bonuses to loyalist agents, calling it a possible personal slush fund.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought the week's densest concentration of institutional strain. New reporting detailed how Stephen Miller had proposed suspending habeas corpus outright, and how Miller and Vice President Vance had separately pushed for invoking the Insurrection Act to suppress protests after ICE agents killed two civilians, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in Minnesota. The administration was also reported to be reclassifying long-term immigrant residents to deny them bond hearings, in apparent defiance of court rulings against the practice. In a starkly asymmetrical response to the Minnesota killings, federal prosecutors charged fifteen protesters with conspiracy for opposing the crackdown — even as the agents involved faced no charges, and even as eighteen of thirty-six earlier cases against protesters had already been dropped, one after a judge found it rested on a false affidavit. FBI Director Patel then posted details from a court-sealed investigation into the UFC attack plot on social media, prompting allegations that he had violated disclosure rules; Trump, asked about the plot at the G7 summit, appeared unaware of it. Trump also threatened Senator Lindsey Graham over his skepticism of the Iran deal, warning he would be "in big trouble" — a threat that drew pushback from Graham and other Republicans asserting Congress's right to review any nuclear agreement. The Kennedy Center board, for its part, missed the court-ordered deadline to remove Trump's name by twelve hours, then certified compliance while the facade sat under a tarp. And reporting confirmed that a $14 million no-bid Reflecting Pool renovation and a promised $200 million East Wing ballroom project, now grown to roughly $600 million, were both running far over their advertised costs.

**Wednesday**

On Wednesday, Trump signed the Iran memorandum of understanding at the Palace of Versailles, having abruptly reversed an earlier plan to have Vance sign it instead. The backlash was immediate: Republican senators including Bill Cassidy, Ted Cruz, and Thom Tillis criticized reported concessions, including a $300 billion fund for Iran and immediate sanctions relief granted without preconditions. Elsewhere, the Justice Department refused to file a court-required declaration certifying that the blocked $1.8 billion fund had actually been halted, citing separation-of-powers concerns — continued resistance to a judicial order rather than compliance with it. The department also settled claims for Michael Flynn and Carter Page at $1.25 million each, using the same judgment-fund mechanism that January 6 defendants convicted of assaulting police were separately pursuing for their own payouts, prompting Senator Adam Schiff to introduce legislation barring such payments. Congressional staff visited the federal prison camp housing Ghislaine Maxwell to investigate allegations of preferential treatment, only to have Bureau of Prisons leadership repeatedly shut down their questioning. And new reporting showed that ICE detention deaths had more than doubled since Trump's second term began, while the agency was found to be purchasing immigrant tax records from a data broker in an apparent workaround of a court order restricting such access.

**Thursday**

Thursday delivered the Iran deal's final unraveling for the week. The administration released the fourteen-point memorandum text, only for Vance's public claim — that sanctions relief was contingent on Iranian behavioral change — to be directly contradicted by the document's actual language, which provided for immediate relief. In a notable counterpoint, Georgia's Republican House Speaker announced the legislature would not redraw the state's congressional map despite Trump's pressure to exploit a Supreme Court ruling weakening Voting Rights Act protections, citing the need for a deliberate process — a rare instance of a Republican-led body declining to use an opening for partisan advantage. At the intelligence community's headquarters, Bill Pulte arrived a day ahead of his official start as acting Director of National Intelligence, requesting a full employee list to plan cuts of potentially hundreds of jobs and asking about bringing classified briefings home. The Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel issued a memo arguing that federal disability law does not require community-based care alternatives to institutionalization, explicitly acknowledging a break from thirty years of settled interpretation. And the administration's denaturalization campaign accelerated sharply, with 29 cases filed in under two months against a total of 166 filed between 2008 and mid-2026, and plans for at least 250 more by October.

**Friday**

The week closed on Friday with Pulte formally sworn in as acting Director of National Intelligence, after Trump cancelled the Senate confirmation hearing of his intended nominee, Jay Clayton, by social media post. Pulte arrived with no intelligence background and a documented history of pursuing politically motivated referrals against Trump's critics. The same day, a federal judge ordered the release of Salah Sarsour, a Wisconsin mosque president and green card holder, finding that immigration officials had likely detained him in retaliation for his Palestinian rights advocacy after Secretary of State Marco Rubio personally signed a memo targeting him — a ruling that found a legal resident's detention had violated his First Amendment rights. In North Carolina, the legislature continued advancing a package of bills granting partisan control over election administration, criminalizing homelessness, and diluting Black voter power, despite sustained public opposition and the governor's objections. In Georgia, DHS reversed course and cancelled plans for a 10,000-bed detention center in a converted warehouse after a small town sued and organized against it. Federal prosecutors indicted fifteen more Minneapolis protesters after infiltrating their encrypted communications, even as the FBI seized a voting rights group's devices and subpoenaed a national voting organization. Trump's fabricated claim that Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had "begged" him for a photo at the G7 prompted a public denunciation from Meloni and the cancellation of a planned visit by Italy's foreign minister. And officials delayed release of a report on voting machine vulnerabilities even as Pulte was directed to investigate claims of "rigged elections."

Taken as a whole, the week showed an executive branch testing the outer edges of its authority on multiple fronts at once — over intelligence leadership, foreign policy, detention, and dissent — while courts, career officials, and even some Republican lawmakers and local governments pushed back, not always successfully and rarely without delay. The Iran memorandum's public collapse, the surveillance lapse, and the installation of an inexperienced loyalist atop American intelligence were not isolated events but connected symptoms of an administration moving fast and disclosing little. Judicial rulings on the Kennedy Center, the anti-weaponization fund, national park exhibits, and a wrongly detained mosque president showed that institutional checks still functioned — but compliance came late, grudgingly, or under visible duress. For a system built on the assumption that power answers eventually to law, this was a week that tested how long "eventually" can stretch before it stops meaning anything at all. ```
Excerpt: The week opened with spectacle and closed with confusion.
