Title: This Week in Democracy: A Fabricated Vandal, a Hostage Housing Bill, and the End of Independent Agencies
Content:
```markdown This week in American governance produced a genuine constitutional turning point wrapped in a strange and telling sideshow. The Supreme Court delivered its most consequential ruling in decades on presidential power even as the president devoted extraordinary personal attention to a fabricated vandalism story about a public fountain. By week's end, a bipartisan majority of the Senate had asserted, then abandoned, its constitutional authority over an ongoing conflict; a popular housing bill sat unsigned as a hostage to voting-law demands; and courts had once again rejected the administration's efforts to seize control of state voter rolls. Taken together, the week showed institutions bending under sustained pressure from a single office, sometimes without much resistance at all.

The pattern began over the weekend, when the Supreme Court issued back-to-back 6-3 rulings that eliminated meaningful judicial review of two major immigration actions. One decision allowed the administration to terminate Temporary Protected Status for roughly 350,000 Haitians and thousands of Syrians who had built lives in the United States under that designation. The other authorized a revived "metering" policy letting border officials physically turn away asylum seekers before they can make a legal claim. Both rulings shared a common thread: they did not merely uphold the administration's immigration policy but stripped the courts of any further ability to examine it. Alongside these rulings, a review of more than 1,200 lawsuits found that 93 percent of ICE street arrests in New York and New Jersey targeted Latino residents — far exceeding their share of the undocumented population in those states — while federal judges separately described some ICE tactics as "abhorrent and illegal." The administration also installed William Pulte, a loyalist with no intelligence background, as acting director of national intelligence over bipartisan objections; he moved quickly to fire roughly 300 people at the National Counterterrorism Center.

It was also over the weekend that a stranger story began, one that would consume disproportionate public attention for days. Trump posted that "Radical Left Lunatics" had cut a "gash" in the reflecting pool at the Lincoln Memorial and poured chemicals into it, despite visible evidence that the damage came from a failed renovation project and routine algae treatment. Nothing suggested a crime had occurred. The claim, however, did not stay contained to social media.

By Monday, the reflecting pool story had become an active law-enforcement matter. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro announced aggressive prosecution over the alleged damage, out-of-state law enforcement personnel were deputized to conduct detainments at the site, and a 67-year-old Olympic canoeist was arrested for touching peeling material near the pool. Trump kept escalating his claims across multiple posts even as the underlying facts remained unchanged. Separately, the National Park Service awarded a no-bid repair contract worth at least $1.7 million to a firm ultimately owned by a Trump campaign donor, with the Interior Department denying any political awareness of the connection. Monday also brought smaller but notable developments: Amazon and Goodreads restricted reviews of Vice President Vance's newly published memoir after a wave of critical feedback, the Treasury Department issued a 60-day waiver on Iranian oil sanctions that Vance described in terms Iranian officials immediately disputed, and Defense Secretary Hegseth removed a widely respected Army Europe commander, drawing criticism from Senator Thom Tillis that loyalty was displacing competence in military leadership.

Tuesday offered a rare glimpse of ordinary legislative functioning — one soon to be undone. The Senate passed the 21st Century Road to Housing Act 85-5, a bipartisan measure meant to lower housing costs and restrict investor purchases of single-family homes, sending it to the House ahead of the midterms. The same day, deep cuts to HIV and AIDS programs advanced on multiple fronts: NIH froze HIV research funding in South Africa, the House proposed a $225 million cut to the Ryan White program, and a 2027 budget proposal would eliminate CDC HIV-prevention funding entirely. Tech-industry Super PACs poured $24.5 million into a single New York primary contest over artificial intelligence regulation, an extraordinary concentration of spending on one House race. Trump also renewed demands that Illinois Governor Pritzker accept National Guard deployment following a violent weekend in Chicago — a proposal Pritzker has repeatedly rejected and sued to block.

By Wednesday, two very different assertions of institutional authority ran in parallel. The Senate passed a war-powers resolution on Iran by a vote of 50-48, with four Republicans joining Democrats to require congressional authorization for continued hostilities — a meaningful reassertion of Article I authority over an unpopular conflict. At nearly the same moment, National Guard troops were stationed around the reflecting pool and fencing restricted public access to the site, enforcing a narrative with no factual basis. Wednesday also brought some of the week's harshest sentences: federal judges sentenced nine anti-ICE protesters from a July 2025 demonstration at a Texas detention facility to terms ranging from 30 to 100 years — the first case applying the administration's antifa domestic-terrorism designation — with one defendant sentenced despite not having been present at the protest. Trump separately called the New York Times "treasonous" over a story questioning the outcome of the Iran conflict and threatened to fold the coverage into an existing multibillion-dollar lawsuit. The Justice Department opened a civil rights investigation into a Brooklyn coffee shop over a political dispute involving a member of Congress, and Reuters reported that the intelligence community was withholding a completed report on voting-machine vulnerabilities ahead of the midterms.

Thursday was the week's pivot point, carrying the heaviest concentration of consequential developments. The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Slaughter to overturn Humphrey's Executor, the 90-year-old precedent shielding independent agency leaders from removal without cause. The decision followed Trump's earlier removal of FTC Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter and eliminates a foundational structural safeguard Congress had built to insulate certain agencies from direct presidential control. The same day, an hour before a scheduled Capitol Hill signing ceremony, Trump abruptly canceled the housing bill signing via social media, calling legislation that had passed 85-5 and 358-32 "of minor importance" and demanding Congress first pass the SAVE America Act's voting restrictions. And at a Capitol lunch that day, Trump confronted Republican senators, including Bill Cassidy, over the previous day's war-powers vote, accusing dissenters of giving "aid and comfort" to Iran. By evening, Senate Republicans had begun retreating from their position.

Thursday also reinforced the week's immigration and courts arcs. The Sixth Circuit rejected the administration's suit for Michigan's voter rolls, and a federal judge permanently blocked provisions of Trump's election executive order, continuing an unbroken pattern of judicial rejection in every voter-roll case decided so far. Fuller reporting on the Texas protester sentences confirmed the 30-to-100-year range, including one sentence tied to possession of leftist literature. A separate report found that ICE and CBP surveillance spending had reached a record $513 million, having doubled in a single year, driven by facial recognition, phone-hacking tools, and autonomous surveillance towers. The Supreme Court also granted border officials broad discretion to deport lawful permanent residents suspected of crimes of "moral turpitude" without requiring clear and convincing evidence. And the costly New York primary fight over AI regulation ended with the candidate who supported the safety legislation losing to an opponent who held the same position — illustrating how spending alone had come to define the race.

Friday brought the direct consequence of Thursday's pressure campaign into full view. The Senate voted 50-47 to block a binding war-powers measure, a day after passing its symbolic predecessor, following Trump's public description of dissenting senators as "losers" and "lunatics." Cassidy was summoned to a White House briefing and reversed his vote; Rand Paul voted present. The reversal closed out, within roughly 24 hours, an episode that had briefly looked like a genuine congressional check on executive war-making authority. Meanwhile, the housing bill remained unsigned, and Trump extended similar hostage tactics to FISA renewal, conditioning it on passage of the SAVE America Act. Representative Anna Paulina Luna shut down House floor operations, Speaker Johnson canceled votes, and Majority Leader Thune adjourned the Senate for nineteen days — leaving both chambers effectively paralyzed over the voting-restriction standoff.

Courts continued to push back against the administration's election-related efforts. Judge Denise Casper permanently barred Trump's proof-of-citizenship voter registration order as unconstitutional, and Judge Indira Talwani struck down an executive order tying mail-ballot delivery to a federal citizenship database. Taken with earlier rulings in the week, these decisions meant courts had rejected essentially every element of the administration's attempt to centralize control over voter rolls and mail voting. At the same time, the Supreme Court's TPS and asylum rulings became fully operative, and the Department of Homeland Security announced that TPS holders must formalize permanent status or accept deportation, with modest financial incentives offered to those who leave voluntarily — turning an abstract legal ruling into an immediate operational ultimatum for hundreds of thousands of people.

The week's closing hours brought an escalation in rhetoric to match the escalation in institutional stakes. At a Faith and Freedom Coalition conference, Trump called Democratic opponents "godless communists" and "animals," framing the midterms as a fight against a communist takeover. Representative Tom Emmer said Somali immigrants "don't assimilate" and should leave the country, and senior adviser Stephen Miller stated plainly that ending birthright citizenship remained an administration goal. Speaker Johnson told an audience that if Democrats retake the House, they will weaponize committees against the president's family and allies, promising, "I run the protection program. We'll take care of you" — an explicit pledge to shield the executive from oversight. Smaller developments closed out the week: California certified a one-time wealth tax measure for the November ballot even as billionaires funded competing measures to block it, and billionaire Leon Black refused to answer House Oversight Committee questions about Epstein-related nondisclosure agreements, prompting subpoenas, while a federal judge separately ordered the Justice Department to produce or justify withholding Epstein-related files by early July.

Viewed as a whole, the week illustrated how quickly institutional constraints can give way under concentrated and personal pressure. A fabricated story about a public fountain produced real arrests, a militarized perimeter, and a no-bid contract for a political donor — a minor absurdity that nonetheless consumed federal law-enforcement resources and restricted public access to a national monument. Far more significantly, the Supreme Court removed a structural safeguard that had protected agency independence for ninety years, at the same time it stripped judicial review from major immigration decisions affecting hundreds of thousands of people. Congress, for its part, showed both capacity and fragility: it passed a housing bill and a war-powers resolution with genuine bipartisan support, only to watch the president hold one hostage and personally pressure senators into abandoning the other within a single day. Courts remained the one institution consistently resistant to these pressures, rejecting the administration's voter-roll and mail-voting efforts in case after case. Whether that judicial resistance can offset the erosion visible elsewhere — in agency independence, legislative leverage, and the treatment of dissent — is a question the coming weeks will begin to answer. ```
Excerpt: This week combined a genuine constitutional turning point with a strange, almost absurd sideshow that consumed disproportionate presidential attention.

Title: This Week in Democracy: A Court Reshapes the Presidency, Even as It Holds a Few Lines
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which the Supreme Court redrew the boundaries of presidential power — expanding it dramatically in one ruling, constraining it in the next — leaving behind a record that resists any single interpretation. It was also a week of record immigration arrests, a $2.2 billion disclosure of the president's personal income, and a congressional report accusing the administration of hijacking the nation's 250th anniversary for corrupt and ideological ends. Beneath the institutional drama, protest and dissent continued to assert a different account of the country's civic life.

The weekend set the tone. On Saturday, the Supreme Court paused lower-court rulings and allowed the administration to terminate Temporary Protected Status for roughly 350,000 Haitians and thousands of Syrians, exposing them to deportation despite State Department warnings that conditions in Haiti remain unsafe. DHS Secretary Mullin and adviser Stephen Miller defended the decision; Ohio's Republican governor publicly broke with the administration over it. At the same time, Trump escalated military strikes on Iranian sites and posted explicit threats that the Islamic Republic "will no longer exist" if diplomacy collapsed further — rhetoric that bypassed the ordinary process of congressional consultation on military action. Nationwide, the 50501 coalition, Women's March, and Next250 organized large demonstrations offering a fuller account of American history, in sharp contrast to a sparsely attended official National Mall fair that Fox News nonetheless described as a success. Speaker Mike Johnson, addressing a conservative conference, warned that a Democratic majority would turn House committees into investigative bodies targeting the president's family, Cabinet, and donors — while promising he personally runs a "protection program" for allies. The weekend also saw a Mississippi police response that deployed teargas against protesters seeking justice for a one-year-old shot and killed by an officer, with authorities withholding body-camera footage, and a mistrial in the federal arson case tied to the deadly 2025 Palisades fire, after a jury deadlocked 10-2 for acquittal.

By Monday, the Supreme Court delivered the week's most structurally significant ruling. In Trump v. Slaughter, a 6-3 majority overturned Humphrey's Executor, the 1935 precedent that had shielded independent agency heads from at-will presidential removal. The decision means the president may now fire leaders of the FTC, NLRB, and roughly two dozen other independent bodies without cause, eliminating a foundational separation between politically insulated regulators and the executive branch. Trump publicly celebrated the ruling as a major expansion of his authority. Yet the same day produced a narrower, more protective outcome: a 5-4 ruling kept Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in her position, finding that Trump had failed to provide required notice before attempting to remove her over unproven mortgage-fraud allegations. The ruling preserved the Fed's independence for now, though it rested on procedural grounds rather than a broader principle, leaving that independence exposed to future challenge under the newly expanded removal doctrine. Separately, the Court held that geofence location-data warrants require Fourth Amendment protections and upheld Mississippi's mail-ballot postmark rule against a Republican National Committee challenge, protecting ballot-counting procedures used in more than a dozen states.

Away from the Court, Senator Bill Cassidy publicly accused Trump of treating Congress as an "appendage," describing a heated confrontation over a war-powers resolution on Iran in which the administration had failed to brief lawmakers. Trump also declined to commit to signing a bipartisan housing bill that had passed the House 358-32, calling it "a big yawn" unless Congress advanced a voter ID measure he favored, and toured a public D.C. golf course with Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to plan a luxury renovation later reported to include removing mature cherry tree groves. Separately, the administration invoked emergency authority to restart a California oil pipeline shuttered since a 2015 spill, prompting a lawsuit from the state's attorney general.

Tuesday brought another major and mixed judicial record. The Court narrowly upheld birthright citizenship, ruling that children born in the United States to undocumented or temporary-status parents remain citizens under the 14th Amendment and rejecting Trump's executive order attempting to redefine the constitutional phrase "subject to the jurisdiction." The margin was thin, and four justices signaled openness to revisiting the doctrine in the future, with Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence leaving room for legislative narrowing later. On the same day, a 6-3 majority upheld state bans on transgender athletes in girls' sports, allowing West Virginia and Idaho to exclude transgender girls from female school sports and rejecting Title IX challenges — a decision expected to embolden similar bans in roughly 25 other states. The Court also struck down limits on coordinated party campaign spending in a case brought by Vice President Vance and Republican officials, removing a safeguard at a moment when the Republican National Committee holds a substantial financial advantage over its Democratic counterpart.

Elsewhere, the Department of Health and Human Services restructured its civil rights office to elevate religious-conscience protections above other enforcement priorities, a move legal experts warned could allow providers to refuse care related to reproductive health, LGBTQ services, and vaccines. The Washington Post also revealed a $500 million no-bid contract for renovation work tied to the White House, the first thread in what would become a week-long story about presidential enrichment. Meanwhile, Speaker Johnson sent the House home without passing the defense authorization bill after a member blocked the floor rule pending unrelated voter ID provisions, and reporting surfaced that the White House had floated mass pardons — a "250 pardons for 250 years" initiative — as a symbolic centerpiece for Independence Day.

Wednesday deepened several of the week's central threads. The Court weakened the Voting Rights Act, giving southern legislatures greater latitude to redraw congressional districts previously protected against racial gerrymandering — a decision experts said would likely reduce Black congressional representation ahead of the midterms. The Justice Department, separately, refused to comply with a federal judge's order to produce Epstein-related documents by a July 2 deadline, citing its own interpretation of statutory redaction requirements — a direct instance of executive-branch resistance to judicial authority. Trump also announced acceptance of a $400 million Boeing 747-8 from Qatar; after bipartisan criticism, the Pentagon formally accepted the aircraft, with plans reported to eventually transfer it to Trump's presidential library.

Immigration enforcement escalated sharply, with roughly 10,000 arrests recorded over five days as officials pursued a directive of 2,000 arrests daily, even as a federal appeals court limited detention without bond hearings to 90 days. A federal judge separately blocked a USPS plan that would have denied mail-ballot delivery to states refusing to share voter rolls, the second judicial defeat for administration efforts to narrow mail voting. Florida's state education board voted to bar undocumented students from all 28 state-funded colleges and universities, and nearly 500,000 New Yorkers lost health coverage as federal Medicaid cuts and expired ACA subsidies took effect.

The day's most consequential emerging story, though, was the first wave of reporting on Trump's annual financial disclosure — a 927-page filing showing $2.2 billion in 2025 earnings, including $1.4 billion from cryptocurrency ventures and $636 million from a memecoin, alongside 22,000 individual stock trades. Additional reporting detailed $8.9 billion in federal funding flowing to mining companies linked to Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, an undisclosed $50 million loan, and stock purchases made the day before a market-moving tariff announcement. An Air Force officer, Major Jason Watson, was arrested at the Capitol for standing in uniform with a sign reading "Impeach. Convict. Remove," and now faces an internal military investigation.

Thursday carried the citizenship ruling into enforcement. One day after the Court's decision, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche directed prosecutors to pursue fraud cases targeting so-called "birth tourism," despite acknowledging the practice accounts for less than 1 percent of U.S. births — using selective prosecution to narrow, in practice, a right the Court had just upheld in principle. An appeals court separately ruled the administration need not restore historical materials on climate change, immigration, and slavery removed from national park sites, permitting long-term alteration of public historical memory. Further reporting connected Trump's sons to at least ten military-contractor investments that had received $3.7 billion in federal funding, even as the Senate rejected a crypto conflict-of-interest amendment along party lines. And a House Democratic subcommittee released a report titled "From Vanity to Insanity," alleging wire fraud, pay-to-play arrangements, and the diversion of nonpartisan 250th-anniversary funds into a shadow entity called Freedom 250 that promoted Christian nationalist messaging while harvesting voter data — a story with roots stretching back to the weekend's contested commemorations.

The week closed on Friday with an unusual legal collision in Louisiana, where a New Orleans grand jury indicted Republican Attorney General Liz Murrill on 16 counts related to alleged intimidation of city officials. The state supreme court quickly stayed the indictment after finding the trial judge had sealed the courtroom in violation of open-court law, a closure during which journalists were briefly detained. House Democrats formally released the full "From Vanity to Insanity" report the same day, alongside reporting on a $68 million taxpayer-funded contract awarded to an allied firm for Independence Day festivities. Legal experts, including Representative Jamie Raskin, outlined plans for expanded oversight of alleged administration corruption should Democrats retake the House majority in the midterms. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani delivered a widely covered Independence Day address framing American identity around inclusion and dissent, directly countering official anniversary messaging. And Trump, in a smaller coda, publicly criticized NATO allies over defense spending as "not reciprocal," despite recent allied increases nearing $1 trillion combined. Notably, the acute Iran conflict that dominated the weekend faded from direct coverage as the week progressed, surfacing only in secondary references to oil markets and economic messaging — a shift in attention rather than a resolution.

Taken as a whole, the week offers a genuinely mixed record of institutional behavior rather than a single trend line. The Supreme Court, in the space of two days, both dismantled a 90-year check on presidential removal power and refused to let the executive redefine constitutional citizenship by decree; it weakened voting-rights protections for minority communities while preserving mail-ballot access and digital privacy safeguards. Enforcement agencies moved swiftly to narrow the practical reach of rulings that didn't go the administration's way, even as courts imposed some procedural limits on detention. Financial disclosures and family business dealings drew bipartisan scrutiny without yet producing consequence, and a sitting attorney general's indictment collapsed amid procedural irregularities of its own. What connects these threads is not a single verdict on the health of American self-government, but a documented pattern: guardrails holding in some places, eroding in others, and the outcome of that contest left, for now, unresolved. ```
Excerpt: This was a week in which the Supreme Court did two contradictory things at once.

Title: A Birthday Speech, a Fatal Traffic Stop, and an Election Commission Left Empty
Content:
```markdown The week the United States marked 250 years of independence opened with celebration and closed with the machinery of its elections left without a single overseer. In between, a federal immigration agent killed a Houston construction worker who was not his target, the only witnesses to that killing were themselves detained, and a president who had spent the holiday warning of "communism" spent the following days testing how far executive power could be pushed against courts, Congress, and the public record. It was not a week of return to normalcy after the anniversary. It was a week of escalation.

The Fourth of July itself set the tone. At delayed remarks on the National Mall and at Mount Rushmore, Trump used the nation's semiquincentennial to attack political opponents as communists, press for passage of the voter-restriction SAVE America Act, misquote the Declaration of Independence, and appear to reference a third term before catching himself. What should have been a nonpartisan commemoration became, in substance, a campaign event delivered from the office of the presidency. The same day, hundreds of masked Patriot Front marchers carried Confederate flags through Washington chanting "Reclaim America," while counter-demonstrators from the Women's March and Veterans Against Fascism gathered nearby. The White House would not say whether the president condemned the march. That evening, an 850,000-firework display at the Lincoln Memorial—the largest in American history—triggered a Code Purple air alert, briefly giving the capital the worst air quality of any major city on Earth; internal documents later showed officials had anticipated the pollution beforehand. Meanwhile, the country logged its deadliest July 4–5 stretch for gun violence in over a decade, with 224 mass shootings and more than 6,600 gun deaths recorded for the year by July 7, including an attack that killed or injured four children near Coney Island. Amid it all, Trump pardoned eleven people, nine of them Clean Air Act violators, even as ICE carried out roughly 10,000 arrests in five days—a juxtaposition of selective clemency and mass enforcement that would prove to be a preview of the week ahead.

By Monday, the fallout from the enforcement surge had not yet become the week's central story, but other threads were already forming. A House committee alleged that Trump officials had misled donors into funding a parallel "Freedom 250" entity rather than the bipartisan America250 program, then steered congressional appropriations toward favored contractors, including the firm that organized the January 6 Ellipse rally. New disclosures showed Trump had personally earned $1.4 billion from family cryptocurrency ventures since taking office—profits he defended by citing his children's "inside information"—while separately, nearly a million memecoin investors lost a combined $3.81 billion as Trump extracted $636 million in fees. The EEOC, meanwhile, rescinded a 47-year-old safe harbor for voluntary affirmative action under Title VII, narrowing workplace remedies nationwide. And in Maine, Democratic Senate nominee Graham Platner faced detailed sexual assault allegations that would soon cost him major endorsements and halt party fundraising in the state.

Tuesday brought the week's first defining tragedy. In Houston, an ICE officer shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old construction worker who had lived in the United States for 35 years and was the father of three, during a traffic stop. He was not the operation's target. DHS claimed he had "weaponized his vehicle," but witnesses disputed the account, and no officer involved wore a body camera. The killing joined a documented pattern of at least eleven fatal ICE shootings since the administration began. The same day, the Supreme Court handed down two major immigration rulings: a 6–3 decision stripped judicial review from most Temporary Protected Status determinations, affecting 1.3 million immigrants including 300,000 Haitians, while a separate ruling approved reinstating "metering," the practice of turning back asylum seekers at the border. Both decisions removed courts from oversight of consequential immigration policy at the same moment enforcement itself was producing a body on a Houston street. Elsewhere, an appeals court handed a rare win to civil liberties, striking down part of Florida's Stop Woke Act as an unconstitutional restriction on professors' speech, with the panel accusing the state of "puppeteering" educators. And in Washington, House Speaker Mike Johnson signaled he would try to push the SAVE America Act through budget reconciliation—a maneuver that cannot be filibustered—to bypass Democratic opposition, extending the voter-restriction push from the holiday weekend into legislative strategy.

By Wednesday, the Houston shooting had become a story not just about a death but about what followed it. The only civilian witnesses—including Salgado Araujo's own brother—were detained by ICE and moved to an undisclosed location, prompting fears among family members and advocates that they would be deported before they could testify to what they saw. The same day, the Justice Department escalated its election-related pressure campaign, sending letters to all 50 states threatening criminal prosecution over unsubstantiated noncitizen-voting claims, then announcing election monitors for 15 jurisdictions across six states and demanding voter data from Lansing, Michigan—all of it concentrated in Democratic-leaning areas. Trump's own public conduct raised separate concerns: at a NATO summit, he referred to Iran as the "Islamic Republic of Japan," called Zelensky "President Putin," and falsely claimed to have settled eight wars, some of which were still ongoing. He also ordered a halt to all trade with Spain over its refusal to permit U.S. airspace use against Iran—an order experts called functionally unenforceable—while separately swapping his Qatari-gifted jet for stated security reasons and offering a false public explanation for the switch. The Pentagon, meanwhile, announced a joint taskforce with the Justice Department to prosecute unauthorized press disclosures, following subpoenas of New York Times reporters, as the White House's official social media account attacked a journalist over a factual video clip. In Memphis, National Guard troops fatally shot 20-year-old Tyrin Johnson during a pursuit, the second officer-involved death tied to a federal anticrime initiative in the city within weeks.

Thursday was the week's institutional turning point. Trump fired the two remaining Democratic commissioners of the Election Assistance Commission by email; the sole Republican commissioner resigned in protest, leaving the body that certifies U.S. election systems with zero commissioners months before the midterms. The move was not an isolated act but the culmination of a week that had moved from rhetoric to structure: a campaign speech demanding voter restrictions, a Speaker maneuvering to pass them without debate, a Justice Department threatening state officials and deploying monitors to opposition strongholds, and now the removal of every person responsible for independent oversight of election administration. The same day, courts pushed the other direction. Judge Kaplan ordered the release of the $5.8 million Trump owed E. Jean Carroll after years of delay tactics; Trump appealed immediately, and the Second Circuit rejected his bid within a day. A separate federal appeals panel rejected the administration's attempt to keep Trump's name on the Kennedy Center, finding no evidence to support its claims. Yet even as courts compelled compliance in these cases, Trump announced he would seek a Supreme Court rehearing of a birthright citizenship ruling the Court had upheld only a week earlier, calling the decision "wrong" and citing a Texas hospital's maternity marketing as evidence of "birth tourism." In Houston, hundreds marched and held vigils demanding accountability for Salgado Araujo's death; LULAC offered a reward for evidence and gathered nearly 70,000 petition signatures. DHS assigned its own Office of Inspector General to investigate the shooting rather than an independent body. Also on Thursday, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche—Trump's former personal lawyer, who has said he holds a "continuing duty of loyalty" to the president—was nominated to lead the Justice Department permanently, with confirmation hearings set for July 16. In the West Bank, Rep. Ro Khanna's delegation was blocked and intimidated by armed Israeli settlers for roughly 90 minutes, with arriving Israeli soldiers, according to Khanna's account, siding with the settlers rather than assisting the congressman. And Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker stated publicly that Trump was "suffering from dementia" and that intervention was needed, a striking response to the president's NATO confusion two days earlier.

The week closed on Friday with the SAVE Act thread reaching its resolution. Trump announced he would not sign a bipartisan housing affordability bill "in PROTEST" unless the Senate passed the SAVE America Act, conditioning approval of popular legislation on unrelated voting restrictions; the bill became law without his signature at midnight after House GOP leadership secured override votes. In Mexico City, President Sheinbaum announced her government would seek criminal charges over the deaths of 17 Mexican citizens in U.S. immigration custody, including Salgado Araujo's, and would back civil suits against detention-center operators—an international escalation over enforcement practices that had begun with a single traffic stop three days earlier. The administration also finalized a rule opening endangered species' habitats to drilling, mining, and development, called by environmentalists the largest such rollback in decades, and appointed a climate science denier to lead the U.S. Global Change Research Program responsible for the National Climate Assessment. A new 500-bed immigrant detention facility was announced for a former Air Force base in Louisiana, expanding capacity even as the Houston case remained unresolved.

Taken as a whole, the week showed two of the republic's core mechanisms—courts and elections—pulling in opposite directions. Judges forced a president to finally pay a judgment he had delayed for years and blocked several agency actions on the record; the same week, the Supreme Court narrowed judicial review of immigration protections affecting more than a million people, and the president moved, without resistance from Congress, to eliminate every independent overseer of federal election administration. A death in Houston—an ordinary man, not the target of the operation that killed him—became the week's clearest human measure of what accountability gaps can cost, compounded by the disappearance of the only witnesses who might have contradicted the official account. Whether that account will ever be independently tested remains, as the week ended, an open question resting with an inspector general who answers to the same department under scrutiny. ```

Title: This Week in Democracy: A Blockade Announced and Reversed, Two Men Dead in ICE Stops, and a President's Speech About an Election He Won
Content:
```markdown This week moved on two tracks at once: a slow-building campaign to reshape the rules governing elections, and a series of sudden, violent episodes in immigration enforcement that twice ended in civilian death. Between them ran an Iran policy that escalated to strikes and a declared blockade before being abandoned within days, a federal judge's finding that the president had engineered a fraudulent settlement with the IRS, and a Justice Department subpoena of journalists over national security reporting. By the time a nationally televised address revived debunked election-fraud claims on Thursday, the week's separate threads had begun to look like a single, coherent pressure campaign aimed at courts, the press, and the machinery of voting itself.

**The Weekend**

The weekend set the tone. The bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law automatically after President Trump declined to sign it — not a veto, but a calculated non-action meant to pressure Congress into passing the Save America Act, a voter-restriction measure that lacked Senate support. He tied renewal of a foreign surveillance law to the same demand. At Camp David, a closed-door meeting on reconciliation legislation excluded moderate House Republicans entirely; attendees had their phones confiscated, and at least one participant left urging a no vote. Overseas, Trump's explicit social media threats against Iran gave way within days to an actual drone strike on an Iranian naval base and further airstrikes after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz — military decisions announced online, without congressional authorization. And in Houston, an ICE agent shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a business owner and father of three who was not the target of the operation, amid a record pace of daily arrests carried out by newly hired and often unvetted agents. The Justice Department, meanwhile, subpoenaed four New York Times reporters to testify before a grand jury over their reporting on Secret Service concerns about the new Air Force One, following an eight-hour FBI leak investigation launched from inside the White House. A Trump-appointed judge separately dismissed seditious conspiracy convictions against Proud Boys leaders tied to January 6, stating outright that the dismissal reflected the president's wish to excuse the violence rather than any legal defect in the case.

**Monday**

The human cost of enforcement policy sharpened further. ICE agent David Brouillette — a man with a documented history of domestic violence allegations and no in-person training — shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian national authorized to work in the United States, during a vehicle stop in Maine. No body camera footage existed. Guerrero, like Salgado Araujo three days earlier, was not the target of the operation. These were two distinct deaths, in two different states, within the same week — not variations on one story but a pattern emerging from separate, independent failures. The same day, Judge Kathleen Williams ruled that Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against the IRS, and the $1.8 billion settlement that followed it, had been manufactured litigation designed to create a personal immunity fund for the president and his family. She sanctioned his attorneys and criticized the Acting Attorney General's testimony as misleading. Elsewhere, the Justice Department opened a grand jury investigation into UAW president Shawn Fain just ahead of contested union elections, and Trump removed three members of an independent federal commission that works with states on election administration — a move Senate Democrats warned threatened the integrity of the coming midterms. Trump also announced, then began walking back, a blockade of Iranian shipping tied to new tolls on the Strait of Hormuz. A joint Human Rights Watch report, meanwhile, documented 52 ICE custody deaths in 500 days, more than double the rate under the prior administration.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought the week's clearest example of executive override colliding with agency judgment. Following the two fatal shootings, Tom Homan announced a suspension of most ICE vehicle stops pending procedural review — a rare acknowledgment that something had gone wrong. Within twenty-four hours, President Trump publicly reversed that decision under pressure from allies, insisting the stops continue as a "crime fighting tool." The Department of Homeland Security aligned itself with his position, and the safety pause evaporated before it could take effect. That same day, ICE officials pepper-sprayed New Jersey Senator Andy Kim during a protest at Delaney Hall in Newark held in solidarity with hunger-striking detainees; police followed with tear gas and dozens of arrests. Trump also signed proclamations shrinking Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments by roughly 90 percent, citing a declared national energy emergency and removing nearly three million acres from federal protection to open them to extractive industry. Judge Williams issued further findings confirming the IRS settlement had been collusive, recommending bar discipline for the government lawyers involved. Tribes, conservation groups, and public health organizations filed a wave of lawsuits challenging agency rollbacks of the Endangered Species Act's habitat-harm standard, FDA vaping guidance, and teen pregnancy prevention funding. Mahmoud Khalil, detained by ICE for 104 days, filed a federal complaint under the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871 alleging a coordinated conspiracy between administration officials and private groups to target and deport pro-Palestinian activists. And at a detention facility in Aurora, Colorado, at least twelve detainees contracted tuberculosis amid reported failures to isolate infected individuals, while a Venezuelan man died in Georgia during a facility transfer after medication was allegedly withheld.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday shifted attention briefly toward institutional resistance. Senate Democrats denied the National Defense Authorization Act the votes it needed to advance, in direct protest of the president's resumption of military action against Iran despite a war powers resolution passed the month before. New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a first-in-the-nation one-year moratorium on new hyperscale datacenters, citing strain on the electrical grid and rising utility costs — a state-level regulatory response that would soon draw federal pushback. Trump imposed a 25 percent tariff on Brazilian goods under Section 301, with Secretary of State Rubio citing bad-faith negotiations; the timing coincided with an active Brazilian election pitting Lula against Bolsonaro's son. Two advocacy organizations sued over executive sanctions targeting International Criminal Court officials and a UN expert, arguing the restrictions violated protected speech and association rights. Supreme Court Justices Kagan and Barrett testified before Congress requesting a $14.6 million increase in security funding, describing swatting incidents and death threats against justices and their families. And after a day of insisting on a naval blockade and shipping tolls, Trump abandoned the plan entirely, citing conversations with Gulf leaders and pivoting instead toward investment agreements — the rhetorical escalation of the weekend meeting its practical limit.

**Thursday**

Thursday was dominated by a single event: a nationally televised address in which President Trump revived claims that China and Venezuela had interfered in past U.S. elections, releasing declassified documents that reportedly undercut his own argument. He called for NBC and ABC to lose their broadcast licenses for declining to air the speech live, and the FCC chair suggested license consequences could follow. The speech's central claims were debunked within hours — by CNN, by Republican Senator Thomas Massie, by John Solomon, the report's own author, and by Senator Mark Warner. The same day, the House passed the Save America Act, which would ban mail-in ballots and impose new voter ID requirements, by bundling it with an unrelated State Department appropriations bill in a party-line 217–209 vote — avoiding standalone scrutiny of a major change to election rules ahead of the midterms. A separate vote exposed a rare fracture among House Democrats: a Massie amendment to cut $3.3 billion in Israel aid failed 314–104, but more than 100 Democrats, including the party whip and former Speaker Pelosi, voted in favor, breaking with decades of bipartisan consensus. More than two dozen House Democrats held a closed-door session gaming out over 100 scenarios for potential executive interference in the 2026 midterms. And White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller delivered a speech framing domestic political opposition as a global terrorism threat, part of a rhetorical pattern that would continue into Friday.

**Friday**

By Friday, the week's separate threads converged. DHS Secretary Mullin escalated threats against state election officials who refuse to comply with federal voter-roll purge demands, warning of fines and imprisonment — despite federal courts having already blocked the underlying data-sharing tool sixteen separate times. He repeated unsubstantiated claims about noncitizen voting and voting-machine vulnerabilities. The FBI notified staff that it would no longer investigate confrontations between the public and ICE agents, eliminating a channel that had previously generated evidence used to prosecute agents involved in violent incidents — a direct institutional consequence of the week's two fatal shootings and the Tuesday reversal of the vehicle-stop pause. Trump fired a U.S. attorney roughly an hour after a judicial panel swore him into office in Washington state. Treasury Secretary Bessent announced a commemorative dollar coin bearing Trump's likeness, using a collectible-currency statute to route around an 1866 law barring living people from U.S. currency. An off-duty Geo Group employee working at the Aurora detention facility shot and injured a protester during a demonstration and was arrested on felony charges including attempted second-degree murder. Secretary Rubio convened a State Department meeting framing domestic "antifa" activity as equivalent to jihadist terrorism, while Miller continued describing protesters in dehumanizing terms. And over 600 communities began a multi-day "Good Trouble Lives On" weekend of nonviolent civic action honoring John Lewis, centered on voter registration, civic education, and, in many locations, demands for ICE accountability.

Taken as a whole, the week documented a widening gap between the pace of executive action and the pace of institutional response to it. Courts pushed back forcefully — a federal judge's finding that a $1.8 billion IRS settlement was manufactured litigation stands as one of the clearest judicial rebukes of executive self-dealing in recent memory, and a wave of lawsuits challenged agency rollbacks on multiple fronts. Congress showed intermittent friction, from a blocked defense bill to a fractured Israel-aid vote to contingency planning against election interference. Grassroots mobilization reached hundreds of communities by week's end. But in immigration enforcement specifically, the pattern ran the other direction: a safety pause reversed within a day, an independent investigative channel closed off entirely, and two civilian deaths absorbed without any announced change in operational practice. Layered against a primetime address reviving debunked election claims, an aggressive push to alter voting procedures ahead of the midterms, and direct threats against broadcasters and state officials alike, the week left a record of institutions still capable of resistance — but increasingly tested by the speed and breadth of the pressure applied against them. ```

Title: War Without a Vote
Content:
```markdown This week began with a legal blow to gun-safety law and ended, five days later, with courts pushing back on multiple fronts against the executive branch — and in between came a war that grew larger in rhetoric while its official record grew smaller. Over seven days, the Iran conflict, immigration enforcement, tariff policy, and voting rights all advanced under executive pressure, while Congress, the courts, and the public tried, with mixed success, to hold the line.

The weekend set the tone. On Saturday, the Third Circuit became the first federal appeals court to strike down a state assault-weapons ban, breaking with every other circuit and teeing up a likely Supreme Court fight over similar laws in more than ten states. That same weekend, the Justice Department filed its first-ever application to a dormant 1996 tribunal allowing the Secretary of State to label noncitizens "alien terrorists" and deport them using evidence they never see — a revival of secret-evidence removal power with no operating history. Immigration enforcement turned deadly again when a federal agent with a documented history of domestic violence fatally shot a Colombian immigrant in Maine. Reporting soon showed that nearly half of more than 400 prosecutions against people accused of assaulting ICE agents had collapsed in court, and that the FBI had quietly stopped investigating fatal ICE confrontations altogether. Underneath it all ran a thread that would recur throughout the week: the Pentagon, it emerged, had concealed three earlier Iranian strikes on U.S. forces before a fatal attack in Jordan became public — an early sign that the war's true cost was being managed rather than reported. Amid it all, roughly 70 "ICE Out" rallies, nearly 700 voting-rights demonstrations, and more than 100 datacenter protests unfolded nationwide, and House Judiciary Chair James Comer acknowledged that the chamber was "basically done working" before the midterms.

Monday brought an unusually dense stack of developments. Trump signed proclamations imposing 50 percent tariffs on Canadian dairy, alcohol, and vehicles, actions Canadian officials called a violation of the USMCA trade agreement. He also reframed the Iran war's objectives after the World Cup final, saying the conflict had grown beyond its original scope, while separately vowing that Iran would "pay" for killed American soldiers — expanding war aims without new congressional authorization. That same event delivered a very different kind of headline: Trump was booed during the trophy ceremony, ushered off stage by FIFA's president, cropped from Spain's official victory photo, and denied handshakes by Argentine players — a public rebuke on a global stage. Domestically, ICE announced it would require body cameras for vehicle stops following fatal shootings in Texas and Maine, reversing an earlier push to cut camera funding by 75 percent. Investigative reporting revealed that SpaceX, Home Depot, Walmart, Toyota, and Google had donated hundreds of thousands of dollars to lawmakers sponsoring ICE-expansion bills, even as Citizens Bank cut credit lines to the two largest private detention operators, CoreCivic and The GEO Group. The administration also sought — then withdrew — subpoenas for New York Times reporters' phone records, including those of family members, tied to coverage of the Qatar-donated Air Force One. Gas prices crossed $4 a gallon for the first time since June, driven by the widening Iran conflict, while new executive orders tightened domestic-sourcing mandates for defense contractors.

By Tuesday, the war's financial and legal dimensions sharpened. Defense Secretary Hegseth testified before the Senate seeking a $454 billion increase to a $1.5 trillion total budget, even as senators caught him contradicting his own earlier claims that Iran's missile program had been "functionally destroyed." Joint Chiefs Chair Caine declined to rule out strikes on civilian infrastructure or further ground escalation. The same day, two separate court rulings tested executive removal power: a newly appointed U.S. Attorney sued after being fired less than an hour into the job, and a federal judge found the government had violated a fired civil servant's due-process rights, rejecting the claim that presidential removal authority overrides civil-service protections. Reporting also confirmed that ICE's year-old body-camera policy remained almost entirely unimplemented — only 3,000 of 13,000 officers were equipped despite adequate funding, a gap linked to at least eight enforcement deaths that went largely unrecorded. On a separate track, Trump declared Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu immune from arrest on U.S. soil after New York's mayor floated reviewing local authority under an ICC warrant. In Arizona, election deniers Alexander Kolodin and Andy Biggs won GOP primaries for the state's top election post and governorship, while Republicans nationally promoted federal voter-ID legislation using a widely mocked comparison to a restaurant's pasta-pass policy. Separately, reporting found the CDC had lost 25 to 30 percent of its staff, leaving the agency less prepared for disease outbreaks than before COVID.

Wednesday deepened both the war and voting-rights threads at once. House Republicans passed a budget resolution authorizing a $95 billion reconciliation package that combined Iran war funding, farm aid, and $10 billion toward the Save America Act — a bill that would ban mail-in ballots nationwide and impose strict voter-ID rules, using reconciliation specifically to bypass the Senate filibuster. The same day, Trump threatened to bomb a bridge or power plant in Tehran for every Iranian strike on shipping, and at a Dover Air Force Base ceremony for four fallen troops, he attributed views to the deceased while warning Iran would "pay a big price" — remarks widely seen as politicizing a solemn military ritual. Elsewhere, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's SNAP cuts stripped food assistance from 440,000 Arizonans, forcing mass caseworker layoffs and leaving vulnerable residents, including an elderly cancer survivor, without adequate food access. Des Moines and Tampa airports opted into a new program privatizing TSA screening, reviving a pre-9/11 model Congress had abandoned for safety reasons. House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan pushed the acting Attorney General to prosecute former special counsel Jack Smith, a move Smith's lawyers called retaliatory. The administration also approved a Saudi nuclear program and granted the UAE broad access to U.S. AI and semiconductor technology — decisions that would draw scrutiny within days.

Thursday was the week's most consequential day. The House passed a $1.15 trillion defense authorization bill embedding the same voting restrictions on a near party-line vote, then separately passed a concurrent resolution calling for an end to the Iran war, 214–208, joined by four Republicans — a symbolic assertion of war powers that carried no binding force absent Senate and presidential action. Trump told Israeli media and Axios he was close to ordering a strike "larger than any prior operation," saying Iran "haven't received enough pain yet," while Hegseth requested another $88 billion in supplemental funding, prompting a senator to ask whether the request functioned as a backdoor substitute for formal war authorization. That evening, the Pentagon's official casualty database dropped overnight from 18 deaths to 14; officials attributed the change to removing troops killed after a declared ceasefire, while a spokesperson cited "temporary data disruptions." Extensive reporting that day detailed a web of financial conflicts: a $2 billion Saudi investment in Jared Kushner's private equity fund coinciding with the new nuclear deal; UAE tech transfers approved over security objections tied to Kushner's holdings; a Pentagon AI office overseen by an official who had personally profited from crypto investments; a Pentagon private-equity arm tied to gains benefiting Trump's son; and outsized returns for Trump Jr. from a firm invested in government-linked companies. Compounding the strain, Brent crude jumped 42 percent in twenty days to above $100 a barrel following Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers, sending Treasury yields spiking and markets selling off. Twenty-five states and Washington, D.C. sued in Rhode Island over FEMA and DHS grant conditions tying more than $740 million in disaster and homeland-security funding to paper-ballot mandates, citizenship verification, and immigration cooperation. A separate suit challenged new tariffs on 60 countries as exceeding presidential trade authority. A federal panel allowed a Tennessee redistricting map splitting Memphis's majority-Black district — eliminating the state's only Democratic-held seat — to proceed under a weakened Voting Rights Act. ICE officers, including some Trump supporters, described denied leave, inadequate training, and chaotic leadership to reporters. And Vance Boelter was sentenced to two life terms plus 40 years for assassinating Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband.

Friday brought a wave of judicial pushback that stood in some contrast to the week's executive momentum. Federal courts halted the termination of work authorization for asylum seekers and TPS holders, dismissed an RNC lawsuit demanding sensitive New Jersey voter data, and paused the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger for 28 days pending antitrust review. The 25 attorneys general formalized their FEMA suit challenging the use of disaster aid as leverage over state election and immigration policy. The Fourth Circuit upheld the release of Georgetown scholar Badar Khan Suri, arrested by ICE over pro-Palestinian speech, affirming habeas rights in a ruling likely headed to the Supreme Court. Separately, the Electronic Privacy Information Center sued DHS over an unpublished policy tracking Americans who observed ICE operations, alleging retaliatory revocation of Trusted Traveler status. Trump threatened new tariffs against the EU over its fines against Apple, Meta, Amazon, and Google, opening a Section 301 investigation. Reporting revealed DHS had diverted $155 million of $170 million appropriated to counter Chinese illegal fishing toward World Cup and America250 security, without fully disclosing where the money went. Ahead of a rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner, 520 journalists signed a letter condemning threats to broadcaster licenses and the earlier subpoenas of reporters' families. Trump signed an order directing signage criticizing alleged bias in Smithsonian exhibits. Federal debt passed 100 percent of GDP, and the administration requested another $11.1 billion in farm aid. And in a final note of dissonance, Trump said he trusted Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping's personal assurances that they would not arm Iran — directly contradicting Hegseth's Senate testimony days earlier that both countries were enabling Iranian actions.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government stretching in several directions simultaneously: a war whose public accounting shrank even as its stated ambitions grew, a legislature that passed resolutions without the power to enforce them, and a string of policy vehicles — defense bills, disaster grants, budget reconciliation — used to carry voting restrictions that might not survive scrutiny on their own. Courts intervened repeatedly, but unevenly, blocking some assertions of executive power while allowing others, including a redistricting map that will shape political representation for years. Beneath the week's headline conflicts ran a quieter story of financial entanglement — family investments, foreign money, and defense-adjacent profit sitting close to decisions of state. None of it was hidden entirely; much of it was reported, argued over, and litigated in real time. Whether that scrutiny translates into accountability remains, as ever, a separate question from whether it occurred. ```
Excerpt: This week's defining tension was a war effectively run by press release.

Title: A History Rewritten, a Cabinet Stalled, and a War Without a Clock
Content:
```markdown This week, spanning July 25 through July 31, brought together four distinct but overlapping stories: a sustained push to reshape how American history is preserved and told, a cabinet confirmation that collapsed over the president's personal financial protections, a war-powers debate that Congress lost for the second time in two weeks, and a false story about a New York City mayor that spread through major news outlets faster than anyone corrected it. Underneath these headline fights, quieter developments — a State Department map with every African country misplaced, a $22 million order for luxury vehicles, a 19-year high in Treasury yields — sketched the texture of an administration operating at full speed across many fronts at once.

The weekend opened with a coordinated set of actions touching historical memory. A Trump-appointed preservation board voted to weaken public and tribal review requirements for federal projects at historic sites, clearing the way for a disputed triumphal arch near Arlington and a mineral-extraction effort at Chaco Canyon. At nearly the same time, the administration ordered warning signs installed at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History and began repainting the Eisenhower Executive Office Building without the customary review process. Individually, each move might have passed as a bureaucratic footnote. Together, they signaled an effort to narrow outside input — from historians, tribal nations, and Congress — over how the government tells the story of the country's past.

The same weekend produced a second test of institutional limits: three days after the Supreme Court struck down the administration's emergency tariffs as unconstitutional, Trump reimposed them, first under Section 122 of trade law and then under Section 301 — authorities that do not require congressional approval. Legal experts noted that these statutes, unlike the one the Court had just voided, could make the tariffs effectively permanent. It was the third attempt in short order to keep the same policy alive through a different legal door, raising a basic question about whether a Supreme Court ruling could meaningfully constrain the executive's approach to trade.

A third weekend story began quietly and would grow for days. The New York Post published a front-page claim that thousands of 9/11 victims' families wanted New York Mayor Mamdani barred from a memorial ceremony, sourced to an online petition. The petition's own organizer later admitted the family-member count was an unsubstantiated guess. Also over the weekend, four House Republicans crossed party lines to support a symbolic resolution demanding troop withdrawal from Iran — a day after backing a $95 billion war-spending package — while the Pentagon quietly revised its Iran-war casualty database, introducing a new operational category that appeared designed to reset the 60-day clock that normally forces a war-powers reckoning with Congress.

By Monday, several of these threads deepened. ICE, which had briefly paused most vehicle stops after two fatal shootings in Texas and Maine, resumed aggressive enforcement within days on Trump's order, despite one of the officers involved having a documented history of domestic abuse allegations that should have disqualified him from hiring. Separately, Taylor Farms — a food company linked to a multi-state cyclospora outbreak — contacted the White House seeking a delay in the government's public health announcement, a request a former FDA commissioner said fell well outside normal practice. At a Michigan rally, Trump reduced the justification for the Iran war to a single unexamined claim, falsely stated he had attended the G20, and misrepresented the source of ammunition shortages, while posting AI-generated images hinting at a future political run. Meanwhile, the 9/11 petition story moved further into the mainstream: CBS News New York and Fox Business both amplified it, with Fox Business citing a figure — 15,000 — with no supporting count. In Arizona, federal contractors felled centuries-old cottonwood trees for a border wall extension despite earlier assurances to preserve nesting habitat, prompting activists to occupy the last standing tree.

Tuesday was the week's most consequential single day. Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis announced they would withhold support for Attorney General nominee Todd Blanche unless the administration provided written confirmation that a $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund — tied to a personal IRS settlement involving Trump — would be eliminated. The Senate Judiciary Committee scheduled, then began wavering on, a confirmation vote. The same day exposed a stark asymmetry in how election irregularities were treated: a New Jersey software error involving fewer than 400 noncitizen votes triggered an immediate federal investigation, subpoena threats, and calls to end automatic voter registration, while news surfaced that California had rejected nearly 150,000 mail ballots in its June primary with no federal inquiry and little media attention. Also on Tuesday, the FCC received petitions to strip license renewals from eight ABC-owned stations following Trump's criticism of the network, prompting a bipartisan group of former FCC chairs to warn that the proceeding was unconstitutional. Trump pressured Health Secretary Kennedy to cut the childhood vaccine schedule further, despite a standing federal court order against such changes. And as gas prices, mortgage rates, and war costs strained household budgets nationwide, Trump announced the White House had ordered 250 Cadillac Escalades at a cost exceeding $22 million. The day closed with reports that ICE was preparing action against roughly 300,000 Haitian Temporary Protected Status holders, arresting people with expired visas at airports — including U.S. citizens' spouses — and that the Office of Refugee Resettlement had shared 460,000 leads with ICE, resulting in more than 12,000 arrests, some involving children and their sponsors.

On Wednesday, the fight over historical memory returned to Congress. A House committee member had coordinated with Christian nationalist activists on questions for a Smithsonian oversight hearing, during which the director of the National Museum of American History was accused of promoting "woke ideology" for examining difficult chapters of the country's past. At a separate hearing chaired by Senator Rand Paul, Dr. Anthony Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right rather than answer questions about COVID-19's origins, describing the proceeding as an attempt to embarrass and imprison him; Paul said he would pursue a contempt of Congress vote. In a party-line vote, the Senate confirmed Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence, despite his having sidestepped questions about the 2020 election and having previously subpoenaed New York Times journalists before withdrawing the subpoenas. Reporting also revealed that the administration had directed Secret Service agents to secretly monitor former FBI Director James Comey's phone after his "86 47" social media post, with agents instructed to report details on their questioning of him directly to the president. Quietly, a deadline passed: Trump did not file for Supreme Court rehearing of the ruling upholding birthright citizenship, despite earlier vowing to do so "immediately," leaving the protection intact for now.

Thursday brought the Blanche standoff to a head. The Senate Judiciary Committee abandoned plans to advance his nomination after Trump declined to formally narrow the immunity arrangement senators had demanded be terminated in writing. Rather than yield, Trump reversed course again, vowing to revive the fund through legislation or executive action — and then floated an extraordinary alternative: "temporarily" withdrawing Blanche's nomination and resubmitting it once Cornyn and Tillis had left office, keeping Blanche as acting attorney general indefinitely in the meantime. The same day, the coordinated pressure on Fauci continued, with multiple Republican senators accusing him of covering up vaccine information and demanding apologies, while a Democratic senator warned the hearings were scapegoating one official for a broader institutional failure. In a rare moment of unanimity, the Senate passed a non-binding resolution opposing any pardon or clemency for Ghislaine Maxwell. Elsewhere, a State Department presentation at an international AIDS conference in Brazil displayed an AI-generated map with every African country misplaced — Nigeria shown inland, Mozambique relocated — bearing an OpenAI watermark. And as the 30-year Treasury yield hit a 19-year high, with national debt approaching $40 trillion and annual interest payments surpassing $1 trillion, neither party offered a serious plan to address it.

Friday closed the week with the Senate's second failed attempt in two weeks to constrain the administration's war-making authority. Following fresh airstrikes launched in response to an Iranian missile attack, the Senate voted 49-50 to reject a resolution requiring troop withdrawal absent explicit congressional authorization — a narrow but consequential defeat that left the earlier casualty-database reclassification's practical effect unchallenged. On voting rights, the administration petitioned the Supreme Court to enforce a mail-voting order requiring citizenship lists, even after 23 states and the First Circuit had already blocked it, while the Kansas Court of Appeals separately preserved a mail-ballot grace period historically responsible for saving tens of thousands of votes. It also emerged that the FBI had requested and received the IP address of a South Carolina voter as part of a fraud investigation, a move a former senior Justice Department official called atypical. Trump demanded the Senate cancel its August recess to pass the long-stalled SAVE America Act. A budget filing revealed that at least one detained hunger striker in ICE custody had been subjected to forced feeding, hydration, catheterization, or blood draws, with an ACLU attorney noting many detainees lack legal representation to contest such orders. And reporting deepened around Representative Max Miller, detailing allegations that he had physically abused his ex-wife and infant daughter, with a restraining order filed and a former girlfriend's earlier allegations resurfacing alongside calls for his resignation.

Viewed as a whole, the week showed several of the same pressures converging from different directions. Efforts to control historical narrative moved from rulemaking to congressional hearings shaped by outside activists. A cabinet confirmation stalled not over policy disagreement but over a president's refusal to relinquish a personal legal shield, forcing an unusual standoff with members of his own party. Congress twice declined to reassert its constitutional authority over war, even as the executive branch adjusted its own recordkeeping in ways that could delay that reckoning further. And a single unverified petition, amplified without correction across several major news organizations, showed how quickly an unsubstantiated claim about a sitting official can outrun any effort to correct it. None of these stories, individually, settled anything. Together, they mark a week in which existing checks — judicial, legislative, and journalistic — were repeatedly tested, and in several instances, did not hold. ```
Excerpt: This week combined an aggressive campaign to control historical memory with a mounting crisis of executive accountability.
