Title: This Week in Democracy: A Fund Falls, an Attorney General Rises, and Citizenship Is Tested Again
Content:
```markdown This week in Washington was shaped by one long argument over who controls the machinery of law enforcement, and by a series of smaller ones over who controls the border, the courts, and the truth. By week's end, the fight over the attorney general's office had been resolved in the president's favor, even as several others remained open.

The week began over the weekend with Trump pressuring the Senate to confirm Todd Blanche, his former personal attorney, as attorney general, threatening to simply leave Blanche in the acting role indefinitely if senators would not yield. At issue was a $1.8 billion fund that critics said was designed to compensate Trump's political allies and potentially shield his family from tax audits — an arrangement Republican holdouts wanted addressed before they would vote to confirm. Elsewhere over the weekend, Trump Media rolled out a premium Truth Social subscription tier selling early access to market-moving presidential posts for up to $100,000 a month, even as the administration sought $10 million in taxpayer money to cover event costs. The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History came under executive pressure over alleged political bias, and Arizona's supreme court ruled that clergy who learn of child abuse through confession have no duty to report it — a decision arising from a case in which three children continued to suffer abuse for years after bishops privately learned of it. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. urged parents to vaccinate against measles while simultaneously repeating misinformation about vaccines, a contradiction unfolding against a 35-year high in measles cases. Ethics concerns also touched Congress: the House ethics committee recommended censuring Rep. Chuck Edwards for staff harassment, while Senator Bernie Moreno called publicly for Rep. Max Miller's resignation over abuse allegations raised by his own daughter.

By Monday, litigation became the week's dominant register. A coalition of 25 states — eventually joined by others, including two Republican governors — sued in the Court of International Trade to challenge tariffs imposed on goods from 60 trading partners, arguing the measures exceeded the president's statutory and constitutional authority. That same day, court records and detainee video showed that ICE had sought court orders to force-feed hunger strikers in at least ten cases, alongside documentation of contaminated drinking water at a California detention facility, often affecting detainees without legal counsel. In North Carolina, the state Senate passed a voter-restriction bill without debating Democratic amendments, removing protesters from the gallery in the process, while the House scheduled votes on companion legislation restructuring courts and elections along more partisan lines. Trump also turned his public anger on U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro after the Justice Department dropped vandalism charges related to a Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool incident that Trump had earlier mischaracterized online — a dispute that would resurface later in the week. Meanwhile, at the state and local level, Washington's governor signed legislation restricting license plate readers, and Monroe County ended its surveillance camera contract early, following reporting that documented 28 cases of officers misusing plate-reader data to track people in their personal lives. At an international terrorism conference, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and adviser Stephen Miller made unsubstantiated claims characterizing left-wing violence as widespread and warranting elimination "by any means necessary."

Tuesday was comparatively quieter but not without consequence. ICE detained a Johns Hopkins pharmacy researcher and a University of Maryland pharmacy instructor at separate airports despite both holding valid work authorization; each was eventually released. A federal judge issued a split ruling on New York's ICE transparency law, blocking the requirement that agents show their faces and identification during enforcement actions while allowing the state's separate ban on local police cooperation with ICE to stand. Reporting also revealed that federal contractors building the Arizona border wall had been broadly exempted from environmental laws, including protections for an endangered bird species. The allegations against Rep. Miller deepened as Senator Moreno detailed specific claims of physical abuse, adding pressure ahead of a looming candidate-replacement deadline. And a dark-money nonprofit called One Nation began a $1.7 million disinformation campaign against Senator Ossoff, generating 78 million impressions with claims that contradicted his actual voting record — a story that would expand considerably by week's end.

Wednesday brought a notable moment of direct democracy alongside further executive and press-related conflict. Missouri voters rejected a measure to eliminate the state income tax by an overwhelming 83.3 percent, along with a related phaseout amendment defeated by similar margins, while renewing a conservation sales tax — a rare instance of voters decisively rebuffing tax-cut ideology despite being outspent by the measure's proponents. New Mexico's attorney general sued the Department of Justice, alleging it had stonewalled the state's criminal investigation into Jeffrey Epstein's activities at Zorro Ranch by missing a deadline to hand over unredacted records. Trump's legal team, meanwhile, moved to block a court-ordered financial disclosure to the BBC ahead of a deadline while pressing forward with a separate $10 billion defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal. The Justice Department also issued, then quietly withdrew, subpoenas to New York Times reporters covering Air Force One security matters. In immigration enforcement, ICE deported a man to Guatemala one day after a federal judge had ordered his removal halted, later calling it a case of mistaken identity; his lawyer said he would be returned. Separately, a former immigration judge sued over what she described as a politically and demographically motivated termination, and federal employees filed a class action challenging the elimination of gender-affirming care coverage.

Thursday marked the week's most direct constitutional confrontation. Trump signed two executive orders narrowing birthright citizenship and targeting birth tourism — just over a month after the Supreme Court had ruled 6-3 that his original 2025 order attempting the same thing was unconstitutional. The same day, the Justice Department petitioned the Supreme Court to lift a block on mail-ballot restrictions while continuing its 30-state lawsuit demanding voter registration data, a suit that had by then been rejected by 21 different judges. The Department of Homeland Security separately demanded that four states purge their voter rolls, threatening prosecution of officials who declined. A Senate subcommittee obtained a backup of Dr. Anthony Fauci's government-era iPhone and voted to refer him for contempt after he had invoked Fifth Amendment protections in an earlier hearing. Journalist Georgia Fort was charged with conspiracy for documenting an anti-ICE church protest — charges that later unraveled somewhat when the Justice Department conceded that false information had been submitted to judges in at least 15 warrant applications, and to a grand jury, in her case. A senior DOJ official reportedly urged prosecutors to "go big" against immigration protesters, a directive tied to at least one Texas case resulting in decades-long sentences. ICE and TSA rapidly expanded airport enforcement targeting people with pending visa and asylum applications, prompting some airlines, including Southwest, to begin resisting agents who lacked judicial warrants. Trump also threatened lengthy prison sentences for officials who leaked reports of U.S. munitions shortages during the Iran conflict, while twenty-four states sued to block a federal demand for welfare recipients' immigration data, and the Senate passed a Russia sanctions bill granting the president broad new tariff authority.

The week closed on Friday with the resolution of its central storyline: Senator Bill Cassidy, the last Republican holdout, announced his support for Blanche, clearing the way for confirmation after weeks of negotiation over the anti-weaponization fund, which had ultimately been rescinded as the price of his ascension. On the same day, Trump signed two more executive orders further narrowing birthright citizenship, calling the Supreme Court's ruling "very unfortunate" and describing his new orders as mere "adjustments" — language that left little ambiguity about the administration's view of judicial finality. New figures showed ICE had detained more than 43,000 people in July, the highest monthly total of the term, while further reporting detailed the prolonged force-feeding of at least ten hunger strikers over months, an FBI decision not to investigate a fatal ICE shooting, and the termination of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and South Sudanese despite ongoing crises in both countries. A new body-camera policy was also revealed to allow ICE to withhold footage of killings from the public. Still, the week's record was not one-sided: an analysis found federal judges had ruled against the administration in 75 of 93 First Amendment cases — a rejection rate far higher than under the prior administration — even as Fort's attorneys moved to have her indictment dismissed on First Amendment grounds. The One Nation disinformation campaign against Ossoff was revealed to be part of a broader network of fake local news sites targeting six states with competitive Senate races, funded through undisclosed dark money and paid social promotion. The Justice Department's own internal watchdog, meanwhile, was found to have been gutted, its staff cut from 29 to 16 and its director fired with no replacement, even as misconduct complaints reached their highest level since 2005. The week ended with smaller but familiar notes of conflict of interest: a sitting federal appeals judge had run a private firm for months after confirmation, and senators were reported to be delaying a hemp product ban at the administration's request, in a move benefiting a company tied to the White House chief of staff's son-in-law.

Taken as a whole, the week traced a familiar but sharpening pattern: an executive branch testing the outer edges of judicial rulings it found inconvenient, an enforcement apparatus expanding with fewer visible checks, and a press and judiciary that, however unevenly, continued to push back. The confirmation of a president's former personal lawyer as the nation's chief law enforcement officer, arriving alongside new executive orders that treated a Supreme Court ruling as negotiable, will likely be remembered less as an isolated news cycle than as a marker of how far institutional boundaries were tested — and, in the Missouri vote and the courts' First Amendment record, where they still held. ```

Title: A New Attorney General, a Vaccine Order, and a President Who Won't Say No to Emergency Powers
Content:
In one week: Trump's personal lawyer took over the Justice Department, the president rewrote childhood vaccine policy by fiat, ICE moved to arm agents with shock gloves, and courts pushed back on the White House ballroom and Kennedy Center takeover — even as Trump's approval sank to 33 percent.

```markdown The week of August 8 through 14 unfolded as a study in contrasts: an administration consolidating personal control over the machinery of government even as courts, career officials, and public opinion pushed back at nearly every turn. By week's end, a president who had installed his own former defense lawyer atop the Justice Department was also facing a 33 percent approval rating, a defeated lawsuit against Harvard, and a blocked construction project he could not simply will into existence.

The week opened with the Senate's confirmation of Todd Blanche as attorney general, a 50-49 vote that required a Republican tiebreaker to succeed. Blanche had defended Trump personally in his criminal cases before serving as acting attorney general, and critics saw his elevation — following his role in the second indictment of James Comey and a contested "anti-weaponization fund" — as confirmation that the Justice Department's traditional independence from the White House had effectively ended. The pattern did not stay abstract for long: within the same weekend, Trump publicly attacked U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro for dropping charges against Olympian David Hearn after her office determined that damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool had resulted from faulty installation, not vandalism. Trump demanded Pirro reverse the decision and insulted both Hearn and his attorney — a rare instance of a president publicly pressuring a specific prosecutor over a specific case involving a private citizen.

The weekend also brought discouraging economic news. The Department of Labor reported a loss of 23,000 jobs in July, with sharp downward revisions to prior months, while polling showed inflation concerns had climbed sharply since 2024, with women accounting for a disproportionate share of workers leaving the labor force. Elsewhere, a D.C. Circuit panel ruled that Trump lacked unilateral authority to build a ballroom on White House grounds without congressional approval, rejecting the administration's national security justification; Trump vowed to appeal. And in Texas, bulldozers arrived at Big Bend National Park to begin border wall construction after the administration waived dozens of environmental and cultural protection laws — despite the area recording only about 100 to 125 unlawful crossings a year.

By Monday, the week's defining executive action arrived: Trump signed an order directing the Department of Health and Human Services to reduce the recommended childhood vaccine schedule, split the MMR shot into three separate doses, and instructed the attorney general to challenge state vaccine mandates. The order bypassed the CDC's normal scientific review process and revived a policy previously blocked in court. At the signing, Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. repeated unproven claims linking vaccines to autism; Louisiana Senator Bill Cassidy, a physician, publicly objected. The same day, the Justice Department unveiled $300 million in "Model Cities" policing grants conditioned on cities adopting federal immigration enforcement and specific homelessness policies — terms several Democratic-led cities declined outright. DHS quietly published a procurement notice seeking up to $20 million for electric-shock gloves for ICE agents, despite manufacturer warnings against their use on vulnerable populations and past deaths linked to similar devices in custody. Monday also brought a North Carolina bill letting the state Supreme Court's Republican majority remove judges without independent review, and reporting that the National Park Service had diverted $323 million to White House grounds even as the Interior Secretary acknowledged a $30 billion nationwide park maintenance backlog. At an ICE facility in Mississippi, detainees reported a gas leak followed by denial of medical care, then a two-day power outage without air conditioning during extreme heat.

Tuesday shifted focus to immigration enforcement's reach into political expression. The State Department disclosed it had revoked more than 175,000 visas since Trump took office — four times the pace under the Biden administration — including cases tied to political commentary, a Turkish student's op-ed on Gaza, and parents seeking birthright citizenship for their children. The same day, reporting revealed that Trump had secretly left Turkey earlier in the month via a catering truck and decoy Air Force One, prompted by a low-confidence CIA assessment of an Iranian assassination threat; he took indicted aide Walt Nauta with him while leaving Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the traveling press pool behind as decoys. The pressure campaign against Pirro's office escalated further, with the White House formally asking Justice Department headquarters to consider new charges against Hearn — an extraordinary departure from the arm's-length relationship prosecutors are supposed to maintain from the White House. Separately, the Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion expanding executive privilege to cover communications between the president and outside advisors, with clear implications for congressional oversight should Democrats retake the House. Reporting also detailed Jared Kushner's purchase of disputed Albanian resort property from a man later accused of drug trafficking, and disclosed that Kushner's private firm had collected substantial fees from governments he was simultaneously negotiating with on the government's behalf. And a watchdog analysis found that Justice Samuel Alito had gained up to $2.9 million from oil and gas holdings as the Supreme Court prepared to hear a climate liability case; calls for his recusal were rejected.

Wednesday brought the week's clearest accounting of presidential enrichment. Investigations documented Trump personally earning roughly $2.2 billion through cryptocurrency ventures, a Truth Social pay-for-access scheme, a $10 billion IRS settlement, and a $400 million plane gift from Qatar, while a UAE-backed $2 billion investment flowed through his World Liberty Financial venture into Binance despite that exchange's history of money-laundering violations. That same day, Intercept Media and the Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Trump over "Truth API," a $100,000-per-month subscription service giving Wall Street firms early access to the president's posts — arguing the arrangement violates equal-access and First Amendment principles governing official government communications. Compounding the financial throughline, Treasury and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network permanently repealed the requirement for companies to report beneficial ownership information and ordered the deletion of already-collected data, reversing a 2020 law designed to combat money laundering by traffickers and kleptocrats. Against this backdrop, a new poll showed Trump's approval falling to 33 percent, with 60 percent of respondents saying he was not honest and trustworthy and 53 percent describing him as too old for the office; a former White House cardiologist publicly questioned his health and fitness to serve. The Justice Department also arrested Heidi Beirich, a prominent former Southern Poverty Law Center executive and extremism researcher, on financial charges her attorney called retaliatory. And press secretary Karoline Leavitt announced she would resign at the end of the month after nearly two years marked by restricted press access, the exclusion of the Associated Press, and a documented pattern of falsehoods.

Thursday tested whether court orders could actually constrain the administration's allies. The Kennedy Center's Trump-aligned board voted to inscribe his name on the building and proceed with a closure plan despite a federal judge's ruling blocking both actions — open defiance of a court order rather than mere resistance to one. The same day, Judge Richard Stearns dismissed the administration's antisemitism lawsuit against Harvard, finding it failed to plausibly allege an ongoing civil rights violation, constraining one avenue the administration had used to pressure universities. Court documents also revealed "Operation Puppet Master," a federal surveillance effort that had infiltrated meetings of progressive organizations, labor unions, and anti-ICE protest groups in Minnesota using undercover officers, chat monitoring, and license plate tracking; fifteen defendants faced federal charges. HHS finalized a rule eliminating Medicaid and CHIP coverage for gender-affirming care for transgender youth, despite roughly 90 percent of nearly 35,000 public comments opposing the change. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth briefed only Republican lawmakers on a proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget, withholding information about Caribbean boat strikes and the decoy Air Force One flight — prompting Republican Senator Thom Tillis to warn the approach could doom bipartisan passage. And Trump signed a memorandum ordering the Navy to revert to steam catapults on a nearly finished aircraft carrier, overriding objections from Navy officials and the system's contractor over cost and schedule risk.

The week closed on Friday with the administration formally asking the Supreme Court to stay the appeals court ruling against the White House ballroom, arguing the project was essential to national security — setting up a direct test of whether the Court would back the executive branch's claim to unilateral authority over public property. In the week's most striking moment regarding electoral process, Trump, prompted by a sympathetic radio host who suggested declaring a national security emergency to impose new voter ID, citizenship, and mail-ballot restrictions, responded only that "stranger things have happened," declining to disavow the idea. ICE and the Transportation Security Administration meanwhile began coordinating airport arrests of individuals with expired visas, including people holding valid work permits awaiting extensions, aiming for roughly 2,000 daily arrests under an expanded definition treating all overstays as criminal — continuing the week's arc from ankle monitors and shock gloves toward broader enforcement authority. Economic indicators darkened further: retail sales fell 0.6 percent against a forecast of 0.1 percent growth, and gas prices hit a record high for the date even as Trump described the economy as strong only "from the standpoint of Wall Street." Two smaller but notable developments closed the week: Columbus, Ohio restricted its police department's sharing of license-plate surveillance data statewide after a public hearing revealed over 15,000 searches potentially tied to immigration enforcement, and Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty to federal stalking charges in the killing of a healthcare executive, with sentencing set for December.

Taken as a whole, the week captured a government moving in two directions simultaneously. The confirmation of a former personal lawyer as the nation's top law enforcement officer, sustained pressure on an independent prosecutor, a unilateral rewrite of vaccine policy, and the accumulation of personal financial gain from the presidency all point toward power concentrating in the hands of one man with fewer internal checks willing or able to resist him. Yet the same week produced an appellate defeat on the ballroom, a dismissed lawsuit against Harvard, a lawsuit challenging pay-for-access presidential communications, and an approval rating scraping historic lows — evidence that courts, career institutions, and public opinion remain functioning, if strained, counterweights. Whether that resistance holds, or whether defiance of court orders at places like the Kennedy Center becomes the template rather than the exception, is a question this week left open rather than settled. ```

Title: This Week in Democracy: A President Who Answers to No One
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which the machinery meant to check presidential power kept declining to use it — even as other parts of that same machinery pushed back hard enough to show the difference was a choice, not an inevitability.

**The Weekend**

The week opened with Attorney General Todd Blanche telling a national television audience that no attorney general should promise to act independently of the president. The remark came just days after his narrow confirmation, which followed the dismissal of his predecessor for insufficient action against Trump's political opponents. It set the tone for a week in which the country's central law-enforcement and regulatory bodies were repeatedly asked, directly or through their actions, whether they served the presidency or the public — and answered in ways that varied sharply depending on which institution was doing the answering.

That same weekend brought a wave of reporting on the immigration court system, where due process appeared to be eroding on several fronts at once. ICE agents made arrests inside courthouses despite the system's long-recognized chilling effect on attendance. "Mega master" hearings, sometimes scheduled with as little as fifteen days' notice, produced more than 53,000 in-absentia removal orders in June alone. More than 100 sitting immigration judges have been replaced by new appointees marketed as "deportation judges," who now grant relief in fewer than 2 percent of the cases they hear. A separate Texas Tribune analysis found children held well beyond the legally mandated 20-day detention limit. Taken together, these findings described a system built increasingly to produce removals rather than adjudicate them.

Financial self-dealing surfaced on multiple fronts over the same weekend. General Dynamics was found to have kept $533 million for an artillery factory that never became functional, with no accountability attached. House Democrats opened an insider-trading investigation after an Energy Fuels executive purchased company stock shortly before a monument-shrinkage decision that benefited the firm. And federal regulators approved a bank charter for World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's cryptocurrency venture, which has already funneled more than $1.6 billion to the family. The president, meanwhile, staged a photo-op crediting himself for a drop in drug prices actually driven by a Biden-era law, and separately claimed inflation was falling and that the United States "totally controls" the Strait of Hormuz — both claims contradicted by available data.

**Monday**

The judiciary offered a more mixed picture. The Supreme Court declined to rehear Trump's appeal in the E. Jean Carroll case, leaving intact the $5 million jury verdict finding him liable for sexual abuse and defamation — a quiet but firm assertion that a jury's finding against a sitting president cannot simply be undone by petition. A federal judge separately blocked the FBI and General Services Administration's plan to relocate FBI headquarters to the Reagan Building, ruling that the $555 million reprogramming exceeded statutory authority and permanently enjoining the agencies from proceeding.

That same day, ABC filed a federal lawsuit against the FCC and its chair, alleging that the agency's demand for early license renewal on eight stations amounted to retaliation for coverage the president disapproved of, including the network's handling of late-night host Jimmy Kimmel. Also on Monday, a federal prosecutor sued over her termination, alleging retaliation for prior enforcement work, while the Justice Department appealed a judge's dismissal of charges against Kilmar Ábrego García — charges the judge himself had called "vindictive." In the Oval Office, Trump threatened to bomb Oman if it interfered with reopening the Strait of Hormuz, said he intended to declare the strait U.S. territory, and dismissed reports of poor conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought a legislative response to the weekend's self-dealing revelations. Senator Elizabeth Warren and nine colleagues introduced a bill to bar presidents, vice presidents, and senior officials from owning or controlling a bank — a direct answer to the World Liberty Financial charter. The Pentagon separately ordered thirty major universities, including Harvard, MIT, and Johns Hopkins, to sever foreign academic partnerships within two weeks or risk losing federal funding. The Justice Department announced it would deploy 1,000 election monitors to polling places for the midterms, citing unspecified voter-fraud concerns — a deployment far larger than the agency's historical practice. And Disney formally joined ABC's suit against the FCC, filing a complaint citing more than 600 document requests and describing a chilling effect on programming decisions; it was the first time in more than fifty years that a major broadcaster had faced this kind of early license review.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday offered one of the week's clearer instances of judicial pushback. The Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed a preliminary injunction limiting immigration enforcement at Quaker, Sikh, and Baptist houses of worship, finding the administration's 2025 enforcement policy likely violated the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. The same day, reporting surfaced describing Christian nationalists with influence in the administration advocating repeal of the Nineteenth Amendment in favor of household voting that would defer to men — a proposal aimed at over a century of constitutional suffrage protection. The week's pattern of attacks on the press also escalated: White House communications director Steve Cheung used vulgar insults against Senator Ossoff, Trump attached derisive nicknames to him, and the official White House rapid-response account attacked a CNN reporter by invoking her children.

**Thursday**

Thursday was the busiest day of the week and, in some ways, its clearest illustration of institutions pulling in opposite directions. Courts blocked two separate executive actions: a federal judge halted the transfer of 17 million commercial driver's license records to federal custody, and another blocked the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA from imposing DEI-related conditions on disaster-relief grants to Salem, Oregon, finding likely violations of separation of powers.

At the same time, the Justice Department defended its prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey, arguing in court filings that his seashell Instagram post could reasonably be read as a coded threat against the president — a prosecution his lawyers continue to call vindictive. Documents obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request showed FCC chair Brendan Carr working closely with the White House and right-wing media figures on license matters even as he oversaw renewal decisions affecting ABC. And reporting deepened on aide Natalie Harp, revealing she had worked at the White House for more than a year without a required security clearance while serving as a key filter of information reaching the president — a lapse that drew bipartisan concern from national security officials, regardless of the personal dynamics also being reported. Trump, meanwhile, gave the press a tour of extensive White House renovations that included materials donated by a campaign contributor, and separately staged a high-speed car race that required modifications to Washington's streets.

**Friday**

The week closed with a Supreme Court intervention that crystallized its earlier posture. Chief Justice Roberts stayed a lower court's order that had blocked construction of Trump's $400 million White House ballroom pending congressional approval, allowing the project to resume while the Court considers the underlying case — even though the appellate court had found the project likely required congressional sign-off.

The Pentagon, separately, fired the publisher, editor, and a reporter of Stars and Stripes, the military's own news outlet, for insubordination following its coverage of conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln and staff defense of editorial independence. The Department of Homeland Security dramatically retreated from its earlier claims about non-citizen voting, admitting after meeting with Nevada officials that it had manually confirmed only 185 non-citizens on the state's voter rolls — down from an earlier claim of nearly 16,000, itself a fraction of a national figure of roughly 278,000 the agency had floated. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent formally ended beneficial-ownership disclosure requirements under the 2021 Corporate Transparency Act, a law originally passed over presidential veto to combat money laundering. And federal budget cuts that reduced food-safety inspection capacity by more than 40 percent were linked to the largest cyclospora outbreak in U.S. history, as gas prices approached record highs and school lunch costs rose 11 percent.

**Assessment**

Read end to end, the week does not describe a single institution failing uniformly. It describes several institutions choosing differently under similar pressure. The Fourth Circuit limited enforcement at houses of worship; district courts blocked a data transfer and grant conditions built on shaky legal footing; the Supreme Court declined to revisit a jury's finding in the Carroll case. But the Attorney General publicly declined to promise independence, the FCC's chair coordinated with the White House against a network he regulates, and the Supreme Court's own stay let a presidential construction project proceed over an appellate court's constitutional concerns.

Alongside these institutional questions ran a due-process crisis in immigration courts, a foreign policy driven by threats and impulse rather than settled process, and a financial picture in which oversight tools were dismantled even as self-dealing surfaced in plain view. None of this occurred by accident; each instance involved a choice by a specific office or official. The record of who chose to check power, and who chose not to, is now part of the public account of how this period was governed. ```
Excerpt: This week's defining thread was the refusal of institutions meant to check the president to actually do so.

Title: Ballots, Beef, and a Lake Renamed
Content:
```markdown This was a week defined by whiplash. A fight over who gets to vote by mail swung back and forth between courts almost daily. A trade relationship with Canada that had taken a year to negotiate collapsed within days and then kept escalating. And a president who spent the week renaming a lake and denying documented deaths found himself, by Friday, facing fresh questions about the money flowing into his family's pockets even as he ran the country.

**The Weekend**

The mail-in voting fight set the tone before the week even formally began. Over the weekend, the Postal Service finalized rules implementing Trump's executive order restricting mail-in ballots, conditioning delivery on compliance with a federal citizenship list. USPS said it would hold off activating the rules pending Supreme Court review, but the finalization alone signaled how far the machinery had already moved.

The weekend's other defining rupture was with Canada. Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from trade talks just before a tariff deadline, citing last-minute demands he called unacceptable, and announced dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs. The breakdown ended nearly a year of negotiations that had appeared close to completion.

Public-health credibility also began fraying early. Trump's claim that the MMR vaccine "may be lethal" went unclarified when Dr. Mehmet Oz declined to directly repudiate it on air, while Rep. Byron Donalds falsely attributed a Florida measles outbreak to illegal immigration rather than low vaccination rates.

**Monday**

USPS's restraint didn't last. A divided 6-3 Supreme Court lifted a lower-court injunction that had been blocking Trump's executive order, ruling on procedural grounds that the challenge was premature rather than addressing whether the order was constitutional. The decision cleared USPS to proceed with weeks to go before ballots needed to reach voters.

The enforcement infrastructure around voting expanded in tandem. USCIS reassigned its entire Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate to screen South African refugees and investigate alleged noncitizen voters, halting routine asylum-fraud screening in the process — a redirection of anti-fraud staff toward politically charged voter investigations weeks before an election. Reporting also surfaced that multiple Republican candidates who had questioned the 2020 election results were now running for governor and secretary of state positions in several swing states, offices with direct authority over certifying future election results.

Immigration enforcement widened elsewhere too: DHS moved forward with plans to spend up to $20 million equipping ICE officers with electric-shock gloves, over objections from civil rights groups citing documented abuse cases.

**Tuesday**

The Supreme Court's clearance reversed almost as quickly as it came. A federal judge found that USPS had actually violated an earlier injunction by sending its final rule to the Federal Register — though she stopped short of ordering a remedy beyond identifying the violation.

Institutional friction surfaced on other fronts as well. Trump's lawyers argued that the Kennedy Center faced inevitable demolition unless the administration's renaming and renovation plans proceeded. And a divided Third Circuit panel ruled that criminal charges against Rep. LaMonica McIver over her conduct during a congressional oversight visit should proceed, finding her actions unprotected by the speech and debate clause — a decision that narrows a long-standing shield for congressional oversight functions.

**Wednesday**

The legal response to the ballot rule widened dramatically: twenty-four states and the District of Columbia, joined by twenty-three Democratic attorneys general, sued to challenge it outright. A judge, citing the Supreme Court's ruling, reluctantly lifted the last standing injunction, allowing the rule to take effect even as the multistate litigation proceeded.

The Kennedy Center dispute escalated too, with DOJ lawyers formally arguing that Trump's "efforts and prestige" were the building's "sole hope" for survival, months after ticket sales and donations had collapsed following the addition of his name to the facility. The Justice Department was active on other fronts as well, suing a Franklin County, Ohio court over a rule blocking ICE arrests near courthouses and signaling it would appeal rather than comply with a judge's order to unredact additional Epstein files material.

Presidential authority expanded formally, too: Trump signed an executive order declaring a national emergency over foreign-made electrical equipment in the bulk-power system, banning its acquisition where a foreign entity holds an interest and centralizing new authority over energy procurement. The same day, DHS rapidly expanded the 287(g) program deputizing local police departments for immigration enforcement — described by the secretary as enabling "quiet" enforcement — alongside a $70 billion funding increase aimed at reaching 2,000 arrests per day. Not everything moved toward more centralized control, however: city councils and county commissions in Asheville, Kendall County, Wylie, St. Paul, Tempe, and Pflugerville all voted to terminate or decline renewal of license-plate surveillance contracts, several citing data-sharing failures — one city discovering 1.6 million unauthorized searches of its data.

**Thursday**

The pendulum on mail ballots swung back once more. Judge Talwani granted a new temporary restraining order, pausing enforcement for fourteen days after finding the states likely to succeed on claims that USPS lacked the statutory authority to impose the rule and that it was unconstitutional.

The Canada dispute, meanwhile, kept climbing. Both governments raised the stakes through the week, and on Thursday Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario — a body of water shared with Canada — "Lake America." Canada rejected the move outright, citing the lake's Indigenous origins, and several U.S. governors publicly dismissed it as well.

The public-health credibility thread connected directly to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.: new documents showed he had given false 2025 confirmation testimony about a 2019 trip to Samoa tied to vaccine skepticism, even as he separately suggested that Pennsylvania's documented measles deaths might have been "fabricated."

Immigration cases illustrated enforcement's growing reach. The wife of an active-duty Army sergeant was deported to Honduras after protections for military families were rolled back, joining at least seven similar cases, and immigrant-rights groups reported dozens of arrests in Danbury, Connecticut, including parents detained in front of children's school bus stops.

Reporting that day also connected the administration's cancellation of offshore wind leases — which redirected $1.2 billion to the energy company RWE — to $900 million flowing into a liquefied natural gas stake owned by a private equity fund run by a Trump inaugural donor, prompting calls for a congressional investigation. Separate reporting found Trump's investment accounts had executed thousands of oil and gas trades during the first quarter of 2026, with his energy holdings rising in value alongside U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Iran.

**Friday**

Trump didn't let the lake renaming go: he displayed a map labeled "LAKE AMERICA" and floated renaming an ocean next, reinforcing the gesture even as the underlying trade dispute continued to escalate toward tariff threats reaching 50 percent on autos and steel. The trade war's domestic costs showed up closer to home as well. Trump announced a suspension of tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef, framing it as consumer relief, and immediately drew backlash from cattle ranchers and farmers — including longtime supporters — who said they felt betrayed by a policy that undercut their own prices to lower costs elsewhere. Underneath both the trade fight and the beef reversal, Treasury Secretary Bessent was intervening directly in currency markets and doubling the bond buyback program, moves that came alongside warnings from a former Federal Reserve governor about a stock market bubble and reports that the government was losing control of long-term interest rates — a quieter but persistent thread of financial fragility running beneath the week's louder disputes.

By week's end, mail-in ballot rules for the midterms remained legally unsettled, five separate rulings deep, with no durable resolution in sight.

The public-health credibility arc extended further still, with reporting tracing Kennedy's 2021 praise of low childhood vaccine uptake at a Lancaster County fair back to the same community where two unvaccinated people, including a newborn, later died of measles. Taken together, the week showed a sitting cabinet health official denying verified deaths while his own past statements and testimony came under sustained scrutiny.

Immigration enforcement's scale became clearer still: ICE detained a record 49,571 people in a single month, and a New York Times analysis found that most of July's arrestees had not been charged with or convicted of any crime, sweeping in legal residents, asylum seekers, and people married to citizens. The same day, GEO Group, a private prison operator, donated $1.4 million to Trump's super PAC weeks after winning DHS detention contracts worth an estimated $160 million annually. Even political allies weren't fully insulated: commentator Milo Yiannopoulos was detained by ICE at a New Orleans airport for a visa overstay, despite his ties to prominent Trump allies, raising its own questions about how selectively enforcement was being applied.

Financial conflicts of interest culminated in a cluster of major disclosures. An examination found Trump had made an estimated $1.4 billion from cryptocurrency products in 2025 while investors in those same products lost $4.7 billion, and separately that a United Arab Emirates national security adviser had invested $500 million in the family's crypto venture at the same time Trump was negotiating AI chip access with that government.

The week closed on the National Mall, where thousands gathered for a "Defend the Vote" march on the sixty-third anniversary of the 1963 March on Washington, with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez framing the coming midterms as a response to eroding rights. It was a fitting bookend to a week that had opened with a symbolic motorsports spectacle staged in the same space.

Friday also brought a Florida grand jury's finding that the DeSantis administration had misappropriated $10 million meant for children's health care, funneling it through a foundation into political committees aimed at defeating a marijuana legalization initiative — a breach of public trust the grand jury documented in detail even while concluding there was insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges. Elsewhere, Republican officials in Wyoming, including the governor, complained that DOJ election monitors had conducted unannounced and overly aggressive visits to polling sites, a rare instance of bipartisan concern about federal overreach into state-run elections. Disinformation also surfaced repeatedly in the week's final days, from a fake attack site linking a Senate candidate to an out-of-state murder to a billionaire-funded PAC running a false ad about a tax initiative.

By the time the week ended, the throughlines were unmistakable even without any single dramatic event tying them together. Voting rules remained genuinely unsettled just weeks before ballots needed to be mailed, decided and redecided by courts working faster than the legal process could fully absorb. A trade relationship built over decades had fractured into retaliatory tariffs and diplomatic theater. Immigration enforcement had grown in reach, funding, and technological capacity, sweeping up people with no criminal record alongside its stated targets. Public officials denied verified facts about vaccines and deaths even as their own records came under scrutiny. And a widening set of financial arrangements — a donor's stake in redirected energy funds, a family cryptocurrency venture enriched by foreign investment, a private prison company's donations following lucrative contracts — pointed to a persistent blurring of the line between public office and private gain. None of it was hidden; courts, journalists, grand juries, and local governments each did their part to document it in real time.
